text:
Uh huh.... California had the same pitch. How has that shaken out?

Let's check.. (and pay attention to the final bit on projected vs. actual cost)

The California High-Speed Rail (CAHSR) project is an under-construction, publicly funded high-speed rail network managed by the California High-Speed Rail Authority. Authorized by voters via Proposition 1A in 2008, the system aims to eventually link major regions of the state with trains capable of reaching speeds up to 220 mph (350 km/h). 

Project Scope and Phases

Phase 1 (Bay Area to Greater Los Angeles): Spans roughly 494 miles (795 km), designed to offer a non-stop express connection between San Francisco and Los Angeles in 2 hours and 40 minutes. [1]
Phase 2 (Extensions): Plans extend the system north to Sacramento and south to San Diego, bringing the total proposed network to 776–800 miles with up to 24 stations. 

Initial Operating Segment (IOS): Active construction is currently concentrated on a 119-mile (171-mile broader footprint) stretch in the Central Valley connecting Merced, Fresno, and Bakersfield. 

Current Status and Timeline

Target Launch: Passenger operations for the initial segment are targeted to begin between 2031 and 2033, with the full Phase 1 buildout projected toward 2039–2040.

Leadership Transition: CEO Ian Choudri resigned in October 2026 following scrutiny and an Office of the Inspector General investigation into consultant travel expenses. Joe Stephenshaw, director of the California Department of Finance, was named interim CEO. 

Trainsets: The authority approved a contract with Siemens Mobility for initial high-speed trainsets, with testing expected to begin by early 2030. 

Construction Progress: Dozens of grade separations, overpasses, and structural viaducts (such as the Hanford Viaduct) have been completed across the Central Valley. 

Costs and Funding

Cost Escalation: Originally estimated around $33 billion to $45 billion in 2008, updated projections place the cost for Phase 1 between $126 billion and $231 billion. The 119-mile Central Valley segment alone is estimated at roughly $36 billion.

Funding Sources: Financed through a mix of state bond proceeds (Proposition 1A), state cap-and-trade greenhouse gas reduction funds, and federal grants.

An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth

Listen · 11:10 min

By Stephanie Nolen
Photographs by Taiwo Aina
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/aO6K2L1cVT
Stephanie Nolen saw nine women bring new babies safely into the world while reporting this story in labor wards in the north of Nigeria.

The maternal drape, as it is called, is helping to solve one of the world’s most intractable health problems.

An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth

A few hours after she nearly bled to death, Husaina Balarabe was serenely unaware that her life had been in peril.

She cuddled her newborn baby, a lush-cheeked boy she had named Aabid, and showed him off to her sisters from her bed in a noisy hospital delivery ward in the northern Nigerian city of Kano.

Ms. Balarabe, a 26-year-old optometrist, had experienced a postpartum hemorrhage, a side effect of childbirth that is the leading cause of maternal death around the world.

She did not die because her midwife used a low-cost, low-tech intervention that was pioneered here and in other maternity wards in some of Africa’s poorest places, and that is now saving lives across the continent.

From the cart, she took a syringe of the drug oxytocin and injected it through an IV to get Ms. Balarabe’s uterus to contract. She added a dose of tranexamic acid, to prompt clotting. She massaged Ms. Balarabe’s abdomen, encouraging more uterine contractions, while another nurse started IV fluids to restore her blood volume. The bleeding slowed, and after a couple of minutes, it stopped altogether.

It was all so swift and smooth that the new mother had no idea there was cause for alarm.

One in every 10 women who give birth experiences postpartum hemorrhage, and at least 70,000 women die from it each year. Almost all of those women are in low-income countries; more women die giving birth in Nigeria than in any other country.

Postpartum hemorrhage occurs after a baby is born, when the placenta separates from the mother’s body, leaving hundreds of blood vessels open and pumping blood. In a normal delivery, the uterus quickly contracts, and the pressure closes those vessels. But if that contraction doesn’t occur or happens too slowly, or if pieces of the placenta are left behind, blood pours out without stopping, and the woman can die in as little as 10 minutes.

Some bleeding is normal in childbirth. The reason many women die is that it is surprisingly difficult to tell if someone is losing too much blood. Research found that even midwives and doctors who have delivered hundreds of babies consistently underestimate how much blood a woman has lost.

“The amount of blood on the couch, on the floor, on the pads, on my clothes, on her clothes, is it 300 or 500 or 1000 milliliters ?” asked Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano who oversaw the Nigerian research into use of the drape. “A lot of times, we don’t realize the amount of blood that a woman has lost because we make a visual assessment and it’s very, very subjective.”

Next came the series of treatments after the pouch became dangerously full of blood. None of those steps are new, but a few years ago, researchers tested what happened when they were all done at once — massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, IV fluids — and quickly. Previously, health workers had been trained to respond by first trying massage and then waiting 20 minutes to see if bleeding stopped. If it didn’t, they tried a drug and waited 20 more.

If it doesn’t stop, the last step is escalation: getting the woman into an operating room or transferring her to a facility that has staff who can stop the bleeding surgically.

“We have not had one death from postpartum hemorrhage since we started this,” said Binta Garba, who has been the head nurse in the labor ward at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital for seven years.

The research convinced her — and she went on a campaign to persuade Nigeria’s health minister to make this the national standard of care.

Now, pairs of midwife-trainers are visiting labor wards across the country to introduce the drape and the bundle. Often, they’re greeted with the same skepticism.

“I thought, We already give oxytocin and tranexamic acid, women still die — you’re wasting my time telling me about something we already do,” Kursiyya Shuaibu, one of the trainers, said of the first time she heard about the new procedure. Then she used it, and saved a woman’s life. “When you bundle it, it’s magic!”

Postpartum hemorrhage also occurs in high-income countries, but women are much less likely to die. They typically have one-on-one care from a midwife or nurse, as well as electronic monitoring of vital signs that can flag a problem early, and blood supply for transfusion is readily available.

Nigeria has high rates of severe postpartum hemorrhage because it has weak primary care. Sixty percent of women are anemic, and there is limited access to birth control. The average woman in the north has seven children, and her risk of hemorrhage rises with each pregnancy.

A quarter of Nigerian women never receive any prenatal care during pregnancy; less than half manage four visits. There is a critical shortage of health care workers throughout the system, from midwives who might screen for high-risk pregnancies to obstetricians who could safely deliver them.

Dr. Galadanci talks fast, walks faster and bristles with impatience to improve the care women receive. She believes the solutions to these basic problems have to be equally simple.

“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite: It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems,” she said. “You don’t need a surgeon to come and save a woman. On a recent afternoon in the maternity ward at the teaching hospital — the best public hospital in Kano — one woman lost 600 milliliters of blood before anyone intervened. Another woman’s drape went unchecked for nearly 45 minutes after her baby was born.

The drapes used for the research in Nigeria were imported from India, and cost about $3 each. That was more than the national health budget could afford.

Dr. Muhammad Ali Pate, the health minister, wants Nigeria to make more of what it needs. So Dr. Galadanci and her team got in touch with a family-run plastic manufacturer in Kano that made plates, forks and containers for things like vegetable oil. Dr. Galadanci showed the chief engineer a drape: Could they make that?

The company made a prototype, but it was clear that any significant production would require custom-built machinery, which it would need to import from Taiwan. The Gates Foundation, which had helped fund the drape research, was eager to scale up the drape’s use, and offered a $600,000 grant. (The foundation has also backed companies in Kenya and South Africa, where the drape was tested, to manufacture them.)

In exchange, the company, Systs Engineering, agreed to sell the drapes for 70 cents each to the national health system. The war in Iran has since pushed up the cost of raw materials, so these days, the drapes cost 80 cents. The company is making them for all of Nigeria, and it has started to export to some neighboring countries.

Dr. Galadanci has now moved on to the next problem: The drape and the bundle are working well in hospitals, but 60 percent of Nigerian women give birth at home. Her research team is testing a kit for community health workers who attend home births. It has an absorbent mat, and when that fills to the corners, it’s a sign a woman cannot lose any more blood and must be taken to a hospital. The kit also contains the drug misoprostol, which causes the uterus to contract, helping to stop bleeding long enough to get a woman to medical care.

The lone obstetrician, Dr. Halima Ibrahim, had three urgent cases waiting for cesareans, and a lone midwife oversaw the delivery ward. One woman was whimpering through the contractions of her 11th delivery, while in the corner, a couple of student nurses used the flashlight from a phone to stitch another woman’s episiotomy.

But the drape helps. “It used to be that we lost a woman every month: You are left holding the baby, and the mother is gone,” Dr. Ibrahim said. “Not any more.”

$300,000 apart on price. Neither side is willing to compromise. Deal closed in 30 days.

How? Seller carry-back financing.

In a recent commercial property transaction in downtown Mountain View, California, the seller wanted to protect his selling price, while the buyer sought to avoid the costs, delays, and uncertainty of conventional bank financing.

Rather than letting the $300,000 price gap derail the transaction, Tim Vi Tran, SIOR, CCIM, President of The Ivy Group, structured a financing strategy that created a win-win outcome.

The results:

✅ Transaction closed in just 30 days.

✅ Buyer secured an interest rate below conventional mortgage rates.

✅ Seller earned monthly interest income by becoming the lender.

✅ Seller potentially benefited from tax deferral through an installment sale, subject to applicable tax rules.

The lesson?

In commercial real estate, successful negotiations aren't always about who gives up more on price. Sometimes, the greatest value comes from how the transaction is structured.

Seller carry-back financing, also known as seller financing or owner financing, can create opportunities that traditional lending may not offer. However, the right conditions must be in place, and this strategy is certainly not suitable for most CRE transactions.

This real-world case study demonstrates why experience as an investor, strategic advisor, and broker matters when navigating complex commercial real estate transactions.

text:
WEEK 9 FIRST LOOK 🏈

The early week breakdown through the lens of StatATL

BRONCOS 🟠@ PANTHERS 🐈‍⬛

Bryce Young ($5,500) is an intriguing option in a matchup that probably won't jump off the page for most of the field.

Denver has seen opposing QBs attempt 30 or fewer passes in four of eight games, those quarterbacks all failed to throw for 220 yards or more than two passing TDs.

The four QBs who attempted 40+ passes all produced at least 288 total yards. 

Young has attempted 36 or more passes in seven of eight games this season, including three games with 40+ attempts.

The ground matchup doesn't stand out for either team, despite DraftKings highlighting bottom-10 matchups for both backfields. 

Carolina held Bijan Robinson and Jahmyr Gibbs under 82 total yards after allowing D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai to each rush for 100 yards earlier in the season.

Jonah Coleman ($5,300) will likely attract ownership after his strong Week 8 performance, but an underwhelming outcome feels possible if the TDs don't break his way.

Chuba Hubbard ($6,500) is more interesting to me, with 29 touches in two of his last three outings.

Through the air, Denver has allowed several strong performances, most notably Jaxon Smith-Njigba (12-134-0), Davante Adams (7-137-0) and Trey McBride (10-111-1).

Tetairoa McMillan, averaging 9.5 targets per game, is my early favorite stacking partner if playing Bryce Young.

COWBOYS 🤠@ COLTS 🐎

My first thought was that this would be an intriguing spot for Javonte Williams, coming off back-to-back games with 25 touches.

The matchup stands out. Indianapolis has allowed Derrick Henry, Kenneth Walker, Jaylen Warren and Bhayshul Tuten to each surpass 150 total yards this season.

The Colts have lost four straight, and I wouldn't be surprised if we see Daniel Jones benched for Anthony Richardson soon as the season continues to slip away.

Dallas presents a solid on-paper matchup for the Colts backfield, but Jonathan Taylor only saw 12 touches last weekend, likely influenced by rumors of a potential trade.

Through the air, the matchup doesn't stand out for CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens. Zay Flowers has been the only WR to crack 20 DK points against Indianapolis all season.

At just $2,900, Brevyn Spann-Ford is an intriguing punt play at TE with Jake Ferguson dealing with an ankle injury.

I'm not sure any Colt is playable currently, even in a plus matchup.

JETS ✈️@ CHIEFS 🏹

Let me preface this by saying I'm not advocating to play Geno Smith ($4,900) on the road here, but the stable of quarterbacks Kansas City has faced this season is far from intimidating.

Daniel Jones, Malik Willis, Justin Herbert, Kirk Cousins, Sam Darnold and Bo Nix twice make up that group. Geno is at least mildly intriguing at his price.

The main challenge is figuring out his stacking partner. Omar Cooper Jr. has two games with 25+ DK points, Garrett Wilson has two, while Kenyon Sadiq and Adonai Mitchell have each exceeded 25 DK points once.

On the ground, Braelon Allen has been incredible in Breece Hall's absence, recording four straight games with 100+ total yards. Hall is expected back this week, unfortunately tempering the excitement around the Jets backfield.

On the other side, Kenneth Walker gets an appealing matchup. He's seen at least 18 touches every week, while Jahmyr Gibbs, Kyle Monangai and Ollie Gordon all exceeded 100 total yards with at least one TD against the Jets.

Of note, Gibbs and Ashton Jeanty also added 60+ receiving yards.

Through the air, the matchup doesn't stand out for any pass catcher.

LIONS 🦁@ DOLPHINS  🐬

Even on the road, this is an interesting spot for the Detroit offense. Miami has allowed 24 or more points in every game but one.

After back-to-back difficult matchups, the game sets up nicely for Jahmyr Gibbs. An opposing RB has topped 22 DK points against Miami in more than half of its games.

Through the air, the best matchup is with Sam LaPorta. George Kittle, Travis Kelce, T.J. Hockenson and Mason Taylor have all recorded at least 59 receiving yards and a TD against the Dolphins.

On the other side, this is a very intriguing spot for Malik Willis.

Every opposing QB has thrown at least two TDs against Detroit, while only Kyler Murray, with 245 passing yards, failed to top 274 total yards.

Detroit's defense had been one we were targeting early in the season but had recently looked much better. However, the Lions suffered multiple significant defensive injuries during their Week 8 game against Minnesota.

If multiple of Brian Branch, Jack Campbell, DJ Wonnum and D.J. Reed were to miss, I'd likely have interest in Willis paired with Malik Washington and/or Caleb Douglas, both in the $4K range.

Greg Dulcich ($3,100) is also appealing, with five or more targets in three straight games. He's only behind Malik Washington in red-zone targets on the year.

BROWNS 🟤@ SAINTS ⚜️

A tough spot for Tyler Shough. Only two QBs have accounted for more than one TD against Cleveland this season, while the last four opposing QBs all failed to throw for 200 yards.

New Orleans offers a middling matchup for Deshaun Watson, who is coming off back-to-back 300-yard passing performances.

At $5,200, Watson has some initial appeal, although teams tend to focus their attack on the ground against the Saints.

Jahmyr Gibbs, Bijan Robinson, Aaron Jones and Jaylen Warren all accounted for at least 117 total yards against New Orleans, with only Warren failing to add a TD.

At $5,400, Quinshon Judkins is intriguing. Jaylen Warren has been the only RB1 not to score against the Saints, despite accounting for 137 total yards.

Through the air, the matchup doesn't stand out for Chris Olave ($7,400). Garrett Wilson (7-104-1) is the only pass catcher to top 20 DK points against Cleveland all season, while Olave himself has only topped 23 DK points once.

The Saints DST initially has some appeal in the mid-range, as Deshaun Watson leads the NFL in sacks taken.

GIANTS 🔵 @ EAGLES 🦅

The Giants are coming off their bye and are a week removed from J.J. McCarthy leading them to a 27-21 win over Houston in his first start with New York.

Philadelphia has been an above-average matchup for opposing QBs this season, and at $4,800, McCarthy has some appeal.

Through the air, CeeDee Lamb, Tommy Tremble, Kalif Raymond, Luther Burden, Puka Nacua and Parker Washington have all topped 19 DK points against the Eagles over the past six weeks. 

That doesn't even include Jalen Coker (6-97) and Tetairoa McMillan (8-86), who also had solid performances during that stretch.

Malik Nabers ($7,300) has seen 51 targets over the past four weeks and has produced four straight games with 110+ yards.

For some reason, he's still priced under $7,500 and initially stands out as my favorite WR on the slate.

On the other side, there's plenty of uncertainty around Philadelphia's receivers early in the week. If DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks were both to miss again, Makai Lemon ($4,700) becomes very intriguing as his role has continued to grow over the past few weeks.

RAMS 🐏 @ COMMANDERS ⛑️

An interesting spot for Matthew Stafford. We've seen some really strong QB performances against Washington this season.

Dak Prescott, Sam Darnold and Jameis Winston all topped 300 total yards with at least three TDs. Darnold and Dak both had four.

We've also seen multiple 30-point DK performances from Stafford this year. It's early in the week, but I expect him to go overlooked, especially without Davante Adams on this slate.

On the other side, Jayden Daniels has some appeal with his rushing ability. Josh Allen ran for over 120 yards and a TD against the Rams a few weeks ago.

The matchup is middling for both backfields, and neither stands out.

Through the air, only three WRs have seen nine or more targets against Washington this season: JSN, Malik Nabers and CeeDee Lamb. 

All three are alpha receivers.

The worst score of the bunch came from Nabers, who managed an 11-121-1 line for 32.1 DK points.

Puka Nacua has seen double-digit targets most weeks and, along with Nabers, jumps out on this slate.

The matchup for Washington's WRs doesn't stand out, but Treylon Burks and Antonio Williams are interesting value options with Terry McLaurin on IR. 

Chig Okonkwo ($3,600) also has some appeal.

TEXANS 🐂@ CHARGERS ⚡️

Another strong on-paper spot for Justin Herbert, but this Chargers offense continues to look unplayable.

On the other side, it's a below-average spot for C.J. Stroud. I'm not sure I'll have interest in either signal-caller this week.

What does stand out is the Houston backfield and the potential for Woody Marks to be the only game in town again this week for the Texans.

Marks has seen 17 or more touches in three straight games and stands out as a solid midrange option at $5,700 if David Montgomery were to miss again.

Through the air, the spot jumps out for Ladd McConkey, as opposing pass catchers have smashed against Houston. I'm just not sure I can get there on an 11-game slate with plenty of other solid options.

Initially, my interest in this game is solely Woody Marks and potentially the Texans DST.

RAIDERS ☠️@ 49ERS ⛏️

Brock Purdy ($6,800) has some appeal as the 49ers expect to welcome back his top receiving weapon, Mike Evans, this week.

The Raiders have already allowed Drake Maye and Tyler Shough to each account for 290+ yards and four or more TDs over the last six weeks. Geno Smith also threw for 294 yards and two TDs last week.

On the other side, the matchup is middling for Kirk Cousins, who doesn't stand out on the road.

The ground game is intriguing for Las Vegas. Ashton Jeanty has seen his workload decrease every week, going from 23 carries in Week 1 to just two last week.

Mike Washington Jr. ($5,200) saw 25 carries last week and is an interesting midrange option.

On the San Francisco side, Christian McCaffrey stands out. 

Opposing RBs have smashed against the Raiders, with Braelon Allen, Kyren Williams, James Cook, Kenneth Walker, Omarion Hampton and Blake Corum all accounting for 100+ total yards and at least one TD.

Through the air, Mike Evans is interesting, especially if pairing him with Purdy. 

George Kittle also has appeal, as Juwan Johnson, Davis Allen and Noah Fant all produced multiple-TD games against the Raiders.

On the other side, Brock Bowers is always in play, but finds himself in a below-average spot at $7,900.

PACKERS 🧀@ PATRIOTS 🟦

On paper, this is a tough spot for both quarterbacks. At $6,300 for Jordan Love and $7,000 for Drake Maye, a ceiling game from either feels less likely than usual.

On the ground, the return of Josh Jacobs has been a significant boost to the Green Bay run game. 

However, New England has yet to allow an opposing RB to top 78 rushing yards, while only Ashton Jeanty has added more than 34 receiving yards.

The Patriots backfield has the better on-paper matchup, but with TreVeyon Henderson likely to return after missing Week 8 with an illness, I'd expect the backfield to revert to a timeshare between Rhamondre Stevenson, Corey Kiner and Henderson.

Through the air, both teams have some appeal.

The Patriots have been beatable in the secondary, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Keon Coleman, Omar Cooper Jr., Luther Burden and Brock Bowers all surpassing 100 receiving yards and a TD against them this season.

As such, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are intriguing, even at their elevated prices above $7K.

On the other side, A.J. Brown ($5,800) would have some appeal if active. 

Jameson Williams, Justin Jefferson, Drake London and Amon-Ra St. Brown have all posted games of 26+ DK points against Green Bay.

CARDINALS 🐦 @ SEAHAWKS 🟢

I was excited about the possibility of playing newly named starter Gardner Minshew ($4,500) this week until I saw that he'd be on the road in Seattle.

Caleb Williams was the first QB to top 190 yards against the Seahawks, throwing for 247. Initially, I don't think Minshew is going to make my player pool this week.

An interesting spot for Sam Darnold ($5,600) on the other side.

Over the past seven weeks, Arizona has allowed Drew Lock, Brock Purdy, Jameis Winston, Jared Goff, Dak Prescott and Bo Nix to all top 19.8 fantasy points, despite none attempting more than 30 passes.

The Cardinals have allowed several notable WR performances, including JSN's massive 9-155-3 outing when these teams met in Week 2.

If playing Darnold, Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the obvious stacking partner with 89 targets on the season.

The ground matchup is middling for both teams, but if Bam Knight (concussion) were to miss with Jeremiyah Love already on IR, Tyler Allgeier ($5,400) would be appealing after a career-high 39.1 DK points last week.

Through the air, Seattle has been one of the stingiest defenses against both WRs and TEs. 

Neither Michael Wilson nor Trey McBride stands out initially, although the Kendrick Bourne fractured tibia may condense Arizona's targets even further.

There are several injury situations that could reshape the slate, particularly in Detroit, Philadelphia, San Francisco and New England.

These are the initial reads, not final decisions. We'll keep evaluating the matchups, roles and ownership as the week develops.

I am listening to other exchanges between ATC and pilots on different days and I am stunned!! WTH are they hiring these days?? Pilots of major airlines are telling the towers they are unable to fly thru these storms and are refusing to continue the flight plan. One declared an emergency and simply told them he was making a left turn heading 260 for severe weather avoidance. My father was a pilot and I never heard about this kind of disregard for safety. I knew things were turning bad in the flight industry but I had no idea it was this bad. My husband flies in and out of West Palm every time he goes to FL. I wish I wasn’t hearing all of this. text:
*The Divine Mother Who Upheld Righteousness; The Compassionate One Who Blessed Her Devotee!*

Once, in a certain village, there lived a poor farmer named Ramayya. He was a devout follower of Goddess Durga. Every morning, before heading to his fields, he would visit the Goddess’s temple to offer his prayers before beginning his day’s work. He would even share a portion of his own meager food with those who were hungry. Through all the joys and sorrows of life, he lived with his thoughts constantly fixed upon the Divine Mother.

In the same village, there lived a wicked landlord who would forcibly seize the lands of poor farmers and subject them to various forms of suffering. He also attempted to take over Ramayya’s land. Refusing to bow down to this injustice, Ramayya stood firmly on the side of righteousness (*dharma*). However, as there was no one to listen to his plea, he felt deeply distressed.

One night, he lit a lamp in the temple of Goddess Durga and prayed, "Mother! I bear no hatred toward anyone. But I beseech You—protect the destitute who are falling victim to this injustice. Grant Your grace so that righteousness may prevail."

That night, he had a wondrous dream. The Divine Mother, radiant and seated upon her lion, appeared before him and reassured him, saying, "My child, do not fear. Never abandon the path of righteousness. The courage to stand up for the truth is the first sign of My grace." The following day, in the presence of the village elders, all the farmers courageously spoke out about the injustices they had suffered. Old documents pertaining to the land held by Ramayya were also brought to light. As the truth emerged, the landlord’s illicit actions were exposed. The village elders took steps to ensure justice was served, and the farmers regained their lands.

Overjoyed, Ramayya went to the temple of the Goddess and offered his salutations. "Mother! It is through Your power that justice has been served," he said, expressing his gratitude. He regarded the dream he had experienced as a sign of the Goddess’s grace.

*The Deeper Meaning of the Story*

The legend of Goddess Durga slaying the demon Mahishasura signifies the triumph of righteousness (*dharma*) over unrighteousness (*adharma*). The power of the Goddess is not limited to the destruction of demons alone; it also provides the inspiration to overcome negative traits within ourselves—such as fear, ego, injustice, and hatred.

True devotion is not merely about seeking the removal of one's hardships. It also encompasses upholding righteousness, standing by the weak, and fighting courageously for the truth. Every devotee who seeks the blessings of the Divine Mother, Durga, must walk the path of righteousness that She has shown. That, in itself, is the true glory of worshipping the Goddess.

text:
As of November 4, 2026, the vote count for the U.S. midterm elections is still underway, and control of Congress remains undecided. One confirmed result is the reelection of Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia—the first key Senate seat to be called tonight. Exit polls indicate that approximately half of the voters view this election as a rejection of Trump, while three-quarters express feeling "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the direction of the country. In the House of Representatives, Democrats are widely favored to regain the majority; however, control of the Senate remains up in the air, with the outcomes of several critical races still too close to call.

Key Results Announced

The Senate race in Georgia served as the clearest early indicator of the night. Democrat Jon Ossoff defeated Republican Representative Mike Collins to secure reelection. Reuters noted that this contest—once expected to be highly competitive—slipped "out of reach" for the Republicans, a shift attributed to declining support for Trump. Ossoff, considered a potential presidential candidate for 2028, has provided a significant boost to the Democratic Party with this victory.

In Virginia, Democratic Senator Mark Warner was declared the winner shortly after the polls closed. In Florida, Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz won a new House seat following a redistricting process.

Voter Sentiment Revealed by Exit Polls

Exit polls conducted by SSRS for several U.S. media outlets offer a clearer picture than the raw seat tallies alone. Nationwide, half of the voters stated that they view the 2026 midterms as "an opportunity to reject the president." Three-quarters of voters expressed feeling "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the country's current trajectory, and 70% indicated a desire for Congress to exert greater checks and balances on the president. The AP Voter Poll provides more specific data on economic anxiety: about 80% of voters report that inflation has caused "severe" or "moderate" financial hardship for their households, making it difficult to afford basic necessities like gasoline and groceries. Roughly half of the voters identified "government corruption" and the "cost of living" as "key" issues influencing their choice for Congress—priorities that rank higher than immigration enforcement, potential conflict with Iran, or the development of AI data centers.

House of Representatives: Democrats Show Strength, but It’s Early in the Count

Democrats need a net gain of three seats to take control of the House (currently, Republicans hold 218 seats, Democrats 214, with 2 vacancies). Real-time analysis from *The Guardian* suggests that Democrats are "currently favored to win enough House seats to take the chamber—without even needing to win any of the 18 districts classified as 'toss-ups' by the *Cook Political Report*." However, as of this writing, the declared House results are largely concentrated in non-competitive districts, with outcomes still pending in over 40 decisive races.

Early vote tallies have revealed some concerning signs for the Republican Party. A report from *https://t.co/BYOm0KyNoV* notes that in Steuben County, Indiana—a rural county where Donald Trump won 70% to 28% in 2024—the Republican candidate’s lead had narrowed to just 8 percentage points with nearly half the votes counted. Early results from Florida also show Democrats leading in both the Senate and gubernatorial races, though it should be noted that Florida typically tallies Democratic-leaning early votes first.

Senate: Where the Real Suspense Lies

With 35 Senate seats up for election, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure a majority. (In the event of a 50-50 tie, Vice President-elect Vance would cast the deciding vote, allowing Republicans to retain control.) The seven states currently classified as "toss-ups" by the Cook Political Report are Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas.

In Texas, the race between Democrat James Talarico and the Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton is exceptionally tight. On-the-ground reporting from DW notes that more than 7.7 million Texans have already cast their ballots—exceeding 40% of registered voters and setting a record for a midterm election. In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins—who previously voted in favor of impeaching Trump—faces a stiff challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson. In Ohio, former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is vying to reclaim a seat, competing against Republican Jon Husted.

However, the reliability of polling warrants caution. On the eve of the election, *The New York Times* pointed out that Democrats held leads in the final polls across "all seven states most likely to determine control of the Senate," while acknowledging that "the Trump era has seen instances where polls overestimated Democratic support." Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini told ABC News that while the political environment is "indeed bad" for the Republican Party, his analysis of over 3,000 Senate polls from the past eight years reveals that 73% of them overestimated support for Democratic candidates—a figure that rises to 93% for polls in Iowa, Ohio, and Michigan.

Background: A Referendum on Trump

The underlying nature of this election is clear. DW’s coverage captures the mood of the electorate: "American voters are heading to the polls feeling weary and frustrated, angered by the soaring cost of living. They are expected to punish Trump and his Republican Party." Trump himself has transformed the election into a referendum on his own leadership, urging his supporters to "pretend that I am on the ballot." However, the fact that he focused his energy during the final stretch of the campaign on deep-red states—such as Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina—rather than on swing states, speaks to the defensive position in which the Republican Party finds itself.

In an interview with Fox News on November 3, Trump claimed that "inflation has been solved." Yet, data released by the Department of Commerce last week showed that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 3.6% year-on-year in September. This gap between his assertion and the lived reality of voters is precisely the point that the Democratic Party has repeatedly leveraged throughout this election cycle.

POLLS CLOSE — The most consequential round of poll closings of the 2026 midterms is here. Polls closed at 8 p.m. ET in 21 states, including three major Senate battlegrounds: Texas, Maine, and Michigan.

All eyes are now on Texas. We expect substantial returns from key Texas counties within minutes of polls closing. Democrat James Talarico is attempting to defeat Republican Ken Paxton, as Democrats seek their first statewide victory in Texas in more than three decades.

We're also watching Governor Greg Abbott's race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa and several competitive House contests.

Maine and Michigan also are key Senate battlegrounds, but they will be much slower to report. In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is hoping to fend off Democrat challenger Troy Jackson. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in a closely contested race for an open Democratic-held seat.

Both states count substantially more slowly than Texas, and it could be several hours before we have meaningful clarity.

The final polls have also closed in Florida, where results from competitive House districts should already be providing useful information about the national environment.

Another race I'm closely watching is Kansas Senate, where Democrats are hoping to make a surprisingly competitive contest out of a normally safe Republican seat. A Democratic victory there would be a remarkable upset and signal a blue tsunami.

Texas should quickly offer some of the most revealing returns of the night. Maine and Michigan will require considerably more patience.

text:
Joe Buck and Peyton Manning: A Potential New Era of Monday Night Football

A Monday Night Football pairing of Joe Buck and Peyton Manning would have the potential to become one of the most compelling broadcast teams in the program’s history. The closest comparison would be Al Michaels and John Madden, who established a successful formula by combining polished play-by-play with entertaining, knowledgeable football analysis. Buck would fill a similar role to Michaels, providing authoritative calls, storytelling and the excitement of prime-time football, while Manning could bring the personality, humor and football expertise that made Madden so popular.

There would also be similarities to Mike Tirico and Jon Gruden, particularly in the technical analysis of quarterback play, offensive schemes and defensive adjustments. However, Manning’s experience as a five-time MVP and two-time Super Bowl champion would give him a unique perspective, especially when explaining what quarterbacks see before and after the snap. Unlike a traditional analyst, Peyton could make complicated football concepts accessible while adding spontaneous humor and personality.

Compared with Buck’s current partnership with Troy Aikman, a Buck-Manning combination would potentially offer a more entertaining and conversational dynamic. Aikman is measured and analytical, whereas Manning could bring a more unpredictable, humorous and interactive approach without sacrificing football credibility.

Ultimately, Buck and Manning could represent a modern combination of the Michaels-Madden and Tirico-Gruden partnerships. Buck would provide the broadcast’s structure and big-game atmosphere, while Manning would supply the personality, quarterback insight and entertainment. If their chemistry translated from the ManningCast to a traditional three-hour broadcast, they could become a defining Monday Night Football pairing.

text:
I want to thank everybody for the support—even the skeptics. Heck, especially the skeptics.

Truth be told, I've always been very customer-service-oriented. This came as a surprise to early @WatchMojo viewers when I moonlighted in the comments section as Mr. X.

To me, engaging with viewers was both an invaluable source of feedback and something of an ombudsman's responsibility. Initially, the comments sections were crickets. Then things exploded. Eventually, I stepped away.

With the Peanut Project, I approached things with the same philosophy: engage with fans to gauge genuine interest, listen to skeptics to identify potential pitfalls and obstacles, and use that feedback to strengthen the mission.

Transparency wasn't a publicity strategy. It was accountability.

Professionally, those who know me understand that I place enormous importance on character, integrity and truthfulness.

So when people started making frivolous personal accusations, I struggled with how to respond. The conventional wisdom is to ignore them. And while I still believe in defending the truth, I recognize that responding in kind to people taking personal shots rarely accomplishes much.

You can take the high road 99 times, but the one time you lose your patience can overshadow the other 99.

That's a lesson worth acknowledging.

Last week, I discussed the many missionaries (below) who have helped generate the incredible momentum behind the Peanut Project. There are many others I haven't yet recognized.

One is Patrick Malone, who played a catalytic role in the effort to bring Major League Baseball back to Washington, D.C., through what became the @Nationals.

Incidentally, Patrick was involved with a competing group when the Lerner family ultimately secured the franchise.

Throughout this process, he's been extraordinarily gracious, generous and constructive with his feedback.

Today, he shared a particularly insightful observation about @MLB expansion:

The sports media treats expansion like the Kentucky Derby.

Pundits handicap the favorites based on bloodlines and past performance, much as they're evaluating the cities competing for MLB's next two franchises.

It's a great analogy. But the best pedigree doesn't necessarily win the race.

For what it's worth, Patrick believes Montréal deserves to be front and centre in the expansion conversation. I've shared a little more with him privately than I have publicly here, though certainly not everything.

And that brings me back to the importance of listening.

We would NOT have identified Carrie-Derick as a potential stadium site had I remained in my own bubble.

Nor would we have recruited @DanEvans108 without the input of people following the project. Thank you, @mattbomberg.

Separately, when I recently ran an idea by our brain trust, Matt offered this perspective:

"Let's consider what the @Montreal_Expos looked like 22 years ago. A complete mess. Twelve different paths and cooks in the kitchen. Zero strategy, always reacting, and their decision-making was always knee-jerk, almost always wrong.

You have crushed this. That's how far you have taken this."

I appreciate the sentiment, but I want to clarify one thing:

The "YOU" is the collective Peanut Project.

The people who have contributed ideas, challenged assumptions, opened doors, offered introductions, identified opportunities and helped solve problems.

Some are household names. Others are anonymous fans. Some are longtime believers. Others began as skeptics.

All have helped.

Going forward, I'll continue reading as many comments as I reasonably can, but I'm going to shift gears a little.

There are simply too many moving parts now, and I need to be more deliberate about where I spend my time and energy.

So, two things:

1. I'll share a dedicated Feedback Form.

If you have potentially instrumental information about land, urban planning, infrastructure, investors, financing, MLB intelligence, partnerships or anything else that could materially advance the project, please use it.

That will ensure your feedback reaches me rather than getting buried in a sea of social media comments.

2. I'll update the Peanut Project Table of Contents.

This has effectively become a full-time job in itself!

For anyone who wants to follow the journey, understand the strategy, explore the research or share relevant resources with others, I'll make it easier to navigate everything we've published.

No obligations, of course.

Ultimately, I never wanted an echo chamber. I wanted a sounding board.

And the skeptics have been just as valuable as the supporters—sometimes more so.

I'll continue to welcome constructive criticism, even when it's uncomfortable. But I'll be more selective about engaging with personal attacks that contribute nothing to the mission.

The goal was never to win arguments on social media.

The goal is to bring the Expos back to Montréal.

Thank you. ⚾

Yes. SBA-backed loans can be used to purchase hotels, motels, inns, restaurants, and other operating businesses. Minority entrepreneurs can qualify, but there is an important distinction: the SBA does not automatically offer lower down payments or preferential loan approval simply because an applicant is Hispanic, Black, or belongs to another minority group.

There are also financing organizations that focus on underserved communities and help entrepreneurs access capital.

### 1\. SBA programs for buying a hotel

| Program                   | Maximum financing                                   | Typical buyer contribution | Best use                                           |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| SBA 7(a)                  | $5 million                                          | Starting at 10%            | Buying an existing hotel and its business          |
| SBA 504                   | SBA portion up to $5.5 million, plus bank financing | Often 15–20% for hotels    | Purchasing hotel real estate and major renovations |
| Community-focused lenders | Varies                                              | Depends on lender          | Smaller acquisitions or additional financing       |

The 7(a) program can finance a business acquisition, equipment, renovations, real estate, and working capital. The 504 program focuses on major fixed assets rather than working capital. Small Business Administration +2

A hotel can qualify when it is an eligible, actively operated hospitality business. Simply purchasing a building to collect rent is different and may not qualify.

### 2\. How much money would you need?

For an illustrative $1.5 million hotel acquisition:

EXAMPLE HOTEL PURCHASE

### $1,500,000

SBA 7(a), 10%

### $150,000

504, 15%

### $225,000

504, 20%

### $300,000

Illustrative minimum equity contributions, assuming eligible project costs equal the purchase price. Closing expenses, operating reserves, renovations, and lender requirements can increase the cash needed.

The 504 program generally requires 15% for special-purpose properties such as hotels, rising to 20% when the business also qualifies as new. The October 1, 2026 SBA acquisition rules retain a 10% minimum equity requirement for initial 7(a) acquisitions. U.S. Small Business Administration +3

Lenders also examine the hotel's operating history, profits, occupancy, management experience, personal credit, and ability to repay. Current 7(a) acquisition underwriting generally requires historical cash flow sufficient to cover debt service at least 1.25 times. WBD +1

### 3\. What minority-owned business assistance exists?

The Minority Business Development Agency (MBDA) helps eligible minority-owned businesses locate financing, establish lender relationships, and prepare for expansion. It does not automatically provide the acquisition loan itself. Minority Business Development Agency +1

In South Carolina, these are useful starting points:

* [South Carolina MBDA Business Center](https://t.co/v5rpqxZZ69) — Columbia; 803-743-1152.

* [Appalachian Development Corporation](https://t.co/KsFKHRPyGH) — Greenville-based SBA 504 financing.

* [SC Small Business Development Centers](https://t.co/gt9uoBnsFU) — assistance preparing acquisition plans and loan applications.

* [SBA Lender Match](https://t.co/dptstoHZYq) — connect directly with SBA lenders.

One significant current restriction: since March 2026, SBA 7(a) and 504 financing has required ownership by eligible U.S. citizens or U.S. nationals residing in the United States. U.S. Small Business Administration.

text:
8 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

Election night in America 2026. I'm Matt Pieper.: “And I'm Stacy Lynn in Washington. Polls have just closed in Pennsylvania, Maine, and several other states, but they're still open in Alaska, where a closely watched Senate race is drawing new scrutiny. The Justice Department is ramping up its criminal investigation into allegations that Democrats recruited a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and take votes away from. Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, prosecutors have issued more than 100 subpoenas and sent at least 20 letters notifying people they're targets of the investigation. Senator Sullivan told reporters voters are confused. I've heard from people who think they voted for the wrong guy and have apologized. Democrat Mary Peltola denies any involvement and no one has been charged. ”

In all - 435 seats in the House and about a third in the Senate are being contested.
In Maine - when it comes to polling - incumbent Senator Susan Collins has seen a swing this election cycle of double digits, that's usually a 3 to 4 percent swing.
So says Colby College professor of government Nick Jacobs.: “A swing of about 15 points from election to election. Uh, it's been 6 years for Susan, but a swing that big is a tsunami. ”
Jacobs says such a dramatic change in the rural vote could really have an impact with congressional races.

Election officials in Southern California are offering a snapshot of turnout - with a little less than three hours to go before polls close.
More than 1.9 million ballots have already been cast in LA County.
That includes 1.5 million vote-by-mail ballots - and nearly 400-thousand voters who have voted in person.
County Clerk Dean Logan:: “To put those numbers in perspective, in the 2022 general elections, so the last gubernatorial election, uh, overall turnout in that election was 28%, and so we still have several hours to go and many more vote by mail ballots that are coming back, coming back in. So that's a clear indication that we're going to see a healthier turnout than we saw four years ago. ”

There ARE issues in some places.
Voters in Westchester County New York have had to resort to a backup system to vote all day - because voting machines have malfunctioned.
Carol Hall from Pelham on what she had to do.: “The physical ballot itself goes into the bag, and instead of, I guess, the machines tabulating the votes, they, they will be counted by hand. ”

There are some early results.
The Associated Press has made its first Senate race call of the night.
Democratic Sen. Mark Warner has been reelected in Virginia.
Warner was overwhelmingly favored to win and the seat is staying in Democratic hands, so his victory does NOT tilt the balance of power in the Senate.
Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans.
Polls have closed in 11 states.
And Democrat Debbie Wasserman Schultz wins election to the House in Florida -  defeating Republican Brent Andersen.

Even working at the International Space Station - has not kept astronaut Anil Menon from casting his ballot - as a resident of Harris County, Texas.
He offered a quick snapshot on social media - of the process of voting from space.: “This is my room that doubles as a voting booth for me. Inside of it is my computer where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County, so I could vote. ”
Crewmates Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney did the same.

Uruguay has unveiled the popemobile that Pope Leo will use during his visit this week to South America.
Local manufacturer NORDEX says the vehicle - which started as a donated Fiat - was built to Vatican specifications.
That includes protection from adverse weather, accessibility and safety during travel.
It earned Cardinal Daniel Sturla's blessing. He noted the quality of the work - suggesting it was carried out impeccably.  He says it will allow the pope to stand if he so chooses.
Pope Leo is set to visit 10 cities during his South American tour beginning Friday - which also includes stops in Argentina and Peru.

text:
AI's most expensive mistake doesn't happen when it answers. It happens earlier, when nobody confirmed what it understood.
On yesterday's AI Daily Brief, @nlw and Nufar Gaspar offered a definition I agree with: slop is work where the person who should have done the thinking skipped it, and the cost lands on whoever receives it.
The data backs it up. A BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab study (2025) found that 40% of US desk workers had received that kind of work in the past month, and each case took close to two hours to sort out.
In the ICAR method, the second step is Confirm, and it's the one people skip most. Before the AI produces anything, ask it to tell you:
1. What it understood you're trying to achieve.
2. Who it's for and what decision it should support.
3. What it's assuming and what information it's missing.
If the answer doesn't match what you had in mind, the problem isn't the model. It's the instruction. Fixing it there takes a minute. Fixing it after you get a polished document that answers a different question takes hours, and sometimes a client's trust.
Over my career I learned that the costly errors are rarely the obvious ones. They're the ones that look right.
I'm adopting one of the episode's tests as a rule: nothing made with AI goes out unless the person signing it can defend every sentence without rereading it.
#AI #TameYourAI #Leadership

In a report from early October 2026, JPMorgan strategist Dubravko Lakos-Bujas pointed out that, since 1950, periods of a "gridlocked" (divided) Congress have been associated with an average 21% gain in the S&P 500 over the subsequent two-year term, compared to an 18% gain when a single party controlled both chambers of Congress. Regarding the strategy of buying AI-related stocks during any potential sell-off following a "blue wave" (a Democratic sweep of both chambers), JPMorgan offered the same advice in an election outlook dated November 2, 2026—reasoning that any legislation aimed at curbing AI expansion would likely be blocked by a presidential veto. The bank’s forecast that AI-related capital expenditures will continue through 2028 has also appeared consistently across several of its research notes; notably, in July 2026, the firm raised its projection for AI data center capital spending by hyperscalers in 2028 to approximately $1.4 trillion.

Historical Returns Under a Divided Congress: 21% vs. 18%

These figures originate directly from a client report by JPMorgan strategist Dubravko Lakos-Bujas dated October 1, 2026. The report states: "Since 1950, congressional gridlock has been associated with a 21% gain in the S&P 500 over the subsequent two-year term, whereas a scenario where one party controls both chambers of Congress has yielded an 18% return from the date of the election." This aligns precisely with the information mentioned in the user's post. Historical statistics from the independent financial website Lederer Associates—drawing on data from LPL Research and Bloomberg—also indicate that, between 1950 and 2019, the S&P 500’s average annual return was indeed higher during periods of divided government than under unified government, although the specific methodology used for categorization (based on combinations of the president’s party and congressional control) differs from the "two-year term total return" metric employed by JPMorgan. Buying the Dip in AI Stocks Following a "Blue Wave": Conditions and Rationale

In a report dated November 2, 2026—the day before the election—JPMorgan Chase identified a "Blue Wave" scenario (in which the Democratic Party secures control of both the House and the Senate) as the most likely outcome, assigning it a 66% probability. The report acknowledged that such a scenario could trigger a sell-off in AI-related stocks, driven by market concerns that a Democratic-controlled government might impose stricter regulations on data centers and technology companies. However, JPMorgan’s core assessment was that any legislation aimed at curbing AI expansion would be unlikely to overcome a presidential veto; therefore, the firm advised traders to "buy any dip" in tech stocks. This recommendation was not based on the premise that a "Blue Wave" would be beneficial for AI, but rather on the view that any negative impacts on the sector would be difficult to enact into law.

AI Capital Expenditure to Persist Through 2028: Quantitative Forecasts from JPMorgan

The assertion—found in user discussions—that "AI spending will remain robust through 2028, regardless of who wins," is supported by several research notes from JPMorgan. In July 2026, the firm raised its capital expenditure (capex) forecasts for AI data centers among hyperscalers—including Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft—projecting approximately $1.2 trillion for 2027 and an increase to roughly $1.4 trillion by 2028. In September of the same year, the bank projected cloud infrastructure capital expenditures at $954 billion for 2026, $1.41 trillion for 2027, and approximately $1.54 trillion for 2028. A separate report from JPMorgan Asset Management, also released in July 2026, noted that analysts expected total AI spending to potentially exceed $3 trillion by 2028, adding that "every revision to this forecast to date has been to the upside." The underlying premise for these projections is that the AI ​​investment cycle is driven by corporate demand and capacity expansion, rather than by the outcome of any single election. Distinctions Worth Noting

The user’s post presents a "divided government" and a "blue wave" as two pillars of the same argument; however, within JPMorgan’s framework, these correspond to distinct scenarios. The historical return statistic of 21% (versus 18%) applies to a "divided Congress" scenario, while the advice to "buy the dip in AI stocks" pertains to a "blue wave" scenario (a Democratic sweep). JPMorgan does not claim that a blue wave itself would yield a 21% two-year return—that figure represents the historical average under a divided government. Combining these two concepts rhetorically reinforces the impression that "the market will perform well regardless of the outcome," but JPMorgan’s actual analysis is segmented by scenario, with each carrying different implications for the market.

text:
Agentic commerce is undeniably overhyped based on current usage

...but, I'd be willing to bet it's massively underhyped based on volume agents will drive in ~3-6 months. 

And, if you're not optimizing your product (software, service, or physical good) for agents, you'll be left behind. 

Why? 

1. As Maia's demo shows - agents are much improved, but still nowhere near perfect. 99% of consumers will churn off an agent if there are any issues or delays. Browser use is still slow / buggy and the ecosystem of connectors / plug-ins available on these agents are nascent. 

Similarly - saving down credentials, handling payments, etc. all have too much friction and uncertainty now. This will all be solved over time. 

2. The VAST majority of consumers still are not using agents. Pick a person off the street in any city other than SF, and they have likely heard of neither Muse nor Instinct. 

These products have (so far) done a fantastic job optimizing for the workflows / use cases of high income, tech-forward SV users. They are still early in doing things that are valuable for the mainstream user on a repeatable basis (retention), especially while being able to offer the product for free. 

This will likely involve unlocking network effects (yes, some consumer agents now are multiplayer but usage is fairly low) and giving people ways to make money / spend time vs. save money / save time (@ekuyda's thesis!) Model costs coming down will help here too. 

3. "Agents" right now generally refer to standalone harnesses built for consumers to use (Instinct, Muse, Fo, Tomo, Pally, Folk, Tab, Daimon and many others). 

These products will continue to grow - and consumers will interact with agentic models more frequently via products like ChatGPT (now at 1.2B WAUs), that can now complete purchases instead of just recommending products. 

As ChatGPT rolls out its wallet and more developers connect plug-ins, I could see a massive increase in % of LLM queries that lead to in-chat transactions. And, early data shows that AI-driven traffic is actually higher conversion and intent than non-AI commerce traffic.

text:
Canva’s restructuring memo runs roughly 1,600 words. “AI” appears zero times. So does “layoff.”

As a goodbye, it’s well done. Melanie Perkins gives one headline figure: 1,271 people, 22% of the company. The exit package is generous: at least six months’ pay, departing staff keep their MacBooks, the one-year vesting cliff is waived for recent hires, and anyone leaving can apply for a US$10,000 grant to start something of their own.

As an explanation, it’s less convincing.

The letter says “new technology” is changing what people create, growth has “slowed for the first time in a decade,” and Canva needs to “refound” itself. The proposed fixes are structural: fewer layers, fewer handoffs, broader ownership. Fair. But those changes don’t fully explain why growth slowed.

Canva’s own disclosures offer more context. In August, it cut its 2026 growth forecast from 30% to 20% after the cost of running AI features forced it to slow their rollout. Canva says it has reduced the cost per AI task by nearly 90% since April.

And on November 3, AFR reported, citing confidential internal data, that annualized revenue stood at about US$3.69 billion in late October, well below the company’s reported US$5.2 billion internal target.

Then there’s the 22%.

“Impacted” bundles three different outcomes: changes to existing roles, relocation requests to hubs such as Sydney, and actual job losses. Add the new expectation for most hybrid staff to spend two or three days a week in the office from January.

From the outside, we still can’t tell how many people will actually lose their jobs.

I’ve spent 11 years working in China tech PR, and I’ve seen how relocation can function as a form of indirect headcount reduction. Employees are offered a transfer to another city. Some can go. Others can’t, and leaving becomes the practical outcome without a conventional layoff.

I have no evidence that’s Canva’s intent. But this is precisely why combining three outcomes into one number matters.

And why leave out AI?

I don’t know. But AI is both raising questions about the economics of Canva’s product and challenging the basic design workflows on which its business was built. Those are uncomfortable questions to leave unanswered in a letter explaining the company’s biggest restructuring.

As a goodbye, Canva did a lot right. As an explanation, it left too much unsaid.

Generous terms buy goodwill. A clear cause buys trust. Canva only paid for the first.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
November 3, 2026
UTAH ELECTION CONTROVERSY: CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION REQUEST FILED AS FEDERAL AUTHORITIES INVESTIGATE SIMILAR ALASKA ELECTION ALLEGATIONS

Salt Lake County, Utah — Today, Sophia (Sophie) Anderson personally delivered a signed, nine-page request for criminal investigation and independent conflict-of-interest review to the Utah Attorney General's Criminal Investigations Division. 

An intake employee acknowledged receipt.
The complaint concerns allegations surrounding Utah's 2024 gubernatorial election, when Richard Kennedy Lyman and Carol Ann Lyman entered the race as write-in candidates against Phil Lyman and Natalie Clawson.

A witness, James Newson, alleged that Richard Lyman reported an offer of $1,000 and a steak dinner to enter the race and interfere with Phil Lyman's campaign.

The allegations were raised in a civil lawsuit that was dismissed without adjudication of whether the alleged financial inducement occurred.

ALASKA: FEDERAL CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION — MORE THAN 100 SUBPOENAS
The Utah filing comes as the U.S. Department of Justice conducts a criminal investigation into similar allegations: that political operatives recruited another candidate, also named Dan Sullivan, to run against incumbent U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska's 2026 election.

According to ABC News on November 3, 2026, federal prosecutors are preparing more than 100 subpoenas and have issued approximately 20 target letters or related notices in connection with the investigation. A federal grand jury is reportedly examining potential conspiracy and donor-fraud offenses.
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy has also directed a separate state investigation into whether the alleged candidate-recruitment effort violated state law.
The Utah and Alaska controversies both raise questions about the recruitment of similarly named candidates and possible voter confusion.

In Utah, the additional allegation of a $1,000-and-steak-dinner inducement raises a specific question under the state's election-bribery law. Sophie's November 3 filing asks Utah authorities to investigate that allegation and determine whether criminal conduct occurred.

UTAH ATTORNEY GENERAL'S CONFLICTS QUESTIONED
Sophie's complaint also requests an independent conflict-of-interest review involving Attorney General Derek Brown.
In December 2023, Lieutenant Governor Deidre Henderson was announced as co-chair of Brown's campaign finance committee. Governor Spencer Cox publicly endorsed Brown in May 2024, and Brown publicly supported Cox over Phil Lyman.

The complaint asks whether these documented campaign relationships warrant independent investigative or prosecutorial review.

ELECTION ADMINISTRATION AND MEDIA QUESTIONS
Sophie also requests examination of the Lieutenant Governor's handling of candidate withdrawal notices and media coverage that prominently displayed photographs of Phil Lyman in stories concerning the withdrawal of Richard and Carol Lyman.

text:
TYRAN STOKES: TALENT VS. RISK

Tyran Stokes is an incredibly talented basketball player. There's a reason he's been considered one of the best prospects in his class for years.

But I think there's a much bigger conversation worth having about the risk involved in making him the No. 1 pick — or even No. 2 — and handing him the keys to an NBA franchise.

This isn't about predicting that he'll fail. It's about taking a serious look at the reported history of disciplinary issues, emotional outbursts, questionable judgment, maturity concerns and questions about how he handles adversity.

When you're investing that much in a player, those things matter.

Here's what people should understand about the situation.

NOTRE DAME / DISCIPLINARY HISTORY

In November 2025, Stokes abruptly withdrew from Notre Dame High School in Sherman Oaks, California, shortly before the start of his senior basketball season.

The school's public statement simply said he had decided to withdraw and explore other opportunities.

However, Sports Illustrated reported that Stokes had been facing disciplinary issues, including altercations with other students, and had served a suspension.

The Journal 425 subsequently reported two physical altercations within a two-week period: one involving a senior student and another involving a 14-year-old freshman. The outlet reported that these incidents played a role in his departure.

To be clear, the school publicly described his departure as a withdrawal, not an expulsion. The specific details of the altercations come from reporting, not a public disciplinary record. But the broader reporting about disciplinary problems and student altercations is significant.

There was also the football situation. Stokes joined Notre Dame's football team during the 2025 season, making his debut on September 26. He appeared in two more games, with the suspension reportedly keeping him out of multiple football games.

I'm not suggesting his limited football appearances are another behavioral issue. The relevant point is that the suspension affected him during that season, too.

ON-COURT ATTITUDE / EMOTIONAL CONTROL

The concerns aren't limited to what happened at Notre Dame.

The Athletic documented several incidents during his time on the grassroots circuit.

At Peach Jam, Stokes was observed failing to get back on defense after turnovers and missed shots, snapping at teammates and coaches, and visibly losing his temper after his Oakland Soldiers team suffered an upset loss.

His outburst was significant enough that people wondered whether he would stick around for the rest of the tournament. He did.

At the Les Schwab Invitational, The Athletic described him as whining to officials during a loss in which Rainier Beach was outplayed by a less talented local team.

There have also been multiple reports about his interactions with opposing crowds.

A South Seattle Emerald feature documented Stokes playing into the heckling from opposing student sections, making gestures toward crowds, talking back and even blowing kisses after making shots.

Hoops HQ has also described his historically aggressive demeanor and tendency to trash-talk opponents.

Some view this as entertaining competitive fire. Others see it as unnecessary theatrics and a potential maturity concern. An experienced referee who worked his games pointed out that Stokes was frequently subjected to hostile heckling and that occasionally responding was only human.

The point isn't that trash talk is inherently bad. It's whether he can consistently channel that energy appropriately, particularly when things aren't going his way.

THE JAMAL CRAWFORD CONFRONTATION

At Hoophall West, Stokes got into a very public shouting match with assistant coach Jamal Crawford during a game against Mater Dei.

Stokes had just hit a three-pointer and started running his mouth. Crawford, frustrated with his defensive effort, shouted at him from the bench. The two exchanged words across the court.

Stokes was subbed out with two minutes remaining in the half and sat at the start of the second half.

This wasn't a minor disagreement behind closed doors. It was a very public confrontation between a highly touted prospect and a respected former NBA player who was trying to coach him.

Crawford later described it as a "blowup that turned into a blessing and a breakthrough." That's an encouraging way to look at it, but the incident itself is still relevant when evaluating how Stokes responds to criticism and accountability.

BODY LANGUAGE / MATURITY / COACHABILITY

Jeff Goodman has publicly described Stokes' body language as "atrocious" at times.

Other scouting reports have raised questions about his motor, demeanor and emotional consistency.

ESPN's Jeremy Woo has also reported that NBA executives have concerns about Stokes' maturity and demeanor, with scouts frequently noting his on-court temper and moodiness.

These aren't isolated criticisms from random fans on social media. They've been recurring themes in scouting and reporting.

OFF-COURT JUDGMENT

Then there's the fireworks video from July 2026, featuring Stokes shooting fireworks alongside Sexyy Red, Rob49 and Skillibeng.

I'm not suggesting there's anything inherently wrong with being around entertainers or musicians. But participating in a fireworks display carries an obvious risk of serious hand injuries, particularly for someone whose basketball career represents an enormous financial opportunity.

It's not evidence of criminal activity or anything else beyond what the video shows. But it is another example of a decision that raises questions about judgment and risk assessment.

WHAT GRASSROOTS SCOUTS ARE SAYING

This isn't just my interpretation of the available history, either.

In a recent post, grassroots scout Eric Guilleminault said:

"There are multiple grassroots scouts including myself who would rather trade the pick than draft him at 1. He's not equipped to be the face of a franchise and it will likely take a few changes in scenery before it clicks."

That's a pretty significant statement from people who have followed Stokes closely throughout his grassroots career.

Obviously, this is one scout's public account of what he's hearing from others, not a verified consensus of NBA front offices. But it reinforces that concerns about Stokes extend beyond what fans see in a box score or highlight reel.

The question isn't simply whether he's talented enough to be the No. 1 pick. It's whether he's ready for everything that comes with being the face of an organization.

THE COUNTERARGUMENT: THERE ARE POSITIVES, TOO

To be fair, there is meaningful positive evidence.

Mike Bethea has praised Stokes as a high-character kid, a good teammate and someone who accepts hard coaching.

Jamal Crawford described their confrontation as a "blowup that turned into a blessing and a breakthrough." He said Stokes responded to accountability and wanted to be coached.

Bill Self has repeatedly praised his coachability. In October, Self said he's coached Stokes as hard as anyone on the team and that Stokes keeps coming back for more. He also said Stokes has made a good effort to fit in at Kansas and has shown progress in maturity.

The Athletic documented Stokes buying shoes and a winter coat for students in need, signing autographs for hours and encouraging teammates during the Hoop Summit.

Stokes himself has acknowledged the criticism. He's talked about still growing up, working through things off the court and learning to manage his emotions.

And Kansas is a new environment. It's entirely possible that the structure, coaching and accountability under Bill Self will help him continue to mature.

That's important. He's young, and people can change. I'm not suggesting his past defines his future.

But positive developments don't mean the concerns should simply be dismissed, either.

WE'VE SEEN THIS BEFORE: "HE'S JUST A KID. HE'LL MATURE."

One of the most common responses to concerns like these is that Stokes is still young. He's a teenager. He'll grow up, mature and figure things out.

And that's certainly possible.

But we've heard similar arguments about other immensely talented prospects. Sometimes those concerns don't simply disappear with age, and the consequences can be significant.

Josh Jackson was one of the most talented players in the 2017 draft and went No. 4 overall. Even before entering the NBA, there were documented concerns about his emotional control, maturity, body language and off-court judgment. He had multiple incidents at Kansas, including a confrontation that resulted in anger-management requirements. His NBA career never came close to matching the expectations surrounding his talent.

Michael Beasley went No. 2 overall in 2008 after an extraordinary college season. But maturity and behavioral concerns had followed him throughout high school and into the draft process. He openly acknowledged being young and still learning. His NBA career was subsequently sidetracked by inconsistency and repeated off-court issues, including marijuana-related incidents and time in treatment. His talent was never the question. Maximizing it was.

Eddie Griffin was considered a legitimate candidate for the No. 1 pick in 2001. Before the draft, there were already serious concerns about his history of fights, suspensions, anger management and ability to handle accountability. He ultimately fell to No. 7, and his NBA career was short and troubled. The warning signs weren't something that suddenly appeared after he became a professional.

Ben Simmons is another interesting example. He was the No. 1 pick in 2016, an extraordinary physical talent and a three-time All-Star. But questions about maturity, leadership and commitment were being raised before he ever entered the NBA. His relationship with Philadelphia eventually deteriorated into a prolonged holdout and a very public breakdown between player and organization. Injuries and mental-health struggles also played major roles in his career, so it's unfair to reduce his situation to attitude alone. But his story is another reminder that extraordinary talent doesn't guarantee a player will maximize his potential or become the franchise cornerstone everyone envisioned.

And Ja Morant is a different but equally important example. He became an NBA superstar, but repeated poor decisions involving firearms resulted in suspensions of eight and 25 games. Morant himself eventually acknowledged that his off-court decisions had negatively affected the organization.

These aren't predictions that Stokes will follow the same paths. Their circumstances are different, and some of these players faced challenges that went well beyond maturity or behavior.

But they illustrate an important point: You cannot simply assume that talent will overcome everything, or that every young prospect will automatically mature out of recurring issues.

Sometimes players do grow up and figure it out. Sometimes they don't. Sometimes the consequences are significant, both for the player and the organization that invested in him.

That's why these concerns should be evaluated seriously BEFORE making a top-two investment, rather than dismissed with the assumption that everything will work itself out.

THERE ARE OTHER PROSPECTS IN THE MIX

I'm not suggesting Stokes should automatically fall down draft boards or that there aren't legitimate reasons to consider him No. 1.

He's currently No. 1 on my personal board.

But he's also not the only prospect in the conversation.

Jordan Smith Jr., Quentin Coleman and Stefan Joksimovic are three other players I believe belong in the discussion at the very top of this draft.

In my evaluation, all three are right there with Stokes in terms of on-court ability, while bringing their own advantages when you factor in age, size, skill sets and overall profiles.

Smith offers outstanding two-way ability.

Coleman brings shooting, burst, defense, passing and feel for the game. He'll also be just 18 on draft night.

Joksimovic led Slovenia to a FIBA U18 championship and is already playing at a high level in the EuroLeague/ACB environment, despite being more than a year younger than Stokes.

And importantly, I haven't seen comparable questions about behavior, attitude and maturity with any of them.

I'm not suggesting any of these players is guaranteed to become a better NBA player. But when you're evaluating the No. 1 or No. 2 pick, the comparison matters.

If you believe multiple prospects are in a similar tier in terms of basketball ability, the additional risks associated with one of them become much more relevant.

Stokes may remain No. 1 on my updated board. I'm still putting the finishing touches on it. But teams should be weighing the entire picture, not just the talent.

THE BOTTOM LINE

The question isn't whether Stokes has the talent to be the No. 1 pick. He does.

The question is whether a team can confidently invest a top-two pick in him, build its franchise around him and make him the public face of the organization.

That means trusting him to handle the expectations, scrutiny, leadership responsibilities, accountability and pressure that come with that position.

There is a difference between having the talent to become a franchise player and being ready for everything that comes with being one.

I'm not predicting Stokes will fail. I'm saying the risk deserves serious consideration, especially when there are other prospects with comparable on-court appeal who don't appear to carry the same concerns.

When you're making a decision this significant, maturity, judgment, emotional control and behavior aren't secondary considerations.

They're part of the evaluation.
