text:
#USMidterms #Trump #Impeachment #Israel #EpsteinFiles

Republicans took a serious electoral hit. Democrats are projected to retake the Senate, and there’s already talk of a third Trump impeachment. Washington is in something of a hurry to mistake a change in the Senate majority for a change in the country.

America remains deeply divided. Some voters may have turned against Trump over the cost of living, the war with Iran, or concerns about corruption while still identifying with the right. Others who voted for him in 2024 may simply have stayed home. We’ll have a better sense of how lasting this shift is when those voters choose a president again.

Impeachment would test something else: how much power Trump still holds over his own party. The House can impeach by a simple majority. Removing him takes two-thirds of the senators present. The November results only begin to tell us how far Republicans are willing to go. It’s one thing for a Republican to wish Trump would stay out of their district. It’s another to vote him out of the White House.

On Epstein, the test for the new Congress is whether it can obtain records, hear from survivors, and establish how the files were handled. Transparency is easier to promise on the campaign trail than to pursue when the inquiry starts making your own side uncomfortable.

On the very day Americans went to the polls, Trump said annual U.S. military aid to Israel would end after 2026. Arms sales, he clarified, would continue. The current agreement runs through 2028, and he offered no details on how he would end the aid early. He was more forthcoming about the electoral upside: it would take an argument away from his opponents. That may be a tactical move, and that’s precisely what makes it revealing. A policy defended for decades as a bipartisan commitment has become a subject a president would rather take off the table on Election Day.

Republicans and Democrats have real disagreements. They also compete in a system where big donors and lobbying groups have access to both parties. Pro-Israel groups spend money trying to shape who makes it onto the Democratic ballot. In Michigan, they spent tens of millions of dollars and the candidate they backed lost the primary. Money can buy airtime and access. Fortunately for voters, the votes still have to be counted.

Between now and 2028, I’m less interested in who declares victory than in what each party does when a decision costs it something with its donors, its allies, or its own base. Trump has offered an early test. He says the aid will end. Let’s see what happens to the money, the weapons, and the votes in Congress.

1️⃣ Trump’s midterm setback offers India some breathing room. After tariffs, threats and insults, a check on his power will be very welcome. A reminder of what India faced in his second term:

2️⃣ THE TARIFF HAMMER: Imposed tariffs reaching 50% on many Indian goods, including a 25% Russian-oil penalty. Indian exporters became collateral damage in his pressure campaign. Rates were subsequently reduced.

3️⃣ THE ECONOMIC INSULT: Dismissed India & Russia as a “dead economies”. Said they could take those economies down together “for all I care”. (You remember who picked that up 🙄)

4️⃣ THE CEASEFIRE CREDIT GRAB: Repeatedly claimed he stopped Op Sindoor. India’s position: Pakistan practically begged for the ceasefire, there was no US mediation or trade bargain. He kept claiming credit anyway.

5️⃣ THE TRADE BLACKMAIL CLAIM: Boasted that threatening BOTH India and Pakistan with 250% tariffs stopped the fighting. His account reduced India’s military decisions to obedience to Washington. India rejected it.

6️⃣ THE KASHMIR INTERVENTION: Offered to help settle Kashmir after a supposed “thousand years”. Injected himself into an issue on which India has consistently rejected third-party mediation.

7️⃣ THE PAKISTAN EMBRACE: Hosted Asim Munir for an unprecedented White House lunch weeks after the conflict. India privately protested that Washington was sending the wrong signal to Pakistan’s military.

8️⃣ THE OIL TAUNT: Announced plans to develop Pakistan’s oil reserves, then suggested Pakistan might someday sell oil to India. This came hours after announcing tariffs on India.

9️⃣ THE MANUFACTURING PRESSURE: Told Tim Cook he did not want Apple expanding production in India for the US market. Then threatened at least 25% tariffs on iPhones manufactured abroad. A direct challenge to India’s manufacturing ambitions.

🔟 THE VISA BLOW: Imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, hitting a route dominated by Indian professionals. The rollout caused panic before clarification that existing visas and renewals were excluded.

1️⃣1️⃣ THE SHACKLED DEPORTEES: His administration returned Indians on a military aircraft, with deportees in handcuffs and leg restraints. Trump made the White House boast about it with music-laced videos.

1️⃣2️⃣ THE PERSONAL CONDESCENSION: Threatened fresh tariffs over Russian oil, saying Modi knew he was unhappy and “it was important to make me happy”. India’s energy security treated as a presidential favour.

1️⃣3️⃣ THE “HELLHOLE” REPOST: Amplified material describing India as a “hellhole”.

India owes no American party its loyalty. The Democrats have low-key been as bad or worse in the past. But after his record of ‘big guy’ diplomacy, Trump cut to size will be welcomed by India.

text:
Wisconsin voters have spoken, and Democrats will hold a governing trifecta for the first time in nearly two decades. Governor-elect David Crowley, Assembly Minority Leader Greta Neubauer, and Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein will set the agenda in Madison.

I congratulate them on their victory.

For years, Wisconsin has thrived under an approach that made important investments while also reducing the tax burden. That balance delivered economic growth, fiscal responsibility, and opportunity for families and job creators. Republicans remain committed to those same principles: lower costs, a lighter tax burden, and an economy that expands opportunity rather than government.

Democrats spent the campaign promising lower costs and relief for families while offering few specifics. Their records tell a clearer story. Under Crowley, Milwaukee County nearly doubled its sales tax and raised property-tax levies in five of his six years. He has argued higher taxes are not a burden. Hold on to your wallets. With full control of state government, that approach is now on track to become statewide policy.

The new Democratic leadership also lacks any real private-sector experience. Crowley built his career in campaign organizing and political staff work. Neubauer and Hesselbein have the same resume. They know politics. Being good at politics will mean paying back their powerful political allies.

Republicans know what it takes to support a family or grow a small business, and we will keep that perspective front and center.

Over the next two years, I know Republicans will stand firmly with the taxpayers and job creators who built Wisconsin’s success. Conservatives will offer constructive alternatives, demand accountability, and make sure voters can see the difference between growing government and growing opportunity.

Many newly elected Democrats presented themselves as moderates; their leadership team has a different agenda.

Wisconsin’s strengths—our workforce, our communities, and our tradition of common-sense governance—are durable. Republicans will work every day to protect those strengths, highlight what is working, and prepare for the moment when voters again choose balance and results over one-party control.

The next two years will test our resolve.  They will also clarify the choice ahead.  We are ready for both.

text:
Republicans spent election night discovering that “pretend I’m on the ballot” was not, in fact, a governing strategy. Trump, displaying his usual breathtaking commitment to personal accountability, offered this masterpiece of political self awareness: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Apparently, the man who spent months demanding that voters treat every election as a referendum on him suddenly developed amnesia when the referendum came back with a resounding rejection. How convenient. It is the political equivalent of totaling your car, blaming the passengers, and then insisting the accident never would have happened if you had been driving. This is the same man who graciously acknowledged that Democrats “did a good job” and declared himself “absolutely willing to accept” the results, while simultaneously floating the veto hat. Nothing says accepting defeat quite like announcing that you intend to obstruct the people who just defeated you. Truly, a masterclass in losing without the inconvenience of admitting it.

Then came Mike Johnson, whose contribution to the evening was apparently to explain that history was always going to win, despite polling that had been practically screaming about a Republican wipeout. “We faced some real odds,” he lamented, which is a fascinating way of describing the consequences of spending two years ignoring every warning sign while confidently marching toward the electoral equivalent of a wood chipper.

And now, naturally, the Republican Party is talking about a “wake up call.” How precious. A wake up call generally suggests that someone intends to get out of bed, examine what went wrong, and make meaningful changes. Republicans, meanwhile, have spent the last two years treating Democratic voters, Democratic candidates, and enormous portions of the American public as existential threats to civilization. They have spent years screaming about communists, invaders, enemies of America, and the supposed destruction of the republic. But suddenly, after getting their political teeth kicked in at the ballot box, they expect Democrats to pull up a chair, pour some coffee, and have a pleasant bipartisan conversation about “core principles.”

Absolutely not.

You do not spend years vilifying an entire political party, questioning its legitimacy, attacking its voters, and treating compromise like an act of treason, only to lose an election and immediately demand cooperation from the people you spent years demonizing. That is not reconciliation. That is political entitlement with a fresh coat of desperation.

And that brings us to what these election results actually mean.

The voters who flipped Texas, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, Iowa, and a string of House seats did not send new Democratic majorities to Washington so they could participate in some adorable bipartisan friendship retreat with the very people voters just rejected. They did not vote for Democrats so Republican leadership could continue dictating the agenda while Democrats politely searched for common ground beneath the rubble.

They voted to STOP the Republican agenda. They voted to reverse what can be reversed. They voted to ensure that the next two years do not become another installment of the same political disaster with a slightly different cast.

Democrats were not elected to serve as unpaid therapists for a Republican Party experiencing the consequences of its own behavior. They were not sent to Washington to provide adult supervision for a movement that spent years treating bipartisanship as a one way street, only to suddenly discover the beauty of cooperation when it found itself on the losing end of an election.

And spare us the inevitable lectures about statesmanship, unity, and reaching across the aisle. Republicans had their opportunity to demonstrate those principles. Instead, they spent years setting fire to the concept of political cooperation and are now apparently shocked that Democrats might not be interested in helping them roast marshmallows over the ashes.

Working with a party that voters just repudiated on its own preferred political terrain is not statesmanship. It is surrender dressed up in a respectable suit. It is handing the losing side the authority to negotiate the terms of its own defeat. It is taking a democratic mandate and feeding it directly into the Republican obstruction machine.

Democrats should not be working with Republicans to salvage their agenda, rehabilitate their reputation, or soften the consequences of an election they lost. Republicans can spend the next two years contemplating the political consequences of their actions without expecting Democrats to rescue them from those consequences.

The newly elected Democratic majorities were not dispatched to Washington to negotiate away the very policies and principles voters elected them to defend. They were elected to USE THEIR MAJORITY.

Stop the agenda. Reverse the damage wherever possible. Exercise the authority voters handed them. And let Republicans experience the extraordinary constitutional concept of losing an election and no longer getting to dictate what happens next.

That is the mandate.

Anything less is rewarding a political movement that has repeatedly and loudly declared Democrats illegitimate, treated compromise as weakness, and only discovered the virtues of bipartisanship once its own political power was threatened.

Republicans spent two years making it abundantly clear that cooperation was beneath them.

Democrats should respect that position.

No bipartisan rescue mission. No political rehabilitation program. No surrender disguised as compromise.

Republicans wanted to govern without Democrats. Now they can discover what it feels like when Democrats govern without them.

text:
My parents paid $42,000 to help me buy my first house. I secretly put my husband's name on the deed because I didn't want my family controlling my future.

When my husband, Daniel, and I got married, we were renting a small apartment in Ohio. We both worked, but between bills, student loans, and everyday expenses, saving for a house seemed impossible.

My parents eventually offered to help us. They gave us $42,000 toward a down payment, telling me they wanted their daughter to have a stable home.

My father made one thing clear: the money was intended to help me secure a home, not to give Daniel's family any ownership.

At first, I agreed.

But Daniel wasn't happy about the arrangement. He said he couldn't spend his life paying a mortgage on a house that technically belonged to his wife.

He told me marriage meant sharing everything.

I understood his argument, and after several conversations, I secretly arranged for his name to be included on the deed.

I didn't tell my parents because I knew they would object.

I convinced myself it was my marriage, my house, and my decision.

text:
Ossoff wins a second Senate term in Georgia, keeping a key seat with Democrats

Jon Ossoff won another term representing Georgia in the US Senate, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and securing a second term in office. The result kept this important Georgia seat in Democratic hands, though the available reporting does not establish that Democrats controlled the Senate after the contest. The BBC described the outcome as a projection for Ossoff and said it moved the swing state further into Democratic control. That projection was issued less than an hour after voting ended, while the reported count at an earlier point showed Ossoff ahead by 63 percent to 29 percent with 56 percent of ballots counted.

The count figures describe Ossoff’s lead at a point when just over half of votes had been tallied, rather than a final margin for the race. The reported percentages show Ossoff well ahead of Collins at that stage, and the report attributed those figures to the Associated Press. The eventual result was reported as a re-election victory, but the facts provided here do not give a final vote total or final percentage margin. The swift projection and the partial-count figures are distinct measures: one described the projected winner, and the other captured the count while votes were still being reported.

Ossoff entered the contest as the Democratic incumbent, having held his Senate position since 2021. His win means he is to serve another term and return to the chamber alongside Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock. The reporting describes the seat as important because the parties were seeking influence in Congress and across the South. That wider significance reflects Georgia’s place in the parties’ efforts to build congressional power and influence in the South.

The campaign offered voters contrasting accounts of what should guide government and what problems deserved priority. Ossoff presented affordability, healthcare and accountability in government as central themes, while his campaign also highlighted economic concerns. The BBC reported that exit polling identified affordability as the leading issue for many voters, without supplying a percentage in the facts available here. Ossoff also made actions by the Trump administration a major subject, pointing to stock trading, business arrangements, the Iran war and trade policy.

Collins, a Republican member of Congress and a firm Trump ally, campaigned in support of Trump’s programme. His stated priorities included stronger immigration enforcement and a smaller federal government, as well as anti-transgender policies. He defended his backing for Trump’s war in Iran and attributed higher living costs to Joe Biden, according to the BBC account. These messages placed the candidates’ approaches side by side: Ossoff stressed economic concerns and oversight, while Collins emphasized Trump’s agenda and immigration enforcement.

The contest was also shaped by scrutiny of reported links involving people associated with Collins’s campaign. The Guardian reported that campaign staff had connections to white nationalists, neo-Nazis and other far-right extremists, describing those reports as a difficulty for Collins’s campaign. CNN reporters said Collins’s son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, had promoted white supremacist and Nazi positions online. Ossoff repeatedly challenged Collins over those reported connections in debates and campaign advertisements.

Campaign resources also differed: Ossoff had raised at least $115.9m for the election cycle, a sum reported as far above Collins’s fundraising. The figure refers to money raised by Ossoff for the cycle, not to the number of votes he received or to a final spending total. The available facts do not give Collins’s fundraising total, so they support a comparison in relative terms but not a precise difference between the campaigns. Nor do these facts show how the fundraising difference affected individual votes; they establish the reported scale of Ossoff’s fundraising and that it exceeded Collins’s.

Georgia’s recent presidential voting history shows why the state’s Senate race was set against a politically competitive backdrop. The state chose Joe Biden in 2020, then narrowly backed Donald Trump four years later. Those presidential results provide context for the state’s importance to party efforts, but they are not measures of the Senate vote in Ossoff’s race. The reporting also notes that a Georgia case alleging an effort by Trump and others to reverse the 2020 election outcome was dismissed after Trump returned to office in 2025.

Ossoff said the task ahead required reform rather than a simple return to earlier conditions, and he acknowledged that significant work remained. His remarks framed the victory as no substitute for further work, without specifying in the supplied facts which reforms he intended to pursue. Georgia Governor Brian Kemp, a term-limited Republican, was considered the favoured prospective challenger to Ossoff but chose not to run. Ossoff had repeatedly said that he did not want to seek the presidency, a point relevant to the political context but not a change in his Senate role. The midterm elections were expected to affect the remainder of Trump’s presidency and decide which party would control Congress, giving the Georgia result significance beyond the individual term.

text:
Me: Art =: Discovering Infinite Connections in Art History

Ai: Art =: Discovering Infinite Connections in Art History is an expansive and visually compelling exploration of humanity's artistic achievements, bringing together an extraordinary selection of artworks from the renowned collection of The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Published in celebration of the museum's 150th anniversary, this ambitious volume offers a fresh and unconventional approach to understanding art, examining the relationships between artistic movements, materials, cultures, historical periods, and visual ideas across approximately 6,000 years of creative expression.

Rather than following the traditional chronological structure of an art history textbook, Art = introduces an inventive system of thematic organization that encourages readers to discover unexpected relationships between artworks separated by centuries, continents, and cultural traditions. Its central premise is that art becomes even more fascinating when viewed through the connections that unite seemingly unrelated objects, images, and artistic practices. A flower, for example, can become a starting point for an exploration that moves from ancient Egyptian imagery and decorative traditions to Dutch Golden Age still lifes, the expressive paintings of Vincent van Gogh, and the monumental floral compositions of Georgia O'Keeffe. Through these visual comparisons, the book demonstrates how recurring subjects, symbols, techniques, and aesthetic concerns continue to influence artistic expression throughout history.

The publication is organized into three principal thematic sections: Material/Technique, Period/Place/Style, and Object/Subject. The first explores the physical and technical dimensions of art, bringing together works according to their materials and methods of production, including drawing, marble, watercolor, wood, and other artistic mediums. The second examines art through historical periods, geographical origins, and stylistic movements, creating opportunities to explore subjects such as Ancient Egyptian art, Impressionism, and Japanese art. The third investigates the objects, subjects, and recurring motifs that have inspired artists across different civilizations, encompassing themes such as flowers, food, motherhood, furniture, jewelry, and self-portraiture.
One of the book's greatest strengths is the extraordinary diversity of its visual material. Paintings, sculptures, photographs, drawings, prints, decorative arts, historical objects, and other forms of artistic production appear throughout its pages, creating an expansive visual dialogue between different disciplines and traditions. The juxtaposition of these works reveals how artistic ideas evolve, reappear, and transform across cultures, while also highlighting the distinctive ways in which individual artists interpret the world around them.

Complementing its extensive imagery are more than 160 essays written by museum curators and art historians. These texts provide historical background, cultural interpretation, and insights into the significance of individual works, allowing readers to move beyond visual appreciation and develop a deeper understanding of the circumstances, ideas, and artistic traditions behind them. A carefully designed color-coded reference system connects artworks, essays, and thematic keywords, making it possible to navigate the publication through multiple pathways and continually uncover new associations. A detachable, fold-out historical timeline provides an additional chronological perspective, balancing the book's unconventional thematic structure with a broader overview of art history.

2. U.S. Midterms: Democrats Win Both Chambers. #BlueWave2026

Democrats have won control of the Senate and are projected by major media outlets to take the House. This marks a major shift in Washington's balance of power, with Democrats positioned to control both chambers of Congress while President Trump remains in office.

The election uncertainty is now giving way to a clearer political landscape. Investors can begin evaluating the likely policy environment rather than trading around unknown election outcomes.

3. Why This Could Matter for Markets and Crypto

Historically, U.S. equities have performed well in the 12 months following midterm elections. U.S. Bank reports an average return of 12.4% across its historical sample, rising to 17.5% for elections since 1980. BlackRock's analysis found an average S&P 500 return of 14.1% in the six months following midterms since 1970.

This is a recurring historical pattern, not a guarantee: stocks have not risen after every midterm, and economic conditions remain decisive.

The removal of election uncertainty may help investors regain confidence and refocus on earnings, interest rates, growth, and investment opportunities.

For crypto, the congressional shift creates a new policy environment:

- Market-structure legislation, including the CLARITY Act, may face a different path through Congress.
- SEC and CFTC jurisdiction, stablecoin regulation, exchange oversight, and consumer protection will remain central issues.
- A Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican White House could produce negotiations, oversight, and potential legislative gridlock.

The opportunity: Greater clarity about political control may reduce one source of uncertainty. The next catalyst for digital assets will be whether policymakers can establish workable rules that support institutional participation, stablecoins, and blockchain innovation.

4. Macro + Crypto Markets

Tuesday's U.S. close was mixed: S&P 500 +0.36%, Nasdaq +0.83%, Dow -0.38%, and Russell 2000 +0.23%.

Bitcoin traded near $77,957 (+1.67%) and Ethereum near $2,297 (+2.12%). Big Tech and AI shares helped support the Nasdaq, while Treasury yields moved higher.

5. Sui Adoption + Infrastructure

- @MercadoBitcoin is bringing SUI, USDC, and USDsui access to its 4.5M Brazilian customers, with broader tokenized-asset expansion being explored.
- Sui's AI-agent initiatives are advancing programmable permissions, spending limits, and verifiable activity. Some capabilities remain in development or testnet.

Bottom Line

Sui's tracked assets are moving higher, and ecosystem development continues across payments, stablecoins, DeFi, tokenized assets, and AI infrastructure.

With Democrats projected to control both chambers of Congress, the political uncertainty surrounding the midterms is largely behind investors. Historical post-midterm performance offers an encouraging backdrop, although it does not guarantee gains. For crypto, the focus now shifts to regulatory negotiations, institutional confidence, liquidity, and real adoption.

text:
$ORCL filed for approximately $20 billion in AI data-center financing, split between roughly $10 billion of common stock and $10 billion of investment-grade bonds. The equity was reportedly offered at an approximately 11% discount, and shares fell 8.76%. The S&P 500 reversed an intraday gain of about 1% to close down 0.51%. Technology lost 2.95%, while flows favored Consumer Discretionary, Financials and Materials. $NVDA also reversed higher trading to finish down 1.26%.

Raising debt and equity together makes expansion costs more visible: bonds add interest and repayment obligations, while new shares dilute existing holders. That does not establish disappearing AI demand, but investors must reassess how much capital incremental revenue requires and how quickly it returns cash. The consequences can extend across GPUs, compute lessors, optics and power equipment.

Stronger borrowers such as $MSFT and $GOOGL may gain relative appeal, although their own free cash flow and capex still require scrutiny; neither should automatically be treated as entirely internally funded. $GS, $MS and $JPM have underwriting opportunities, while $RSP, $XLY and $XLF offer ways to track rotation. Deutsche Bank’s same-day upgrade of Tech to overweight highlights emerging valuation disagreement, requiring confirmation from earnings and flows.

A large order still raises the question: how much cash must be committed before it pays? Watch Oracle’s new-issue concession, financing terms elsewhere and this week’s AI earnings. Rising funding costs become more consequential if they produce project delays or order revisions. Successful financing and improving cash recovery would provide a firmer foundation for a technology rebound.

RHAPSODY OF REALITIES DAILY DEVOTIONAL 

PASTOR CHRIS OYAKHILOME

WEDNESDAY 4TH, NOVEMBER 2026

THE SINLESS SUBSTITUTE

For It Is Not Possible That The Blood Of Bulls And Of Goats Should Take Away Sins (Hebrews 10:4 KJV).

     The Bible lets us know that due to Adam's transgression, every man born into this world was born into sin. It says by one man’s disobedience, referring to Adam, many were made sinners (Romans 5:19). And there was no permanent salvation from sin until Jesus Christ. 

     To provide permanent salvation, the sacrifice for sin had to be sinless. But there was none. No man qualified. This is why the blood of animals could never save mankind. The sacrifices offered under the Law had to be repeated continually because, as the Bible says, “it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” 

     An animal is a lower order of being. How then could the blood of a lower being take away the sins of man or purify the human soul? It couldn't. A sinless man had to take our place. That's why the Lord Jesus came into the world. He had to be born of a virgin so His life wouldn't be touched by sinful man. Every human life comes from the seed of a man, but the life of the Lord Jesus came from the Word of God. 

     The angel came to Mary with God's message, declaring that she would bear a Son who would save His people from their sins. Mary received that Word, and she conceived. The Word of God is seed, and from that incorruptible seed the Lord Jesus was born. 

     John opens his Gospel with these remarkable words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). This same Word by which God created all things became flesh and dwelt among us. He was the living Word manifested in human form. 

     Untainted by Adam's fallen nature, He alone qualified to become the perfect sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. Blessed be God! Jesus became the sinless substitute who took your place. Through His perfect sacrifice, you've received eternal life and His righteousness, and have been brought into everlasting fellowship with the Father.

          PRAYER

Dear Father, Thank You For Your Wonderful Plan Of Redemption. Thank You For Sending Jesus, The Living Word Made Flesh, To Become The Perfect And Sinless Sacrifice For Our Salvation. I Rejoice That Through His Finished Work, I’ve Received Righteousness, And Eternal Life, And I Have Been Brought Into Everlasting Fellowship With You, In Jesus' Name. Amen.

FURTHER STUDY

John 1:1 & 14 KJV 
In The Beginning Was The Word, And The Word Was With God, And The Word Was God. And The Word Was Made Flesh, And Dwelt Among Us, (And We Beheld His Glory, The Glory As Of The Only Begotten Of The Father,) Full Of Grace And Truth. 

Hebrews 9:11-14 KJV
But Christ Being Come An High Priest Of Good Things To Come, By A Greater And More Perfect Tabernacle, Not Made With Hands, That Is To Say, Not Of This Building;  Neither By The Blood Of Goats And Calves, But By His Blood He Entered In Once Into The Holy Place, Having Obtained Eternal Redemption For Us. For If The Blood Of Bulls And Of Goats, And The Ashes Of An Heifer Sprinkling The Unclean, Sanctifieth To The Purifying Of The Flesh:  How Much More Shall The Blood Of Christ, Who Through The Eternal Spirit Offered Himself Without Spot To God, Purge Your Conscience From Dead Works To Serve The Living God?

1 Peter 1:18-19 KJV
Forasmuch As Ye Know That Ye Were Not Redeemed With Corruptible Things, As Silver And Gold, From Your Vain Conversation Received By Tradition From Your Fathers; But With The Precious Blood Of Christ, As Of A Lamb Without Blemish And Without Spot:

text:
Daily meditation with Zac Poonen
04.11.2026

A New Attitude of Mind - Giving Our Maximum to the Lord

Written by :   Zac Poonen 

Many religious people are legalistic and are under the law. They think in terms of the minimum necessary in order to please God. This is why they calculate exactly how much 10% of their income comes to and then offer it reluctantly to God. In the Old Testament, this attitude finally ended up in the Israelites offering blind sheep and sick bulls as sacrifices to the Lord (Mal. 1:8).

It is possible to have an identical attitude to the New Testament commandments. A sister can think in terms of the minimum necessary in order to keep the letter of the Word that commands her to be subject to her husband; or the minimum necessary covering required for her head in the meetings - without the beauty of her hair being totally hidden! Men and women can think in terms of the minimum necessary in order to be 'spiritual' without altogether giving up everything. "What is the minimum that I have to give up of this world?" is a question that is always in the minds of such people. Such people can never be spiritual. They can only be religious.

Jesus' attitude was totally different. He never sought to discover what the minimum requirement was, to please His Father. On the contrary, He sought to find out what the maximum was, so that He could offer everything to the Father. Therefore He sought to find out the spirit behind each commandment. Thus He knew that it was not enough to merely avoid adultery in the flesh (even though that was the minimum required by the law). He understood that the spirit behind that commandment was that one should not even lust (covet) in one's heart. Likewise, He saw that anger and murder were similar. And so on. Thus, He understood the spirit behind each commandment.

An earthly bride who is deeply in love with her bridegroom never thinks of the minimum necessary to please her partner. On the contrary, she thinks of what the maximum is that she can do. This is the attitude of the bride of Christ too.

It is here that we see the distinction between the servant and the bride. Those under the law can only be servants. The employee works for wages and is therefore very calculative in his service. He measures his work by the clock. If he works overtime, he expects extra wages. One who is a son (or a wife), on the other hand, will work for any length of time - not for reward, but out of love. Herein lies the difference between religiosity and spirituality.

The attitude of mind that thinks, "What can I get out of the Lord?", leads to religiosity. On the other hand, the attitude that thinks, "What can the Lord get out of the one earthly life that I have?", will lead to true spirituality. It will then become natural for us to go the second mile when the minimum requirement is to go just one mile.

text: Every state is different when it comes to veteran benefits, and what percentage disabled veterans need to be in order to access those benefits. 22 states offer property tax discounts if you are 100% disabled from military service, Oregon is not one of them. In Oregon a veteran can get a free hunting and fishing license with a 30% rating, in California it’s a 50% rating to get that. When I lived in Illinois I was told to just keep a document showing my rating with me at all times when I fish and it’s free, that felt really weird. text:
The election result in Washington kills off the last comfortable lie Whitehall has clung to: that Britain can indefinitely outsource European deterrence to an erratic American superpower while treating our own armed forces as an optional domestic savings account.

When Donald Trump walked back into the Oval Office promising a negotiated settlement within twenty-four hours, the establishment genuinely believed his transactional bluster could bypass the bloody reality of Russian revanchism. Twenty months later, that illusion is dead. You cannot real-estate-deal your way out of an existential war of conquest, and the front lines in the Donbas didn’t freeze just because Mar-a-Lago demanded a photo-op. What Trump’s return did do, however, was brutally expose the sheer cowardice of Western Europe’s political class. For nearly two years, he held a mirror up to NATO: demanding Europe fund its own backyard instead of freeriding on American taxpayers. Instead of treating that as a wake-up call to urgently rebuild sovereign industrial capacity, Burnham and the European uniparty spent twenty months doing what they do best—holding summits, drafting hand-wringing communiqués, and shuffling Treasury spreadsheets to hit an arbitrary 2.5% target that largely exists on paper.

Now the midterms have delivered a split Washington, and anyone who thinks Democratic control of Congress magically rescues Kyiv’s logistical pipeline hasn’t been paying attention to how Capitol Hill works.

Over the next two years, Ukraine will be trapped in the crossfire of American institutional civil war. Yes, a Democratic House and Senate will enthusiastically pass monster supplemental aid packages, but Trump still sits as Commander-in-Chief. He controls Presidential Drawdown Authority, Pentagon delivery schedules, targeting clearances, and intelligence-sharing protocols. Every arms package will be tied up in legislative extortion, with Democrats demanding unconditional shipments and the White House slow-walking deliveries or withholding advanced systems as leverage for leverage's sake. The American arms spigot isn't turning off, but it will be erratic, volatile, and held hostage to 2028 presidential posturing.

For those of us who believe in both Ukrainian national sovereignty and serious British national renewal, the forecast for the next two years is brutally simple: Europe has run out of runway.

Ukraine’s survival and our own eastern flank cannot be conditioned on the mood swings of swing voters in Pennsylvania or the whims of an administrative state at war with its own president. If we believe a sovereign nation has the right to defend its borders against foreign invasion—the most fundamental principle of any serious patriotic foreign policy—then Britain has to stop pretending press releases deter artillery shells. Starmer's Labour, like the Tories before them, love posing as Churchillian defenders of democracy while our domestic ammunition factories run on peacetime single shifts, the Royal Navy cannibalsises frigates for spare parts, and the British Army shrinks to a ceremonial border patrol.

Between now and the end of Trump's term, the geopolitical reality will force a complete reckoning. The uniparty model of foreign policy—loud moral posturing backed by hollowed-out hardware—is finished. If Reform is to offer a genuinely serious alternative to the establishment’s managed decline, this is the ground we have to own: true sovereignty requires unyielding self-reliance. That means ditching the Treasury bean-counters, rebuilding our domestic steel and propellant manufacturing, committing to a real, unvarnished 3% of GDP spent purely on frontline lethal capability, and ensuring British kit actually exists in stockpiles rather than Whitehall consultation papers.

Trump has washed Washington’s hands of unconditional European security guarantees.

text:
We Catholics make the Sign of the Cross
But do you know why??

The Catechism of the Catholic Church recommends the practice of sanctifying our daily life with sacramentals, chief of which is the Sign of the Cross. Many Catholics don’t know that the Sign of the Cross is a sacramental!.

When we make the Sign of the Cross before we begin any activity, we elevate whatever it is we are doing. It becomes an opportunity for drawing nearer to God.

When you sign yourself, think of all the mysteries contained in the cross. It is not enough to form it with the finger. You must first make it with faith and good will. . . . When you mark your breast, your eyes, and all your members with the sign of the cross, offer yourself as a victim pleasing to God.
           St. John Chrysostom 

This simple act of making the sign of the cross reminds us that: 

1. We have been bought and purchased by the finished work of Christ on the cross (“sign of the cross”).

2. We have been marked with the name of the Triune God in our baptisms (all Christians baptisms are in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit). 

3. We continue to look and trust in Christ at all times and situations. 

4. We boldly and unashamedly declare to the world that we are Christ-followers.  

When is it appropriate to make the sign of the cross? 

Anytime throughout the day, you feel led to or whenever you desire to be reminded of God’s presence with you and your reliance upon Him. You may do it before an especially important meeting, when you are being tempted by sin, as you drive, when you pray, before and/or after meals, and when you wake up and when you go to bed.   

During the worship service, it is especially appropriate to cross oneself at:

(1) the beginning of the service during the Invocation (in the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit), 

(2) after the Declaration of Grace; 

(3) during the Creed when we declare our belief in the resurrection (“Resurrection of the body”),

(4) After receiving the Holy Eucharist,

(5) Upon receiving the closing benediction when the Priest makes the sign of the cross upon the congregation.  

May the Lord’s grace and peace be upon us all every day. Amen

In the name of the Father, and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.  Amen

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it "unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 billion?

🧐 The 2026 midterm results are exposing the limits of partisan gerrymandering as an electoral strategy. Across the country, Democrats have secured significant victories in congressional districts whose boundaries were deliberately redrawn to give Republicans a structural advantage.

The mid-decade redistricting campaign, particularly in states carried by Donald Trump in 2024, was intended to translate Republican advantages in state-level mapmaking into additional congressional seats and help protect the party's grip on the House. Yet the results have not delivered the gains Republicans were counting on. In several districts, Democratic candidates have overcome boundaries designed to make their path to victory considerably more difficult.

My home state of Florida offers a particularly striking illustration. Governor Ron DeSantis and the Republican-controlled legislature pursued a new congressional map intended to strengthen the party's position by creating additional Republican-favourable districts. Yet Democrats won three of the four targeted seats. The results are especially significant because Trump had carried these districts in 2024, demonstrating that previous presidential voting patterns did not necessarily translate into Republican support in the midterms.

The underlying assumption was that carefully engineered electoral maps could provide a durable political advantage. But district boundaries cannot guarantee voter loyalty, compensate for declining support or neutralize a broader shift in the political environment. Nor can they fully contain an electorate whose priorities and voting behaviour have changed.

This does not mean gerrymandering has lost its influence. It means its effectiveness has limits. Republicans sought to reshape the electoral playing field through geography, only to discover that they could not control the voters themselves.

The broader takeaway is that redistricting can influence the distribution of political power, but it cannot manufacture a mandate. When voters move decisively in the opposite direction, even carefully constructed electoral advantages can begin to unravel.

text:
Statement on the Phoenix City Council District 8 Race
and the Cause of Conservatism:

The first numbers are in, and they are what they are.

Of the 24,401 early ballots so far tabulated in District 8, the incumbent holds 18,185, Mr. Abasciano 4,126, and the Rev. Jarrett Barton Maupin, Jr. 2,090. Those figures are real. They are also incomplete. They record the early vote only. They do not yet include the full complement of Election Day in-person ballots, nor the late-turned mail and drop-box ballots that Arizona law permits to arrive on Election Day itself and that must still be
verified and counted. 

The early snapshot is the early snapshot. It is not the vote.

We do not pretend the present arithmetic is flattering. Nor do we pretend that an unfinished count is a finished verdict. South Phoenix has spent years watching taxes rise, utility rates climb, and services lag while the same voices insist the status quo is progress. 

Maupin has placed a different premise on the ballot: that the community does not require another steward of higher levies and slower growth, but a Level I trauma center, a homeownership fund that converts tenants into owners, and relief from the burdens that fall hardest on working households. 

Those are not racial propositions. 

They are conservative ones, offered to voters long told that such propositions are unavailable to them.

The cause of conservatism, in this campaign and in the larger moment it reflects, is the refusal to treat race as a permanent political destination. For generations the progressive order has insisted that certain communities must remain inside fixed silos. Across the country, and inside racial categories once treated as electoral monoliths, measurable shares of Black and Latino voters have begun to detach from that coalition on the practical issues of crime, schools, housing costs, and the size of the public claim on private earnings. That detachment is not a betrayal of identity. It is the ordinary exercise of judgment by people who have concluded that the silo no longer delivers the goods it promised. 

Maupin’s candidacy is one local instance of that reconsideration: a Black and Latino minister and civil-rights figure standing against the assumption that his
community’s interests are permanently aligned with higher levies and administrative expansion.

Conservatism does not demand that voters abandon their history. It simply declines to let history be invoked as a veto on arithmetic, on public order, and on the right to own what one has earned. 

In District 8 the unfinished count will eventually
settle the immediate contest. 

The deeper contest, over whether racial silos remain the organizing principle of urban politics or whether they yield to a politics of results, will continue regardless.

It sets itself against the silo with une résistance inébranlable and proclaims an end to the leftist reign of
benign disdain.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Chris, perhaps you should understand how the oil industry works before declaring this bad news for Canada.

Valero is acquiring an existing Houston refinery, not discovering new American oil reserves or eliminating demand for Canadian crude.

American refineries are among the largest buyers of Canadian oil, particularly heavy crude from Alberta’s oil sands. Canadian Western Canadian Select often trades at a discount to WTI, making it attractive to refineries equipped to process it.

Valero initially plans to restart light, sweet crude processing, but the facility also offers potential future expansion into heavy, sour crude processing. That could actually create additional demand for Canadian oil.

And here’s the part you seem to have missed: Canada supplies roughly 60% of U.S. crude oil imports. American energy security and Canadian oil production are deeply interconnected.

So explain something, Chris. How exactly does an American company purchasing an existing refinery constitute bad news for Canada?

You’ve provided absolutely no evidence to support that conclusion. You’ve simply taken an American business announcement and turned it into another anti-Canadian talking point.

A refinery acquisition isn’t an oil discovery, Chris. Understanding the difference would be a good place to start.

text:
This is for anyone building automation and AI agents for cold email or outbound outreach.

Most people are still targeting local service businesses that live on Instagram and Facebook. The bigger money is in professionals who are active on LinkedIn, selling high-ticket services to clients with real purchasing power and already understand the value of systems.

Here are the niches worth prioritizing

1. Cosmetic / Plastic Surgeons & Med Spas

They sell elective procedures to affluent clients. Focus on Miami, Los Angeles, New York, and Dallas (plus London, Dubai, and Sydney). Their biggest leak is slow follow-up (most lose the majority of paid leads because coordinators respond too late) and high no-show rates on consultations. One agent can watch new form submissions and missed calls, enrich the contact, and send a personalized reply within minutes while logging everything into the practice management system. Another can run inside the CRM to qualify procedure interest and budget before the patient coordinator ever sees the lead, then automatically offer available consultation slots. A third agent tracks show rates and re-engages no-shows or stalled inquiries with relevant before-and-after context so the practice stops losing high-intent patients to slow human follow-up.

2. Luxury Real Estate Agents & Brokers

They sell multi-million-dollar properties to high-net-worth buyers. Strong markets include Miami, Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco (plus London, Dubai, and Sydney). They waste time on tire-kickers and lose deals from slow response. You can build an agent that monitors listing inquiries and portal leads, pulls property preferences and financial signals, then responds with matching inventory while updating the CRM. Another sits in the CRM to continue the conversation, ask qualifying questions about timeline and budget, and only book showings once the prospect clears basic filters. One agent I have seen any realtors ask about is one that watches their calendar, sends property-specific reminders, flags no-shows immediately, and re-engages cold leads with new inventory so they only spend time on serious buyers.

3. Cosmetic Dentists & High-end Orthodontists

They sell smile makeovers, veneers, and elective work to professionals who pay out-of-pocket. Target Los Angeles, Miami, New York, and Dallas (plus London, Dubai, and Melbourne). Most practices miss 30–50% of new-patient calls and convert less than half of the ones they answer. For instance, what happens if they have an agent that can answer or text back missed calls instantly, capture the reason for the visit, and offer booking options while syncing to the practice software. Another works inside the CRM or patient system to qualify insurance versus cash-pay status and treatment interest before the front desk gets involved. A third agent manages the calendar side, sending prep forms, reducing no-shows, and following up on incomplete treatment plans so the practice fills higher-value elective slots instead of chasing every inquiry.

4. High-asset Family Law / Divorce Attorneys

They handle complex, high-value cases for executives and business owners. Strong cities include New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago (plus London and Dubai). They get buried in low-quality inquiries while missing serious cases that need a fast, professional response. One agent can monitor website forms and after-hours messages, enrich the contact with public asset or business signals where available, and send a calm, professional first response that starts the qualification process. Another lives in the CRM to continue the dialogue, ask high-level questions about the situation and asset range, and only surface or book consultations for prospects who clear the firm’s thresholds. A supporting agent tracks open inquiries, re-engages those who went quiet, and keeps the attorney’s calendar protected so time is spent on high-asset matters rather than screening calls.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Rhapsody Of Realities 4 November 2026: The Sinless Substitute
For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins (Hebrews 10:4).
The Bible lets us know that due to Adam’s transgression, every man born into this world was born into sin. It says by one man’s disobedience, referring to Adam, many were made sinners (Romans 5:19). And there was no permanent salvation from sin until Jesus Christ.

To provide permanent salvation, the sacrifice for sin had to be sinless. But there was none. No man qualified. This is why the blood of animals could never save mankind. The sacrifices offered under the Law had to be repeated continually because, as the Bible says, “it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.”
An animal is a lower order of being. How then could the blood of a lower being take away the sins of man or purify the human soul? It couldn’t. A sinless man had to take our place. That’s why the Lord Jesus came into the world. He had to be born of a virgin so His life wouldn’t be touched by sinful man. Every human life comes from the seed of a man, but the life of the Lord Jesus came from the Word of God.

The angel came to Mary with God’s message, declaring that she would bear a Son who would save His people from their sins. Mary received that Word, and she conceived. The Word of God is seed, and from that incorruptible seed the Lord Jesus was born.
John opens his Gospel with these remarkable words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). This same Word by which God created all things became flesh and dwelt among us. He was the living Word manifested in human form.

Untainted by Adam’s fallen nature, He alone qualified to become the perfect sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. Blessed be God! Jesus became the sinless substitute who took your place. Through His perfect sacrifice, you’ve received eternal life and His righteousness, and have been brought into everlasting fellowship with the Father.
PRAYER

Dear Father, thank you for your wonderful plan of redemption. Thank you for sending Jesus, the living Word made flesh, to become the perfect and sinless sacrifice for our salvation. I rejoice that through His finished work, I’ve received righteousness, and eternal life, and I have been brought into everlasting fellowship with you, in Jesus’ Name. Amen.

text:
Defence at a Crossroads: Sir Tony Radakin’s Warning for Britain

As Admiral Sir Tony Radakin steps away from his role as Chief of the Defence Staff, Britain bids farewell to one of the most influential military leaders of a generation. His four years as the professional head of the Armed Forces coincided with a period of extraordinary geopolitical uncertainty, from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and escalating tensions in the Middle East to a renewed focus on NATO’s collective security responsibilities. A former First Sea Lord, Sir Tony became the first Royal Navy officer in two decades to lead the Armed Forces. Throughout his tenure, he established a reputation as a moderniser, championing greater integration with allies, accelerating the adoption of emerging technologies including artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and driving efforts to prepare the UK’s military for a more complex and contested security environment. Yet as he leaves office, Sir Tony’s final reflections offer a stark warning for ministers and defence planners alike. While welcoming the Government’s commitment to increase defence spending and its ambition to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035, he argues that pledges alone will not guarantee Britain’s security. “The promises and commitments are really welcome, but the jury remains out until percentages become pounds and pounds become capability.” ⬇️

text:
WHAT I'M WATCHING TODAY — WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 2026
Another important session for AI infrastructure, semiconductors, enterprise software and the broader economy.
$APP, $QCOM, $ARM, $COHR, $DDOG and $UBER are among the companies in focus, alongside ADP employment, ISM Services and the Treasury refunding announcement.
But I'm watching something bigger than whether companies beat earnings estimates.
Can AI demand continue driving earnings growth while inflation, financing costs and increasingly demanding valuations put pressure on investment returns?
MACRO — U.S. (ET)
🔹 8:15 AM — ADP Employment: +67K expected vs +90K previously.
🔹 8:30 AM — Trade Balance: −$107.9B expected vs −$105.6B previously.
🔹 8:30 AM — Treasury Refunding Announcement.
🔹 9:45 AM — S&P Global Services PMI: 57.9 expected vs 58.8 previously.
🔹 10:00 AM — ISM Services PMI: 54.8 expected vs 54.9 previously.
🔹 10:00 AM — ISM New Orders: 59.8 previously.
🔹 10:00 AM — ISM Employment: 50.1 previously.
🔹 10:00 AM — ISM Prices Paid: 74.0 previously.
🔹 10:30 AM — EIA Crude Oil Inventories: −1.892M barrels previously.
ADP and ISM Services are my two main macro releases.
Private-sector hiring is expected to slow from the previous reading, while services activity is expected to remain in expansion.
But I'll be paying particular attention to ISM Prices Paid.
After a previous reading of 74.0, the question is whether services price pressures are easing or remaining elevated.
Strong growth supports corporate earnings, but persistent inflation could keep Treasury yields and financing costs higher for longer.
The Treasury refunding announcement also matters because government borrowing requirements influence bond supply and the broader cost of capital.
EARNINGS — BEFORE THE BELL
🔹 Uber — Bookings, mobility demand, delivery growth and free cash flow.
🔹 Novo Nordisk — Wegovy pill momentum, obesity market share and guidance.
🔹 McDonald's — Comparable sales, consumer spending and pricing.
🔹 Circle — USDC circulation, reserve income and stablecoin adoption.
🔹 Datadog — Cloud observability, AI workloads and enterprise spending.
🔹 CVS Health — Insurance costs, pharmacy operations and profitability.
🔹 GlobalFoundries — Foundry utilisation and semiconductor demand.
🔹 Hut 8 — Power infrastructure, Bitcoin mining and AI/HPC opportunities.
EARNINGS — AFTER THE BELL
🔹 AppLovin — Advertising growth, AXON monetisation, margins and free cash flow.
🔹 Qualcomm — Smartphones, automotive, edge AI and margins.
🔹 Arm Holdings — Licensing, royalties, AI compute and data-centre exposure.
🔹 Coherent — Optical networking, AI data-centre demand and profitability.
🔹 HubSpot — Enterprise software, CRM growth and AI monetisation.
🔹 Viavi Solutions — Optical testing, networking and AI infrastructure.
🔹 SiTime — Precision timing, communications and data-centre demand.
🔹 Centrus Energy — Nuclear fuel, HALEU supply and government contracts.
🔹 American Superconductor — Grid infrastructure, power systems and backlog.
🔹 Solaris Energy Infrastructure — Power infrastructure and data-centre opportunities.
🔹 Figma — Enterprise adoption, collaboration software and monetisation.
🔹 Snap — Advertising demand, user engagement and profitability.
🔹 Albemarle — Lithium pricing, production costs and cash flow.
🔹 Lumen Technologies — Fibre infrastructure, enterprise connectivity and debt.
MY MAIN FOCUS
1. APPLOVIN — CAN THE GROWTH JUSTIFY THE VALUATION?
AppLovin remains one of the most interesting AI-driven advertising businesses.
I'll be watching advertising growth, AXON performance, adjusted EBITDA margins and free cash flow.
The operating leverage is impressive, but expectations are high.
For me, the question is whether AppLovin can sustain its growth and profitability as the business scales, particularly as competition and valuation expectations increase.
2. COHERENT + VIAVI + SITIME — AI NETWORKING AND OPTICAL INFRASTRUCTURE
As AI clusters become larger and more complex, demand for optical connectivity, testing and precision timing becomes increasingly important.
I'll be watching data-centre orders, product mix, capacity expansion, margins and guidance.
But strong demand doesn't automatically translate into attractive returns.
The real question is how much of the AI infrastructure opportunity these companies can convert into profitable revenue and sustainable cash flow.
3. ARM + QUALCOMM — THE NEXT PHASE OF COMPUTE
Arm and Qualcomm provide different perspectives on the semiconductor market.
Arm's licensing and royalty economics offer exposure to expanding compute architectures, while Qualcomm's diversification beyond smartphones remains central to its investment case.
I'll be watching data-centre adoption, edge AI, automotive demand and the quality of revenue growth.
For both companies, the opportunity is significant, but execution and monetisation matter more than the AI narrative alone.
4. DATADOG + HUBSPOT + FIGMA — ENTERPRISE AI MONETISATION
Enterprise software companies are increasingly embedding AI into their products.
But adoption alone isn't enough.
I want to see whether AI features are generating incremental revenue, improving customer retention and supporting operating margins.
There's a difference between customers experimenting with AI and businesses being willing to pay more for it.
That distinction will become increasingly important as enterprise AI spending matures.
5. CIRCLE — STABLECOIN ECONOMICS
Circle provides an interesting test of whether growing stablecoin adoption can translate into sustainable shareholder returns.
I'll be watching USDC circulation, reserve income, distribution costs and the sensitivity of profitability to interest rates.
More USDC in circulation is encouraging, but the economics depend on how much revenue Circle retains and what happens to yields.
6. CENTRUS + AMSC + SOLARIS + HUT 8 — POWER INFRASTRUCTURE
AI infrastructure is creating opportunities across nuclear fuel, grid equipment, power generation and data-centre development.
But these businesses have very different economics.
I'll be watching contracted demand, capital requirements, project execution and the path from investment to cash generation.
Power availability is becoming a competitive advantage in AI infrastructure.
The question is which companies can turn that advantage into durable earnings without taking excessive financial risk.
MY TAKE
Today's earnings provide another opportunity to test the AI investment thesis across several layers of the ecosystem.
Arm and Qualcomm represent compute.
Coherent, Viavi and SiTime represent connectivity and networking infrastructure.
Datadog, HubSpot and AppLovin represent software and monetisation.
Centrus, American Superconductor and Solaris represent the power infrastructure needed to support the buildout.
Capital → Power → Compute → Networking → Utilisation → Revenue → Free Cash Flow → Returns
I remain bullish on the long-term AI opportunity, but I'm becoming increasingly focused on the quality of growth.
AI demand can remain strong while individual companies struggle to generate attractive returns.
That's why I'm paying as much attention to margins, cash flow, financing costs and guidance as I am to headline revenue growth.
The opportunity is real. The returns still need to be earned.

text:
What’s next for Ukraine after the US elections?

1.  The lame-duck Congress matters. Trump and Republicans retain control until January 3. The December 11 funding deadline creates an opportunity to shape FY2027 spending, and a major new Ukraine appropriation remains unlikely.

2. Peace negotiations are entering a critical period. President Zelenskyy may feel emboldened by the Democratic sweep, but Trump still controls US diplomacy and key weapons deliveries.  Trump can be constrained on sanctions and returning blocked assets; he cannot be forced to offer security guarantees or military assistance, except by horse trading.  Democratic leaders will have more ability to horse trade in appropriations etc if Ukraine has friendly relations with the White House. Congress can weigh in on security guarantees and a treaty would be approved by the senate.  

3. Divided government changes the equation, but not necessarily in Ukraine’s favor. Democrats can increase oversight and pressure, but they cannot simply force Trump to provide additional military assistance or deliver weapons.  

4. The political clock is ticking. By late 2027, Washington will be consumed by the 2028 presidential campaign. Ukraine cannot assume American attention will increase.

My recommendations for Ukraine:

1.  First, don’t spike the football.  This election was not about Ukraine; they shouldn’t pretend it was. Trump has two months with a Republican Congress. Lame-duck presidents can wield considerable influence, particularly when outgoing legislators are seeking appointments, jobs, or final legislative victories. Personal grievances and political favors can matter enormously during this period.

2. Second, stay out of American partisan politics. Ukraine needs a bipartisan coalition in Congress, united around a concrete agenda for military assistance, reconstruction, sanctions, and peace. Democratic support alone is not enough. Do not send out the Vindman type surrogates who will be tempted to make it look like Ukraine is celebrating the election or calling for investigations, etc.  

3.  Build bipartisan support for security guarantees now. Security Guarantees and rebuilding are an opportunity for consensus.  A formal US security treaty would require the consent of two-thirds of the Senate.  Washington loves rebuilding and they love to project power and the shining city on the hill.  Building consensus here for maximum support should be low hanging fruit.   

4. 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗱𝗼𝗿.

Ukraine may do well to look outside politics for an accomplished founder or CEO with gravitas, strong ties to Ukraine’s business community, and a deep understanding of the country’s reconstruction needs. Someone who can speak credibly for Ukrainian businesses, attract American investment, and make deals in Washington.  

The bottom line: Trump’s electoral defeat doesn’t mean Ukraine’s strategic position has improved. The next eight weeks may shape Ukraine’s prospects for the next two years. Kyiv needs to navigate them carefully.
