•Nature & Grace & Faith & Soteriology 
•What God’s Universal Salvific Will Compels
•Election & Predestination 

Divine election and predestination in Patristic and Catholic thought affirms God’s eternal plan to save while generally preserving both the gratuity of grace and real human free response. It rejects both Pelagian self-sufficiency and any positive divine predestination to damnation.

Patristic Orientations:

Pre-Augustinian and especially Eastern Fathers typically treated election as unconditionally Gifted to all then layered with foreknowledge and free human response. They stressed Grace-Funded free will, human responsibility, and God’s Concrete provision for the salvation of all. This was the dominant trajectory, especially after the Cappadocians and in the Damascene synthesis, though it was not perfectly uniform—Origen, for example, is more complex.

Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Clement, and others emphasized free choice and moral accountability. God knows who will believe or refuse, but the decisive reason for reprobation lies in human dispositions rather than an arbitrary divine decree. 

John Chrysostom and other Greeks linked predestination to foreseen perseverance in virtue or faith as Election is in part layered with bare / exhaustive foreknowledge of free acts.

John of Damascus, a major synthesis of Eastern tradition, states the classic position: “While God knows all things beforehand, yet He does not predetermine all things. For He knows beforehand those things that are in our power, but He does not predetermine them. For it is not His will that there should be wickedness nor does He choose to compel virtue.” 

Predetermination concerns what is not in free human power; free acts are foreknown but not predetermined. He also distinguishes God’s antecedent will (that all be saved) from His consequent will (which takes account of free human response).

Augustine against Pelagius insisted that the beginning of faith, the good will, and perseverance are gifts of grace, not the fruit of unaided free choice. Predestination of the elect to glory is therefore gratuitous (ante praevisa merita), grounded in God’s free mercy rather than foreseen human merit. On reprobation he tended toward a more passive or “negative” account (God permits some to remain in the massa damnata), though some of his later language is stronger than pure permission, and later interpreters have long disagreed on how far he went toward positive predestination to damnation. Pre-Augustinian consensus was more consistently synergistic and conditional; 

The Second Council of Orange (529) was confirmed by Rome and represents a moderate or “semi-Augustinian” settlement. It firmly establishes the absolute priority of grace against Pelagianism while deliberately stopping short of Augustine’s later particularist views on election and predestination.

The whole person is damaged by original sin; free will is weakened and bent. Grace must precede every saving response. Even the beginning of faith, the desire for baptism, the good will, and any truly good act come from God’s prevenient grace, not from unaided nature (Canons 3–8, 25, and the concluding statement). Free will is restored sufficiently. The council explicitly rejects predestination to evil: “We not only do not believe that any are foreordained to evil by the power of God, but even state with utter abhorrence that if there are those who want to believe so evil a thing, they are anathema.”

It makes no positive statement about an eternal, unconditional election of a fixed number of individuals to glory ante praevisa merita. It does not teach that grace is irresistible or that only the predestined receive efficacious grace while others are passed over by a sovereign decree. It leaves the question of whether (and how) grace can be resisted unaddressed in any particularist direction. 

What the Priority of Grace Does and Does Not Entail

Grace precedes every saving movement of the will (the beginning of faith, the desire for baptism, the good will, any truly good act). No such movement arises from unaided nature. 

To say that grace must precede is not the same as saying that this preceding grace infallibly guides the will. 

To say that a saving response is not from unaided nature is not the same as saying that the will is infallibly guided so that free refusal is impossible.

The canons (especially 3–8 and 25) and the concluding statement establish priority and necessity. They do not establish infallible efficacy. It is the language of real enablement and real responsibility, not of a grace that always succeeds. Later Catholic theology (Trent and the post-Trent debates) has read Orange precisely this way: 

sufficient/prevenient grace is truly necessary and truly enabling; it is not, by that fact alone, infallibly efficacious. The difference between “not unaided” and “infallibly guided” is preserved.

Catholic teaching incorporates Augustinian emphases on the necessity and gratuity of grace while retaining the broader Patristic insistence on free will, universal salvific will, and the absence of positive predestination to hell.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church states that when God “establishes his eternal plan of ‘predestination,’ he includes in it each person’s free response to his grace” (CCC 600), and that “God predestines no one to go to hell; for this, a willful turning away from God (a mortal sin) is necessary, and persistence in it until the end” (CCC 1037), citing Orange and Trent. 

The Council of Trent, Session VI, teaches that free will, moved and awakened by God, cooperates by assenting and is not merely passive (Canon 4). No one may claim certain knowledge of being among the predestined without special revelation (Canon 15). The grace of justification is not restricted solely to those predestined to life while others are predestined to evil (Canon 17). Justification is a free gift that nevertheless involves free human cooperation; merits are real but themselves the fruit of grace.

God truly and sincerely wills the salvation of all (1 Tim 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9). Christ died for all. Sufficient grace is offered such that salvation is a real possibility for every person. There is no positive reprobation (no decree that anyone shall sin or be damned independently of free refusal). Damnation is the consequence of free, persistent rejection of grace.

To accurately map the boundaries of the permitted theological schools, Catholic theology draws a sharp distinction between predestination to initial grace and predestination to glory. All orthodox schools agree that predestination to initial grace—such as the first prevenient movement of the will toward God—is granted strictly ante praevisa merita (prior to any foreseen merits) as a pure, unearned gift. The theological fracture occurs entirely over predestination to final glory. Within Catholicism two schools are permitted, neither defined as the exclusive Catholic position, and as we will see shortly, both schools are restrained by the wider catechism. The Báñezian account holds that predestination is ante praevisa merita. Efficacious grace operates by physical premotion that infallibly yet freely elicits the will’s consent. Merely sufficient grace confers real power but does not infallibly obtain the act. The gratuity of final perseverance is strongly emphasized. The Molinist account holds that God has middle knowledge of free counterfactual responses. He elects those whom He foresees will freely cooperate under the graces He chooses to distribute. Grace is rendered efficacious by free consent; the distinction between sufficient and efficacious grace is more on the side of the free response under God’s infallible foreknowledge.

The theological boundaries defining these permitted schools were formally codified following the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1598–1607), a fiercely contested debate over the mechanics of grace and free will. Recognizing the limits of theological certainty, Pope Paul V formally concluded the dispute by allowing both the Thomist and Molinist schools to operate freely, strictly forbidding either side from condemning the other as heretical, and concluded that subtle nuances left both as nonequivalent to Calvinism’s approach. This papal decree established the enduring dual-school framework. 

Further, neither of the two schools are permitted to reach too far because, crucially, the wider Arc of Christendom and the wider Magisterium comport and therefore place a non-negotiable guardrail around how both schools define God’s universal provision: 

Catholic teaching strictly forbids rendering “sufficient grace” as a practically sterile concept. If sufficient grace were modeled as a theological fiction—one that grants a theoretical capacity but never actually results in conversion without a selectively withheld “infallible push”—it would reduce the Universal Salvific Will to an ontological fiction and an insincere gesture. Because predestination to evil is condemned as heresy, Catholic theology precludes any scenario where God provides grace that is fundamentally insufficient for actual conversion. The sufficient grace offered to all humanity must carry a real, actionable potency for actual conversion, strictly excluding the selective withholding of genuine saving means. This ensures God’s universal offer remains authentically viable, guaranteeing that any failure to convert rests exclusively on the human will’s active resistance, never on a structural deficit in God’s saving provision.

In both accounts, grace is prior and necessary, free will is real and cooperative, and there is no positive predestination to damnation. Heaven is primarily the work of God’s grace as He is the Sole Bank and provides all requisite funding.

Patristic thought and Catholic magisterial teaching converge on free will, the universal salvific will, and the rejection of positive reprobation. Catholic teaching more fully incorporates Augustine’s insistence on the absolute priority of grace (via Orange and Trent) than the earlier Fathers did, while remaining far from later Calvinist double predestination or irresistible grace. The enduring Catholic framework is that God’s eternal plan of predestination includes, rather than overrides, each person’s free response to grace.

The Limits of Orange:

Orange secures the necessity and priority of grace and rejects positive reprobation. It does not define, require, or affirm the doctrine of unconditional particular election that later appears in high Augustinianism and Calvinism. Some later medieval Augustinians (and, of course, the Reformed) have read certain of Augustine’s texts as supporting such a doctrine, but that reading is not demanded by Orange itself or by later Catholic magisterial teaching. Patristic thought and Catholic theology have consistently housed structures that have converged into the reading of Orange it that fashion: the gratuity of grace is required; a particularist decree that determines final destiny independently of free response is not.

It does not define or affirm a doctrine irresistible Grace nor of unconditional particular election. Any use of Orange that treats the council as settling the question of resistible versus irresistible grace, or as settling the question of unconditional election, moves beyond what the text itself states. The council remains limited to the priority of grace and the rejection of predestination to evil.

Concluding Part 1 of 2:

Transitioning from the scholastic frameworks of the De Auxiliis era to the modern Magisterium, the Arc of Christendom’s 1st 1600 years continues to Travel. 

For example in Protestantism it is less than 20% ((approximately 13%)) of Protestants that deploy Monergistic Determinism in the map of Conversion. ((screenshot)). 

Similarly, in Catholicism Pope Benedict XVI’s three encyclicals—Deus Caritas Est, Spe Salvi, and Caritas in Veritate—reframe the historic guardrails described earlier through a relational and Christological lens rather than the metaphysical mechanics of grace. By identifying God’s antecedent motive strictly as a self-communicating agape that inherently seeks all of humanity, Benedict affirms that God universally funds the real, actionable means for conversion. This vision solidifies the rejection of "sterile grace" while maintaining the strict boundary against universalism; as Spe Salvi notes, definitive, willful self-exclusion from this love remains a tragic possibility for those who irrevocably destroy their desire for truth. 

Formally these “encyclicals” transcend permitted theological speculation and formally require the "religious submission of intellect and will" (obsequium religiosum). Therefore, while the precise mechanics of predestination remain open to Thomist and Molinist debate, the underlying reality—that God’s genuine love guarantees viable, universally offered saving grace for every human person—stands as a binding, authoritative doctrine that conclusively precludes any theology of selective withholding.

Concluding Part 2 of 2:

33 Key Voices Across The First 1,600 yrs of Christendom whose theological metaphysics opposed Westminster’s Guaranteed Fall of “Not By Bare Permission” 
→
1. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) — Angels and men created free. Foreknowledge is not causal determination.
2. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) — No coercion with God. Man is cause to himself of becoming wheat or chaff.
3. Tertullian (c. 155–220) — Adam willed the sin he committed. The Fall is not a necessity God imposed.
4. Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215) — Virtue and vice require real choice. Fate does not author the first sin.
5. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) — Autexousion against Valentinian determinism. God does not create anyone wicked.
6. Methodius of Olympus (d. c. 311) — God is not the author of evil. Evil begins in a will that could have kept the command.
7. Archelaus (c. 320) — Anti-Manichaean: devil and man fall by refusing the commandment, not by nature or fate.
8. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — Creatures are mutable by nature, not predetermined to sin. Defilement is from turning, not from God’s making.
9. Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) — The soul is inherently autexousios (self-governed) as the image of its Creator. Humans do not sin by necessity, cosmic fate, or biological drive, but entirely by the exercise of real-time choice.
10. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — God’s eternal foreknowledge neither restricts nor compels the human will; human nature “fell ill” in Adam with mortality, but individual destiny is determined by real-time choice, not an arbitrary divine blueprint.
11. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) — Evil is a voluntary choice. It originates entirely inside the creature’s defect.
12. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) — Image of God includes being without a master. Ruin and return hang on deliberate choice.
13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
→ 
A Few More 
→ 
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.

13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
→ 
A Few More 
→ 
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.

text:
WE DESERVED THAT

Republicans lost because we stopped being Republicans. We abandoned our principles. We became Trump's bitch. And whatever he said, no matter how preposterous or unconstitutional, no matter how contrary to truths we've stood for for generations, we acquiesced to.

We became a party of thugs and suck-ups. If you were close to Trump, you became a thug, trashing and destroying other Republicans who weren't Trump enough. If you weren't close to Trump, you became a suck-up, fawning before his name and whim.

The party became a cult, an obsequious and groveling embarrassment to the party's heritage and beliefs. We sold our soul, and it showed.

We broke our pact with the people and violated our oath to the Constitution. And so we suffered one of the worst political beat downs of the last 100 years.

And we deserved it.

And so did he. Donald Trump. He deserved it. He acted like a king and the people rose up against him. 

That means Ukraine has a chance to survive, and so does NATO, and the Kennedy Center, and maybe we can be friends with Canada again. Vladimir Putin takes a hit, like Elon Musk, and so does the cabal of Trump and cabinet business connections who have whored out federal policy for personal profit.

The Supreme Court may be ripped apart, and it seems unlikely any federal judge nominees will be confirmed from this Republican president or the next. 

And the Republican Party is sidelined in national politics. As it ought to be.  Its recent conduct has demonstrated that it offers nothing of substance or principle.

And now the vultures will fight over the bones, the grifters trying to milk the party and its most ardent supporters for the last bit of cash, or maybe a spot on Fox or a podcast. 

While those of us who are actually Republicans, the ones who have been pushed out of the party, will try to remind people of what we once stood for, and why those principles are still the best protectors of individual liberty and national interest.

But for now we reap the whirlwind. 

Democrats will wield their mandate like a sword, dismembering anything that doesn't jibe with their world view. They will have their day in the sun, and time will tell how wisely they use it. Will they moderate, or will they be extreme? Will they keep the keys to the car, or will they lose them themselves in another two years?

There will be change, in a direction few Republicans will like. And there will be impeachments, and maybe there should be impeachments.

And maybe we Republicans should spend some time re-embracing principle and patriotism, and laying aside personality and party. Maybe we should try to remember who we are.

Maybe we should go back to being Republicans again.

Rev War Tales
Virtue as Well as Valor
4 November 1775, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Samuel Adams writes to James Warren in Massachusetts. The letter emphasizes that virtue, not armies alone, will preserve liberty. Adams, a delegate to the Continental Congress, tells Warren that the eyes of mankind are on the new government of Massachusetts. “We may look up to Armies for our Defence,” he writes, “but Virtue is our best Security.” He then offers the lines that have often been quoted: “For no People will tamely surrender their Liberties, nor can any be easily subdued, when Knowledge is diffusd and Virtue is preservd. On the Contrary, when People are universally ignorant, and debauchd in their Manners, they will sink under their own Weight without the Aid of foreign Invaders.” He urges that the principles of virtue be taught early, even to children, and that the ancestral institutions for that purpose be encouraged by the government. Warren was then active in the Provincial Congress at home.  #RevWar #History #AmRev #RevWarTales

text:
China's pause on its gallium export ban against the United States is set to lapse November 27, and the part that matters most to the Pentagon was never paused. The prohibition on supplying U.S. military end users stayed in force throughout the truce.

In many defense applications, neither gallium arsenide nor gallium nitride has an effective substitute.

Beijing has used that position in stages. It imposed export controls in August 2023, banned gallium exports to the United States in December 2024, and suspended that ban for one year in November 2025, which leaves the restriction available whenever China wants it back.

Allied supply offers less cover than the import data suggests. Canada, Japan and Germany provided about two-thirds of U.S. gallium imports from 2021 to 2024, but much of that metal is recycled from scrap that ultimately relies on Chinese feedstock, so a tighter Chinese grip would reach those suppliers too.

Washington's response has moved from grants to ownership. The Department of War took a $400 million equity stake in Atalco's Gramercy, Louisiana refinery, the last alumina refinery in the country, which targets about 55 tons of gallium a year, and committed $174 million toward a gallium plant at Alcoa's Wagerup refinery in Western Australia alongside Australia and Japan.

Both projects build capacity measured in years, while the deadline is measured in weeks. The open question is whether those stakes buy the United States supply or only time.

text:
The writing is on the wall with Quinn Hughes, and Minnesota fans don't want to acknowledge it.

1. He wants to play with his brothers. This isn't some fantasy Devils fans invented. Jack, Luke, and Quinn have all acknowledged the desire to play together. New Jersey already has two of the three.

2. The timing couldn't be better. Quinn becomes a UFA in July 2027. Jack is signed through 2030, and Luke through 2032. This is the perfect opportunity to unite all three without waiting years and hoping their contracts align again.

3. Minnesota has had months to extend him. He's been eligible since July 1, and Bill Guerin recently admitted he hasn't even spoken with Quinn's representatives in a long time. For a franchise player you're supposedly certain is staying, that's not exactly reassuring.

4. New Jersey can afford him. With the cap increasing to $113.5M, moving contracts like Dougie Hamilton's $9M and Connor Brown's $3M creates a realistic path to offering Quinn around $20M annually while maintaining a competitive roster.

5. The Brock Faber argument is ridiculous. Nobody denies Faber is an excellent defenseman. But you're seriously arguing Quinn would abandon the opportunity to play alongside both brothers because Brett Pesce isn't Brock Faber? Quinn is a Norris Trophy winner. He doesn't need Faber to be elite.

6. New Jersey isn't asking him to sacrifice winning for family. Jack Hughes, Nico Hischier, Jesper Bratt, Timo Meier, Arseny Gristyuk, Luke Hughes, and Quinn Hughes would form an incredibly talented foundation. He'd be joining a team with legitimate Stanley Cup aspirations, not abandoning his career for a family reunion.

And here's the biggest point: Signing a seven-year extension in Minnesota could mean spending the rest of his prime without ever sharing an NHL locker room with both brothers.

He has the opportunity to get paid superstar money, compete for a Stanley Cup, and play alongside his two brothers in the same organization.

Minnesota can offer him money, Brock Faber, and a competitive team.

New Jersey can offer him all of that, plus something Minnesota simply cannot replicate.

The question isn't why Quinn Hughes would leave Minnesota. It's why he'd pass up this particular opportunity to join New Jersey.

text:
The 31st Alabama Infantry Flag: “God and Our Native Land” Beneath the Smoke of the Western Theater

Some Civil War battle flags became famous because they flew over massive armies. Others became unforgettable because of the message stitched directly into the cloth itself.

The battle flag of the 31st Alabama Infantry Regiment belongs to that second story.

At first glance, the design immediately stands apart from most Confederate regimental colors of the American Civil War. Instead of the familiar square battle flag associated with the Army of Northern Virginia, the 31st Alabama carried a personalized variation of the Confederate First National Flag, often called the “Stars and Bars.”

The flag featured red-white-red horizontal stripes with a blue canton in the upper left corner. At the center of the canton stood a large white Christian cross surrounded by thirteen white stars arranged in a circular halo. Encircling the cross were the words:

“GOD AND OUR NATIVE LAND.”

Across the center white stripe appeared the unit designation in bold yellow lettering:

“THIRTY FIRST ALABAMA.”

The flag reflected something deeply personal about many Civil War regiments, especially those raised early in the war before Confederate standardization became widespread. These banners often carried the identity of the communities that created them. In the case of the 31st Alabama, the flag combined religion, state pride, and military service into a single battlefield symbol.

The regiment itself was organized in Talladega, Alabama, in March 1862. More than 1,100 men initially joined from counties including Talladega, Shelby, Cherokee, Randolph, Montgomery, and Calhoun. Like thousands of young Southern volunteers entering Confederate service in 1862, many believed the war would be short. Few could imagine the scale of destruction waiting ahead.

The flag was reportedly presented to the regiment by the women of Talladega around April 1862. Similar ceremonies occurred throughout both the Union and Confederacy during the Civil War. Communities gathered to sew flags, offer speeches, and send local men off to war beneath banners carrying the hopes of entire towns.

For the soldiers of the 31st Alabama, this flag became far more than decoration.

It marched with the regiment through Tennessee, Kentucky, Mississippi, and Georgia as the Western Theater became one of the bloodiest regions of the war.

The regiment initially served under General E.K. Smith before joining Confederate operations around Vicksburg under General Edward D. Tracy’s brigade. During the Vicksburg Campaign in 1863, the 31st Alabama fought in some of the hardest combat of its existence.

At Port Gibson in May 1863, the regiment suffered severe casualties attempting to slow Union General Ulysses S. Grant’s advance toward Vicksburg. Days later came the Battle of Champion Hill on May 16, one of the decisive engagements of the campaign.

It was there that the regiment lost its famous colors.

Private Albert G. Trussell of the 17th Iowa Infantry captured the flag during the intense fighting around Champion Hill. In Civil War combat, losing a regimental flag often meant a unit had been shattered, overrun, or forced into retreat amid close-range chaos and black powder smoke.

Yet the regiment continued fighting.

The surviving men retreated into the defenses of Vicksburg and endured the long siege until the city surrendered on July 4, 1863. After exchange and reorganization, the 31st Alabama later fought through Chattanooga, the Atlanta Campaign, Hood’s Tennessee Campaign, and finally the Carolinas Campaign before surrendering in 1865 with only a fraction of its original strength remaining.

Today, the original 31st Alabama flag survives as one of the most distinctive Confederate regimental flags preserved from the Civil War. More than cloth and stitching, it represents the faith, sacrifice, local identity, and brutal realities faced by Alabama soldiers who fought across the Western Theater from 1862 until the Confederacy’s collapse.

text:
Success in an African family comes with a punishment that no court imposes and nobody announces. It usually begins with a phone call from an auntie who has not spoken to you since your last visit home.

"Hello, my child. How are you? We thank God for you."

You relax. Then she clears her throat.

"Your cousin has been sent home from school. They need only a little money."

By the time you have finished answering the greeting, the little money has grown large enough to give your bank account high blood pressure.

Welcome to the life of the family gatekeeper.

In many African families, whoever lands a good job, builds a business or moves abroad receives a new position without applying for it. The family appoints you chief financial officer, emergency contact, career adviser and marriage counsellor, with occasional duties as official recipient of complaints against God. The appointment is permanent and comes with no medical cover and no salary review.

While you were struggling, relatives were understanding, and some even offered prayers. Once your fortunes improve, the family takes a keen interest in your finances. People who could not remember your birthday suddenly know which day of the month you are paid. Your success becomes public property.

You may have worked for twenty years, skipped holidays, endured a difficult boss and lived on tea while paying your own children's school fees. None of that enters the family's calculations. They see the car, the house, the foreign trip or the photograph taken outside an air conditioned office, and they conclude that money has become your permanent companion.

One of the most dangerous sentences in family life is "We know you can manage." It sounds like praise, but it is usually a request wearing a necktie.

A brother needs capital. An uncle needs hospital fees. A niece is joining university. Someone's rent is overdue, and another relative has found an exciting investment in poultry, fish farming or a shop whose entire business plan is "People must eat." You are expected to contribute because you are doing better than the rest. Asking questions makes you look unkind, and suggesting that the applicant prepare a budget may be taken as an attempt to introduce Western civilisation into a family meeting.

The gatekeeper is supposed to open the gate even when nothing is left behind it.

There is a spiritual side to this as well. Some people sincerely believe God blessed them so that they could lift their families out of poverty. Others see support as a cultural duty, a way of remembering those who helped them when they had nothing. These beliefs can be beautiful, and anyone who shares success with parents, siblings and struggling relatives deserves respect. Trouble starts when generosity becomes compulsory and the beneficiary begins to treat it as an entitlement.

Helping a younger brother finish college is one thing. Paying his rent at thirty five because he has never quite found himself is another. You can help a relative start a business, but you cannot finance for ever the enterprises that collapse whenever the owner is asked to wake before ten. At some point even the most generous person must ask whether the family is being helped towards independence or growing comfortable with dependence.

This is where black tax comes in. The term describes the financial pressure that many successful Black people feel when supporting extended family. No government collects it, no receipt is issued, and the Kenya Revenue Authority does not send an officer to check what you gave your cousin last Christmas. Yet the burden can be heavy. Money meant for savings, a mortgage, retirement or your children's education gets redirected to family emergencies, and the sibling who looks wealthy may be privately struggling. The family goes on regarding this person as rich even when the account balance begins to resemble a neglected borehole.

🗓️रमा एकादशी बृहस्पतिवार, नवम्बर 5, 2026

📍एकादशी तिथि प्रारम्भ  - 11:03 AM, नवम्बर 04
 ◽️ एकादशी तिथि समाप्त - 10:35 AM, नवम्बर 05

Falling beautifully in the holy Kartik month right before Diwali, Rama Ekadashi is a sacred day dedicated to the joint worship of Lord Vishnu and Goddess Lakshmi (Rama).

 It is a divine opportunity to clear deep karmic obstacles, quiet material distractions, and welcome immense peace and prosperity into home. 🌸🪔

🚩 Spiritual Significance

◽️Karmic Purification: Scriptural texts like the Brahma Vaivarta Purana state that this fast frees devotees from the sins of both past and present lives.

◽️Ultimate Liberation: The spiritual merits earned today surpass grand Vedic rituals, granting both material abundance (Aishwarya) and Moksha (liberation).

◽️Astrological Balance: Falling under a Jupiter-ruled tithi, this day calms the Moon's influence on our emotions and digestion, making a light or fasting routine highly beneficial.

📜 The Story of Faith: Shobhana & Chandrabhaga

The Puranas recount the story of Prince Shobhana, who was physically weak but attempted the strict fast out of duty. 

Though he succumbed to thirst and hunger, his external compliance earned him a celestial kingdom. However, because his fast lacked deep faith, the kingdom remained temporary and invisible. 

His wife, Princess Chandrabhaga, a lifelong devotee, transferred her accrued spiritual merits to him. 

Her pure devotion turned his invisible realm into a permanent, divine paradise, proving that sincere faith matters most to the Divine.

🪐 ASTROLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE

◽️Guru (Jupiter) represents wisdom, dharma and spiritual growth.

◽️Lakshmi Tattva symbolises abundance, harmony and prosperity.

◽️Ekadashi observance encourages mental discipline and emotional balance.

🕉️PUJA VIDHI & SACRED PRACTICES

🚩Wake up early, take a holy bath and offer prayers to Shri Hari.

🚩Offer Tulsi leaves, flowers, fruits and bhog to Lord Vishnu.

🚩Worship Maa Lakshmi with devotion and light a ghee diya.

🚩Observe Nirjala, Phalahar or Satvik vrat according to your capacity.

🚩Read or listen to Rama Ekadashi Vrat Katha.

🚩Recite Vishnu Sahasranama & perform naam japa.

🚩Donate food, clothes or essentials to those in need.

🚩Maintain purity in thoughts, speech and actions.

🚫 WHAT TO AVOID

🔻Onion, garlic and tamasic food.
🔻Anger, gossip and harsh words.
🔻Overindulgence and negative thoughts.
🔻Ego, dishonesty and unnecessary arguments.
🔻Grains, beans and pulses as per vrat tradition.

📿 SACRED MANTRAS

॥ ॐ नमो भगवते वासुदेवाय ॥

॥ ॐ श्रीं महालक्ष्म्यै नमः ॥

Ekadashi is more than fasting. It is an opportunity to purify the mind, release negativity and strengthen devotion.

☑️Replace fear with faith.
☑️Replace greed with gratitude.
☑️Replace anger with forgiveness.
☑️Replace ego with humility.

text:
A rattlesnake's tail holds a muscle that fires about 50 times every second, for hours, without tiring.

You cannot tap a finger that fast for even one second.

And that is the harmless end of the animal.

Stay with me. By the end of this post you will know how it sees heat, how it lies with sound, how it decides who gets venom and who gets a warning, and why the thing everyone fears is almost never the thing that hurts people.

Bookmark this. You will want it on your next hike.

---

1/ THE ENGINE NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Everyone knows the sound. Almost nobody asks what makes it.

Muscle biologists did. What they found inside a rattlesnake's tail has a name: the shaker muscle.

It contracts roughly 50 times per second at normal operating temperature. In warm conditions, measurements climb toward 90.

Now the part that breaks intuition. Fast muscles usually burn out. Sprint muscles run on stored fuel, scream for a few seconds, then fail. That is the trade: speed or endurance, pick one.

The shaker muscle refuses the trade.

In lab experiments it kept this pace going for hours.

How? It is packed with mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and its internal calcium handling is tuned to switch on and off at a speed most muscles cannot reach. It is built for exactly one job, and it does that job better than almost anything in your body does anything.

Think about what that means. An animal with no limbs and no real voice solved the problem of making loud noise by building one of the fastest sustained engines in the vertebrate world and bolting it to its tail.

That is the warning system. Hold on to that word, warning. It is about to get complicated.

---

2/ THE RATTLE IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK

Picture a baby rattle with beads inside. That is the picture almost everyone carries around.

It is wrong.

There are no beads. The rattle is a stack of hollow, interlocking segments made of keratin, the same protein that builds your fingernails and hair.

When the shaker muscle drives the tail, the segments slap against each other. The noise is the sound of the animal's own body clapping.

The design trick is how the stack gets built. A rattlesnake sheds its skin several times a year. When most snakes shed, the tail tip slides off with everything else. A rattlesnake's tail tip has a bulge that stops the old scale from slipping free. So the old tip stays behind. One shed, one new segment. Next shed, another.

Which gives us the most repeated myth in the American outdoors: count the rattles, know the age.

Don't.

Young snakes can shed several times a year, so segments pile up faster than years pass. And long rattles break. Wild adults often carry a damaged, shortened rattle, or none at all. A newborn has a single bump called a button, and it stays silent until a second segment arrives.

So a silent rattlesnake is not a safe rattlesnake. A big rattle is not proof of an old one. The sound is a signal, not a gauge.

---

3/ THE SOUND IS A LIE (A GOOD ONE)

In 2017, researchers published a result that changes how you hear this animal.

They recorded rattlesnakes as a threat got closer. The snakes did not simply rattle louder. They changed the pitch, jumping from a lower rattling rate into a much higher one.

Then they tested humans. People listened to rattles and were asked to judge how far away the snake was.

The result: the higher-pitched rattle made listeners believe the snake was closer than it really was.

Read that again.

The rattlesnake is not only warning you. It is manipulating your sense of distance. It rings a false alarm in your auditory system so you stop, jerk back, and give it more room than the truth required.

Researchers described it as an acoustic illusion, a trick that works because brains evolved to treat a sound that suddenly rises in pitch as something rushing toward them.

And the likely target was never humans. The leading idea is that rattles evolved to stop heavy hoofed animals, bison and similar grazers, from stepping on a snake that has no armor and no speed. A big animal that hears a sudden buzz and swerves is a snake that lives.

We just happened to wire our ears into an alarm system built for buffalo.

Respect the sound. Millions of years of survival engineered it to work on you.

---

4/ THE SQUIRREL THAT ANSWERS WITH HEAT

Here is a story that sounds invented.

The California ground squirrel is a regular menu item for rattlesnakes. So the squirrel evolved a response that borders on science fiction.

When it meets a rattlesnake, it kicks sand, faces the snake, and waves its tail high and fast. That is called tail flagging. Nothing unusual yet.

Then researchers pointed thermal cameras at it.

The tail is heating up.

Squirrels facing rattlesnakes push warm blood into the tail so it glows in infrared. And snakes see infrared. The squirrel is sending a message in a language the snake's heat sensors can read: I see you. I am healthy. I am not worth the strike.

Experiments with robotic squirrels backed it up. A fake squirrel with a heated tail made rattlesnakes retreat more than a cold one. The heat is the argument.

And it gets better. Adult squirrels carry proteins in their blood that neutralize a portion of rattlesnake venom. They also chew shed snake skin and smear the scent on their fur, wearing the predator's smell like a disguise.

So the next time someone says nature is simple, remember a rodent with a blood chemistry set, an infrared signal, and a perfume made from its enemy.

---

5/ THE SNAKE THAT HEARS WITH ITS JAW

A rattlesnake has no external ears and no eardrum. By the old textbook, it was deaf. The modern picture is more interesting.

It feels the ground. Vibrations travel through the jaw and bones into the inner ear, so it can sense footsteps long before you see it. Sound traveling through the air reaches it too, but mostly at low frequencies.

Your steps are a drumbeat to it. The heavy tread of a person in boots is loud news in the snake's world.

It is one reason rattlesnakes so often rattle early, or slip away before you notice them at all. In plenty of encounters, the snake knew about you first.

---

6/ THE SENSE YOU DO NOT HAVE

Between each nostril and eye, a rattlesnake carries a small hollow pit. Inside is a membrane thinner than tissue paper, wired with nerve endings.

Its job is to feel heat from a distance. Not touch it. Feel radiation traveling through the air.

Estimates of its sensitivity point to changes of a few thousandths of a degree Celsius. In practice, that means a snake in the dark can tell a warm mouse from the cooling ground it sits on, and tell you where a warm body ends and the night begins.

Here is the twist scientists confirmed in 2010. The molecular sensor inside the pit is a protein called TRPA1.

You have TRPA1 too. In humans, it is the receptor that fires when you eat wasabi or horseradish. The same protein that makes your sinuses burn from a green paste is the one a snake rewired into a heat sensor.

Evolution did not invent a new tool. It took an old one and changed what it was listening for.

And the brain does something stranger. Signals from the pits and from the eyes converge in the same region of the snake's brain, where individual neurons respond to both. In classic experiments, snakes with their eyes covered still struck warm moving targets with deadly accuracy.

It does not have vision plus a heat sensor. It has one merged picture. A thermal overlay on the visible world, built into the hardware.

---

7/ THE HUNT: BITE, LET GO, FOLLOW THE SMELL

This one surprised me more than the venom.

A rattlesnake hunting a rodent does not hold on. It strikes, injects, and releases immediately.

Why? Because a mouse or a ground squirrel can bite back, and even a small rodent can injure a snake's face. So the snake does the safest thing: it lets go and backs off while the venom works.

Then it goes looking for its own kill.

Scientists call it strike-induced chemosensory searching. The snake flicks its forked tongue, collects chemical particles, and delivers them to an organ in the roof of its mouth. The fork gives it two samples, one from each side, which works like a stereo nose. It can sense which way a scent trail turns and follow it to the body.

Experiments show snakes can pick out the trail of the animal they envenomated from the trails of others.

So the real hunting method is: ambush, inject, retreat, track, eat. Patience, chemistry, and a nose you have to see to believe.

---

8/ THE HYPODERMIC NEEDLE WITH A HINGE

A rattlesnake's fangs are hollow, like hypodermic needles, and they fold.

At rest, they lie flat against the roof of the mouth, wrapped in a tissue sheath. When it strikes, the mouth opens nearly flat, the fangs swing forward, lock, and drive in. Then the muscles around the venom glands squeeze.

The whole event is over in a fraction of a second. About the speed of a blink, give or take.

Two details most people miss.

First, the fangs are disposable. They break, wear out, and get replaced by spare fangs waiting behind them in line. A rattlesnake grows new ones a few times a year.

Second, the snake controls the dose.

Venom costs energy. It takes days to weeks to rebuild what is spent, and the same chemistry helps the snake digest its food. So the animal meters. A bite meant for prey can carry a lot of venom. A defensive bite can carry little or none. These are often called dry bites, and estimates suggest roughly one in five venomous bites involve no venom at all.

That is not mercy. It is accounting.

A defensive strike is the last line of an argument that started with the rattle, the posture, the stare. By the time fangs are used, the snake has already spent all its cheaper options.

---

9/ A COCKTAIL, NOT A POISON

"Venom" sounds like one substance. It is closer to a pharmacy.

Rattlesnake venom is a blend of dozens of proteins and peptides. Different pieces do different jobs. Some break down tissue and make blood vessels leak. Some interfere with clotting. Some loosen the tissue around the bite so the rest spreads faster. A serious bite can look like a body being digested from the outside in, which is exactly what the venom is partly designed to start.

The recipe is not fixed.

It changes between species. It changes between populations of the same species a few valleys apart. In some species it changes between baby and adult, so a newborn can carry venom with a different chemical profile than its mother's.

And in some populations, notably certain Mojave rattlesnakes, the cocktail includes a neurotoxin that acts on the nervous system, a trait that is rare among North American rattlesnakes. Same continent, same genus, completely different clinical picture.

This variability is why doctors take every bite seriously, and why treatment follows symptoms and progression, not just the snake's name.

---

10/ THE PLOT TWIST: THE POISON THAT TREATS

Here is where the story flips.

Venom proteins are brutally precise. They hit blood pressure, clotting and platelets with surgical specificity. Pharmaceutical chemists noticed that precision is exactly what drugs need.

A pit viper from Brazil inspired captopril, a landmark blood pressure drug in the ACE inhibitor family that millions of people have taken.

A small rattlesnake from the southeastern United States, the southeastern pygmy rattlesnake, inspired eptifibatide, an antiplatelet drug used during heart attacks and emergency heart procedures.

Another viper, the saw-scaled viper of Asia and Africa, inspired tirofiban, used for similar purposes.

So somewhere in a hospital cardiac unit tonight, a patient may be held together by a molecule modeled on one a snake designed to wreck its prey's blood.

Evolution spent tens of millions of years tuning these molecules against living nervous systems and circulatory systems. Labs now mine that library. We have catalogued only a sliver of it.

---

11/ THE ANIMAL THAT RUNS ON SUNLIGHT

Rattlesnakes are ectotherms. They do not burn food to make heat. They borrow it. The sun is their engine.

That is why you find them where the ground is warm: stone, asphalt, the sunny side of a boulder. Their muscles work best in a narrow temperature range, and everything about their behavior is a negotiation with that range.

Too cold, and they are sluggish. Too hot, and they die within hours, so in desert summer they retreat to burrows and come out at night.

It also makes them absurdly efficient. A mammal your size spends most of its calories keeping a furnace burning. A snake spends almost nothing. Some rattlesnakes eat only a handful of meals in a year, and some go months between them.

Flip it around: because they live on borrowed heat, they love the exact places we build roads and trails. Which is how most close encounters begin.

---

12/ WHY YOUR BRAIN FLINCHES BEFORE YOU DO

Remember how you reacted the first time you heard that sound. Before thinking. Before deciding.

Researchers have a theory about that. Snakes were such a persistent threat to early primates, the idea goes, that evolution tuned our visual system to spot them. In experiments, neurons in the brains of lab-raised monkeys that had never seen a snake responded faster to snake images than to other images. Studies with babies as young as six months found stronger stress responses, like pupil dilation, to snakes than to other animals.

Nobody taught them. The fear is, at least in part, pre-installed.

That is a gift, because it keeps us alive. It is also a trap, because fear without information makes people do stupid things: panic, stomp, swing a shovel, or worse, reach.

The fear gets you to stop. The knowledge gets you home.

---

13/ THE NUMBERS THAT SPOIL THE MOVIE

Let's talk about how dangerous this animal actually is.

In the United States, venomous snakes bite on the order of 7,000 to 8,000 people each year. Rattlesnakes account for most of the serious ones.

Deaths: around five per year, nationwide.

Five.

For comparison, bees, wasps and hornets kill roughly a dozen times more Americans annually. Dogs kill several times more than that. Lightning and car crashes with deer both outnumber snakes by a wide margin.

If rattlesnakes were villains, they would be the worst-performing villains in the history of the genre.

Why so few deaths, when the venom is serious? Three reasons.

One. Modern antivenom and emergency care work.
Two. Many bites are partial or dry.
Three. The animal wants nothing to do with you. It evolved a warning system whose entire purpose is to avoid the fight. You are not food, and a snake that spends venom on non-food is a snake that goes hungry.

Fear is a feeling. Risk is a number. The two have almost nothing to say to each other here.

Do not misread this. Five deaths a year does not mean bites are harmless. A bite can leave permanent tissue damage, lost function, long hospital stays and months of recovery. The point is not that it is safe. The point is that it is avoidable.

---

14/ WHO ACTUALLY GETS BITTEN

Here is the uncomfortable bit.

Studies of snakebite cases keep finding the same pattern. A large share of bites land on the hands and arms. A substantial share involve someone who knew the snake was there, and decided to move it, poke it, photograph it up close, or kill it.

Hikers who simply walk past are the minority.

The most dangerous moment around a rattlesnake is not meeting one. It is deciding to be brave.

The rule is the same on a trail, at a campsite, or in your yard.

Stop moving. Freeze for a second and locate it. Rattlesnakes can strike roughly a third to half their body length, so the safe distance is bigger than you think. Back away slowly and give it an exit. Go around with plenty of room, ten feet or more is a sensible target.

Do not throw things. Do not try to pin it with a stick. Do not pick it up, even if it looks dead.

Especially if it looks dead.

Which brings us to the most unsettling fact in this post.

---

15/ THE HEAD THAT BITES AFTER DEATH

A rattlesnake's bite reflex can keep working after the snake is dead.

Documented cases describe severed heads still biting and injecting venom, in some reports for up to an hour after death. The nerves, fangs and venom glands do not know the animal is gone. Touch the mouth, trigger the reflex.

Doctors have treated people for envenomation from snakes that were, by every ordinary definition, dead.

It is not a haunted-house story. It is neurology. Reflex arcs run on local circuits, and cold-blooded animals keep their tissue responsive far longer than we do.

Practical lesson: never handle one. Not to move it, not to bury it, not to hang it on a fence for a photo, not because it "seems finished."

---

16/ IF IT HAPPENS ANYWAY

Quick, boring, life-saving. Screenshot this.

Call emergency services right away, and get to a hospital that can give antivenom. Time matters more than anything else on this list.

Stay calm and keep still. A racing heart moves venom faster.

Take off rings, watches and anything tight near the bite before swelling starts.

Keep the bitten limb still, around heart level.

Note the time of the bite. If you can, mark the edge of the swelling with a pen.

Do not cut the wound. Do not suck out the venom. Do not apply a tourniquet. Do not use ice. Do not use electric shocks, which people have really tried. Do not drink alcohol. Do not try to catch or kill the snake. A phone photo from a safe distance helps, but only if you can get it without risk.

Every folk remedy from the movies makes outcomes worse. The most effective treatment ever built is a hospital and a few vials of antivenom.

---

17/ THE ANTIVENOM STORY, AND THE PRICE TAG

Here is the part nobody puts on a hiking sign.

Modern rattlesnake antivenoms are built from antibodies. In one widely used version, sheep are immunized with small amounts of venom, their blood produces antibodies, and the antibody fragments are purified into a treatment that grabs venom proteins and neutralizes them. Another common version is made using horses.

It is one of the oldest ideas in modern medicine, using animals as living factories, and it still works.

It is also expensive. A single vial can run to thousands of dollars on a hospital's price list, a serious bite can need several vials, and hospital bills in the six figures are well documented in American snakebite cases.

Which gives the cruelest part of the story. The treatment exists. The cost of it can punish the victim after the venom already did.

If you hike in rattlesnake country, understand your health coverage before you need it. Nobody wants to compare insurance plans while their hand is swelling.

---

18/ THE PART THAT DOES NOT FIT THE MONSTER STORY

Rattlesnakes do not lay eggs. They give birth to live young, usually in late summer.

And here is where the cold, mindless reptile myth cracks.

Mothers often stay with their newborns for the first days, until the babies complete their first shed. Researchers who tracked rattlesnakes have documented females guarding young, and groups of mothers gathering at shared nursery sites. Experiments have also suggested that rattlesnakes can tell relatives from strangers, and prefer the company of kin.

This is a snake with a social life. Not warm and fuzzy, but real.

Even more striking is the pace. Many rattlesnakes grow slowly, mature late, and reproduce only every few years. Some species live two decades or more in the wild, and timber rattlesnakes have been recorded approaching thirty. A female may raise only a handful of litters in her life.

Slow life, few offspring, deep attachment to home ground. That is the profile of an animal that is easy to wipe out and hard to rebuild.

---

19/ THE WARNING THAT GETS THEM KILLED

Now we reach the paradox.

The rattle exists to avoid conflict. It is a transaction: I tell you I am here, you leave, and nobody bleeds.

But the same sound that tells a hiker to step back also tells a person with a shovel exactly where to swing.

Some biologists suspect that in places where people kill rattlesnakes on sight, the animals that rattle least are the ones that live longest. Quiet snakes survive, quiet snakes breed, quiet snakes become the population. People in several regions have reported snakes that freeze silently instead of buzzing.

The evidence is still thin and debated, and I want to be honest about that. But the logic is hard to dismiss.

A rattlesnake that stops rattling is not more dangerous by temperament. But it deletes the one signal that let both of us avoid the encounter.

---

20/ THE SNAKE THAT BECAME A FLAG

America picked the rattlesnake as a symbol before it picked almost anything else.

In 1751, Benjamin Franklin published a satirical proposal that Britain, which was shipping convicts to the colonies, should receive rattlesnakes in return. In 1754 he published the "Join, or Die" cartoon, a snake cut into pieces, urging the colonies to unite. By the Revolution, the rattlesnake was everywhere, and the Gadsden flag, a coiled rattlesnake over the words "Don't tread on me," became one of the most recognized flags in American history.

In 1775, writing under a pseudonym, Franklin published an essay praising the animal. His argument: it never begins an attack, never surrenders when attacked, and always gives fair warning. He even noted that its rattle had thirteen segments, one for each colony.

Whatever you think of the flag today, the original logic is the whole post in one sentence: a creature that warns first, strikes last, and does not quit.

Two and a half centuries later, the real animal still behaves exactly like that.

---

21/ A FAMILY OF ABOUT THIRTY-SIX

Rattlesnakes exist only in the Americas, roughly three dozen species from southern Canada down to Argentina. Arizona alone has 13, the most of any US state.

The variety is wild. The sidewinder throws loops of its body sideways across hot sand so only two points touch the ground at a time. Tiny pygmy rattlesnakes carry rattles that sound like a distant insect. The eastern diamondback is the heaviest venomous snake in North America, and big adults can top ten pounds.

Each one is a different answer to the same question: how do you survive as a legless, cold-blooded ambush hunter in a world full of things that want to step on you or eat you?

---

22/ MYTH CHECK

1. They chase people. No. A rattlesnake crawls at a few miles per hour and wants distance, not you.
2. They only strike when coiled. No. Coiling helps, but they can strike from other positions.
3. They always rattle first. No. Some bites come with no warning.
4. Babies are always worse. The evidence says adults can inject far more venom.
5. Count the rattles to learn the age. No.
6. Cut and suck the wound. No. It makes things worse.
7. A dead snake is a safe snake. No.
8. They hate water. No. They swim well.
9. They are aggressive. No. Defensive and aggressive are not the same thing.

---

THE FIVE-LINE VERSION

A muscle that never tires. A sound that lies about distance. A sensor borrowed from wasabi. A venom that doubles as medicine. A mother that stays.

Everything about this animal is engineered for one goal, and it is not to hurt you. The goal is to avoid ever needing to.

The rattle is not a threat. It is an offer. Take the deal.

That is the whole story: an animal built to win by never having to fight. The scariest sound in the desert is also the most polite one. It asks for nothing except a few more steps of distance. 

If this changed one thing you believed:
Repost so the next person who meets one does not step closer.
Reply with the strangest animal defense you know.
Follow for more science that makes the world stranger than the fear.
Bookmark it for the hike.

Next time you hear that sound in the dry grass, remember what it costs the animal to make it.

Back away. Slowly. Say thanks.

text:
Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI | Isabel O'Brien, CNBC

Key Points

- Politicians including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Google following reports that the company would restrict search at schools that ban AI.

- Google responded to the outrage, saying that Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search will be turned off by default, and schools can choose to turn one or all of them back on.

- Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated.”

---

Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools.

In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely.

Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media.

"Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion."

Google responded later in the day. In a post on X, the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit.

"We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork."

The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment.

Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon.

Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service."

It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information.

In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram.

The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June.

The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an "unacceptable risk" rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms.

Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024.

WHEN A MEDICAL EMERGENCY BECOMES A USE-OF-FORCE ENCOUNTER

On October 25, 2026, Dwight Jackson was putting up Halloween decorations outside his home in Chattahoochee, Florida, when he suffered what his family describes as a seizure. His brother called for medical assistance, and paramedics responded. What followed has become another troubling example of why law enforcement must distinguish medical impairment from intentional resistance before escalating to electrical force.

According to Jackson and his brother, paramedics were already treating him when a police sergeant arrived, intervened physically and used a TASER. Jackson maintains he was not combative but was recovering from a medical emergency. Police Chief Michael Miller offered a different account, saying EMS requested assistance with a combative patient and that Sergeant Price encountered physical resistance, including Jackson pulling on his body armor.

On October 28, Miller announced that Price had been dismissed, citing conduct and demeanor that failed to meet departmental standards. A separate video showed the sergeant arguing with an EMS employee. The dismissal is established, but the department has not publicly demonstrated that every alleged electrical deployment was unjustified. The precise number of activations and the circumstances surrounding them remain important unanswered questions.

But the larger issue reaches well beyond this particular officer or department.

A person emerging from a seizure may be confused, disoriented, frightened or unable to process commands. Physical movement during a medical emergency does not necessarily establish intentional resistance, although genuine threats to responders must still be addressed. Recognizing that distinction is fundamental to determining whether force is necessary, what level is appropriate and whether the encounter should remain primarily under medical rather than enforcement control.

This is precisely where the narrowing TASER use-case thesis becomes important. TASER remains an essential less-lethal tool when circumstances justify electrical incapacitation. But as courts, medical authorities, training standards and oversight bodies more carefully distinguish active aggression from passive resistance, confusion and inability to comply, the boundaries around its appropriate use become more clearly defined.

The operational challenge is what happens below that threshold.

Pasadena’s Independent Police Auditor recently examined behavioral-health encounters and found that an enforcement-first approach could compress time, reduce tactical options and accelerate encounters toward force, even when the eventual TASER deployment was found within policy. The auditor recommended scenario-based training, better crisis recognition, deliberate pacing and improved coordination with specialized responders.

Chattahoochee illustrates why those distinctions matter in practice. Officers responding to medical emergencies need training that helps them recognize impaired behavior, coordinate with EMS, assess actual threats and avoid converting a medical problem into a force problem unnecessarily.

And when genuine safety concerns require intervention, officers need appropriate tactics and tools that provide meaningful alternatives before electrical incapacitation becomes necessary.

As the TASER use case narrows, the middle expands. That expanding middle creates a capability gap requiring new training, better tactics and effective non-lethal options.

Not every encounter in that middle requires another device. Sometimes the appropriate capability is medical recognition, coordinated restraint, distance, patience or allowing paramedics to continue treatment. The objective is to give responders the judgment, training and resources to select the appropriate intervention rather than defaulting to force.

That is the larger lesson from Chattahoochee. The question is not simply whether an officer encountered resistance. It is whether the officer correctly understood what was happening, whether the response was proportionate and whether another approach could have resolved the situation more safely.

The Expanding Middle cannot be filled by telling officers what not to do. It must be filled by teaching and equipping them to do something better.

The Florida-based company had offered passengers the option to rent or buy long-term residences aboard the ship, which had been sailing around the world for more than 755 days. Many had paid tens of thousands of dollars to live on board for years

text:
🤝 $ACB Receives Friendly Offer from $OGI. (Will $CURLF Come Back Over the Top?)
— Anthony Varrell @V_arrell 

Three months after Curaleaf went hostile, Aurora Cannabis has an answer: a friendly, board-approved, fully financed merger with Organigram Global that values Aurora at C$7.80 per share, or roughly C$561 million on a fully diluted basis. That’s a 93% premium to Aurora’s unaffected price on August 10 and, more to the point, a 21% premium to the current implied value of Curaleaf’s bid. Curaleaf’s response on Tuesday was a statement that acknowledges the deal, questions its terms, calls Aurora “a significantly smaller, underperforming and less liquid company,” and says its own bid “remains outstanding.” It did not say the word “raise.”

What Organigram is offering

The structure is the tell. Aurora shareholders can choose C$7.80 in cash, 5.8626 Organigram shares, or C$3.75 cash plus 3.0431 shares, with proration against caps of C$253.6 million in cash and 205.8 million Organigram shares. That optionality is designed to beat Curaleaf on exactly the ground where Curaleaf is weakest. Curaleaf’s offer is 0.4013 of its own shares plus US$1.00 cash, capped at US$5.00. With CURA stock having slipped since October, that package is worth roughly US$4.60 today, or around C$6.45. Organigram is offering C$7.80 with a real cash election, and for Canadian holders who take stock, a tax-deferred rollover that Curaleaf’s U.S.-listed paper can’t provide.

The financing is already in place. BAT is buying 141 million Organigram shares at C$1.33 for about C$187.5 million, and ATB has underwritten up to C$210 million in credit facilities, including a C$115 million term tranche earmarked for the acquisition. Both boards approved unanimously. Aurora’s special committee recommended it. Fairness opinions came from BMO on the Organigram side and Fort Capital and Origin Merchant on Aurora’s. BAT signed an irrevocable voting agreement that survives six months past any termination, and directors and officers of both companies are locked up. Aurora’s board is now formally telling shareholders to reject Curaleaf, withdraw tendered shares and vote for Organigram.

The combined company would be the largest Canadian LP by a wide margin, with more than C$50 million in identified run-rate synergies, Aurora’s EU-GMP footprint in Germany and Australia bolted onto Organigram’s domestic scale and BAT’s balance sheet. Aurora holders end up with about 35% of the economics and 42% of the vote. Special meetings are targeted for December, closing for January 2027, subject to German FDI clearance and B.C. court approval.

Curaleaf’s position

Curaleaf’s statement is a holding action. It says the Organigram announcement omits a break fee, post-closing governance and BAT’s investor rights, which is fair; the press release doesn’t disclose them, and the arrangement agreement will. It argues its own bid offers “a stronger capital markets profile, greater certainty and speed to close, and greater anticipated synergies,” without quantifying any of those. It takes a shot at BAT’s “disappointing cannabis investment track record,” which is accurate and also irrelevant to whether BAT’s C$187.5 million clears. And it accuses Aurora’s board of “gross dereliction of their fiduciary duties” for refusing to engage, a line that only makes sense if Curaleaf was prepared to pay more than it has offered.

That’s the question.

Can Curaleaf go higher?

Mechanically, yes. A hostile bidder can amend its offer at any time before expiry, and Curaleaf’s expires December 4, before Aurora’s shareholder vote. Nothing in Canadian takeover law prevents it. The constraint is capacity, not permission.

The bigger problem is that Curaleaf would be bidding against a package Aurora’s board has already endorsed, with synergies Aurora’s advisors have already blessed and a strategic partner, BAT, that has a lock-up. A revised hostile bid would have to be high enough that Aurora’s board couldn’t credibly maintain its recommendation without breaching its own fiduciary duty, which means not just matching but clearing C$7.80 by a visible margin, probably C$8.25 or higher. At that price, Curaleaf is paying roughly 14x Aurora’s forward EBITDA for a company whose own management guides to declining revenue, in a transaction Curaleaf’s lenders will have to approve.

What Curaleaf can do instead

There are three other plays, none of them great. It can vote against the arrangement by buying Aurora shares in the market before the December record date and campaigning for a no vote; the deal needs two-thirds of votes cast plus a majority-of-the-minority, so a determined 20% block could sink it. It can challenge the lock-ups and deal protections in court if the arrangement agreement contains a break fee or no-shop that looks preclusive, though Canadian courts rarely intervene on those grounds. Or it can walk, let the bid expire December 4, book the exercise as having forced Aurora into a sale and move on to the Florida and European priorities it has been talking about all year.

Watch for the arrangement agreement on SEDAR+. The break fee size, the matching rights and BAT’s governance terms will tell you how much room Curaleaf has. A break fee under 3% and a standard right-to-match clause means the door is open. A fee at 4% plus BAT board seats means Aurora built this deal to be unbreakable.

The read

Curaleaf wanted Aurora’s Leuna facility, its German market share and its cash at a discount, and it bet that Aurora’s board had no alternative. It was wrong. Organigram showed up with BAT’s money, a cash election and a premium, and the board took it. Curaleaf can raise, but every dollar it adds now goes to the shareholders of a company it called underperforming, to top a deal it called inferior, using stock it says is undervalued. That’s a hard story to tell your own investors. The smarter move may be to make Aurora’s shareholders prove they prefer C$7.80 in a December vote, and let the market decide whether Curaleaf’s walkaway was the best trade it made all year.
