📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't.” ~ Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897). ☄️

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

November 4 has a charmingly unhinged definition of progress.

On this date, a future president married the woman who would later stare down the country with more backbone than half the men in the room. A saloonkeeper invented a gadget to catch his own staff stealing, because apparently trust is for people who enjoy bankruptcy. An archaeologist's workers uncovered the opening act of one of history's greatest finds, and somehow the world didn't immediately trip over itself rushing to see what came next. A notorious gambler got shot after a poker game and took every useful detail with him, which is frankly the most on-brand exit imaginable. And an embassy was seized, kicking off a hostage crisis that kept Americans captive for over a year while the rest of the world practiced its most serious concerned-face.

Then there's the scientist whose fortune crossed an ocean, helped found an institution he never got to see, and whose remains eventually crossed that same ocean in a coffin escorted by a famous inventor—because apparently even in death, some people get an extraordinary send-off.

So yes. November 4 has been busy making a mockery of linear time.

Humanity calls it progress. That's adorable. Sweet, even. We invent machines to catch thieves, dig up dead kings to admire their gold, shoot each other over card games, and then spend fourteen months arguing about who gets to go home. We've conquered nature, apparently. Still haven't figured out how to behave like civilized goddamn adults.

Cue the chaos. Let's roll. 💥

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

In 1879, an Ohio saloonkeeper received a patent for an invention that would eventually become a fixture in retail establishments.

What unusual experience helped inspire the machine?

[A] He watched a bank teller accidentally destroy a day's receipts.

[B] He discovered that his employees were secretly altering their handwritten accounts.

[C] He witnessed a mechanical counter aboard a steamship and realized it could record sales.

[D] He watched a slot machine pay out money without keeping track of the winnings.

👇 (Answer at the end of the issue.)

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

💍 1842 — ABRAHAM LINCOLN MARRIES MARY TODD: A BROKEN ENGAGEMENT, A SECRET COURTSHIP, AND A WEDDING THAT ALMOST DIDN'T HAPPEN 🏛️

On November 4, 1842, Abraham Lincoln married Mary Todd at the home of her sister in Springfield, Illinois.

It was not a straightforward romance.

Mary was intelligent, politically ambitious, well educated, and accustomed to a more comfortable life than the one Lincoln could offer. Lincoln was a tall, awkward, frequently melancholy young lawyer whose ambitions considerably exceeded his finances.

They met in Springfield in 1840. Their courtship developed quickly, but in January 1841 Lincoln broke off their engagement. The separation devastated both of them, and they largely avoided one another for more than a year.

Eventually, the relationship resumed quietly through mutual friends.

So quietly, in fact, that Mary did not tell her sister Elizabeth—whose home would host the wedding—that she and Lincoln had reconciled until the wedding day itself.

On November 4, the couple married in Elizabeth's Springfield home. Lincoln was 33; Mary was 23.

They began married life in modest circumstances, renting a single room at the Globe Tavern. Their first son, Robert Todd Lincoln, arrived on August 1, 1843. Three more sons followed: Edward, William, and Thomas. Only Robert survived into adulthood.

Mary would become First Lady in 1861, enduring the pressures of the Civil War, the deaths of two of her sons, and the assassination of her husband in 1865.

Their marriage was complicated, sometimes difficult, and often misunderstood. But it began with a broken engagement, a secret reconciliation, and a wedding Mary apparently managed to keep secret until the last possible moment.

Some love stories begin with a grand gesture. This one began with a second chance.

🧩 TRIVIA: The newlyweds' first home was a single room at the Globe Tavern. Their first child, Robert, was born less than nine months after the wedding.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A second chance can change the course of a life—and sometimes the course of a nation.

───────────────

💰 1879 — THE CASH REGISTER: A SALOONKEEPER'S DISTRUST BECOMES A BUSINESS REVOLUTION 🛎️

On November 4, 1879, James Ritty and his brother John received a United States patent for an improved cash register and indicator.

James operated a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and worried that employees might pocket customers' money instead of recording every sale.

His inspiration came during a steamship journey to Europe. Ritty noticed a mechanical device that counted the revolutions of the ship's propeller. He wondered whether a similar mechanism could count something more useful to a saloonkeeper.

Money.

Back in Dayton, he enlisted his brother's mechanical skills. Their machine used keys corresponding to monetary amounts; pressing a key advanced a mechanism that recorded the transaction. It also rang a bell, alerting customers that a sale had been entered.

The brothers called it the Ritty's Incorruptible Cashier.

It was not yet the modern cash register, but it offered business owners something valuable: a mechanical record that did not depend entirely on an employee's honesty.

The Ritty brothers eventually sold their interests. John H. Patterson later acquired the business and developed it into the National Cash Register Company, helping turn the invention into a major commercial industry.

A machine designed to keep bartenders honest had found a much larger market.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original inspiration was a counter measuring a steamship's propeller revolutions. Ritty adapted the principle to record sales.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Distrust is not always admirable. Occasionally, however, it produces an invention that changes the world.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🏺 1922 — THE FIRST STEP TOWARD TUTANKHAMUN: ONE STAIRCASE, THOUSANDS OF YEARS, AND AN ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERY FOR THE AGES 🔱

On November 4, 1922, archaeologist Howard Carter and his Egyptian workers uncovered a step cut into the rock in the Valley of the Kings.

It was the first step toward the tomb of Tutankhamun.

Carter had spent years searching for the young pharaoh's burial place. His financial backer, George Herbert, the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, was losing patience. After years of disappointing results, Carnarvon was prepared to end the excavation.

Carter persuaded him to finance one final season.

The decision proved extraordinary.

As workers cleared debris near the tomb of Ramesses VI, the buried step appeared. Further excavation revealed a staircase descending into the earth. By November 5, the team had uncovered a sealed doorway bearing the marks of the royal necropolis.

Carter stopped, secured the site, and sent word to Carnarvon in England. The earl hurried to Egypt.

On November 25, the team opened the first sealed doorway. The following day, Carter made an opening through the second sealed doorway and peered into the darkness of the antechamber. When Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything, Carter gave the answer that became famous:

“Wonderful things.”

Beyond the entrance lay an astonishing collection of objects: statues, furniture, ceremonial equipment, chariots, and treasures that had remained buried for more than three thousand years.

The tomb had suffered ancient intrusions, but much of its extraordinary contents survived. Its discovery transformed the world's understanding of ancient Egyptian royal burial practices and became one of archaeology's defining moments.

It began not with a golden crown or a jeweled treasure chest, but with one step noticed beneath the dirt.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Griffith Institute at the University of Oxford preserves and digitizes Carter's excavation records, photographs, and journals.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes an extraordinary discovery begins with one more step when everyone else is ready to stop.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎲 1928 — ARNOLD ROTHSTEIN: THE GAMBLER WHO TOOK HIS FINAL SECRET TO THE GRAVE ♠️

On the evening of November 4, 1928, New York gambler Arnold Rothstein was shot after attending a high-stakes poker game at the Park Central Hotel in Manhattan.

Known as “The Brain” and “The Big Bankroll,” Rothstein had become one of the most influential figures in New York's underworld. He was associated with the 1919 Black Sox scandal and had a reputation for treating gambling as a business of calculation, influence, and manipulation.

The circumstances of the poker game and the shooting were murky. Rothstein was reportedly summoned to the game, where a dispute over money may have turned violent.

He was shot in the abdomen and taken to the hospital.

Police wanted to know who had pulled the trigger.

Rothstein refused to tell them.

He understood the underworld's rules, and he apparently had no intention of breaking them—even with his life at stake.

He died on November 6, two days after the shooting.

George McManus was charged with the murder but acquitted. Investigators suspected that the killing involved a gambling debt, but the case was never conclusively solved.

The man who had made a career of calculating other people's risks had encountered one he could not control.

He entered a poker game and left with a fatal wound—and a mystery that outlived him.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rothstein was shot on November 4 but died on November 6. His refusal to identify his attacker helped preserve the mystery surrounding the murder.

🐍 MACHIAVELLIAN: Rothstein's reputation rested on his ability to manipulate games and people. His own murder produced no definitive answer about who had outplayed him.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A lifetime spent calculating other people's risks does not guarantee control over your own.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🏛️ 1979 — THE IRAN HOSTAGE CRISIS: AN EMBASSY SEIZED, 52 AMERICANS CAPTIVE, AND 444 DAYS THAT SHOOK THE WORLD 🇮🇷

On November 4, 1979, Iranian students stormed the United States Embassy in Tehran and seized American personnel.

The students were furious that the United States had admitted Iran's former monarch, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, for medical treatment. The Shah had been overthrown earlier that year, and many Iranians regarded Washington as responsible for supporting his regime.

Sixty-six Americans were initially taken hostage.

Six diplomats, however, escaped the embassy during the takeover and found refuge with Canadian diplomats. Their situation was perilous: discovery could have placed them in the hands of the captors.

The CIA and Canadian government devised an extraordinary extraction plan. The Americans would pose as a Canadian film crew scouting locations for a fictional science-fiction production. A fictitious company, Studio Six Productions, and false identities helped make the story credible.

On January 28, 1980, the six diplomats were successfully extracted from Iran. The operation later inspired the film Argo.

The larger crisis continued.

Thirteen hostages were released during the early months. Fifty-two remained in captivity. In April 1980, the United States attempted a military rescue, Operation Eagle Claw. Mechanical failures and operational problems forced the mission to be abandoned at Desert One. During the withdrawal, a helicopter collided with a transport aircraft, killing eight American servicemen.

The failed mission was a devastating setback. The hostages remained captive while negotiations dragged on.

Finally, after 444 days, the remaining 52 Americans were released on January 20, 1981, the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated.

The crisis profoundly damaged relations between the United States and Iran. What began as an embassy seizure became one of the defining diplomatic confrontations of the twentieth century.

🧩 TRIVIA: The six diplomats rescued through the Canadian Caper were extracted on January 28, 1980. The operation remained classified until 1997.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Courage takes many forms: enduring captivity, risking a rescue, or protecting people whose lives depend on your silence.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY'S CORNER

THE MAN WHO GAVE AMERICA A SMITHSONIAN

Good day.

On a January morning in 1904, a procession moved through Washington toward the building now known as the Smithsonian Castle.

Inside a flag-draped coffin were the remains of a man who had died in Italy seventy-five years earlier.

The man escorting him home was Alexander Graham Bell.

Bell was not bringing home a relative, a fellow inventor, or a former president. He was returning the remains of a scientist whose fortune had created one of America's great institutions.

The man's name was James Smithson.

And the remarkable part of the story is that Smithson had never visited the country that received his fortune.

To understand why his remains were making that journey, we must go back to November 4, 1829.

On that day, Smithson's will was proved in England.

He had died in Genoa, Italy, several months earlier, on June 27. His will, written in 1826, made his nephew, Henry James Hungerford, the principal beneficiary. But Smithson included a remarkable contingency: if his nephew died without children, the estate would pass to the United States of America to establish an institution in Washington “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men.”

It was an astonishing bequest.

Smithson was not an American. He had never set foot in the United States. Born in France as James Lewis Macie, he was educated at Oxford, became a naturalized British citizen, and built his reputation as a chemist and mineralogist.

Smithson's nephew died in 1835 without an heir. The contingency in the will took effect.

The United States accepted the bequest, and diplomat Richard Rush was sent to England to secure the estate. In August 1838, Smithson's fortune arrived in New York aboard the ship Mediator, packed in eleven boxes of British gold sovereigns.

The gold was taken to the United States Mint in Philadelphia, melted down, and converted into American currency.

The final amount was $508,318.46.

In estimated 2026 purchasing power, that would be roughly $18.4 million—a modern comparison based on reconstructed historical consumer-price estimates, not an exact measure of economic influence.

Not an estimate. Not a rounded figure. Forty-six cents included.

The sum was enormous for its time—roughly one and a half percent of the federal budget. But Smithson had left no blueprint for the institution he wanted. Congress debated what to do with the money. A national university was proposed. So were a library, an art gallery, and an observatory.

The debate lasted years.

In 1846, Congress finally established the Smithsonian Institution.

The man whose name it carried had never seen Washington. He would never walk its halls, examine its collections, or meet the people whose lives would be changed by the institution his fortune made possible.

And the mystery remained: why had a British scientist, born in France, chosen to leave his fortune to a country he had never visited?

Smithson's surviving writings do not provide a definitive answer. We should not pretend to know what he never told us.

But we can see what he believed in. He devoted his life to scientific inquiry and the pursuit of knowledge. His will used language broad in its ambition: an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge—not merely for the benefit of one family, one class, or one nation.

Perhaps the phrase “citizen of the world” is an apt way to describe the reach of his legacy. It is not a formal citizenship claim. Smithson was a naturalized British subject, born in France, whose final gift crossed the Atlantic and became an institution serving people around the world.

And that brings us back to Alexander Graham Bell.

By 1903, the cemetery in Genoa where Smithson had been buried faced displacement. The Smithsonian's Board of Regents appointed Bell to oversee the removal of Smithson's remains and their return to Washington.

Bell and his wife traveled to Genoa. Smithson's remains were carefully transferred, placed aboard the steamer Princess Irene, and carried across the Atlantic. They reached New York in January 1904, then continued to Washington.

On January 25, a procession escorted the coffin from the Navy Yard to the Smithsonian Building. The coffin was draped in American and British flags.

Bell delivered the remains to the Institution, declaring:

“And now...my mission is ended and I deliver into your hands...the remains of this great benefactor of the United States.”

The remains were eventually placed in a crypt at the north entrance of the Smithsonian Building.

He gave a country he had never visited a gift that would outlive him by centuries. His name became known to generations who would never know the details of his life. His fortune became museums, research, collections, and discoveries available to people who might otherwise never have encountered them.

And perhaps that is a kind of belonging no passport can confer.

James Smithson did not need to live in America to become part of its story. He did not need to see the Smithsonian to shape its future. His generosity gave him a place in the lives of people he would never meet.

And now you know the rest of the story.

Good day.

·        ·        ·        ·        ·        ·        ·        ·        ·        ·

🧬 HUMAN: James Smithson reminds us that a life can be measured not only by what we accumulate, but by what we give to people we will never meet. He left no children, but his generosity created an institution that has educated, challenged, and inspired generations. How far might one thoughtful act travel after we are gone?

AGNIPATH: A DISASTER Policy By Modi Govt And Unhappy New Year For Gurkhas*
*By Col Diptangshu Chaudhury
https://t.co/CGg0UTIVsQ

Objectives of Agnipath are more political than military.

The Agniveer scheme faced flaks,fresh accusations from Leader Of Opposition Shri Rahul Gandhi in the Lok Sabha, prompting the Indian Army to post a clarification on the news. The scheme, since 2022, has been the centre of controversy with many protests within the Indian Army as well as from veterans demanding the government to rollback the scheme. 

What is Agniveer ?
The Agniveer or Agnipath scheme, announced in June 2022, recruits soldiers in the Army, Navy, and Air Force on a four-year contract, with 25 per cent retained for a further 15 years. It recruits young people to serve in the Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force for a short duration of four years. The scheme targets young individuals in the age group of 17.5 to 21 years. Training and employment: Recruits undergo rigorous training and serve in various capacities within the armed forces during their tenure. After completing their service, Agniveers receive a financial package which includes a lump sum payment and benefits. Additionally, they are provided with skills and experience that can help in future employment opportunities. Only a certain percentage of Agniveers may be absorbed into the regular armed forces based on their performance and the needs of the military. Unlike traditional recruitment, Agniveers are not entitled to a pension.

Why this Criticism ?
Critics argue that the four-year tenure does not provide long-term job security for recruits, leaving them uncertain about their future after their service ends. Additionally, Agniveers do not receive pensions, which is seen as a major drawback for those seeking long-term employment and financial stability. The scheme might impact the morale of the soldiers, knowing that their service is temporary and not on par with the regular forces in terms of career progression and benefits. The worry that a short-term service model could affect the overall effectiveness and professionalism of the armed forces. Any soldier to be technically and militarily competent takes a period of minimum 05 years to be trained to be deployed against adversaries. As also when a Agniveer dies in line of duty, he gets only ex-gratia and no family pension. His family or NoK getting no other benefits which a NoK of regular soldier gets. *Isn’t this a big anomaly differentiating death of a soldier in line of duty?*

Following the announcement of the Agniveer scheme in June 2022, there were widespread protests across Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan and other States. Under the Agnipath scheme, the 'Agniveers' are to be enrolled under the respective Service Acts, and a one-time package of Rs 11.71 lakh will be given to each youth once their service of 4 years comes to an end. The scheme offers no gratuity or pensionary benefits. Those protesting have complained that the new scheme hinders their claim for monetary benefits, such as pensions, since the Centre plans to absorb only 25 per cent of the 'Agniveers' after the completion of their 4-year tenure. Protesting youths say that they will be left in a lurch with no retirement benefits after serving the four-year tenure under the scheme.

The Flaws :
The basic military training of only 04 months of Agnipath runs the risk of “casting the armed forces, already short of manpower, into turmoil with a radical and untried new recruitment system. After four years’ service, an Agniveer will only be a partially-trained soldier and not ready to fulfill the often technologically-dependent and complex functions required of a fully-trained soldier even in civvy street or corporate environments. Given the parlous security situation on the country’s northern and western borders as well as the ongoing domestic turbulence, this is not the best time to cast the armed forces –

text:
Here @McIlroyRory  and all the news ⛳️⛳️
Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, 4 November 2026 - Rory McIlroy is aiming to turn his remarkable record in Abu Dhabi into a long-awaited victory as he hunts history at the DP World Tour Play-Offs.

The Northern Irishman arrives at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, staged by the DP World Tour and Abu Dhabi Sports Council, in the unfamiliar position of chaser as he seeks a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title and fifth in a row.

He currently sits third in the Race to Dubai Rankings Delivered by DP World behind leader Eugenio Chacarra and Patrick Reed but with enhanced points on offer at the fourth Rolex Series event of the season, any of those three or fourth-placed Casey Jarvis could end the week on top.

Out of those four, history would suggest the advantage would lie with McIlroy, with the Northern Irishman having four second and six third-place finishes at this event, with two of those thirds coming at Yas Links in the last two seasons.

He also has seven wins in the UAE in the neighbouring Emirate of Dubai - where we head next week for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship - and would dearly love to complete his unfinished business in Abu Dhabi.

"I feel like the UAE in general has been a good place for me," he said. "It's crazy to think that the 15 years that I've been coming here with how many times I've been in contention, I haven't been able to get over line.

"Hopefully this year I give myself another chance. I feel like we played at Abu Dhabi Golf Club for a lot of years and then from coming here recently, the course is definitely growing on me. I think the first time I played it, I probably didn't enjoy it as much as I enjoy it now.

"I think a big part of that is conditioning of the course and how great the greens are and the surrounds and the fairways and everything.

"I'd love to win. I need a big week to give myself a real chance going into Dubai next week, as well. Hopefully I play well and at least give myself another chance."

A man educated in the history of the game, career Grand Slam winner McIlroy already shares the record for most Major wins by a European and cut an emotional figure when he matched Seve Ballesteros' haul of six Harry Vardon Trophies in 2024.

He is now looking to match Colin Montgomerie''s all-time tally, an achivement that has been high on his list since he started his season in Australia almost 12 months ago.

"It's always a goal," he said. "You just hope you play well in the big tournaments early in the year so you give yourself a chance at this time of the year to win it.

"Hopefully, the experience of playing this course a few times and then the experience of being in this position of trying to win season-long races, whether it be in Europe or America, and having done that for quite a few years, hopefully that experience gives me a little bit of an edge."

McIlroy will play round one in the company of his two closest rivals, reigniting a history with Reed that has seen the pair go head-to-head on several occasions, most notably at the 2016 Ryder Cup and 2023 Hero Dubai Desert Classic.

It will, however, be the first time he has played alongside Chacarra and he is looking for ward to seeing the Spaniard up close.

"I think just from watching him, he seems to excel on difficult golf courses," he said. "So I'd say he's got a good attitude and the right attitude about how he does things.

"It looks like he's quite a feel player. Sort of hits a lot of different shots. But I'm looking forward to playing with him here over the next couple of days. He's had a great season.

"I'm sure he's very high on confidence at the minute, too. It will be interesting. Patrick obviously in there as well.

"I know I need a good week this week and we're going to be playing alongside each other. So we are going to be keeping an eye and seeing how each other is doing but I'm excited for that. Pic credit to DPW tour press release

text:
Rebecca Morgan was thirty-four years old, the eldest of four children.

From the moment she graduated from college, her family treated her salary as a family resource.

Her younger brother needed school fees.

Her sister needed money for rent.

Her mother needed medication.

Her father needed help with the family business.

Rebecca rarely said no.

She had spent years postponing her own plans because there was always someone who needed something.

When she finally received an offer to study architecture in California, she was overjoyed.

It was a two-year programme she had dreamed about since university.

She planned to tell her family during Sunday dinner.

But before she could speak, her father announced that her younger brother, Michael, had been accepted into a private medical school.

Everyone celebrated.

Then her father turned to Rebecca.

"We'll need you to handle his tuition. You're the one with a stable income."

Rebecca's smile disappeared.

She explained that she had received a scholarship and planned to leave in three months.

The room went silent.

Her mother looked disappointed.

Her sister called her selfish.

Her father said, "You are the eldest. Your siblings need you. You can pursue your dreams later."

Rebecca asked one question.

"When exactly is later?"

Nobody answered.

text:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀?

THE BUSINESS ARCHIVES with theBuabee: @McDonalds 

In 1948, two brothers running a successful restaurant in San Bernardino, California, made a decision that probably looked like a step backwards.

They closed their restaurant.

Not because the business was failing. Not because customers had stopped coming.

They had noticed something about the way their business operated.

Although their restaurant offered several items, hamburgers accounted for approximately 80% of their sales.

They were running a relatively complicated operation to serve customers who mostly wanted a few simple things.

So instead of trying to expand the menu, attract more customers or hire more people, Richard and Maurice McDonald decided to simplify the entire business.

They removed most of the menu, eliminated carhop service and redesigned their kitchen.

But the most interesting change wasn't what they stopped selling. It was how they organised the work.

𝙏𝙝𝙚𝙮 𝙙𝙞𝙫𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙙 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙠𝙞𝙩𝙘𝙝𝙚𝙣 𝙞𝙣𝙩𝙤 𝙨𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙨𝙚𝙙 𝙨𝙩𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨. 𝙀𝙖𝙘𝙝 𝙚𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙤𝙮𝙚𝙚 𝙝𝙖𝙙 𝙖 𝙨𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙛𝙞𝙘 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙥𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙞𝙗𝙞𝙡𝙞𝙩𝙮, 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮 𝙝𝙖𝙢𝙗𝙪𝙧𝙜𝙚𝙧 𝙛𝙤𝙡𝙡𝙤𝙬𝙚𝙙 𝙖 𝙧𝙚𝙥𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙖𝙗𝙡𝙚 𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙘𝙚𝙨𝙨.

The objective was to make food faster, cheaper and more consistently.

They called it the 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐞 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦.

Let's think about what they had actually done.

They weren't just improving a restaurant. They were making the process of running a restaurant easier to reproduce.

And that distinction would become extremely important.

Fast forward to 1954, Ray Kroc visited their restaurant and saw the potential in what the brothers had created.

𝑯𝒆 𝒅𝒊𝒅𝒏'𝒕 𝒋𝒖𝒔𝒕 𝒔𝒆𝒆 𝒂 𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒄𝒆 𝒔𝒆𝒍𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒉𝒂𝒎𝒃𝒖𝒓𝒈𝒆𝒓𝒔. 𝑯𝒆 𝒔𝒂𝒘 𝒂𝒏 𝒐𝒑𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒎𝒐𝒅𝒆𝒍 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒃𝒆 𝒓𝒆𝒑𝒍𝒊𝒄𝒂𝒕𝒆𝒅 𝒂𝒄𝒓𝒐𝒔𝒔 𝒎𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒊𝒑𝒍𝒆 𝒍𝒐𝒄𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔.

He went on to help expand McDonald's through franchising, opening his first restaurant in 1955. In 1961, he acquired the brothers' business rights.

The brothers had figured out how to make the restaurant operation repeatable. Kroc helped turn that model into a much larger franchise business.

And this is what I find particularly interesting about McDonald's:

A restaurant can have 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐨𝐝, 𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐫, but if its success depends 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐟𝐞𝐰 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐨, expanding becomes difficult.

The McDonald brothers approached this differently. They designed a process that could be 𝙩𝙖𝙪𝙜𝙝𝙩, 𝙧𝙚𝙥𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙚𝙙 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙞𝙢𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙙.

Instead of relying on every employee to figure things out independently, the business had a defined way of operating.

And that is an important distinction between simply running a successful business and building one that can scale.

𝘼 𝙗𝙪𝙨𝙞𝙣𝙚𝙨𝙨 𝙨𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙡𝙙𝙣'𝙩 𝙝𝙖𝙫𝙚 𝙩𝙤 𝙧𝙚𝙞𝙣𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙝𝙤𝙬 𝙞𝙩 𝙙𝙚𝙡𝙞𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙨 𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙪𝙚 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮 𝙩𝙞𝙢𝙚 𝙞𝙩 𝙜𝙧𝙤𝙬𝙨.

There's a lesson here for everyone of us building a business.

We often think growth means doing more: more products, more employees, more customers and more locations.

But sometimes, the better question is:

text:
Content warning: this post concerns the 1913 murder of a 13 year old girl and the aftermath of the commutation and lynching of the man convicted of killing her.

On Thursday, November 4, 1915, 111 years ago, The Jeffersonian, Thomas Edward Watson's weekly in Thomson, Georgia, printed on Page 4 "The American Law Review, on the Frank Case," Watson's own editorial number 095. On Page 2 it printed a reader letter, "From a Florida Doctor," number 238, on the same subject.

Mary Anne Phagan, 13, was murdered at the National Pencil Company on Saturday, April 26, 1913. A Fulton County jury convicted Leo Max Frank on August 25, 1913. The Georgia Supreme Court and the United States Supreme Court left that conviction standing. On June 21, 1915, Governor John Marshall Slaton, who had been Frank's lawyer before he took office, commuted the death sentence to life. On August 17, 1915, Frank was taken from the state prison farm and hanged near Marietta.

Watson reprinted and answered an American Law Review piece that treated the Frank case as a lesson on American criminal procedure and "Lynch law." The Review blamed form over justice and attacked outside newspapers and petitions that tried to overturn Georgia's courts by popular clamor. It also criticized Slaton for commuting instead of either hanging a guilty man or pardoning an innocent one.

Watson agreed that Georgia's courts had weighed the evidence and that the jury's verdict stood. He corrected the Review on one point: Judge Leonard Strickland Roan and the Georgia Supreme Court had both passed on the sufficiency of the evidence, not the jury alone. He closed by reminding readers that Slaton had been Frank's lawyer, and he pointed them back to the sworn evidence synopsis in his September magazine.

The Florida doctor, Dr. C. M. Yearwood, wrote that until he read the evidence in the Jeff he had doubted Frank's guilt, and that the Jeff had "enlightened" him and others. He called Mary's murder the most fiendish crime ever committed on a pure Christian girl, and he praised Watson for printing the facts when the daily press would not. The Law Review editorial and the Florida letter are below.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

Appendix: Full transcripts

The Jeffersonian, Thomson, Georgia, Thursday, November 4, 1915.

Page 4. Article number 095.

The American Law-Review, on the Frank Case

THE earnest and persevering efforts of The Jeffersonian to counteract the manufactured prejudice against the State of Georgia, is bearing fruit.

A change of tone in many papers is apparent, and many individuals of other States who studied my synopsis of the official evidence which convicted Leo Frank, have published letters, setting outside editors right as to the facts.

When The Jeffersonian called attention to the Atlanta Constitution of June 22, 1913, in which the new partnership of Slaton with Rosser was announced, and showed that Slaton had been Leo Frank's lawyer, throughout Slaton's gubernatorial term, a wet blanket fell on the agitation against our State.

Outsiders at length began to understand our deep indignation at Slaton's perfidy, in acting in the double capacity of our Governor and Frank's lawyer.

The September-October number of the American Law-Review (St. Louis, Mo.) editorially discusses lynch law and the Frank case, and does so with a judicial temper and legal ability altogether admirable.

Read it, and see how completely this National Law Review sustains the position taken more than a year ago by The Jeffersonian.

The tragic end of the Frank case in Georgia offers a new text for a sermon on American criminal procedure. It is a new phase of Lynch law. Now Lynch law is unknown in countries where justice, not form, is the court's motto. In the United States procedure is king, and this judicial monarch has little care whether right is overthrown or wrong triumphs, so long as his claims to precedence are respected.

Lynch law is the natural result of a lack of confidence and respect by the people in their courts and magistrates. The Docket recalls no instance of it, where one suspected of a crime and put on trial, had been acquitted by a jury, with the full concurrence of a bench of judges. But when a criminal has been found guilty by Twelve men and on appeal to a higher court his conviction has been set aside, not on the ground that in the opinion of the Bench the man was not guilty, but because the word "the" has been omitted in the indictment or all the "i's" had not been dotted or all the "t's" crossed, then it is that Judge Lynch takes a hand. It is the protest of the people against what they regard as the treason of the judicial authorities. An indignant and outraged community can see no other method of righting the wrong than to take the law into their own hands, and mete out the punishment which the law has declared, but which the Courts are seeking to nullify.

Frank was convicted of a murder by a jury of twelve men after a long trial in which he was defended by able and astute counsel. All the technicalities which our American criminal procedure gives to the accused his lawyers took advantage of. His case was appealed to the State Supreme Court and the Supreme Court of the United States. These tribunals affirmed the judgment. The State of Georgia had a Board of Pardons to assist the Governor in his prerogative of mercy and to this body the condemned man appealed, but his appeal was rejected. But while the law was being followed by the State with exactness, a host of newspapers, mostly in other States, began a "campaign" to reverse the decisions of the properly constituted State and Federal tribunals. People thousands of miles away from the scene were urged to give their opinions that Frank was not guilty, and from all over the land the response came and the Georgia authorities were deluged with petitions from men and women from Texas to Minnesota and from New York to California that Frank be not hanged. Of course, everybody who was opposed to capital punishment signed these petitionsâ€”for to these persons the guilt or innocence of the accused was immaterialâ€”they belong to that class of our Citizens who are against the enforcement of any law which they do not approve of. To these must be added the sentimentalists who admire a criminal more than they do an honest citizen, and who delight to send flowers and gifts to the death cells. And finally there is that large body of men and women who think themselves qualified to decide any question that may be submitted to them at a moment's notice, and who are delighted to be called upon to criticise any official action of any kind in any part of the land or of the world. And this "campaign" began, it should be remembered, long before the case had been submitted to the appellate courts, and was therefore, as a matter of law, a gross contempt of those courts, and in any country where the judicial tribunals are stronger than the newspapers, would be severely punished by fine and imprisonment.

The State of Georgia, in so far as the investigation and punishment of crime committed within its territory is concerned, is an independent sovereignty. It has established courts and forms of procedure, and all the rights of accused persons are preserved by its Constitution. And that its courts have the confidence of its citizens in as high a degree as those of its sister States there is no doubt, and that the decision in the Frank case was approved by the people of Georgia there is also no doubt. But now came a host of outsiders who declared that Frank was innocent; that his judges were weak, cowardly and perjured. Perhaps had this come in the form of a declaration by some kind of judicial authority in other States, a body of men who had taken the time to examine the evidence, and pass upon the facts, with the patience and care of a high International tribunal, the people of Georgia would not have resented it, they might have welcomed it. But when it came from a mob, what could you expect?

Certainly the people of Georgia might well protest against this method of procedure in the trial of one accused of a great crime. That there are grave defects in our judicial system everyone must admit. But would trial by referendum be an improvement? Very few people we imagine would be willing to have the question of life and liberty submitted to a popular vote. Every civilized nation has determined that the guilt or innocence of one accused of crime and the punishment to be meted out to the criminal shall be decided by regular Courts of Justice presided over by trained jurists and that the questions of fact shall be submitted to twelve menâ€”a jury of his peers. This is the best that civilization has been able to evolve so far in its history. These tribunals may sometimes err, whereby innocent men are sent to the gallows and guilty men are set free; but no human system is perfect and mistakes will occur sometimes in any system. But the agitation in the Frank case was a protest against this historical and well ordered method. It was a clamor that questions of guilt or innocence should be decided, not by the established tribunals, but by popular vote. It was a demand that those tribunals should solve the problem, not according to the opinions of its judges founded upon the evidence, but upon the views of the multitude, founded upon sentiment and rhetoric.

It is perfectly clear that this is a denial and a negation of all law, and of all authority. We cannot try issues of this kind in this way; we cannot decide the guilt or innocence of an accused man or woman by a show of hands in a town meeting or by counting noses on the street. And the people of no State in the American Union are going to acquiesce in this kind of proceeding. No citizen of one State is willing to submit to the inhabitants of the other States the question whether the decisions of its own tribunals are wrong and must not be enforced. And this is what happened in Georgia. Its courts withstood the popular cry, but a weak and sentimental Governor whose term was about to expire, yielded to the clamor, and overturned the judgments of the courts, without at all denying their correctness. The action of the Governor of Georgia showed a woeful ignorance of the historical reasons for the power of pardon which the Constitution had vested in him.

The editor of the Law Review proceeds to speak of the origin of the pardon-power, giving it a broader scope than it can legally exercise in Georgia, under our Constitution of 1877.

Then he adds:

The Governor (from his public statement explaining his action) was of opinion that there was a reasonable doubt of Frank's guilt. Under these circumstances had he allowed Frank to go to the gallows, because of the clamor of the Georgia mob for his life, he would have been false to his oath and a traitor to the great office which he held. People might have criticised his judgment, but no one could have impugned his motive, had he set Frank free, because he believed that there was a reasonable doubt of his guilt. But when he sentenced him to imprisonment for life for a crime of which he believed him to be innocent, he showed that same fear of public clamor which it was alleged that the judge and jury which tried Frank were unable to resist. The statutes of Georgia said that one convicted of murder in the first degree should die. This sentence, wherever he is able to find extenuating circumstances which so often exist even in the case of the highest crime, the Governor is given power to change. If Frank murdered the young girl in the same manner charged, can you find one extenuating or alleviating fact? The evidence shows none; the friends of Frank never suggested one. If Frank was guilty he richly deserved to be hanged; if he was innocent, it was a crime in the Governor to permit him to pass his life in prison.

And the mob, which a little later came along and executed the sentence which the judicial tribunals had passed, was really more logical than the Executive, for it acted on the assumption that Frank was guilty, and that, if guilty, no penalty but death fitted the crime.

All things considered, this calm, deliberate judgment is a stinging rebuke to Slaton, and a complete exoneration of the mob which executed the sentence which the judicial tribunals had passed.

To say that the Vigilantes of Cobb County were more logical than the Governor who commuted, is to repeat in different words what I have contended ever since the execution of Frank.

Slaton's course cannot be defended at all, because it is so obviously and hopelessly illogical.

That's why Samuel Adams' attempt to defend him was so lame and limping.

If Frank was guilty, it was an executive abuse of power to commute his sentence.

If Frank was innocent, or if there was a reasonable doubt of guilt, it was a pusillanimous act to deny him a pardon.

True, he had not asked for one, and Slaton, when he was "Honeymooning" in the North, actually intimated that he did not grant Frank a pardon because Frank had not asked for it.

He was cynical enough to say, that it was not customary to give more than was asked!

In other words, he left an innocent man under a life-sentence, because the innocent man had not requested freedom.

The Law Review makes one serious mistake of fact, when it states that no tribunal excepting the jury passed upon the question of Frank's guilt.

It seems quite difficult to convince outsiders to the contrary, and to prevail on them to accept the truth, namelyâ€”

That Judge Roan had to weigh that very question when, months after the trial, he decided against Frank the motion for a new trial; and

That the Supreme Court of Georgia carefully weighed the evidence against Frank, and pronounced it sufficient to support the verdict of the jury.

The great American public will settle down to the right view of the Frank case, when it becomes generally known that Governor Slaton was Frank's lawyer, and that the evidence on which the man was convicted was conscientiously weighed by our highest Court, and found sufficient.

The full synopsis of the sworn evidence, published in our September magazine put a sudden end to the clamor against our State.

Page 2. Article number 238.

FROM A FLORIDA DOCTOR.

Dear Sir: About six weeks ago ten of us subscribed for your paper, and until I read the correct evidence in the Leo Frank case, I had my doubts of Frank's guilt, but your Jeff has without a doubt enlightened my mind and many others. Certainly, beyond any question, Leo Frank committed the most fiendish crime ever committed on a pure Christian girl; and when officers such as Governor Slaton uphold sentiments as he did in this case, then the law-abiding men will rise up to defend our womanhood without fear of what our "enlightened North" may say or do. We need thousands of editors of your typeâ€”men who are not afraid to do their duty, whether or not their papers sell. Our daily press has hurt us very bad in not publishing the true facts of this case. When we have more men who will do their duty and make the people know the truth, these crimes will be more scarce, and Jew money will keep out of our courts.

You have many friends in Florida, and will have more when they read your papers; and Floridians stand just as squarely for you as does anybody in Georgia.

May your good work prosper for many years to come.

Fraternally yours,
DR. C. M. YEARWOOD.
Florida.

References

Watson, T. E. (1915, November 4). The American Law Review, on the Frank Case. The Jeffersonian. https://t.co/bmZX9UJiNL

Yearwood, C. M. (1915, November 4). From a Florida doctor. The Jeffersonian. https://t.co/kWrEo9OyZ8

text:
Dear Governor-elect @pweiser, 

First, allow me to congratulate you on your victory yesterday, as campaigns are a grind. Though I did not cast my vote for you, I still sincerely wish you wisdom and discernment in this new role. Despite our differences, Scripture commands Christians to pray "for kings and all who are in high positions" (1 Timothy 2:2) and to seek the welfare of the city where God has placed us (Jeremiah 29:7), and so I wish to share that our family will be praying regularly for you in this role overseeing our state. 

As you prepare to take office, I offer some counsel from a book you likely are familiar with, that being the book of Daniel. Daniel, serving in Nebuchadnezzar’s court, told the king the truth, and the central truth he told him was this: "the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will." (Daniel 4:17). Your victory on Tuesday was given by God, and must be rendered unto Him. Colorado is not yours, nor the Democratic Party's, nor does it truly even belong to us voters here. It belongs to the Lord's, and you will ultimately answer to Him for how you govern it these next four years.

My counsel is both wisdom and warning, and a reminder that God is the one ruling, and thus out of all the sincerity of my heart, I offer this wisdom to you now. Nebuchadnezzar went on to set up a golden image on the plains of Dura, setting himself up against the God of heaven. He created a rival religion, with its own creed, its own liturgy, and its own penalty for hersey and demanded that all people go along with it, lest the weight and power of the king's power be turned on them. 

Colorado, both under your predecessors and with the support of your past office, has raised its own image, that of the autonomous self. It declares that man may become woman, that marriage is not the Lord's to define, and that the child in the womb may be killed at any point before birth. Like the satraps and officials of Nebuchadnezzar did many years ago, your office has played its part in demanding public homage, that all would bow before this false idol. Jack Phillips was hauled before a Civil Rights Commission and taken to court for more than a decade straight because he would not bow. Similarly for Lorie Smith, your office defended the state's efforts to force her to bow. The Kelly Loving Act carries on this effort, equating gender ideology as a civil rights violation. 

These are not neutral ideologies, for there is no such thing. These policies you and many of your predecessors have pushed demand the same homage that Nebuchadnezzar demanded on the plains of Dura, that we bow before an idol made by man. I ask you to abandon this course of action and govern with an appropriate fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of all wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). 

In Daniel 4, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great tree that grew and covered the whole earth, and then was cut down. Daniel's counsel to him is my counsel to you: "break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed, that there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity" (Daniel 4:27). Nebuchadnezzar did not listen and carried on in his arrogance. A year later he stood on his palace roof and said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power?" (4:30). That night he was driven out to the fields, to eat grass like an ox until he learned that “the Most High rules the kingdoms of men” (4:32) and began to walk in submission and repentance before the Lord.

While your party may preach a message of "justice", I am afraid that you have conflated true righteousness and justice with that which "sets itself up against the knowledge of God" (2 Corinthians 10:5).

NORTH ROYALTON, OHIO HAS LOST A FIREFIGHTER, A HUSBAND, AND A FATHER OF TWO

Firefighter/Paramedic Ryan Milligan, 36, of the North Royalton Fire Department, died Monday night after becoming trapped in the basement of a burning house in Broadview Heights.

His crew had gone on mutual aid to the house fire on West Royalton Road.

A second firefighter, Andrew Protsman, 38, was seriously hurt and is expected to recover.

Milligan grew up in Seven Hills and had served with North Royalton since August 2016. He also served on the Seven Hills fire department and graduated from Normandy High School in 2009.

He had just signed up for the lieutenant's exam.

He leaves behind his wife, Laura, and two young children.

Rest in peace, Ryan. 

You were the best America has to offer, and you always will be.

text:
Content warning: this post concerns the 1913 murder of a 13 year old girl and the legal fight over the man convicted of killing her.

This is a catch-up post. We missed this article on its anniversary, so we are sharing it now.

On Wednesday, June 11, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Journal printed a card on page 6: "T. B. Felder Accounts for Subscriptions Received." The deck read, "Says Only $102 Was Paid Into Fund to Employ Burns Detectives."

Mary Anne Phagan, 13, was murdered at the National Pencil Company on Saturday, April 26, 1913. Her boss, factory superintendent Leo Frank, was convicted of her murder that August.

Who was Felder? Thomas B. Felder was a well known Atlanta lawyer of the firm Felder, Anderson, Dillon & Whitman. In May 1913 he said he had lived in Atlanta 23 years and had once been a solicitor general, which is a district prosecutor. He kept one foot in respectable Atlanta and one foot among men like Colyar, whom Felder's own witnesses swore was a forger and a jailbird.

In May 1913, Felder led a public drive to raise money to bring the William J. Burns detective agency into the Phagan case. He said it was to find the killer. The police said it was something else.

THE DICTOGRAPH

A dictograph was an early hidden microphone. On Wednesday, May 21, 1913, detectives hid one behind a dresser in Room 31 of Williams House No. 2, a hotel at 34-36 North Forsyth Street. Wires ran through a keyhole to Room 32, where stenographer George M. Gentry took down every word he could hear in shorthand and later swore to it (The Atlanta Journal, May 23, 1913).

In Room 31 sat Felder, A. S. Colyar, and G. C. Febuary, the secretary to Chief of Detectives Newport A. Lanford. Febuary typed the police affidavits in the Phagan case. They were kept in the chief's safe.

Here is what the record shows Felder saying.

He wanted the papers. Febuary asked, "You want the Coleman affidavit and all other Phagan affidavits that I can get hold of." Felder answered, "Yes." (J. W. Coleman was Mary's stepfather.)

He named a price. "If the papers will do what you think they will do, I will give you a thousand dollars for them."

He promised protection from the law. When Colyar warned that stealing the papers could mean prison, Felder said, "Penitentiary, hell. They can't put you in the penitentiary as long as Hugh Dorsey is solicitor general." Then: "Why I can control the judge, the mayor and Hugh Dorsey."

He also talked of dirt on the two police chiefs, Chief of Police Beavers and Chief Lanford. The plan was to hand off the files at East Lake, outside the city.

Think about what that means. A private lawyer offered a police clerk $1,000 to take secret murder files out of the detective chief's safe, while the case was still open. That is a bribe offer, caught on a wire and sworn to under oath. Honest men looking for a killer do not buy the evidence out the back door.

THE DEFENSE VERSION

Felder's side said it was a frame up. Felder gave The Atlanta Constitution four sworn statements calling Colyar a lifelong crook who should not be believed (May 25, 1913). Burns agent C. W. Tobie swore no one had asked him to work for Frank (same day).

OUR ANSWER

Attacking Colyar does not erase the record. The words were taken down by Gentry, not Colyar, and they are Felder's own words. And notice whom Felder trusted with his deal: a man Felder himself publicly branded a crook.

Who was paying? On the same record, Felder told how he offered to represent Mary's stepfather for free, saying "it isn't necessary for you to pay me any money, that has all been arranged." Chief Lanford said openly whose side Felder was on. On June 10, 1913, The Atlanta Journal reported that "Lanford charges that Felder was employed by Frank and is seeking for that reason to shield him."

So the Burns fund was not about finding the truth. It was a way to steer the hunt, with the police files in hand, away from Leo Frank.

THE ARTICLE

Less than three weeks after the dictograph story broke, Felder gave up. His card says only $102 was ever paid in. Each of the three daily papers, the Journal, the Constitution and the Georgian, had pledged $100, and none of those pledges was paid. He gave the money back, paid the costs from his own pocket, and said his connection with "the controversy" was ended. He asked the papers to stop printing anything that reflected on him "either as a lawyer or an individual."

The people of Atlanta had stopped giving. They had read the dictograph.

The case against Leo Frank never needed Felder or his fund. It was built by Atlanta's detectives and Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, proved to a Fulton County jury, and upheld by the Georgia Supreme Court.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

Appendix: Full article transcript

The Atlanta Journal, Last Edition,

Wednesday, June 11, 1913,

Vol. XXXI. No. 108,

PAGE 6, COLUMN 1.

T. B. FELDER ACCOUNTS FOR SUBSCRIPTIONS RECEIVED

Says Only $102 Was Paid Into Fund to Employ Burns Detectives

Attorney Thomas B. Felder Wednesday morning issued a card to the public in which he accounts for the funds subscribed to employ the Burns detectives to work upon the Phagan murder case. He reports that but $102 was collected.

Mr. Felder announces that all subscriptions paid in have been returned to the subscribers and that those who have subscribed but have not yet paid are not expected to do so. He submits a letter and detailed statement from C. N. Anderson, the treasurer of his law firm, in which it is stated that the expenses incident to the employment of the Burns detectives have been charged to Mr. Felder's personal account.

In conclusion Mr. Felder says that his connection with the controversy is ended and that he will, in due season, ask a committee from the bar association to pass upon the regularity of his employment in the Phagan case.

MR. FELDER'S CARD.

Following is Mr. Felder's card:

"To the Public:

"I beg to subit [sic] a statement of receipts and disbursements in connection with your contributions to the fund that it was proposed to raise for the employment of the Burns agency to investigate the murder of Mary Phagan:

"First. I submit a letter addressed to me by Mr. C. N. Anderson.

"Second. A statement prepared by Mr. Anderson, showing all moneys received by my law firm.

"Third. Mr. Charles I. Ryan, who was designated as custodian of the fund without his knowledge or consent, informs me that he has already returned to the contributors whatever money was paid in to him.

"Fourth. The Atlanta Journal subscribed $100, and I am informed that certain subscriptions were made to it. This subscription has not been paid in and is not expected, and The Journal is hereby requested to return to the contributors any sums that it has received.

"Fifth: The Atlanta Constitution subscribed $100, and I am informed that certain subscriptions were made to it. This subscription has not been paid in and is not expected, and the Constitution is hereby requested to return to the contributors any sums that it has received.

"Sixth. The Atlanta Georgian subscribed $100, and I am informed that certain subscriptions were made to it. This subscription has not been paid in and is not expected, and the Georgian is hereby requested to return to the contriubotrs [sic] any sums that it has received.

HUNDREDS OF DOLLARE [sic] SUBSCRIBED.

"In addition to the above and foregoing, permit me to say in conclusion that additional sums aggregating several hundred dollars were subscribed by the public, but were not paid, and payment has not been and will not be requested.

"With the above and foregoing statement, I pledge the public not to trespass further upon their time and patience, as my connection with the controversy is ended. I will in due season ask a committee from the Bar association to pass upon the regularity of my employment in the Phagan case, and make its report, in accordance with the evidence.

"I request the newspapers in the city of Atlanta in the future to refrain from publishing any statement that can be by the public construed as a reflection upon me either as a lawyer or an individual.

"THOMAS B. FELDER."

MR. ANDERSON'S LETTER.

Mr. Anderson's letter to Mr. Felder, regarding the subscriptions, follows:

"Atlanta, Ga., June 9, 1913.

"Mr. T. B. Felder,

"Felder, Anderson, Dillon & Whitman, City.

"Dear Sir:

"In connection with the business of the above stated firm, of which I am a member, I occupy the position of treasurer. All letters addressed to the firm are placed upon my desk and are distributed by me, all moneys and checks paid in are turned over to me for appropriate disposition.

"I have received from contributions to the Burns fund $102. Several of the contributions were anonymously made; in the majority of the other cases contributors requested that their names be withheld, and in some cases the addresses of the parties making the contributions were unknown to me. Under your direction, I am returning to the contributors the several amounts contributed by them, where the names and addresses of the contributors are known, and I am directed by you to return the balance upon their request.

"I also desire to say that you have directed me to charge whatever disbursements have been made, which, by the way, are several times over larger than the contributions that have come in, to your personal account. This I have done.

"I beg to remain,

"Very truly yours,

(Signed)

"C. N. ANDERSON."

DETAILED STATEMENT.

The detailed statement of funds paid in, as prepared by Mr. Anderson, follows:

May 15—Check, Joseph Hirsch $25.00
May 15—Check, anonymous 30.00
May 16—Check, anonymous 1.00
May 16—Check, anonymous 5.00
May 17—Check, not authorized to give name 1.00
May 17—Check, not authorized to give name 1.00
May 17—Check, not authorized to give name 25.00
May 17—Check, not authorized to give name 5.00
May 23—Check, not authorized to give name 1.00
May 26—Check, not authorized to give name 5.00
May 26—Check, not authorized to give name 3.00
$102.00

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it "unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 billion? Hi

text:
When We Ask God to Follow Us | The Mid-Week Memo | November 4, 2026
Our new book, Embracing the Way, launches November 24! For the next four weeks, we’re sharing excerpts that offer a glimpse of the journey. This week, Colleen shares a question that interrupted her success.

Twenty years ago, I—Colleen—sat on a runway in Miami after facilitating a strategic-planning session for a room filled with highly accomplished people.

By almost every outward measure, my life was going well. I was earning good money, receiving praise for my work, and developing a reputation for being able to “read the tea leaves”—to recognize what was happening in an organization and anticipate what needed to happen next. I had even surprised myself with how successful I had become.

As I sat there reviewing the day and quietly congratulating myself, something happened that changed the trajectory of my life. It felt as though an invisible hand reached into my carefully constructed life and awakened me with a question:

What good is it for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul? (Mark 8:36 NIV)

I had known that verse for years. But on that runway, it was no longer an abstract teaching. It became deeply personal.

I had spent much of my life asking what I could accomplish. I had not stopped long enough to ask what all that striving was doing to me—or whether the life I was building was the life God was inviting me to live.

I wrote the verse on the first page of my to-do journal. That placement was fitting. My life had become organized around things to accomplish, problems to solve, and goals to reach. But now another question had entered the conversation:

What is my life really for?

By that point, I had been a Christian for more than twenty years. I loved God, believed in Jesus, and knew the truth of the gospel. The question was not whether I was committed to Christ. The question was whether I was surrendering my actual life to Him.

Could I belong to Jesus and yet build much of my life around achievement, recognition, control, and self-reliance? Could I believe the right things about God while still living as though everything depended upon me? Gradually, I began to recognize the prayer beneath much of my activity: God, here is what I have decided to do. Will You please join me and bless it?

I was asking God to follow me.

The point: Following Jesus begins with surrendering the life we keep asking Him to bless. This week, ask Him: “Where am I asking You to follow me instead of following You?”

Excerpt source: Introduction, The Life We Were Made For, pages 1–2.

text:
If you're a Catholic, I want you to know that from now until November 8, you still have an opportunity to obtain a PLENARY INDULGENCE for the souls in Purgatory. Especially for your loved ones. 
Listen carefully so that you don't miss anything.

All you have to do is devoutly visit a cemetery and pray for the dead, even if it is just a mental prayer.

But there are other conditions you must fulfil if you want to obtain a plenary indulgence. Let me explain.

First, you must be in a state of grace. You must also have the intention of gaining the indulgence and offering it for a deceased soul.

Second, you must visit a cemetery between November 1 and November 8 and pray for the departed. You don't necessarily have to visit the grave of the particular person you are praying for. Any cemetery will do.

Third, you must receive sacramental confession. The good thing is that one confession can suffice for several plenary indulgences. You don't have to go for confession every single day.

Fourth, you must receive Holy Communion. However, you need to receive Holy Communion each time you want to gain a plenary indulgence. So, if you want to gain five plenary indulgences over five days, you need to receive Holy Communion five times.

Fifth, you must pray for the intentions of the Holy Father. One Our Father and one Hail Mary are sufficient for this. You can, of course, say more prayers if you wish.

Sixth, and this is very important, you must be completely detached from every sin, including venial sin. This means that you must sincerely reject every attachment to sin. If you fulfil all the other conditions but lack this complete detachment, you may obtain only a partial indulgence.

Now, you should also know that there is an important distinction here.

You cannot apply a plenary indulgence to another living person, but you can apply it to somebody who has died by way of suffrage.

Pope St. Paul VI explained this in his writing, "Indulgentiarum Doctrina." He says:

"Partial as well as plenary indulgences can always be applied to the dead by way of suffrage."

Now, what do we mean by suffrage?

When we say suffrage, we mean that we cannot independently release a person from Purgatory by our own authority. Rather, we offer the indulgence to God on behalf of that soul, and God applies it according to His mercy.

So, you can offer a plenary indulgence for a particular deceased person, including a loved one.

Let me give you guys a few final clarifications.

You can gain only one plenary indulgence per day under the ordinary rules. One confession can cover several indulgences, but each indulgence requires its own Holy Communion and prayer for the Pope's intentions.

You do not have to fast, give alms, recite the Rosary or say any special prayer formula to obtain this particular cemetery indulgence.

Also, remember that the indulgence is specifically for the faithful departed. You are not obtaining another plenary indulgence for yourself on those same days.

So, between now and November 8, let us remember the souls in Purgatory. Visit a cemetery, pray for the departed and offer the indulgence for them.

Remember, the souls in Purgatory can no longer obtain indulgences for themselves. But we, the Church militant, can assist them through our prayers and the spiritual treasures of the Church.

Let us not forget the faithful departed. They need our prayers too.

Musa Abdraim, a 52-year-old former boxer and father of five, was at the airport seeing off relatives when he heard screaming. He walked up and offered to swap places with the hostage, telling the attacker: “Take me hostage instead of her.”

The attacker agreed. When he was briefly distracted, Abdraim grabbed the knife with his bare hands, wrestled him down, and held him until police and airport security piled in.

Ron DeSantis Had a Very Different Night Than Greg Abbott….. And It Says Something About His Brand.

Look at Florida and Texas.

Two large states. Two nationally known governors. Two very different outcomes on the same night.

In Texas, the incumbent governor lost. The Senate race also went the other way.

In Florida, Republicans held the governorship and the Senate seat.

DeSantis wasn’t on the ballot. But the governing identity he spent eight years building was part of the election. The candidate who won campaigned on continuing that direction.

That gives him something rare: a brand that survived a change in leadership on a difficult night.

Texas produced the opposite result in a state considered deeply red.

One of the harder tests of any brand is what happens after the person who shaped it is no longer the face of it.

Florida and Texas just offered two different case studies.

Whether that changes how people view DeSantis’s future is an open question.

After last night, the conversation looks different.

How do you think this shapes the future?

THE PRESS
•PEN International said Monday that at least 17 journalists were killed over the past 12 months in circumstances possibly linked to their reporting, in at least six countries: Mexico 6, Guatemala 4, Colombia 2, Peru 2, Ecuador 2 and Haiti 1.
