text:
Hundreds of fire ants. One hole. Not a single one of them in charge.

Read that again, because the last part is the one that should bother you.

Nobody is giving orders in this footage. There is no foreman, no scout captain, no queen standing at the edge of the tunnel pointing a tiny arm at the dark. And yet something is being decided, collectively, in real time, by creatures whose individual brains hold a few hundred thousand neurons. For comparison, yours holds roughly 86 billion.

So how does a crowd of insects with almost no individual intelligence behave like it has a plan?

That question is the real subject of this video. The hole is just the stage.

Let me tell you what you are about to look at, without telling you what happens.

Fire ants are not a fringe species you have to hunt for in some remote jungle. They are one of the most successful insects ever to travel the planet with human help. The red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta, is native to South America. It reached the United States in the 1930s, most likely arriving through the port of Mobile, Alabama, hidden in cargo. Within a few decades it had spread across the American South, and it has since turned up in Australia, China, Taiwan and beyond. A creature smaller than a grain of rice crossed an ocean and rewrote the map.

You can tell a lot about an animal from how it travels. This one travels as a society.

And a society is exactly what you are looking at, even when the frame seems to hold only a few ants at a time. What you see on the surface is a tiny sample of something much larger underneath. A mature fire ant colony can number in the hundreds of thousands of workers. Most of them are below ground right now, in a network of chambers and galleries that can reach down several feet into the soil. The ants you spot on top are the visible edge of a body that mostly lives out of sight.

Think about that scale for a moment. The mound is not a pile of dirt. It is the outer skin of a structure that was excavated grain by grain, by animals with no blueprint, no architect, and no concept of the word "mound."

Now add the hole.

A hole is a different kind of object from a mound. A mound is something the colony built. A hole is something they have to deal with. It is an opening into the unknown, and for a species whose survival depends on knowing exactly what is happening around the nest, an unknown opening is not neutral. It is a question the whole colony has to answer, and it has to answer it without anyone who understands the question.

This is where fire ants become genuinely unsettling to think about.

When one ant finds something interesting, it does not report to a supervisor. It leaves a chemical trace. Other ants pick that trace up with their antennae, follow it, and add their own. The more ants that walk a route, the stronger the signal gets, and the stronger the signal gets, the more ants walk it. That loop is the entire engine. It has no memory of its own, no goals, no opinion. It just amplifies whatever the first few ants happened to find.

Which means the outcome of a situation like this can hinge on something as arbitrary as which ant got there first.

I keep returning to that. The most organized-looking behavior in the animal kingdom is built on a foundation of small accidents that happen to snowball.

Here is the part most people never learn about fire ants, and it changes how you watch them.

They are not just good at marching in lines. They are one of the few animals known to behave, under the right conditions, almost like a material. Researchers who study them describe a colony that can flow like a liquid and hold its shape like a solid, depending on what the moment demands. When floodwater rises, workers lock their bodies together into a floating raft with the queen and the young protected inside. The raft sheds water. It rotates its members from the bottom to the top. It can drift for a long time and come ashore intact.

Think about the design problem that raft solves. Every single ant in it is a bad swimmer. Every single ant in it will drown alone. Together, they are a boat that nobody built and nobody steers.

That is the creature you are about to watch investigate a space it has never seen.

I want to be careful here, because I am not going to oversell this. I am not going to tell you the ants are afraid, or curious, or brave. I do not know what an ant feels, and neither does anyone else. What I can tell you is that the way they collectively approach an unfamiliar space has been studied, and the findings are stranger than any story I could invent.

Take tunneling. Engineers at Georgia Tech spent years watching fire ants dig in lab setups, and one result stuck with the scientific community. In a tunnel, you would expect traffic jams. Narrow passage, many workers, two-way movement. Any human construction crew would gridlock. Instead the ants kept the flow moving, and a surprisingly large share of them did very little of the actual digging. Something like a third of the workers did the bulk of the work while the others stayed put, and that apparent laziness seems to help keep the passage from clogging. Inefficiency, at the individual level, is part of what makes the group efficient.

That finding alone should make you suspicious of every assumption you carry about teamwork.

So when you see a crowd of them pressing toward a dark opening, you are not watching chaos, and you are not watching a plan. You are watching something in between, a system that has no word in ordinary language. Scientists call it collective behavior. Everyone else just calls it creepy.

And the stakes, for the ants, are not abstract.

An opening that appears where no opening was before is a risk to the nest, or a resource for it, and the colony cannot tell which until it explores. Explore too little, and you miss food or a way to expand. Explore too much, and you spend the lives of workers on nothing. The colony has to price that tradeoff without any individual understanding it, using only the sum of thousands of tiny, local decisions.

That tradeoff is the quiet drama in the footage. Not danger in the cinematic sense. Something older. The cost of finding out.

Now let me widen the lens, because the ants are only half of this story.

Every piece of footage like this has two parties, even when only one of them is visible. There is the colony, and there is the person who decided that the colony was worth watching. That second party is easy to forget, and it is the one who set the entire situation in motion.

Think about what it takes to even film this. It takes someone who looks at the ground and sees something other than ground. Most of us walk over thousands of these societies in a lifetime without registering a single one. We treat the soil beneath our feet as a surface, when it is closer to a city.

There is a number I like to use to reset my sense of proportion. Researchers who have tried to weigh the world's ants against the world's humans have come up with estimates that put the combined mass of all ants in the same conversation as the combined mass of all people. Ants are not a footnote to the planet. They are one of its main characters, and we have been reading the book without noticing them.

That changes the tone of a short video about a hole.

It stops being a novelty clip and starts being a rare window. For a few seconds, a very large and very old form of intelligence, one that does not look like anything we usually call intelligence, becomes visible at human scale.

And here is where people split into two camps.

The first camp watches and feels wonder. They see a living machine made of living parts, and they want to know how it works. They send the clip to a friend with a single line: look at this.

The second camp watches and feels something closer to unease. Fire ants have a reputation, and it is earned. The name is not a metaphor. The sting delivers venom built largely from alkaloids, and for most people it produces an immediate burning sensation, followed by a small white pustule within a day. The ants do not sting once and leave. They tend to grip with their jaws and sting repeatedly, which is part of why a disturbed mound is something people learn to respect early and permanently. For a small share of people, a sting can trigger a serious allergic reaction, and that is a medical emergency rather than an inconvenience.

So the second camp is not being irrational. They are remembering a mound they stepped on once, years ago, and the next several hours of their life.

What fascinates me is that both reactions are completely correct at the same time.

The same animal that is an engineering marvel is also a genuine ecological and public health problem. In the places where it has spread, it has been blamed for harm to ground-nesting wildlife, damage to crops and electrical equipment, and injuries to people and livestock. The species that built a raft out of its own bodies is also the species that has cost economies billions of dollars. You do not get to pick which of those facts to keep.

I think this is why the footage grips people the way it does. It sits exactly on the line between admiration and wariness, and you cannot fully resolve it in either direction.

Let me raise something else, because it is the thing I found myself thinking about long after I watched it.

We have a habit of imagining that being small means being simple. It is such a deep assumption that we rarely notice we hold it. A fire ant weighs almost nothing, lives for a short time, and has a brain you could not see without magnification. By any ordinary measure it is a trivial animal.

And yet a few hundred thousand of them, linked by nothing but touch and scent, can survive floods, dig structures that outlast seasons, divide labor without a manager, and respond to novelty without anyone knowing what novelty is.

If the whole is smarter than the parts, where exactly does the intelligence live?

It does not live in the ant. You can examine one for as long as you like and you will never find it. It does not live in the queen, who is far less of a commander than the word suggests. It does not live in the mound. It appears only in the interaction between them, the way a melody does not live in any single note.

I find that idea both beautiful and slightly vertigo-inducing. It means intelligence is not always a thing an animal has. Sometimes it is a thing a crowd does.

Which brings me back to the footage, and to what you should actually watch for when you press play.

Do not watch for the dramatic moment. Watch for the hesitation. Watch for the way the group commits to something before anything has been settled. Watch the difference between an individual that moves and a colony that decides. If you look closely enough, you will start to see the exact point where one turns into the other, and I promise that once you notice it you will not be able to stop noticing it.

I am deliberately not telling you what the ants find, or whether they find anything at all. That is not coyness. It is that the answer matters less than the way the question gets asked, and the way a question gets asked is something you can only really understand by seeing it with your own eyes.

There is one more thing, though, and I will say it plainly because it is true.

Somewhere in the final seconds, something shows up that I did not expect, and it quietly reframes everything that came before it. I will not tell you what it is. I will only tell you that the first time through, I missed what it meant, and the second time through I could not look at anything else.

Here is the part I cannot shake.

For all of human history, the most advanced societies on Earth that were not ours were being built a few inches from our shoes. Not on another planet. Not in the deep ocean. In the dirt at the edge of the path, in the yard, in the gap between two paving stones. We built telescopes to look for intelligence among the stars while a species with a very different mind kept running its civilization at the height of our ankles.

That is not an argument for fear. It is an argument for attention.

And attention is exactly what this video asks of you.

One more thing, about what the ants actually perceive, because it makes the whole scene feel stranger.

An ant does not experience the world the way we do. Sight is a minor sense for most of them. Their reality is built from smell, taste and touch, delivered through a pair of antennae that work like a combination of nose, fingertips and radio. Every surface carries a chemical message. Every passing nestmate leaves a note about who they are, where they have been and what job they are doing. A fire ant crossing a patch of soil is not looking at it. It is reading it.

So the dark opening that seems so mysterious to us is, for them, a page covered in writing we cannot see. Whatever the colony learns in there, it learns through scent that no human nose could parse, in a language of molecules that was fully developed before the first flower bloomed.

Which means that even when we watch closely, we are watching only the movement, never the conversation. We see bodies. They are exchanging meaning.

That gap is part of why this footage is hard to look away from. You can sense, without being able to prove it, that you are missing most of what is going on. The surface is quiet. The signal underneath is deafening.

And you are about to watch it unfold in real time.

Let me go deeper on why this matters, because the ants have been solving problems for far longer than we have been naming them.

Ants as a group have been around for well over a hundred million years. They were already working out logistics, defense, farming and construction while the ancestors of most modern mammals were still small and nervous. Whatever strategy they use to handle the unknown, it has been tested against ice ages, extinctions, floods and fires. Time is the only peer reviewer that cannot be bribed, and this approach passed.

So when a colony meets something unfamiliar, it is not improvising from scratch. It is running a routine that has been refined across more generations than there are words in this post.

What does that routine look like? In broad terms, it looks like a gamble with very good odds.

Send out a few explorers. Let them wander more or less at random. If one stumbles onto something, mark the path. If the path is good, more ants follow and reinforce it. If it is a dead end, the chemical trail fades on its own, because the scent evaporates and nobody refreshes it. The system forgets automatically. That is a quietly brilliant feature. A bad decision does not need to be corrected by anyone, because it simply stops being repeated.

Humans spend enormous energy trying to admit mistakes. Ants built mistake-forgetting into the chemistry.

Engineers noticed. Entire families of computer algorithms for routing deliveries, directing network traffic and organizing swarms of simple robots were inspired by exactly this behavior. When a logistics company finds an efficient route through a tangle of possibilities, there is a reasonable chance that an insect solved a cousin of the same problem long before a computer did.

So the colony in this footage is not only an animal. It is a working prototype of ideas we are still catching up to.

Now let me bring it back to the emotional core, because this is where the video stops being a science lesson and starts being something you feel.

There is a very specific human instinct at play whenever we see a dark opening. We lean toward it. We want to know what is inside. It is the same instinct that pushed people into caves, down shafts, across oceans and, eventually, off the planet. Curiosity about the unseen is one of the oldest drives we have.

What is strange is that the ants seem to share a version of it. Not as a feeling, as far as anyone can prove, but as a behavior. Faced with an opening, the colony investigates. It sends bodies into the dark and waits to hear back through scent and touch.

Two very different minds, one very old impulse.

And that is the quiet emotional engine of this video, if you let it be. A human looks at an ant colony and wonders what it is doing. An ant colony, in its own way, looks at an opening and wonders what it is. Neither can explain itself to the other. Both are trying to find out.

I know that sounds like a stretch for a short clip of insects and soil. Watch it and decide for yourself whether it is.

There is also a harder question hiding underneath all this, and I would rather say it out loud than pretend it is not there.

What do we owe the things we watch?

When we turn our attention onto a living system, even a very small one, we are never fully neutral. Our presence changes what we observe. Our shadow falls across it. Our hands, our tools, our curiosity all arrive as forces in a world that was running quite well before we showed up. The act of looking is an act of intervention, whether or not we admit it.

That is true for ants, and it is true for every wild thing that has ever been filmed for our entertainment.

I am not saying the answer is to stop looking. Attention is how we come to care, and care is how anything gets protected. A species nobody notices is a species nobody defends. But I do think the best nature footage carries a quiet awareness of its own footprint, and the most honest way to watch it is with that awareness switched on.

So here is the question I would leave with you before you press play.

Is curiosity a form of respect, or a form of intrusion?

I do not think the answer is one or the other. I think it depends entirely on what we do after we find out.

Let me add one more layer, because the soil itself deserves a moment.

We tend to treat ground as inert. Something to build on, drive on, dig up and forget. But the top layer of earth is one of the most densely populated places in existence, and ants are among its busiest engineers. Their tunneling moves soil, mixes nutrients, lets water through and lets air in. Where they thrive, the ground behaves differently than where they do not. They are not just living in the landscape. They are quietly editing it.

Fire ants are a special case, because they edit it aggressively. Where they establish, they reshape the community around them, sometimes pushing out the native insects that used to fill the same role. That is the uncomfortable side of their success. The thing that makes them impressive is the same thing that makes them hard to live beside.

Understanding that does not make the footage less compelling. It makes it more honest.

Because the truth about nature, almost always, is that the most fascinating animals are rarely the simplest to love. They are tangled up with our history, our economy, our fears and our mistakes. The ants did not choose to travel in ship cargo. We carried them. The consequences are partly ours.

Which is one more reason to look closely.

Here is what I think is actually happening when a video like this spreads.

People are not sharing it because ants are cute. They are not. People are sharing it because it hands them a feeling they rarely get from a screen: the sense that the world is bigger and stranger than the version they walk through every day. A few seconds of footage punctures the assumption that nothing interesting is happening at ground level. Suddenly the yard has depth. Suddenly the dirt has a population. Suddenly you are not alone in your own garden, and never were.

That sensation, the little jolt of scale shifting, is worth more than most things the internet offers.

And it is free. It is under your feet right now.

A quick note on the word "hidden," because it carries more weight than it seems to.

Hidden from whom? Not from the colony, which maps its own territory with a thoroughness no surveyor could match. Not from the soil, which holds every tunnel and chamber in perfect silence. The only party for whom anything is hidden is us. We are the ones standing outside the map, peering in through a single opening, trying to guess the shape of a structure we cannot enter.

That asymmetry is the quiet tension of the whole scene. A world that knows itself completely, and a visitor who can only glimpse a fraction of it.

Most of what matters in nature works like that. The important part is usually underground, underwater or under the leaf, and we spend our lives interpreting a surface.

So when you see an opening, treat it as an invitation to humility.

You are looking at the door, not the house.

Let me give you something practical, because a post this long should leave you with more than a mood.

When you watch this, try a small experiment. Ignore the individual ants completely. Let your eyes go soft and treat the whole moving surface as one creature. You will notice something odd almost immediately. The group has a kind of body language. It swells toward certain spots and thins out from others. It hesitates as a mass and then commits as a mass. Individual ants vanish into the pattern, and what remains looks uncomfortably like a single animal thinking.

Then flip it. Pick one ant and follow it for a few seconds. You will see something that looks far less impressive: a tiny, jittery body bumping into things, turning, retracing, changing its mind. Nothing about that single animal suggests it is part of a grand design. It looks lost.

Both views are true. That is the entire trick.

A fire ant worker does not live long as animals go. Its whole life is a handful of weeks to months of small, repetitive jobs. It will never understand the colony it belongs to. It will never know the colony has a history. And yet the colony it serves can persist for years and spread across a continent.

If you wanted a clean picture of how a short life can matter inside something long, you could do worse.

There is a human parallel here, and it is a little humbling.

Most of us live as the lost single ant. We make small local decisions with partial information, bump into obstacles, retrace our steps, and rarely see the larger pattern our choices belong to. We assume nothing we do adds up to anything. And then, occasionally, a thousand small choices, made by people who never met, quietly bend the course of a city, a movement, a culture.

Nobody in that crowd planned it. It just snowballed from whoever got there first.

I am not saying ants hold the secret to human society. I am saying they are one of the clearest demonstrations we have that large outcomes do not require large intentions. Sometimes a thing becomes enormous simply because enough small things leaned in the same direction at once.

That is a hopeful idea and a frightening one, and the footage lets you feel both.

Let me return to the hole one last time, because I think it deserves to be treated as more than a prop.

Every living thing has to deal with openings. Doors, gaps, cracks, dark spaces where something unknown might be waiting. A rabbit meets them. A child meets them. A scientist meets them. An entire colony of insects meets them, all at once, with hundreds of bodies and no one to ask what to do.

How a living system handles an opening says almost everything about it. Whether it rushes in or hangs back. Whether it sends one volunteer or ten. Whether it treats the unknown as a threat or an opportunity. Whether it can change its mind halfway through.

That is why I think this particular clip is more than a curiosity. It is a compact study in how life approaches what it does not understand.

And that, not the ants, is the thing worth carrying away.

And if you only take one question from all of this, take the oldest one: how does a crowd with no leader know what to do next? Scientists are still refining the answer. The ants have been living it for ages.

I have tried to write this without spoiling the footage, and I have tried to be honest about what I know and what I do not.

I know the species. I know the scale of the society behind the surface. I know a few of the mechanisms that make the group behave the way it does. What I do not know is what you will take from the moment itself, because that part is not in the facts. It lives in the watching.

So I am going to leave out the ending on purpose.

I will say only this. When the video finishes, you may find yourself looking at the ground differently for the rest of the day. You may slow down at the edge of a lawn. You may catch yourself crouching beside a sidewalk crack like an idiot, watching a line of tiny bodies carry a crumb across a distance that, for them, is a journey.

If that happens, the video did its job.

Small bodies. Enormous questions. Almost no one is watching them closely enough. That is the whole deal, and it is more than enough reason to look.

You have been walking above a city your whole life.

Go and watch it, slowly.

Genuinely how many midfielders can you think currently that’s on the level of Rice? That can do everything he does effectively like this? Tackles, ball carrying, creativity, physicality, what do you want that he doesn’t have?? I can only think of Bellingham right now. No one else. 

He combines everything you can think of in one person. He can win the ball back, drive through midfield, break lines with his passing, create chances, arrive in the box, score goals and still have the physical capacity to track back and defend.

You can mention players like Rodri, Valverde, Vitinha and Bellingham, but even with those names, you’re talking about different profiles and different strengths. Very few midfielders offer the same combination of athleticism, defensive responsibility, ball progression and attacking contribution.

But the craziest thing is his consistency. Every match day, you’re guaranteed at least 7.5/10 performance. He hardly get a bad game at all. It’s just like those all timer players we usually rate. 

He’s arguably the best midfielder in the world right now.

text:
Study Notes - (Pulpit Version Explained) Psalms 134:1-3
EXPOSITION
THE" Little Psalter" of" Songs of Ascents" terminates here with a short psalm, due probably to the compiler—a psalm of four lines only. It consists of two portions:
(1) A call from those without the temple, upon God’s servants, who conduct his service within his house during the night season (1Ch_9:33), to praise and thank the Lord in their name for his met-ties vouchsafed to them (Psa_134:1, Psa_134:2); and
(2) a response from those within the temple, who ask God to" bless out of Zion" those who have addressed them. The psalm is very suitable for pilgrim-bands arriving, as they commonly would, late in the day at the temple gates, and announcing their arrival to those within, who would be expecting them, and would call on God to bless their pilgrimage to them (Psa_134:3).
Psa_134:1
Behold. The word calls attention to an immediate need—something that is to be done, and to be done at once. Bless ye the Lord. This must mean "for us"—"on our behalf." Thank God for having brought our journey to a prosperous end. All ye servants of the Lord, which by night stand in the house of the Lord; i.e. ye special servants of the Lord, priests and Levites, now standing within his courts, and engaged in his worship. The temple was never left without a body of priests and Levites, to keep it and sing praises in it.
Psa_134:2
Lift up your hands. The attitude of prayer and praise (Psa_63:4; Psa_119:48; Psa_141:2). In the sanctuary; rather, towards the sanctuary; i.e. towards the holy of holies. Others render, "in holiness." And bless the Lord (compare the first clause of Psa_134:1).
Psa_134:3
The Lord that made heaven and earth (comp. Gen_1:1; Psa_115:15; Psa_121:2; Psa_124:8; Psa_146:6). Bless thee out of Zion. God was regarded as dwelling in Zion, and therefore as giving his blessings out of Zion (comp. Psa_20:2; Psa_53:6; Psa_128:5).
HOMILETICS
Psa_134:1-3
God and man; reciprocal relations.
"It must needs be a matter of conjecture who the speakers are" in this short psalm; but these three verses bring before us the reciprocal relations existing between our God and ourselves, particularly as those engaged in his worship. "Bless ye the Lord … the Lord bless thee."
I. IN APPROACH AND NEARNESS OF SPIRIT. We draw nigh unto him, and he draws nigh unto us (2Ch_15:2; Jas_4:8). We come up to his house to "seek his face’ (Psa_27:8), and he seeks us; he finds us; he makes us conscious of his presence. He manifests himself unto us as not unto the world. And when we leave the sanctuary, and (partly through the help we have gained there) cherish the sense of God’s near presence, and feel that we are "with him ’ everywhere, then is he "with us," not only in nearness of spiritual presence (Psa_139:1-24.), but in fullness of Divine sympathy and the putting forth of Divine power on our behalf.
II. IN PRAYER ON OUR PART, AND IN COMMUNICATION OF TRUTH ON HIS PART. We speak to him in prayer (Psa_134:2). With uplifted hands, in reverent adoration, we pour out our heart in humble, earnest supplication, or in renewing before him and unto him our solemn vows. We may do well to put it to ourselves in these simple terms—that we are together, that with one voice and one thought and hope we may "speak to God." Then we listen as he speaks to us. As we listen to the reading of his Word, we may feel—Surely this is nothing other than God speaking to our hearts. Such a thought should make him that reads and those who hear feel that this is not the least important part of Divine worship, and is not undeserving of our best effort and attention. The preacher in the sanctuary should set before him as his high aim, as his noble and holy function, so to declare his message that, through his human voice, God will be speaking to the people of his charge. Thus, before leaving the house of God, we shall have reverently spoken to him; he will have graciously spoken to us.
III. IN BLESSING. "Bless ye the Lord … the Lord bless thee."
1. We bless God as we offer him our lowly but sincere adoration; as we ascribe to him all power, wisdom, faithfulness, holiness, mercy, patience; as we present to him the tribute of our praise for all his past kindness to us, and especially for his grace to us in Christ Jesus; as we thank him for all he has promised to us in the near and in the further future.
2. He blesses us as he lifts on us the light of his reconciled countenance; as he enlightens our understanding, and enables us to perceive new and fuller truth, or recognize familiar truth more clearly or vividly; as he kindles in our waiting heart a stronger flame of gratitude and love; as he stablishes and strengthens our soul in our purpose of devotion; as he draws out our sympathies with all that suffer and are in need; as he sends us forth from his presence confirmed and enlarged in heart, rejoicing in himself and in his service. It may be added that:
(1) If we honor him, he will honor us (1Sa_2:30).
(2) If we love him, he will love us (Jhn_14:21).
(3) If we crown him Lord of our heart and life, he will crown us with the crown of eternal life.
HOMILIES BY S. CONWAY
Psa_134:1-3
The songs of degrees’ doxology.
This series of psalms ends, as all service of worship should, with the voice of praise and thanksgiving. It is ill if our prayers and varied waiting upon God do not bring us into the spirit which would bless the Lord, and bid all others do the same. That spirit is present in this psalm. Note—
I. THE EXHORTATION HERE GIVEN. "Behold, bless ye the Lord." Now, this psalm, being placed here at the end of the series, bids us look back and trace, in the psalms that have gone before, the manifold reasons wherefore we should bless the Lord. The first of these psalms, Psa_120:1-7; tells of deliverance from cruel enemies; Psa_121:1-8; of God’s continual preservation of his people; Psa_122:1-9; of joy and delight realized in the worship of the Lord; Psa_123:1-4; of waiting continually upon God in times of trouble; Psa_124:1-8; of deliverance from fierce foes; Psa_125:1-5; of experience of God’s guardian care; Psa_126:1-6; of the joy of God’s salvation; Psa_127:1-5; of the Lord alone being our sure Keeper; Psa_128:1-6; of God’s grace and goodness sweetening the home; Psa_129:1-8; of afflictions many, but of preservation in them all; Psa_130:1-8; of God’s blessed uplifting; Psa_131:1-3; of the soul kept in the peace of God; Psa_132:1-18; of the prosperity of the Church; and Psa_133:1-3; of her unity; and now in Psa_134:1-3, there is, as there well may be, the command to bless the Lord. What a long list it is of mercies, and help, and deliverances, and blessings unspeakable! If men will look back along their lives, they too will bless the Lord.
II. To WHOM IT IS ADDRESSED.
1. To all servants of the Lord. For there is none that has not good reason for obeying it. But especially:
2. To them "who by night stand in the house of the Lord." Now, here allusion is made, so it seems, to those whose office it was to minister before the Lord during the night watches—there were priests and Levites who had duties by night as well as by day (1Ch_9:33). There was "a night watch of choristers who kept up the worship of God through the silent hours." Two verses of the psalm seem to have been the salutation of the congregation addressed to them, and Psa_134:3 is their response.
3. And God has yet many servants whose duty is to serve him through the night hours. The sleepless ones—those who from one cause and another have to say, "Thou holdest mine eyes waking." Well is it for such to employ those hours in the praise of the Lord (cf. Psa_63:5, Psa_63:6). And such as the sailor pacing the deck in the night watch, the sentry on guard, the nurse in her ward,—well is it for them in the night to bless the Lord.
4. Or, we may take the night as telling of the night of sorrow—those times of darkness and depression through which we all have to pass (see Paul and Silas in the dungeon at Philippi, at midnight singing praises unto God). How often have these psalms been used by God’s people at such hours, and with what rich results in the quickening of faith and hope and joy in God!
5. And if, as some maintain, there was no later service in the temple than the evening sacrifice, then the many evening congregations gathered together may take these words as addressed to them.
III. HOW IT IS TO BE OBEYED. They were to "lift up their hands to the sanctuary." The body should bear its part; posture and gesture help the spirit.
IV. WHAT COMES OF SUCH OBEDIENCE. The Lord will bless us (Psa_134:3). He who hath all power, who made heaven and earth, he will bless the soul that worships him (cf. Psa_135:3). All who have thus drawn near to God have found that he draws near to them.—S.C.
HOMILIES BY R. TUCK
Psa_134:1
Representative worshippers.
From a Targum we learn that "the custom in the second temple appears to have been this: After midnight the chief of the doorkeepers took the key of the inner temple, and went with some of the priests through the small postern of the Fire Gate. In the inner court this watch divided itself into two companies, each carrying a burning torch; one company turned west, the other east; and so they compassed the court to see whether all were in readiness for the temple service on the following morning. In the bakehouse, where the mincha (meat offering) of the high priest was baked, they met with the cry, ’All well!’ Meanwhile the rest of the priests arose, bathed themselves, and put on their garments. They then went into the stone-chamber (one half of which was the hall of session of the Sanhedrim), and there, under the superintendence of the officer who gave the watchword and one of the Sanhedrim, surrounded by the priests clad in their robes of office, their several duties for the coming day were assigned to each of the priests by lot." It should be always borne in mind that, in the Divine idea, the entire people of Israel made up a nation of priests. Every man was regarded as a consecrated man, separated unto the honor, worship, and service of Jehovah. What were called the actual priests were only representatives of these universal priests, and they were only daily doing materially what every man-priest of the nation was pledged to do, and if he was a true and worthy man, was trying to do 
spiritually. If this point can be clearly seen, a new interest will be found to attach to the various doings of the representative priesthood. Men are always learning from them what they should be and what they should do in a spiritual sense. One thing is set prominently in this psalm. The work of the priests is to "bless Jehovah." This they do in a formal manner by lifting up their hands and voices, waving the censers, etc. Let an Israelite see or hear a priest blessing God, and his heart ought at once to respond, saying, "That is just what I ought to be doing, with heart, and lip, and deed, and above all by the thankful, trustful, devoted spirit of my life."—R.T.
Psa_134:2
Holy hands.
(For the high-priestly benediction, see Numb, 6:24.) Raising suppliant hands is the formal, bodily sign of earnest prayer. Every mental or moral state has its corresponding natural bodily attitude or movement; and raising and stretching forth the opened hands in a receptive attitude is the natural bodily attitude accompanying petition. There is an important alteration in this sentence. It should be, "Lift up your hands to the sanctuary;" and the figure is of the priests turning towards the holy of holies, where the symbol of God’s presence rested, and stretching forth hands of supplication towards it (see Solomon’s attitude at the dedication of the temple).
I. THERE IS AN ELEMENT OF PRAYER IN ALL BLESSING OF GOD. There is for man; there may not be for angels. Man can never offer even his praise without a sense of his unworthiness. So he must always mingle a prayer for pardon and for pitying mercy with his thanksgivings. And he can never draw near to the Divine presence without a sense of need. So say what he may of God, or to God, in his praises, he finds that he always has something to ask for. His dependence always wants to find expression. We are always wrong if there is no prayer in our praises.
II. THE ELEMENT OF PRAYER FINDS EXPRESSION IN UPLIFTED HANDS. Kneeling in prayer is to a great extent a modern device. Easterns stand to pray. So did our forefathers. And so do those who now lead prayers at prayer-meetings. Stretching forth the hands is now regarded as the act of benediction, as in the Catholic and Scotch Protestant Churches. But it is such a universal and natural expression of supplication that it might very wisely be restored to use in private as well as public acts of prayer and praise. The apostle bids us "lift up holy hands, without wrath and doubting."
III. THE UPLIFTED HANDS MUST BE HOLY HANDS. The priests had to wash their hands, as a sign of their putting away all self-indulgence and self-will and all gathered evil before engaging in the praises of Jehovah. And it is the absolutely universal law, "Be ye clean that bear the vessels of the Lord." The symbol of the soul-cleanness which goes with sincerity and gains for us acceptance, is the washed and holy uplifted hands.—R.T.

text:
Interior of Iemitsu’s Mausoleum, Nikkō - Taiyū-in (大猷院) - 1890s 🇯🇵

Japan Through 152 Photographs (circa 1890-1900) 📷🇯🇵
This photograph offers a rare glimpse inside Taiyū-in (大猷院), the mausoleum of Tokugawa Iemitsu (1604–1651), the third shogun of the Tokugawa dynasty, located within the temple complex of Nikkō. Completed in 1653, the mausoleum was built after Iemitsu’s death and reflects his deep reverence for his grandfather, Tokugawa Ieyasu, whose own mausoleum stands nearby at Tōshō-gū.

The interior of the worship hall, or Haiden (拝殿), is richly ornamented with gilded pillars, elaborate carvings and a coffered ceiling. Historical descriptions record 140 dragon images painted across the ceiling, creating an extraordinary decorative canopy above the ceremonial space. The adjoining Ai-no-Ma (相の間), or intermediate chamber, connects the worship hall to the main hall, the Honden (本殿).

Although Taiyū-in shares the elaborate architectural language of Tōshō-gū, its decoration is more restrained. Gold and black form its dominant palette, in contrast to the white and gold associated with Ieyasu’s shrine. This distinction was intentional: Iemitsu wished his own mausoleum to express devotion to his grandfather rather than rival the grandeur of Tōshō-gū.

Today, the Haiden remains accessible to visitors, while the Honden is viewed from outside. The photograph preserves the richly decorated interior of a seventeenth-century memorial complex, offering a record of craftsmanship and religious architecture from the early Edo period.

text:
Ieyasu’s Tomb, Nikko (徳川家康の墓・日光東照宮奥宮) - 1890s 🇯🇵

Japan Through 152 Photographs (circa 1890-1900) 📷🇯🇵

This photograph, bearing the original catalogue caption “1678. Ieyasu’s Tomb, Nikko,” shows the mausoleum monument of Tokugawa Ieyasu within the Okumiya, or Inner Shrine, of Nikkō Tōshō-gū.

At the centre stands a bronze hōtō (宝塔), a reliquary pagoda with a broad roof and a tall ornamental finial. Its richly decorated metal surfaces rise above a stone enclosure, while stone guardian figures stand on either side of the approach. In front of the monument are bronze ritual vessels and an incense burner, arranged as offerings at this sacred site. The surrounding cedar trees create a secluded setting befitting the resting place of one of Japan’s most influential rulers.

Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616), founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, died in 1616. In accordance with the arrangements made after his death, he was transferred from Kunōzan in Shizuoka to Nikkō in 1617, where his spirit was enshrined as Tōshō Daigongen. The original tomb monument was made of stone. It was later reconstructed in bronze, in a Chinese-inspired style, around the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century.

The Okumiya lies beyond the main shrine buildings, reached by a long flight of stone steps through the forest. Its more secluded location contrasts with the elaborate public architecture of the main Tōshō-gū precinct.

This nineteenth-century photograph preserves the appearance of Ieyasu’s tomb monument, its bronze ornamentation and the ritual objects placed before it.
author: photovoyages
authorBio: Old & Vintage

text:
Pillar Door of Temple Gate, Nikko (日光の寺院の門) - 1890s 🇯🇵

Japan Through 152 Photographs (circa 1890-1900) 📷🇯🇵

This photograph, numbered 1596 in Kusakabe Kimbei’s photographic series, presents a detailed view of a temple gate in Nikko. Rather than showing the entire structure, the composition focuses on its architectural elements: the supporting pillars, wooden doors and decorative construction that formed the entrance to a sacred precinct.

In traditional Japanese religious architecture, a gate was more than a passage between two spaces. It marked the transition from the everyday world into the grounds of a temple or shrine. Its proportions, materials and ornamentation expressed the importance of the site and established a formal approach for worshippers.

Nikko is particularly renowned for the elaborate architecture of its religious monuments. The shrines and temples associated with the Tokugawa family were developed and embellished during the Edo period, especially under the patronage of Tokugawa Ieyasu and his grandson, Tokugawa Iemitsu. Their buildings combined sophisticated woodworking, elaborate metal fittings, lacquer and decorative carving.

The pillars were essential structural elements, supporting the heavy roof and framing the entrance. The doors, meanwhile, served both a practical and ceremonial purpose, controlling access to the sacred space while contributing to the visual richness of the architecture.

Although the precise identity of the gate in this photograph remains uncertain, its catalogue title preserves the original description used for the image. The hand-coloured albumen print offers a close study of the craftsmanship and architectural vocabulary that made Nikko one of Japan’s most distinctive religious centres during the late nineteenth century.

text:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) (PART B) “He was carried aloft in the chariots of the Spirit” (En 70:2). In Jubilees 31:16 Isaac is represented as prophesying, and in 25:13 it is said of Rebekah that the “Holy Spirit descended into her mouth.” Sometimes the action of the Spirit is closely connected with the moral life, although this is rare. “The Spirit of God rests” on the man of pure and loving heart (XII the Priestly Code (P), Benj. 8). In Simeon 4 it is declared that Joseph was a good man and that the Spirit of God rested on him. There appears at times a lament for the departed age of prophecy (1 Macc 9:27; 14:41). The future is depicted in glowing colors. The Spirit is to come in a future judgment (XII the Priestly Code (P), Levi 18); and the spirit of holiness shall rest upon the redeemed in Paradise (Levi 18); and in Levi 2 the spirit of insight is given, and the vision of the sinful world and its salvation follows. Generally speaking, this literature is far below that of the Old Testament, both in moral tone and religious insight. Much of it seems childish, although at times we encounter noble passages. There is lacking in it the prevailing Old Testament mood which is best described as prophetic, in which the writer feels constrained by the power of God's Spirit to speak or write. The Old Testament literature thus possesses a vitality and power which accounts for the strength of its appeal to our religious consciousness.
3. The Spirit in the Wisdom of Solomon
We note in the next place a few teachings as to the Spirit of God in Wisd. Here the ethical element in character is a condition of the Spirit's indwelling. “Into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter: nor dwell in the body that is subject unto sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in” (The Wisdom of Solomon 1:4 f). This “holy spirit of discipline” is evidently God's Holy Spirit, for in 1:7 the writer proceeds to assert, “For the Spirit of the Lord filleth the world,” and in 1:8, 9 there is a return to the conception of unrighteousness as a hindrance to right speaking. In The Wisdom of Solomon 7:7 the Spirit of Wisdom comes in response to prayer. In 7:22-30 is an elaborate and very beautiful description of wisdom: “In her is an understanding spirit, holy, one only, manifold, subtle, lively, clear, undefiled, plain, not subject to hurt, loving the thing that is good, quick, which cannot be letted, ready to do good, kind to man, steadfast, sure,” etc. “She is the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness,” etc. No one can know God's counsel except by the Holy Spirit (9:17). The writer of The Wisdom of Solomon was deeply possessed of the sense of the omnipresence of the Spirit of God, as seen in 1:7 and in 12:1. In the latter passage we read: “For thine incorruptible spirit is in all things.”
4. The Spirit in Philo
In Philo we have what is almost wholly wanting in other Jewish literature, namely, analytic and reflective thought upon the work of the Spirit of God. The interest in Philo is primarily philosophic, and his teachings on the Spirit possess special interest on this account in contrast with Biblical and other extra-Biblical literature. In his Questions and Solutions, 27, 28, he explains the expression in Gen_8:1: “He brought a breath over the earth and the wind ceased.” He argues that water is not diminished by wind, but only agitated and disturbed. Hence, there must be a reference to God's Spirit or breath by which the whole universe obtains security. He has a similar discussion of the point why the word “Spirit” is not used instead of “breath” in Gen in the account of man's creation, and concludes that “to breathe into” here means to “inspire,” and that God by His Spirit imparted to man mental and moral life and capacity for Divine things (Allegories, xiii). In several passages Philo discusses prophecy and the prophetic office. One of the most interesting relates to the prophetic office of Moses (Life of Moses, xxiii ff). He also describes a false prophet who claims to be “inspired and possessed by the Holy Spirit” (On Those Who Offer Sacrifice, xi). In a very notable passage, Philo describes in detail his own subjective experiences under the influence of the Holy Spirit, and his language is that of the intellectual mystic. He says that at times he found himself devoid of impulse or capacity for mental activity, when suddenly by the coming of the Spirit of God, his intellect was rendered very fruitful: “and sometimes when I have come to my work empty I have suddenly become full, ideas being, in an invisible manner, showered upon me and implanted in me from on high; so that through the influence of Divine inspiration I have become greatly excited and have known neither the place in which I was, nor those who were present, nor myself, nor what I was saying, nor what I was writing,” etc. (Migrations of Abraham, vii).
In Philo, as in the non-canonical literature generally, we find little metaphysical teaching as to the Spirit and His relations to the Godhead. On this point there is no material advance over the Old Testament teaching. The agency of the Holy Spirit in shaping and maintaining the physical universe and as the source of man's capacities and powers is clearly recognized in Philo. In Philo, as in Josephus, the conception of inspiration as the complete occupation and domination of the prophet's mind by the Spirit of God, even to the extent of suspending the operation of the natural powers, comes clearly into view. This is rather in contrast with, than in conformity to, the Old Testament and New Testament conception of inspiration, in which the personality of the prophet remains intensely active while under the influence of the Spirit, except possibly in cases of vision and trance.
III. The Holy Spirit in the New Testament
In the New Testament there is unusual symmetry and completeness of teaching as to the work of the Spirit of God in relation to the Messiah Himself, and to the founding of the Messianic kingdom. The simplest mode of presentation will be to trace the course of the progressive activities of the Spirit, or teachings regarding these activities, as these are presented to us in the New Testament literature as we now have it, so far as the nature of the subject will permit. This will, of course, disturb to some extent the chronological order in which the New Testament books were written, since in some cases, as in John's Gospel, a very late book contains early teachings as to the Spirit.
1. In Relation to the Person and Work of Christ
(1) Birth of Jesus
In Mat_1:18 Mary is found with child “of the Holy Spirit” (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, ek pneúmatos hagı́ou); an angel tells Joseph that that “which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Mat_1:20), all of which is declared to be in fulfillment of the prophecy that a virgin shall bring forth a son whose name shall be called Immanuel (Isa_7:14). In Luk_1:35 the angel says to Mary that the Holy Spirit (pneuma hagion) shall come upon her, and the power of the Most High (δύναμις Ὑψίστου, dúnamis Hupsı́stou) shall overshadow her. Here “Holy Spirit” and “power of the Most High” are parallel expressions meaning the same thing; in the one case emphasizing the Divine source and in the other the holiness of “the holy thing which is begotten” (Luk_1:35). In connection with the presentation of the babe in the temple, Simeon is described as one upon whom the Holy Spirit rested, to whom revelation was made through the Spirit and who came into the temple in the Spirit (Luk_2:25-28). So also Anna the prophetess speaks concerning the babe, evidently in Luke's thought, under the influence of the Holy Spirit (Luk_2:36).
It is clear from the foregoing that the passages in Matthew and Luke mean to set forth, first, the supernatural origin, and secondly, the sinlessness of the babe born of Mary. The act of the Holy Spirit is regarded as creative, although the words employed signify “begotten” or “born” (γεννηθέν, gennēthén, Mat_1:20; and γεννώμενον, gennō̇menon, Luk_1:35). There is no hint in the stories of the nativity concerning the pretemporal existence of Christ. This doctrine was developed later. Nor is there any suggestion of the immaculate conception or sinlessness of Mary, the mother of our Lord. Dr. C.A. Briggs has set forth a theory of the sinlessness of Mary somewhat different from the Roman Catholic view, to the effect that the Old Testament prophecies foretell the purification of the Davidic line, and that Mary was the culminating point in the purifying process, who thereby became sinless (Incarnation of the Lord, 230-34). This, however, is speculative and without substantial Biblical warrant. The sinlessness of Jesus was not due to the sinlessness of His mother, but to the Divine origin of His human nature, the Spirit of God.
In Heb_10:5 the writer makes reference to the sinless body of Christ as affording a perfect offering for sins. No direct reference is made to the birth of Jesus, but the origin of His body is ascribed to God (Heb_10:5), though not specificallya to the Holy Spirit.
(2) Baptism of Jesus
The New Testament records give us very little information regarding the growth of Jesus to manhood. In Luk_2:40 a picture is given of the boyhood, exceedingly brief, but full of significance. The “child grew, and waxed strong, filled with wisdom (m “becoming full of wisdom”): and the grace of God was upon him.” Then follows the account of the visit to the temple. Evidently in all these experiences, the boy is under the influence and guidance of the Spirit. This alone would supply an adequate explanation, although Luke does not expressly name the Spirit as the source of these particular experiences. The Spirit's action is rather assumed.
Great emphasis, however, is given to the descent of the Spirit upon Jesus at His baptism. Mat_3:16 declares that after His baptism “the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming upon him.” Mrk_1:10 repeats the statement in substantially equivalent terms. Luk_3:22 declares that the Spirit descended in “bodily form, as a dove” (σωματικῷ εἲδει ὡς περιστεράν, somatikō̇ eı́dei hōs peristerán). In Jhn_1:32, Jhn_1:33 the Baptist testifies that he saw the Spirit descending upon Jesus as a dove out of heaven, and that it abode upon Him, and, further, that this descent of the Spirit was the mark by which he was to recognize Jesus as “he that baptizeth in the Holy Spirit.”
We gather from these passages that at the baptism there was a new communication of the Spirit to Jesus in great fullness, as a special anointing for His Messianic vocation. The account declares that the dovelike appearance was seen by Jesus as well as John, which is scarcely compatible with a subjective experience merely. Of course, the dove here is to be taken as a symbol, and not as an assertion that God's Spirit assumed the form of a dove actually. Various meanings have been assigned to the symbol. One connects it with the creative power, according to a Gentile usage; others with the speculative philosophy of Alexandrian Judaism, according to which the dove symbolized the Divine wisdom or reason. But the most natural explanation connects the symbolism of the dove with the brooding or hovering of the Spirit in Gen 13. In this new spiritual creation of humanity, as in the first physical creation, the Spirit of God is the energy through which the work is carried on. Possibly the dove, as a living organism, complete in itself, may suggest the totality and fullness of the gift of the Spirit to Jesus. At Pentecost, on the contrary, the Spirit is bestowed distributively and partially at least to individuals as such, as suggested by the cloven tongues as of fire which “sat upon each one of them” (Act_2:3). Jhn_3:34 emphasizes the fullness of the bestowal upon Jesus: “For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God: for he giveth not the Spirit by measure.” In the witness of the Baptist the permanence of the anointing of Jesus is declared: “Upon whomsoever thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and abiding” (Jhn_1:33).
It is probable that the connection of the bestowal of the Spirit with water baptism, as seen later in the Book of Acts, is traceable to the reception of the Spirit by Jesus at His own baptism. Baptism in the Spirit did not supersede water baptism.
The gift of the Spirit in fullness to Jesus at His baptism was no doubt His formal and public anointing for His Messianic work (Act_10:38). The baptism of Jesus could not have the same significance with that of sinful men. For the symbolic cleansing from sin had no meaning for the sinless one. Yet as an act of formal public consecration it was appropriate to the Messiah. It brought to a close His private life and introduced Him to His public Messianic career. The conception of an anointing for public service was a familiar one in the Old Testament writings and applied to the priest (Exo_28:41; Exo_40:13; Lev_4:3, Lev_4:5, Lev_4:16; Lev_6:20, Lev_6:22); to kings (1Sa_9:16; 1Sa_10:1; 1Sa_15:1; 1Sa_16:3, 1Sa_16:13); sometimes to prophets (1Ki_19:16; compare Isa_61:1; Psa_2:2; Psa_20:6). These anointings were with oil, and the oil came to be regarded as a symbol of the Spirit of God.
The anointing of Jesus with the Holy Spirit qualified Him in two particulars for His Messianic office. (a) It was the source of His own endowments of power for the endurance of temptation, for teaching, for casting out demons, and healing the sick, for His sufferings and death, for His resurrection and ascension. The question is often raised, why Jesus, the Divine one, should have needed the Holy Spirit for His Messianic vocation. The reply is that His human nature, which was real, required the Spirit's presence. Man, made in God's image, is constituted in dependence upon the Spirit of God. Apart from God's Spirit man fails of his true destiny, simply because our nature is constituted as dependent upon the indwelling Spirit of God for the performance of our true functions. Jesus as human, therefore, required the presence of God's Spirit, notwithstanding His Divine-human consciousness. (b) The Holy Spirit's coming upon Jesus in fullness also qualified Him to bestow the Holy Spirit upon His disciples. John the Baptist especially predicts that it is He who shall baptize in the Holy Spirit (Mat_3:11; Mk 18; Luk_3:16; see also Jhn_20:22; Acts 15). It was especially true of the king that He was anointed for His office, and the term Messiah (משׁיח, māshı̄aḥ, equivalent to the Greek ὁ Χριστός, ho Christós), meaning the Anointed One, points to this fact.
(3) Temptation of Jesus
The facts as to the temptation are as follows: In Mat_4:1 we are told that Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil. Mrk_1:12 declares in his graphic way that after the baptism “straightway the Spirit driveth (ἐκβάλλει, ekbállei) him forth into the wilderness.” Luk_4:1 more fully declares that Jesus was “full of the Holy Spirit,” and that He was “led in the Spirit in the wilderness during 40 days.” The impression which the narratives of the temptation give is of energetic spiritual conflict. As the Messiah confronted His life task He was subject to the ordinary conditions of other men in an evil world. Not by sheer divinity and acting from without as God, but as human also and a part of the world, He must overcome, so that while He was sinless, it was nevertheless true that the righteousness of Jesus was also an achieved righteousness. The temptations were no doubt such as were peculiar to His Messianic vocation, the misuse of power, the presumption of faith and the appeal of temporal splendor. To these He opposes the restraint of power, the poise of faith and the conception of a kingdom wholly spiritual in its origin, means and ends. Jesus is hurled, as it were, by the Spirit into this terrific conflict with the powers of evil, and His conquest, like the temptations themselves, was not final, but typical and representative. It is a mistake to suppose that the temptations of Jesus ended at the close of the forty days. Later in His ministry, He refers to the disciples as those who had been with Him in His temptations (
Luk_22:28). The temptations continued throughout His life, though, of course, the wilderness temptations were the severest test of all, and the victory there contained in principle and by anticipation later victories. Comment has been made upon the absence of reference to the Holy Spirit's influence upon Jesus in certain remarkable experiences, which in the case of others would ordinarily have been traced directly to the Spirit, as in Luk_11:14, etc. (compare the article by James Denney in DCG, I, 732, 734). Is it not true, however, that the point of view of the writers of the Gospels is that Jesus is always under the power of the Spirit? At His baptism, in the temptation, and at the beginning of His public ministry (Luk_4:14) very special stress is placed upon the fact. Thenceforward the Spirit's presence and action are assumed. From time to time, reference is made to the Spirit for special reasons, but the action of the Spirit in and through Jesus is always assumed.
(4) Public Ministry of Jesus
Here we can select only a few points to illustrate a much larger truth. The writers of the Gospels, and especially Luke, conceived of the entire ministry of Jesus as under the power of the Holy Spirit. After declaring that Jesus was “full of the Holy Spirit” and that He was led about by the Spirit in the wilderness forty days in Luk_4:1, he declares, in Luk_4:14, that Jesus “returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee.” This is followed in the next verse by a general summary of His activities: “And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified of all.” Then, as if to complete his teaching as to the relation of the Spirit to Jesus, he narrates the visit to Nazareth and the citation by Jesus in the synagogue there of Isaiah's words beginning, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” with the detailed description of His Messianic activity, namely, preaching to the poor, announcement of release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord (Isa_61:1 f). Jesus proclaims the fulfillment of this prophecy in Himself (Luk_4:21). In Mat_12:18 a citation from Isa_42:1-3 is given in connection with the miraculous healing work of Jesus. It is a passage of exquisite beauty and describes the Messiah as a quiet and unobtrusive and tender minister to human needs, possessed of irresistible power and infinite patience. Thus the highest Old Testament ideals as to the operations of the Spirit of God come to realization, especially in the public ministry of Jesus. The comprehensive terms of the description make it incontestably clear that the New Testament writers thought of the entire public life of Jesus as directed by the Spirit of God. We need only to read the evangelic records in order to fill in the details.
The miracles of Jesus were wrought through the power of the Holy Spirit. Occasionally He is seized as it were by a sense of the urgency of His work in some such way as to impress beholders with the presence of a strange power working in Him. In one case men think He is beside Himself (Mrk_3:21); in another they are impressed with the authoritativeness of His teaching (Mrk_1:22); in another His intense devotion to His task makes Him forget bodily needs (Jhn_4:31); again men think He has a demon (Jhn_8:48); at one time He is seized with a rapturous joy when the 70 return from their successful evangelistic tour, and Luke declares that at that hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit (Luk_10:21; compare Mat_11:25). This whole passage is a remarkable one, containing elements which point to the Johannine conception of Jesus, on which account Harnack is disposed to discredit it at certain points (Sayings of Jesus, 302). One of the most impressive aspects of this activity of Jesus in the Spirit is its suppressed intensity. Nowhere is there lack of self-control. Nowhere is there evidence of a coldly didactic attitude, on the one hand, or of a loose rein upon the will, on the other. Jesus is always an intensely human Master wrapped in Divine power. The miracles contrast strikingly with the miracles of the apocryphal gospels. In the latter all sorts of capricious deeds of power are ascribed to Jesus as a boy. In our Gospels, on the contrary, no miracle is wrought until after His anointing with the Spirit at baptism.
A topic of especial interest is that of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Jesus cast out demons by the power of God's Spirit. In Mat_12:31; Mrk_3:28 f; Luk_12:10, we have the declaration that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is an unpardonable sin. Mark particularizes the offense of the accusers of Jesus by saying that they said of Jesus, “He hath an unclean spirit.” The blasphemy against the Spirit seems to have been not merely rejection of Jesus and His words, which might be due to various causes. It was rather the sin of ascribing works of Divine mercy and power-works which had all the marks of their origin in the goodness of God - to a diabolic source. The charge was that He cast out devils by Beelzebub the prince of devils. We are not to suppose that the unpardonable nature of the sin against the Holy Spirit was due to anything arbitrary in God's arrangements regarding sin. The moral and spiritual attitude involved in the charge against Jesus was simply a hopeless one. It presupposed a warping or wrenching of the moral nature from the truth in such degree, a deep-seated malignity and insusceptibility to Divine influences so complete, that no moral nucleus remained on which the forgiving love of God might work. See BLASPHEMY.
(5) Death, Resurrection and Pentecostal Gift
It is not possible to give here a complete outline of the activities of Jesus in the Holy Spirit. We observe one or two additional points as to the relations of the Holy Spirit to Him. In Heb_9:14 it is declared that Christ “through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish unto God,” and in Rom_1:4, Paul says He was “declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead” (compare also Rom_8:11).
As already noted, John the Baptist gave as a particular designation of Jesus that it was He who should baptize with the Holy Spirit, in contrast with his own baptism in water. In Jhn_20:22, after the resurrection and before the ascension, Jesus breathed on the disciples and said “Receive ye the Holy Spirit.” There was probably a real communication of the Spirit in this act of Jesus in anticipation of the outpouring in fullness on the day of Pentecost. In Act_1:2 it is declared that He gave commandment through the Holy Spirit, and in Act_1:5 it is predicted by Him that the disciples should “be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence”; and in Act_1:8 it is declared, “Ye shall receive power, when the Holy Spirit is come upon you.”
It is clear from the preceding that in the thought of the New Testament writers Jesus is completely endued with the power of the. Holy Spirit. It is in large measure the Old Testament view of the Spirit; that is to say, the operation of the Spirit in and through Jesus is chiefly with a view to His official Messianic work, the charismatic Spirit imparting power rather than the Spirit for holy living merely. Yet there is a difference between the Old Testament and New Testament representations here. In the Old Testament the agency of the Spirit is made very prominent when mighty works are performed by His power. In the Gospels the view is concentrated less upon the Spirit than upon Jesus Himself, though it is always assumed that He is acting in the power of the Spirit. In the case of Jesus also, the moral quality of His words and deeds is always assumed.
2. The Holy Spirit in the Kingdom of God
Our next topic in setting forth the New Testament teaching is the Holy Spirit in relation to the kingdom of God. Quite in harmony with the plenary endowment of Jesus, the founder of the kingdom, with the power of the Spirit, is the communication of the Spirit to the agents employed by Providence in the conduct of the affairs of the kingdom. We need, at all points, in considering the subject in the New Testament to keep in view the Old Testament background. The covenant relations between God and Israel were the presupposition of all the blessings of the Old Testament. In the New Testament there is not an identical but an analogous point of view. God is continuing His work among men. Indeed in a real sense He has begun a new work, but this new work is the fulfillment of the old.

text:
Bronze Gate, Nikko - Inukimon (鋳抜門) - 19th century 🇯🇵

This photograph captures the bronze gate known as Inukimon (鋳抜門), located within the inner sanctuary of Nikkō Tōshō-gū. The gate stands along the approach to the mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, whose tomb lies beyond the stone steps leading into Okunoin.

The structure is distinguished by its dark metalwork, decorative roof fittings and imposing double doors adorned with circular emblems. Two bronze komainu, traditional guardian figures resembling lions or dogs, stand on stone pedestals on either side of the entrance. Their alert expressions and carefully modelled bodies give the small gateway a solemn, protective presence.

The gate was constructed in 1650, during the early Edo period. Its name refers to its distinctive casting technique: the principal structural elements, including the roof, pillars and walls, were cast in bronze and assembled to form the gate. The work is attributed to the metalworker Shiina Iyo, whose craftsmanship also appears in the bronze guardian figures.

The komainu have their own history. Earlier versions were made of wood and later replaced with stone figures before the bronze gate and its guardians took their present form. They stand watch over the approach to Ieyasu’s final resting place.

Beyond the gate lies the inner sanctuary and the bronze pagoda containing the remains of the first Tokugawa shogun. Unlike the monumental Yōmeimon, which is celebrated for its elaborate painted carvings, Inukimon is notable for the solemn character of its bronze construction.

This nineteenth-century photograph preserves the appearance of the gateway and its guardian figures during the Meiji era.

text:
Top Images, Great Gate, Nikko (日光東照宮・陽明門) - 19th century 🇯🇵

Japan Through 152 Photographs (circa 1890-1900) 📷🇯🇵

This photograph records a richly decorated sculptural panel high on the Great Gate, or Yōmeimon (陽明門), at Nikkō Tōshō-gū. The original catalogue caption identifies the subject as “Top Images Great Gate Nikko,” directing attention to the elaborate carvings positioned above the main entrance.

The composition brings together three human figures and a deer, set against an intricately decorated architectural background. The figures wear elaborate robes with carefully rendered patterns and colours. One holds a long staff, while another appears to carry a small object. Beside them, the deer stands among carved foliage and rock-like forms. The arrangement combines human and animal imagery in a carefully balanced decorative scene.

Completed in 1636 under the direction of Tokugawa Iemitsu, Yōmeimon is among the most celebrated structures in the Tōshō-gū complex. Its elaborate decoration includes more than 500 carvings, depicting animals, mythical creatures, children, sages and scenes drawn from Chinese stories and traditions. These images were not merely ornamental: many conveyed moral lessons, auspicious wishes and ideals of harmony and good government.

The deer is a familiar symbol of longevity and good fortune in East Asian visual culture, although the precise identities of the three figures in this particular panel have not been firmly established.

Often called the “Gate of Higurashi,” or the gate one could admire until sunset without growing tired of it, Yōmeimon reflects the extraordinary craftsmanship of early Edo-period Japan. This nineteenth-century photograph preserves a close view of one small section of its extensive sculptural programme, allowing details of the original decoration to be examined beyond the scale of the monumental gate itself.

text: St. Abercius, Equal to the Apostles #October22 #Prologue #History Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia under Antoninus and Marcus Aurelius, shepherd of a tiny flock in a pagan city. During a loud idol festival he burned with God’s zeal, walked into the temple and smashed every idol. The mob came to kill him, but three young madmen, foaming and howling, fell at his feet, and he drove the demons out of them. Anger turned to amazement, and five hundred pagans asked for baptism on the spot. He opened the eyes of the proconsul’s blind mother, and in Rome healed the emperor’s daughter. Offered gold, he said: “Riches are not needed for one who considers bread and water a royal meal.”

Is your pickleball serve missing the power to dominate rallies? Imagine unleashing a whip-like serve that rockets past opponents, racking up 3–4 points in a row with aces or weak returns you can smash. Walter, a 53 year old recreational pickleball player, went from frustration to triumph, transforming his serve from inconsistent and lackluster to a game-changing weapon. Once a source of double faults and easy returns, his serve became a point-winning force, thanks to his coach’s guidance and a breakthrough in technique. His journey, peppered with a bit of humor from his home life, offers a roadmap for any player eager to add speed and control to their game.

Walter loved pickleball but dreaded serving. His attempts either plopped into the net or sailed past the service box, costing him points and confidence. During local club matches, opponents easily returned his weak serves, putting him on the defensive. His coach, Sarah, a seasoned pickleball instructor, saw the problem clearly: Walter’s serve lacked a reliable foundation. “Power without accuracy is useless in pickleball,” she told him.

text:
Back in 1999, schools all over America banned Pokémon cards because kids kept talking each other out of their best ones at the lunch table. That's how a whole generation learned to haggle.

The kids who came after them learned the same hobby on apps where you never have to say a word. The kid at this table still has an AirPod in, slides his card across, and waits for somebody to give him a number.

The timing lines up almost perfectly. Pokémon Black and White came out in Japan on September 18, 2010, and Instagram hit the App Store 18 days later. The kids who grew up on that generation of Pokémon were the first ones who could buy and sell almost anything without talking to another person.

The 1999 playground was brutal by comparison. Schools from New Jersey to Washington State banned the cards, partly because older kids kept fleecing younger ones. One Florida school spent four hours searching a lunchroom for a single $75 card a kid had lost. Every trade happened face to face, somebody told you no, and you had to figure out whether to counter.

Now the price comes from TCGplayer and the sale happens on eBay. Whatnot, where you bid on cards with your thumb during a livestream, moved more than $8 billion in goods last year, and trading cards are its biggest category. On those apps a deal has exactly one step. You show the item and wait for an offer.

The stuff outside the hobby that used to teach kids how to talk to strangers faded on the same timeline. Back in July 1978, 71.8% of American 16-to-19-year-olds were working or looking for work. By July 2025 it was 42%, and teens picked up 801,000 summer jobs, the fewest since the BLS started counting in 1948. About 46% of 16-year-olds had a driver's license in 1983, and by 2018 it was closer to a quarter. Even ordering coffee went quiet, since Starbucks now takes 31% of its US orders through the app.

Psychologists Roger Schank and Robert Abelson had a word for this back in 1977. They called them scripts. Their famous example was a restaurant, where you walk in, get seated, order, eat, pay and leave, and adults do it on autopilot because they've done it a thousand times. "Hey, I'm looking to sell this, what would you give me?" is a script too. You learn it the way you learn a free throw, by doing it badly in front of people until it stops feeling weird.

A kid in 1999 had run that script on the bus a hundred times by fifth grade. Plenty of kids now run it for the first time at a convention table with a camera on them.

A mall job used to pay a teenager $5.15 an hour to learn that, and this vendor taught it to him for free.

🚨 REAGAN’S WARNING: GIVE VOTERS SOMETHING TO VOTE FOR—OR WATCH THEM STAY HOME. 🔥

After the Republican disaster of 1974, Ronald Reagan offered an explanation Washington needed to hear: Look beyond the people who voted. Look at the people who didn’t—and ask why they saw too little difference between the parties.

That warning should haunt every Republican who confuses having an “R” beside their name with giving Americans a reason to trust them.

“The Democrats are worse” is an argument against Democrats. It is not a governing vision.

What will YOU defend?
What will YOU fix?
Which promises will YOU keep when keeping them becomes politically inconvenient?

My takeaway from Reagan: Expand the coalition through conviction. Give more Americans a reason to embrace your principles. Don’t make those principles disappear in pursuit of applause.

Constitutional limits. Individual liberty. Fiscal discipline. Public safety. Opportunity people can actually feel in their lives.

Campaign on them. Govern by them. Produce results.

Reagan, a former Democrat, later put his own political journey plainly: “I didn’t leave my party; my party left me.”

Republicans should remember that loyalty can be lost, too.

Voters are citizens to be persuaded, not possessions to be counted.

Watch this. Then ask whether our leaders are offering Americans a cause worthy of their confidence—or merely another fundraising email.

A comeback begins when the promises become performance.
