text:
Johnny Sins is probably the most recognizable man in porn history. The bald guy who’s been a doctor, a plumber, a teacher and an astronaut, and has become a meme on every corner of the internet. Before all that, he was a construction manager in Las Vegas who hated his job. His first paycheck in porn was $100.

His real name is Steven Wolfe. He grew up in Pittsburgh, finished college, and went into construction management. He worked 12 hours a day, six days a week. After a year he decided he couldn’t do it for the rest of his life. He quit and moved to Los Angeles.

He had no connections. This was 2006, before social media, so he answered ads on Craigslist. Almost all of them were junk. The few real ones were amateur directors who were happy to pay the girl but saw no reason to pay the guy. So he worked for free.

One of those early shoots was for a small website that later grew into Brazzers. Then came the first paycheck: $100. Then an agent signed him and got him a contract. $400 a scene, plus a $100 raise every three months. By the end of that contract he was making $800 a scene. He realized he was earning more in a day than a doctor or a lawyer.

He never thought it would last. It did. He worked for more than 15 years and got into the industry’s Hall of Fame. In 2019 he retired and spent six months living on a beach in Mexico.

Then Covid hit. Studios stopped releasing new scenes, everyone was stuck at home, and fans moved to OnlyFans. So he came back, but as a business owner, not an employee.

Today he runs his own production company. He shoots 15 to 25 scenes a month, mostly on his phone, at home. His OnlyFans is free to follow, and he charges per video. Co-stars aren’t paid a fee: they trade content, and each of them sells their own copy. Almost zero overhead. OnlyFans takes 20%, and that’s his biggest cost.

And the studios noticed. He says they now offer performers more money and treat them better, because they know those performers can simply go make the same money on their own.

His estimated net worth is around $5 million. Not Jenna Jameson money, not Sophie Rain money. But he did what almost nobody in that industry does: he stopped being the product and started owning it.

Would you quit a stable corporate job to work for free in an industry where most people walk away broke?

Oprah Winfrey’s bosses wanted to fire her

She was under contract, so to avoid paying it out they demoted her instead

They put her on a talk show

She told the story at Stanford. She started in television at 19 and became an anchor in Nashville right away. Her father still gave her an 11 o’clock curfew, even though she was the one reading the 10 o’clock news

In 1971 she was making $10,000 a year and got an offer from Atlanta for $40,000. Her boss told her she didn’t know what she didn’t know and needed to stay until she learned to write. He couldn’t give her 40. He could give her 12. She stayed, because she felt he was right

By 22 she was in Baltimore making $22,000. When she hit $25,000, her father told her she’d hit the jackpot and would never make more money than that

But reporting felt unnatural. After covering a fire, she went back with blankets for the family, and her boss sent her a note asking what the hell she was doing

Then she was demoted. The station wanted to fire her, but she was under contract, so they moved her to a talk show to run out the clock. Her first interview was with the Carvel ice cream man and all his flavors. The moment she sat down, she knew she’d found home

Around the same time, she found out her co-host was paid more than she was for the same job. She went to the general manager. He asked if she had children. No. Did she own a home? No. A mortgage? No. So why, he asked, did she need the same money? She said thank you for your time and walked out. She didn’t sue. She filed it away and started preparing to leave

When Chicago called, everyone except her best friend Gayle told her she’d fail. Phil Donahue was the king of talk there. Her station offered her a car and an apartment to stay. She said no. If she failed, she’d find out what was next

Years later, with The Oprah Show on the air, she ran into that general manager again. She calls it one of the sweetest moments of her life

Her definition of luck is simple: preparation meeting the moment of opportunity

The demotion that was supposed to get rid of her is what made her

Would you have taken the $40,000?

text:
Representative Trent Kelly is going back to Washington. The Republican from Saltillo won reelection Tuesday night in Mississippi's 1st Congressional District, defeating Democrat Cliff Johnson and Libertarian Johnny Baucom, and keeping one of the most reliably Republican seats in Mississippi in Republican hands.

CNN and the Associated Press called the race just after 9 p.m. Central, with Kelly above 64 percent and 57 percent of the vote reported. The latest AP count, with 99.75 percent of precincts reporting — 403 of 404 — and an estimated 95.92 percent of votes counted, has Kelly at 138,744 votes, 58.7 percent, to Johnson's 94,273 votes, 39.9 percent. The race is called; the totals remain unofficial until certification.

The win extends a decade in the House for Kelly, a Saltillo native. He first arrived in Congress through a 2015 special election held after the death of Representative Alan Nunnelee, when Kelly was serving as district attorney for Mississippi's 1st Judicial District. The district he represents runs across northeastern Mississippi, from DeSoto County to the Golden Triangle — Tupelo, Southaven, Columbus, and Starkville — and the seat has been held by Republicans for decades.

Kelly also carries a soldier's record into the work. He served in the Mississippi Army National Guard, deployed in connection with Operation Desert Storm and the Iraq War, and rose to the rank of major general. In Washington he serves on the House Armed Services Committee, and his campaign emphasized military readiness, veterans' affairs, border security, agriculture, and federal spending.

Johnson, an attorney and civil-rights and public-interest advocate, campaigned on health-care access, voting rights, public education, and economic inequality. Baucom campaigned on limited government and individual liberty. The voters of District 1 have now given their verdict, and Kelly will return to the House for another term.

THE GOOD NEWS: The day after an election, the Christian's first duty toward those in authority is not complaint or celebration — it is prayer. "First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way." (1 Timothy 2:1-2) Representative Kelly, his family, and every leader sworn in from this election need exactly that from the churches of northeast Mississippi — steady prayer, offered in thanksgiving, so that all of us may lead peaceful and quiet lives.

Come Alive in Christ. Grace to all.

text:
Every time I publish something about the far right, a certain kind of reply turns up. No argument, no figure, no source, just abuse. And more often than I'd expect, when I click through to the profile there is a football club in the bio.

That is an observation, not a finding. Plenty of British men on X name a club in their bio, so the only honest way to test it is to compare, and I am now logging replies properly. But the question underneath it is not new. Football crowds have been a recruiting ground for the far right, and at times a street army for it, for decades.

The link between the far right and football firms is documented, and it has been used to build street movements twice in recent memory.

The English Defence League appeared after clashes in English city centres in 2009 and 2010. In a 2010 paper, criminologists Jon Garland and James Treadwell examined the EDL and its affiliate Casuals United, and asked whether their ties to hooligan firms gave the EDL a pool of violent supporters. They concluded the group was the most serious threat to public order and community cohesion in the UK since the National Front's heyday in the 1970s.

The Football Lads Alliance followed in 2017. The anti-fascist magazine Searchlight names John Meighan as its founder, says it grew out of "football lads", the term the firms use for themselves, and says most marchers at the first demonstration came from hooligan firms in London and the South East. It put the 7 October 2017 march at about 10,000, within estimates of 5,000 to 20,000. The FLA says it opposes all extremism and is not racist. Searchlight disputes that and describes it as a far-right street movement, which is its own characterisation, not a finding of a court or regulator.

There are three overlapping reasons, and none of them needs football fans to be worse people than anyone else. This is analysis and interpretation, not a finding.

The first is tribe. Football runs on us against them: colours, chants, rituals, a deep suspicion of outsiders. Those instincts map easily onto nation, race and religion, and political groups that trade on that boundary know it.

The second is infrastructure. A ground puts thousands of young men in one place on a regular schedule. Hooligan firms add networks, loyalty and experience of street confrontation, which is exactly what a street movement needs and cannot easily build from nothing. That is what the EDL and the FLA borrowed.

The third is status. Arie Kruglanski's significance quest theory argues that the need to matter, to be respected and to be someone, drives people toward groups and causes that offer it. 

A lot of working-class lads get belonging from football but not always respect, and extremist groups offer both. I use it here as a lens, not as proof that it explains any particular person's reply.

Most football supporters have nothing to do with any of this. The people in the EDL and FLA stories were a minority drawn from an enormous and varied crowd, and a football club in a profile bio says very little about someone's politics.

The terraces are also contested ground, not far-right by nature. Some of Europe's best-known ultras groups, such as those at St Pauli, Livorno and Bologna, are openly anti-fascist, and in England charities like Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card have spent decades pushing racism out of the game. Whether a club's hardcore support leans right depends on local history, who organises it and whether anyone challenges it.

I just find it interesting and I will be logging true replies against pure abusive replies.

text:
The mission society said she wasn't good enough. Years later, with war at her door, a tiny London housemaid led more than a hundred orphans over the mountains of China on foot.

Her name was Gladys Aylward. Born in Edmonton, North London, in 1902, the daughter of a postman, she went into domestic service in her early teens. She became convinced God was calling her to China.

The China Inland Mission accepted her for a three-month preparatory course. She struggled with the language, and they did not offer her further training.

She went anyway. She saved her wages, and on 15 October 1930 spent her life savings on a train ticket across Siberia, while the Soviet Union and China were fighting an undeclared war. She was detained by the Russians, slipped away with local help, got passage on a Japanese ship, crossed Japan with help from the British consul, and sailed on to China.

In the mountain town of Yangcheng, Shanxi province, she joined an elderly missionary, Jeannie Lawson. They ran an inn for mule drivers, the Inn of the Eight Happinesses, and in the evenings told their guests the stories of Jesus.

She became the local government's "foot inspector," touring villages to enforce the new law against binding girls' feet. She stepped into a violent prison riot and pushed for prison reform. In 1936 she became a Chinese citizen. People called her Ai-weh-deh, "the virtuous one." She took in orphans and adopted several herself.

Then Japan invaded. In 1938 (some accounts say 1940) the fighting reached her region. With the children in her care in danger, she led more than a hundred orphans out over the mountains, sleeping in the open and crossing the Yellow River, wounded and sick, caring for them herself until they reached safety.

Why it matters: the church in China has often been carried not by the polished and approved, but by ordinary people who simply would not leave. Aylward stayed until 1949, when the new communist army was hunting missionaries. Refused re-entry later, she settled in Taiwan in 1958, founded an orphanage, and died on 3 January 1970. She is buried in Taiwan.

Hollywood later cast a tall Swedish star to play her in The Inn of the Sixth Happiness (1958). She was mortified by it. She was small, dark-haired, and sounded like North London. That was the point.

"But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty." (1 Corinthians 1:27, KJV)

"Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me." (Matthew 19:14, KJV)

The mission said no. God said go. What door has been closed in your face that you still feel called to walk through?

Sources: Alan Burgess, The Small Woman (1957); English Wikipedia, "Gladys Aylward"; SOAS Special Collections, Gladys Aylward archive; Bible (KJV), 1 Corinthians 1:27 and Matthew 19:14; images via Wikimedia Commons (public domain and CC licences).

the country. last night, we witnessed, to call it a wave, i don't think would be fully accurate. it's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the united states, blue states, red states, everything in between. and the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of florida. all statewide races, us senate, governor, attorney general, chief financial officer, and agriculture commissioner, were held and won by our republican candidates. and i don't think there's any other state that can say that given all the carnage that was inflicted last night. we also saw the passage of amendment 3, which is the beginning of our property tax elimination efforts in the state of florida. i got a resounding yes vote. i'm very proud of everyone that had been a part of that. and i know that that's something that's very meaningful for a lot of floridians. the truth is, and this is something that i push for over many months and even over the last year, had amendment 3 not been on the ballot, i don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out. people wanted to vote yes on that. and then many of them ended up climate, minimize house losses, even though i didn't think we could keep the house. maybe keep the senate. that would have been a win. if you lost two or three senate seats, that would have been a big win for a midterm election. we knew it could be worse, but i don't think most of us thought it would be quite this bad. the democrats will likely go into january with 56 us senate seats and as much as 258 us house seats. and so what that does, not only is that gonna totally change the dynamic of the next two years to the detriment, of course, of president trump, this is gonna last far beyond just seats in this climate. there was no way you were gonna be able to hold that many seats. but i think some of the losses probably could have been mitigated with better governance.”

A person: “but it's not what you say about the ways that the republican party is going. should republicans look to you as some kind of savior going forward?”

Ron DeSantis: “there's no saviors in politics. i mean, i think people need to understand elected officials are supposed to be servants. you know, you're not gonna get salvation through an elected official. i think people can look at florida and show how you can deliver big results and how you can build a durable coalition. because the reality is you're probably not gonna face an election climate this bad, perhaps in our lifetime in terms of what happened. i mean, losing the senate race in mississippi, which looks like it's gonna happen, who would have thought that was possible? we almost lost louisiana. people weren't focusing on that. that was a 1% victory in louisiana, which i'm sure the president probably carried by 30 points. losing a us senate seat in south carolina, no one would have thought that was possible. heck, even six months ago, you probably could have gotten 99% odds in some of these prediction markets, taking the republican to win at that point. so that's just the reality. so we've shown how it can be done. i think it's gonna take time to dig out of the hole that was there. that's just the reality of the situation. but our voters, did they come out like they did four years ago? not as much. eight years ago, not as much. but i think once we saw what was happening, we did a good job turning out a sufficient number of voters. i absolutely think amendment 3 had a lot to do with that. and of course, i was the chief person to do that. i mean, both governor elect donald's r. p. o. f., they were saying, "come help the governor. "keep the governor's wins on the board. "make sure that we continue. "don't let them take that away." and that was really enough for people to do. and i would run into people over the last six weeks or so, and they would say, "all right, i'm gonna vote for them." 'cause you said, "i don't know." they didn't even know a lot of the candidates, but they said that we were gonna do that. so i think we earned some trust with the voters 'cause we've delivered. but ultimately, politics is only part of life, and do not look to that for salvation. just look to it for people tell you they're gonna do things, and then they do it. i think voters appreciate that. and what i said i would do, we've done. now i think there'll be a next generation that'll come in on the heels of me being here. and if they follow that and just do listen to people and make sure you're using conservative principles to come up with good solutions, you'll be successful in florida in the future. i have no doubt about that. i'm gonna let the legislature kind of get their feet under them. i'm not just gonna throw something on them. we knew this would be something we needed to do. there's a lot of ideas that we've been tossing around for the last six months, and i know that they're gonna want to do it. but we wanna make sure that we land it in a good way. so i'll work with them, i'll probably let them pick the dates. i'm basically on lame duck duty at this point. so i'm very flexible in terms of being able to do it. but yeah, we gotta do it, and it will be, and i think what it'll do is it'll set the schedule for further homestead expansion, obviously, because we want people to be able to get that. but also limiting local governments from just doing an end run around the amendment and taxing them in other ways. miami-dade county voted for this 65-35, our biggest county. i mean, that's a huge, huge mandate for this thing. so we wanna make sure people are saving money. and that is gonna, i think, require a taxpayer bill of rights where we're not allowing to just go and put fees or do play games. that's why we did the business reduction. so they can only raise five instead of 10 like they can do now. they said it would be a tax shift. it's not gonna be a tax shift. it's gonna be a reduction. and then i'll also work with the legislature to provide a pool of funding that we can issue grants to local governments for core needs. and these local, you know, it's like some of the rural, they voted for it over one. people said, oh, rural won't vote it. look at some of the things in rural, what they did. overwhelmingly, they did. but people say the rural tax base isn't as strong. it's not. but it's budget dust to help them with their sheriff's departments. i mean, you're talking about tens of millions of dollars in grants would be able to handle the quote shortfall. so we'll be able to do that. there'll be a transition period. so we'll work with them on that. and i think people are gonna be very excited to get some much needed relief. you know, there's certain things that you can't control directly. indirectly, we've done a lot on the insurance market. you know, they just announced another reduction or another rebate on the auto side. you're gonna see another reduction in citizens insurance in south florida, probably by the end of the year, beginning next year. i'm very confident of that. and i'm very confident that carriers are going to continue to offer lower rates because now you have a lot to choose from. and what consumers are doing, they're getting, they get a high premium, they're looking around, and they're finding they can save money. that's how you drive it down through consumer choice and competition. so that is underway. we've already seen that. we've had the lowest increases in the country the last two years, which no one would have thought was possible. so you're gonna continue to see reductions there, which is relief, which is meaningful for people, 'cause that's tough. but the property tax, man, that's gonna be such a breath of fresh air for people. i mean, this--”

A person: “do you want that special session, though, before you leave office?”

Ron DeSantis: “it has to be. it has to be implemented by january 1st, per the amendment. so yes, so my term goes till the fourth or fifth or sixth, who's counting? but that's the plan, yeah. and you know, look, i don't know how it got to that point, but i'm glad since i was involved with this, you know, i wanna make sure that we land it right. i think it's important.”

A person: “what parts of the president's agenda do you think is most vulnerable, now that democrats have taken back so much from congress?”

Ron DeSantis: “so i think with the, one, they can shut down any appointments, right? so if you have 56 democrats, if, and i don't think justice thomas or alito would retire under those circumstances, but you know, justice scalia didn't either, and hopefully nothing happens, but you know, you never know with life, right? so if there were to be a vacancy, i think the chance of confirming somebody is zero over the next two years. i think the chance of putting people into serious cabinet roles that have strong conservative credentials is close to zero as well, because i don't think you'd get the votes to confirm 'em. so i think that for sure on the senate side is gonna be a huge hindrance compared to where they were, because you know, even when republicans had the majority, you would have some of these republican senators that wouldn't vote, right? the democrats almost always would be against anyone that would be put up. you know, i fail to see how, if you are nominating a replacement for justice alito, first of all, i've said i want alito to stay for another 10 years, 'cause i think he's a great justice, but if you're doing that, what, show me how you get 50 votes with 56 democrats. i don't see it, right? so that is gonna be a huge issue going forward. and then i think the other thing is, is they have the gavels, and so they're gonna launch a lot of investigations, and it's gonna be in both chambers, it's gonna probably be across multiple committees, and that's a sea change in how washington operated over these last two years, and i think they're gonna be able to throw a lot of sand in the gears, attempt to throw a lot of sand in the gears of the inner workings of the administration. so appointments and confirmations, and then the oversight and investigatory, those are probably the two biggest. i don't know policy-wise what there's gonna do, but i will tell you this, they've got enough senators now and house members, they could have dsa people, they're still gonna hold democrat majorities on key votes if they need it, they could do a budget reconciliation bill and put it on the president's desk. it may not be what republicans want, and so then he'd be in a situation where he'd have to veto legislation, budget bills, so i think you're gonna see a lot more conflict between the congress and the executive.”

A person: “are you satisfied with the margins that moody and donald won by? you mentioned a harsh political climate, but when you ran for re-election in 2020, you won by more than 19 points.”

Ron DeSantis: “well, look, i told these guys from the beginning, and this is something we saw in special elections for the last 18 months. donald trump won the state by 13 points. i said the line of scrimmage has moved 10 points in the democrats' direction, and that is about what happened in florida, maybe even a little bit more, so that's the new line of scrimmage, so if you think you're gonna waltz in and win by 13 points, forget about what we did in '22. we told them that wasn't viable. you're not gonna do that, but you're not gonna win by 13 under the circumstances, so you're in a low single-digit race. i told everybody over the last 90 days we are gonna be in a low single-digit race. i do not think those races were in the bag. i think that there were definitely circumstances where we could've gone the way of texas, no question about it but the line of scrimmage moved 10, 12, 13 points in florida. it moved some of these other places 20. in texas, it moved 20 points. if you look at what president wanted by in 24 to what their senate candidate won there. even the governor, i mean, he had been elected statewide overwhelmingly multiple times for multiple offices. you know, that wasn't a close race. i mean, he lost that pretty significantly, so texas probably swung 20 points. our line of scrimmage held better here, but i was under no illusion that that's just the way it is, and when there's a wave, you just have to deal with it. we had a wave in '18, blue wave, they took the congress, but the circumstances this time were much more challenging, not even close.”

A person: “were you surprised that the four congressional seats that were supposed to shift republican through the districting went democrat?”

Ron DeSantis: “no, because i said the line of scrimmage shifted 10 to 15 points, and so those races, now look, i think cd9, i carried by 26 points four years ago. most of them i carried by 15 or more. maybe the coastal one, i maybe did less than that, but we knew the shifts were gonna happen. it just is what it is. you know, we had 20 republicans going into the election. we have 20 republicans in our congressional delegation now, so it is what it is. now, you saw retrenchment on our incumbents from where the president was two years ago to where they were, but when the primary was over, i had a lot of these people here at the house, and we sat them down, we're just socializing. i said, "if the president won your district by 13, "you're in a low single-digit race. "just understand that." the line of scrimmages move. why? democrats had their best turnout they've ever had in the modern history of florida. would they get 68% turnout of their registered voters? they've never gotten that high in a midterm. they've never beaten us in turnout as a percentage in a midterm. the only thing that saved us is we just have so many more republicans than they do. so they did that, and then no party affiliate voters came out much stronger. and you know, that's kind of like a rule of thumb. when i ran four years ago, it was a lower npa turnout. when npa turnout goes up, it's usually because they're not happy. when it's low, it's usually because, you know, they think things are fine, right? and so you saw that. so all those factors, we definitely built in 10, 15 points. and look, we had to change the districts because of calais. i knew it was coming down. i knew that district was not viable. i opposed it four years ago, but there really wasn't case law to support my position at that time, but i knew which way it was going. so we had to do that. but you know, these other ones, that's just the way the cookie crumbles. i mean, you know, you have opportunities and you have to ask. i mean, it's not easy running for congress. i helped all those guys. you know, we helped them raise money. we did stuff. but when you're down ballot like that, you know, especially as a first time candidate, it's hard to buck the trends. it's just the reality. it's hard to buck the trend. so then the question for florida is, are we gonna continue to do what kind of built this firewall and take it to the next level? that will end up giving future candidates in those seats great opportunities to run and win. if you go a different direction and you start losing support, well then those are districts that they may continue to carry. who knows, right? depending on how things shake out. but i told them the line of scrimmage was shifting 10 points at a minimum. i think nationally, you're gonna find that the line of scrimmage probably shifted from 24, 15 to 20 points on average, i think was what it was.”

A person: “this is a rejection. you said nationally this was a rejection of republicans not being able to vote democrats. why is that the case?”

Ron DeSantis: “i think that's just how midterm elections typically go. people come out and they're more apt to vote when they're upset or angry at something and they vote to send a message rather than, oh, you know, i have a positive reason to come out. now it can happen. four years ago in florida, we drove the turnout in a positive way, right? that's why we had a big turnout. but i just look at how are they campaigning, right? and they were running. i mean, these congressmen. you know, i'm like watching these. i'm watching the world series. i see the ad, you know, so-and-so voted against releasing the epstein files. and i'm like, you know, that's a bad vote. we ran as republicans on saying we need to do that. and then you actually have people in the congress voting against release when the attorney general said she had all this horrific stuff on her desk and that people were gonna be held accountable. it's untenable. when you have people going in trading stock, how is it that, so, you know, look, i have credibility on this. i've never traded a stock since i've been in elected office. and i'm poorer for it. i was actually pretty good at it, you know, in my spare time before i got into this. but my view was how do you have no investment acumen and then all of a sudden get elected to congress and then you're outperforming warren buffett? how does that work? oh, you just happened to buy something related to an industry where you're on a committee and then it goes up 150%. and we see that. but those ads hitting those congresspeople, i thought were devastating ads. why, you know, luna was right. why don't they ban the congressional stock trading? it would be a breath of fresh air for everybody, you know, if they were able to do it. so i just saw how they were running and it was really a rejection of what was going on in dc. and our candidates didn't have their footing. and i made comments over the last week or two because when i was seeing this, they didn't have a great positive case for themselves. they were flat-footed. they were trying to explain this or explain that in ways that weren't landing with voters. it's tough. midterms are tough. i mean, i think if you look, the sixth year of a presidency almost always suffers defeats. it's very rare that you gain seats. almost always lose and usually lose big. obama lost big. bush lost big. nixon, the tail end, was cataclysmic. truman lost. i mean, that was a unique situation after the war. but that's kind of the nature. but yes, i don't think the democrats ran on a positive agenda. and in fact, if you look around the states, even in states where republicans got wiped off the face of the earth, the voters were approving conservative ballot measures. they supported photo id when that was on the ballot, even in blue states. they supported amendments against taxation, limiting property tax, not just in florida, but income tax limitations. california even voted against some of the taxes. so the electorate that showed out was obviously voting d up and down the ballot, but on individual issues, they were not, this is not the democrat socialists of america. and the democrats have a variety of people that ran. some were more liberal, some came more moderate. the energy in their party is on the left. we've seen that. if these guys get in and do that, that will induce a reaction. i don't know if it'll be 28, but eventually it'll induce a reaction in, i think, a negative way. but i don't see what their positive agenda was. they were saying they were against what was going on in washington. people that were upset at that, they got 'em out to vote, and that's why they won these races.”

text:
THE DISSOLUTION OF THE GLOBAL ORDER AND THE RETURN OF GRAVITY: THE END OF CONVENIENT PEACE AND THE RESTRUCTURING OF THE 21ST CENTURY

For nearly four decades, the Western world operated under the comforting sedation of a false premise: the belief that history had ended and that multilateral trade had permanently extinguished tribal instincts of conquest, resource scarcity, and war.

The architecture appeared extraordinarily convenient. Europe outsourced its cheap energy to Russia, transferred its industrial manufacturing engine to coastal China, and delegated its territorial defense to the American taxpayer and American soldiers. 
The international community transformed into a hyper connected supply apparatus optimized for maximum margin and maximum vulnerability.

That illusion is dead.

What gathers on the horizon of the coming decades is neither a passing diplomatic dispute nor a cyclical downturn; it is the structural dissolution of the Pax Americana and the unyielding return of geopolitical gravity. Analyzing this future with intellectual rigor demands discarding both the theatrical panic of doomsday prophets and the cynical optimism of bureaucratic elites who pretend the foundation remains intact.

1. THE EXHAUSTION OF THE AMERICAN LEVIATHAN

The foundational pillar of the postwar settlement was Washington’s willingness to act as the world’s default security underwriter.

Corporate commentary reflexively reduces this shift to the personal preferences of @DonaldTrump. 
That diagnosis is historically superficial. 
American strategic retrenchment was not birthed by a single executive; it emerges from the financial and psychological exhaustion of a society bearing unsustainable debt, coping with the deindustrialization of its heartland, and watching middle class families depleted by stubborn inflation and inconclusive foreign entanglements across the Middle East.

The midterm election outcome, cementing a deadlocked capital through an adversarial divide between the presidency and Congress, merely accelerates a reality that was mathematically inevitable: the United States no longer possesses either the fiscal balance sheet or the domestic political consensus to subsidize the defense of global commons.

When the White House demands that NATO member states lift military spending toward 3% or 4% of GDP while imposing protective tariffs across historical allies in Europe and Canada, the message is definitive: the free security umbrella is permanently closed. Every capital must now fund its own preservation.

2. THE RESURGENCE OF RESOURCE ANXIETY AND THE AWAKENING OF EUROPE

It is against this structural void that one must interpret what would have sounded unthinkable a decade ago: the return of civil defense mobilization and emergency stockpiling directives across advanced European democracies.

The security assessment delivered by former Finnish President Sauli Niinistö to the European Commission, alongside the direct distribution of crisis booklets to more than 5 million Swedish households, are not theoretical drills. 
They are formal acknowledgments of institutional fragility. 
When stable governments formally instruct civilian households to hoard bottled water, non perishable provisions, power sources, and emergency medical kits to survive at least one full week of systemic grid collapse, they are conceding that modern supply networks can sever without warning.

Europe confronts an existential convergence: paralyzed by green energy regulations that crippled heavy industry, reliant on distant maritime lifelines, and surrounded by conventional and asymmetric threats on its eastern flanks, the continent recognizes that cargo routes, undersea communications cables, and power grids are prime kinetic targets. 
Food security has ceased to be an agronomic issue; it has become the immediate perimeter of territorial defense.

3. THE EURASIAN MIRAGE AND THE LATIN AMERICAN TRAP

As the transatlantic sphere fractures, the Eurasian axis advances, anchored by the transactional alignment of Beijing, Moscow, and Tehran. 
Packaging their ambition under the rhetoric of multipolarity and BRICS de dollarization, this coalition markets an insulated alternative financial system detached from Western oversight.

A dispassionate assessment exposes the fatal flaw in this narrative: Eurasia does not offer a rules based global market; it offers the substitution of legalistic Western influence with a network of autocracies.

The Brazilian government commits a catastrophic strategic error by tying national policy to this Eurasian pivot. Seduced by superficial anti imperialist posturing, the administration hands over logistical corridors, state financing mechanisms, and agricultural output to the sovereign sphere of the Chinese Communist Party. 
By tethering national interests to an authoritarian bloc defying the West, Brasília achieves zero true autonomy; it merely places the country’s economic survival beneath the leverage of regimes that employ commercial monopolies as instruments of diplomatic subordination. 
Should global shipping corridors close or secondary sanctions trigger, Brazil will quickly discover that it possesses zero blue water naval power to protect its grain and iron ore exports.

4. REALISTIC HORIZONS: THE SECOND ORDER FRICTIONS AHEAD

What defines the strategic landscape ahead? Not instantaneous Hollywood style nuclear cataclysms, but a grinding, systemic recalibration:

First: The fragmentation of international commerce into regional trade fortresses. 
The era of frictionless international logistics delivering low cost goods in 24 hours has drawn to a close. 
The world enters a regime of higher structural inflation, driven by localized manufacturing redundancy, high energy defense outlays, and reshoring costs.

Second: The geopolitical weaponization of food and calories. 
Agricultural output will absorb compounding stress from costly fertilizers, crop protection restrictions, and acute competition over water and seed patents. 
Those who grow food hold strategic leverage, but only if they retain the institutional power and sovereign currency to shield their yields from bureaucratic confiscation.

Third: The test of societal fortitude. 
As comfortable material certainty erodes, domestic political divides will test institutional resilience. 
Fragile societies, accustomed to administrative entitlement and paralyzed by ideological factionalism, will collapse into paralysis. 
Only communities grounded in individual agency, moral discipline, fiscal prudence, and an uncompromising commitment to truth will withstand the incoming pressure.

Human history was never an uninterrupted march toward frictionless prosperity. 
It remains, at its foundation, a demanding cycle of moral endurance and material trials. 
The era of convenient assumptions is over. 
Lucidity is no longer merely an intellectual virtue; it is our indispensable defense.

"The era of convenient peace is over. When Europe orders households to stockpile rations and the United States closes the global tab, lucidity stops being an intellectual virtue and becomes the sole tool of survival."
- Mooska

text:
The Cheesecake Factory is a reminder that some of the best opportunities in the market don’t always look exciting at first.

According to the chart, $CAKE was up 124% in 2026 through late October, while the S&P 500 was up around 10%.

A restaurant chain outperforming the market by that much deserves a closer look.

The interesting part is that the business has been growing alongside the stock.

In Q3 2026:

• Revenue reached $1.03 billion, up nearly 14% year over year.
• Comparable sales at Cheesecake Factory restaurants grew 15.2%.
• Adjusted earnings came in at $1.02 per share.

That comparable-sales number matters. It suggests the company isn’t relying only on opening more locations to grow; its existing restaurants are generating more sales too.

My thesis is simple: The Cheesecake Factory has built a brand that people recognize, return to, and choose for more than just dessert. Its extensive menu and dining experience give it a broad audience, while concepts like North Italia and Flower Child offer other avenues for growth.

But a great business and a great investment aren’t always the same thing at every price.

After a rally like this, the question is whether Cheesecake Factory can keep growing sales and earnings enough to justify what investors are paying today. Higher labor and food costs, weaker consumer spending, or slowing restaurant traffic could all challenge the thesis.

What I’m watching next:

• Can existing restaurants sustain strong sales growth?
• Can the company protect margins as costs change?
• Can its other restaurant brands expand profitably?
• Does the valuation leave room for future upside?

The lesson isn’t to buy a stock just because it went up 124%.

It’s to pay attention when an established business starts delivering results that change what the market expects from it.

Sometimes the opportunity isn’t hidden in the next big technology trend.

Sometimes it’s sitting at a restaurant table.

text:
Tulsa Jack Blake wasn't the kind of outlaw who craved headlines or dime-novel fame — he rode fast, lived hard, died with his boots on, and almost nobody remembers his name. He operated in the shadows of the 1890s frontier, a dangerous era when Indian Territory was still a lawless maze of river bottoms, hidden trails, and outlaw hideouts where men like him could vanish for weeks at a time. 

Train robbers, horse thieves, whiskey smugglers, and armed gangs moved freely through that rough country, and Blake moved right along with them — connected to the violent networks that kept deputy marshals riding hard and sleeping light. He wasn't just a criminal. He was a product of a world where survival meant staying one step ahead of the law, and where one bad morning could end everything.

By 1895, that morning had come. Posses were closing in, tracking Blake through the kind of terrain that swallowed men whole — dense forests, rocky trails, isolated ranches where ambushes hid behind every treeline. Picture it: dust-covered deputies riding beneath a brutal frontier sun, rifles across their saddles, horses lathered from miles of relentless tracking, while somewhere just ahead, an armed man pushed his exhausted animal harder, knowing exactly what capture meant. 

When the confrontation finally came, Blake didn't reach for surrender. Revolvers fired, horses panicked, smoke drifted low through the brush — and when the chaos settled, Tulsa Jack Blake lay dead in the dirt, his story ending not in a courtroom or on a scaffold, but right there in the open frontier where he had always lived.
No famous last words. No dramatic trial. Just a man, a gunfight, and the unforgiving land that witnessed both. Blake's life was short, violent, and mostly forgotten — swallowed by the same era that made him. 

But there's something haunting about that final pursuit, those last desperate miles with posses tightening behind him and nowhere left to ride. The frontier didn't offer second chances, and Tulsa Jack Blake used every one he had. So the question that lingers is a simple one: in a world that brutal, where every sunrise might be your last — how long could you have lasted?

A person: “governor, on amendment 3, you're right, i mean, i believe it's the most popular thing on the ballot last night, but also, at the same time, voters involved in miami-dade approved property tax referendum to fund schools. and so i just wanted a couple of questions. one, do you still think that amendment 3 or 60% had legislation not carved out schools from it? and then, is that something you're particularly gonna look at in the special session, limiting the ability of both governments, even in red areas, to vote a referendum like that on the ballot?”

Ron DeSantis: “so 3 applies to every taxing authority except school districts, and that's what will be implemented. what i think, how you deal with school districts, i think the legislature believed, and i think with some reason, is we have this fefp. it's got pluses and minuses. there'll be opportunities to do a rewrite of that with the committee that's gonna start next year. you may be able to do a rewrite in a way that will provide strong funding for schools in a way that can still provide relief for homestead property owners. i think there's ways to do it, but i think that they felt it was better to do that vehicle if you were gonna do it rather than try to do it in here. so yes, i mean, it would've been susceptible to political tax, obviously, and it is what it is, but i just, i've looked at the economic base of this state, and i know we have a lot of a tax base of people that are not homestead owners, so the more we can get to homestead to just be tax-free, i think that's the better. that is not gonna be a part of the implementing bill in terms of the school districts. there's not gonna be anything that's gonna change on that, but i think the legislature is gonna address the f. b. f. p. i think if the next governor, if byron wants to get to a point where a lot of republican voters wanted to have tax-free homestead, then you're gonna have to come up with solutions on that, but we've had a big commitment to education. i've increased funding for school districts, for teacher salaries, for all these things over the years. i'm a product of public schools, so we're gonna do that, but how do you do that, and can you do it in a way that is giving people more breathing room on their primary residence? you may be able to do that. i don't think that was the major issue. i mean, people will say, if you look in texas, big shift among latino voters, but why did they shift in favor of republicans? they did because of bidenflation. they did because the border was open. they did because of the crime policies which were weak, and i think now they're looking, mortgage rates are over 7%, gas is $4 a gallon, grocery prices have gone up, and all these, and so i think it was more kitchen table issues and bread and butter issues than that. i know that there have been complaints about how that was handled, and like i said the other day, we have responsibility to enforce the law. no one's done more at the state level to support enforcement of immigration laws, and we have, since i've been governor, crossed a wide variety of ways, but if you look at some of the things that happened like minnesota, there was an effort to generate a spectacle, i believe, for press purposes, and that ended up not being effective. this is an important thing that you're doing. it's not about necessarily creating conflict on the streets. it's, you know, we have laws, people came in. if they have a right to be here, great. if they don't, then we'll enforce the law. so i'm not saying it wasn't a factor, but i do not think it was the driving factor. i don't think it was the driving factor in south florida, even though you did have some people that were concerned about it, and you know, if someone's an american citizen, you know, they shouldn't be involved with dhs at all, and that would have been mistakes if that happens. i don't think that was the intent of the administration. you did have some people that had been here for a lot longer than just when biden let everybody in, so it was an issue, but it was not the overriding issue. i think if gas was $2 a gallon, if inflation was lower, and if some of these other issues, you know, were shaking out a little bit better, i think that you would have seen, you know, different, at least different trends. you know, the results still would have been tough, because it was that. yes.”

A person: “your term ends in january, as you mentioned. what do you envision your next chapter looking like, and do you have any plans to run for any entire office?”

Ron DeSantis: “we'll talk about anything i'm doing on the other side of this. i still got more work to do. we'll work 'til the lights are out, and cross that bridge when we get to it.”

A person: “governor, you mentioned that the statewide resistance might really look at florida as a place to spend money that they've been doing for years. talk about their role in the industry in florida.”

Ron DeSantis: “well, look, they've spent a lot of money in florida over the years. they've spent a lot, i mean, in 2018, they spent a lot. in 2020, they spent a lot. they did spend in '22 against me, and they abandoned in '24, because i think they realized, you know, they weren't getting a lot of bang for the buck. we do have a pretty strong voter base. our voter registration has continued to improve, and all that, and so i think the question is, if you couldn't win in this year, you know, what circumstances are gonna create the opportunity for you to win statewide in florida? i mean, ashley moody won by, what, 150,000 votes? byron won by 100,000, uthmeyer won by 130,000, whatever. that's kind of the high-water mark for them, right? now, maybe if they would have spent money, maybe that would have had an effect. i don't think it gets them over the finish line, even if they had put money in, but look, republicans ultimately will decide that in the sense that if these guys get in and do a good job, florida will be out of reach. if they get in and fumble the ball, then all of a sudden you're giving an opportunity for the dems to come back in florida. i am concerned, just nationally, i mean, if you think about it, we got wiped out in ohio. that's a huge part of our national coalition, to have ohio in the republican column. we got wiped out in texas, the biggest anchor we have in republican politics. so really, florida is the last main anchor standing. i think that means that there's gonna be a special emphasis on making sure we increase fortifications as republicans and that we get this right. and i'm not gonna be looking over anyone's shoulders and you gotta do this, you gotta do this come january, but i think that everyone that was on that ballot can look at florida and then compare to the rest of the country and know that there was a reason why we did, we were able to withstand the worst of circumstances here. so if they build off that, i think florida will still be out of reach. but look, if we were all sitting here, even a month ago, and someone offered you odds that texas, some would say the senate was gonna go because you saw, but if you said, i will bet you that texas governor, lieutenant governor, ag, land commissioner, railroad, whatever they have, supreme court, will all go dem, not one of you would have taken that bet. some of you may have wanted to see that, but you wouldn't have taken that bet because you would have known that just doesn't happen in texas, right? so that's a wipe out. so i think florida republicans should know that there's nothing guaranteed in this. politics is changing, it always does. there's always these cycles. and i'd say specifically now the ground, when i was running for reelection, we had the issue advantage. they indulge in covid hysteria. we were the free state of florida. they were pursuing woke ideology. we said, we're gonna protect you from that. they had bad policies on letting criminals out. we are law and order. on issue after issue, we had the strong advantage. and then we had a record that backed it up. so the win was at our back and we did it. well, the issues change as time goes on. so now what were some of the issues that you saw where democrats were able to outflank republicans? how you approach big tech, how you approach the issue of hyperscale data centers. i was one of the few republicans, and we got the legislature to say, you can't raise utility rates. the psc you saw with this duke proposal. so this is the law in florida and that protects consumers. but i think you had some republicans that are like, oh yeah, just eminent domain somebody's farm and give it to a hyperscale data center. you see why these rural voters were revolting over that. so there's a time and a place to be able to do certain development, but why aren't they going into urban core areas that have been hollowed out and doing it? why are they taking farmland or taking ranches and things like that? and the democrats showed an appreciation for some of these rural people who were likely not democrats. and i think the republican view was just saying, oh, you're just gonna have to grin and bear it. we had a more balanced approach in florida for sure about that. but even just how you approach big tech companies, should you give them immunity for 10 years or should we have a coherent framework that's gonna channel technological development in a positive way but mitigate on the negative? that's something. these flock cameras, this happened very quickly. law enforcement uses cameras, normal cameras. that's not anything new. this is one where they're taking data, they're harvesting data about who's going through, they're giving it to private companies, they can create dossiers, they can sell the data, they can do all that. and is that something that we want to have? and so obviously i took action, the legislature here is gonna have to address that. but nationally, that becomes an issue. so there are all these things that happen and you've gotta be responsive to voters. you use your conservative principles to solve these problems and you don't indulge in left wing policy making but to just ignore them as issues. i don't think that's a viable strategy. we of course tried to do the ai bill of rights that the senate passed 38 to one last session in the house. they refused to do it. is that what the voters wanted you to do to not even have a debate over maybe the most significant issue that's affecting society right now and likely will in the future? i think the voters expect you to debate these things and offer solutions. so that's an issue that needs to be addressed here in florida and throughout the country. but we are in a very volatile political era. things shift quickly and the leaders just gotta recognize that and don't act like whatever worked even two years ago in a campaign is necessarily gonna work today or would work going forward. i mean i knew republicans were in trouble when i was reading an overview about what were they running ads on and they're spending hundreds of millions of dollars across the country on transgender ads. and look, i fought disney on gender ideology. we did the boys, protected the girls from the boys going in sports years ago. we've made sure that schools, all this stuff, the surgeries on minors we outlawed. so we have taken that issue the way i think we should have and handled with good public policy. but that was not the issue motivating voters. and it was kind of like an attempt to just scare republicans to vote. but i think, and i think they ran some in florida, but like our voters, they know we took care of that, right? so that wasn't speaking to their concerns. it was effective four years ago. voters were glad that we were standing up against some of the insanity that was happening. i see this guy in michigan that got elected. they asked him about, "well, why should a boy be in a girl's locker room?" he's like, "oh, well, they're gonna see this "on the internet anyway, so what's the difference?" oh yeah, i think parents think there's a big difference for that. but that was the view and people didn't want that and we were able to go. but the ground shifts and the emphasis then is on different things. four years ago, we were in the peak woke era. it alienated a lot of people. rightfully so, it alienated me. so we were fighting back against that. well, now the issues are different. and republicans, it seemed like, and some of the ads i was seeing with how much money they were spending, they really were fighting yesterday's battles. so we are gonna do the special session. i'm gonna let the legislature propose when they wanna do it. i think they should do it when it's convenient for them. we'll get that done. and i don't know that there's, there may be some housekeeping items i wanna do. i'm gonna talk to jim and sam and see. but that's important. we knew this day was gonna come and we're ready for it. thank you.”

One, evidently pro-Trump, is not pleased with my satisfaction that Abdul El Zayed won in Michigan. He said "you Muslims take what you can't give". I asked how. He argued in Muslim-majority countries, non-Muslims dare not run for office let alone win elections. I told him he spoke from a position of ignorance and sought to educate him. Other lawyers who thought he had a point listened, their demeanor betraying their misguided belief I wouldn't be able to disprove the point. 

I am aware Christian and other non-Muslim minorities hold parliamentary seats in predominantly Muslim countries like Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Egypt, Iraq, Malaysia, Indonesia, Pakistan, and even Iran. When I mentioned these countries, they all shouted "Iran?!" in disbelief. I went further to say that even in some of these countries, seats are RESERVED for religious minorities. They could not belief it so I persuaded them to let us confirm or disprove my point on the internet. 

After confirmation, they shifted the goal post to make Saudi Arabia and Afghanistan the centrepieces of the discussion, arguing the point of zero tolerance for other religious beliefs. One even argued Christians dare not travel to Saudi. I laughed at his ignorance and proceeded to educate him. 

Yes, truth be told, Muslims cannot revel in the incredible freedom countries like USA and the UK provide to all and sundry on one hand and then hypocritically condone discrimination against non-Muslims in the heartlands of Islam on the other hand. While every nation is within its right to entrench values and systems that suit them, equal opportunities such as the ones offered by some Western countries are the kind that promote true shared humanity. 

Strict religious values are inherently discriminatory when placed under the microscope of instruments such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights but sovereignty is also one principle international law carefully wraps in cotton wool. America was a hotbed of racial and even religious discriminations until changes occurred. In Europe, Catholics and Protestants could not even tolerate each other. Even within Islam, Sunnis and Shias were at each other's jugular. Nowadays, secularity and liberal democracies have taken roots around the world. Turkey, which was once an empire, is now 100% democratic. Egypt was autocratic for many years but democracy has taken firm roots now. 

Saudi Arabia is a conservative country and it is not a democracy. One family rules the country with the concurrent application of Islamic Law. Its equivalent is The Vatican, which is seat of the Catholic Church (by far the largest Christian denomination in the world). Under International Law, it is a country within a country. It even has a seat in the United Nations Organization. Still, while non-Muslims can live and work in Saudi, non-Christians can also visit The Vatican as tourists. 

Afghanistan is a special case but a closer look at the majority of how conservative Muslim countries evolve will reveal one form of American influence or the other in the journey that has taken them to where they are today. Afghanistan, Somalia and Iran were definitely indirectly led on their current paths with American actions and in actions during periods America had dalliance with ruling elements in the three countries. Saudi is America's greatest lapdog or prized asset, whichever you prefer, in the Middle East as at today despite its so-called conservatism. 

In all, I prefer a world where our diversities become our common strength. We are all creatures of one Supreme Being.

Pakistani Americans invested tremendous hope and energy in supporting Republicans and President Trump, believing his administration would stand for democracy around the world, particularly in Pakistan. This came after deep disappointment with the Biden administration’s failure to meaningfully address Pakistan’s democratic crisis.

When little changed, many Pakistani Americans, like millions of others, began losing faith in the system. There was a growing perception that a few million dollars spent on lobbying could influence American foreign policy, regardless of democratic principles or human rights.

But yesterday’s midterm elections have offered a renewed sense of hope. The Michigan Senate race involving @AbdulElSayed and the enormous political spending in Texas have brought renewed attention to a fundamental question: Can money and powerful interests outweigh the will of American voters?

These elections are a reminder that American democracy is bigger than any billionaire, lobbying firm, or foreign regime. Political spending may buy access and influence, but it cannot guarantee the support of voters.

For Pakistani Americans, our message should be clear: Don’t lose hope, don’t lose focus, and don’t underestimate the strength of American democracy.

Move forward with renewed confidence, unity, and energy. Stay engaged, make your voices heard, and stand firm on democratic principles.

We cannot afford to miss what could be one of our most important opportunities to make a meaningful difference.

The Lancia Y10 Turbo (also sold as the Autobianchi Y10 Turbo in Italy, France, and Japan) was launched at the Geneva Motor Show in March 1985. 

Positioned as a luxury, high-performance micro-hatchback, it stood out as one of Europe's smallest production turbocharged cars of its era.  

Designed under Tom Tjaarda, the Y10 turned heads with its sharp wedge silhouette, Kamm-tail rear, and matte-black tailgate. The flagship Turbo variant combined this avant-garde styling with lightweight performance.

Engine Tech: 

The Turbo relied on a 1.05-litre carb-fed engine reinforced with sodium-filled exhaust valves, Magneti Marelli Digiplex ignition, an electric fuel pump, and an intercooler setup inspired by period Formula 1 practice.  

Exterior Styling: 

Distinguished by subtle red pinstripes on the front and rear bumpers, side "Turbo" body decals, bespoke multi-spoke alloy wheels, and a redesigned front air dam to house the intercooler.  

Interior & Equipment: 

Offered a premium cabin relative to its segment, featuring optional Alcantara trim, sport seats, a boost gauge built into the dashboard instrument cluster, and high-end options for its day like power windows, central locking, and digital climate control.  

Production of the original carbureted Turbo ended in 1989 when it was succeeded by the naturally-aspirated 1.3 i.e. GT. Today, surviving original Y10 Turbos are rare and sought-after collectibles among Italian hot hatch enthusiasts.

Ayn Rand’s stories are stories about the struggle of the individual against the collective and they’re gripping. When I first read Atlas Shrugged, I couldn't put the book down. It became a 12 and then a 14, and then a 16 hour-a-day exercise. Human nature doesn't change. That struggle existed a hundred thousand years ago. That struggle exists today. What does change is technology. A hundred thousand years ago, an enraged human being could maybe kill 10 other people. And today, an enraged human being can kill a hundred million people. So as technology advances, our thoughts about ethics and morality and technology and civility have to evolve.

Today, we struggle with the challenge of authority. You know, Lord Acton said, absolute power corrupts absolutely. And, the only difference between absolute power today and absolute power 10,000 years ago is today we have a company that listens to everything a billion people say. We have another company that answers the questions that 4 billion people ask. We have companies that deliver the food and all of the goods that you need to survive to hundreds of millions of people. We have one company that delivers all of the business software to 80 million corporations and directly serves billions and billions of employees.

Now, if I asked you the question, “If you got ejected out of the third biggest country in the world, or if I denied you privileges to live in any of the five largest countries in the world, would your life go on?”  Probably. Now, what if you actually got canceled by Apple, Amazon, Facebook, Google tomorrow? The question is, would your life go on? What? Stop and think a little bit about what happens if they simply turned off your account, seized your photos, turned off your messages, took your documents. What if Microsoft just denied you access privileges?

Could you run a business? Could you work?

A big question. I used to make the joke: Apple's the most valuable company in the world because there's never been a company in the world as valuable as Apple. It legitimately is the most valuable because it can change the lives of a billion people over the weekend by shipping some electricity. And that is not something we struggled with a hundred years ago. So the question really is, what happens if this goes on? Companies get bigger, we've got big tech. Governments get bigger as the companies get bigger. When the company serves 3 billion people, that means one bureaucrat can make one phone call to that company and potentially turn off all of the information flowing to all 3 billion people over the weekend, right? This is a new idea and it's a disturbing idea. The story of Atlas Shrugged is the story of individuals struggling against the collective and eventually they realize it's a corrupt and a rigged game, and they can't succeed at it. The solution that John Galt offers is to withdraw from the corrupt economy. So, should we follow John Galt's example?

Should we just withdraw from a corrupt economy? Can we? Well, obviously we haven't. To paraphrase George Patton: You don't win wars by dying for your country -- you win wars by making the other guy die for his country. And, we don't want to be martyrs, we want to be winners. And that is the challenge we face today. There's no point in going on strike unless you've formed a union first. Just going on strike without the organization in advance is just self-inflicted martyrdom. Bitcoin is a union. I'm going to leave the thought and continue with my speech. We'll come back to it at the end.

There's a freedom saga in the history of the human race. What is that saga? Somebody grows up, they struggle against the collective, life is oppressive. They can't farm, they can't live, they can't worship, they can't celebrate, they can't breathe. So what do they do? Well, they go over the horizon. Beyond this horizon. We travel somewhere over the hill. After that, we go to the new world. We get on a ship. If you're a Hugenot, if you’re a Protestant in a Catholic land, if you're a Catholic in a Protestant land, if you're a second son, if you're a Quaker, at some point you get on a ship, you go to the new world. What happens after you settle the new world, if it gets too oppressive on the east coast? Go west, young man, and we go west. We want to get away from too many politicians, too much government, too many well-intentioned individuals trying to help us with more laws, more government services.

Well, in the 20th century, Peter and I are both aeronautical engineers. We read every science fiction writer and the great romantic science fiction tomes from Heinlein, et cetera, were all about: Earth being too crowded -- we’ve got to get off this planet. We;ve got to go to space. Elon Musk channels this aspiration every day. But in general, we all grew up thinking in the seventies and the eighties: go to space. Now, the problem is, it turns out to be fairly expensive to go to space. We didn't quite make it. We figured out how to send millions of people to the new world, and we sent millions of people west, but we couldn't yet send millions of people to the moon or Mars or the next habitable G-type star. So where is the next frontier for those thirsting for freedom? Cyberspace. And here I pause and I ask you to, like Steve Jobs said: Think different.  Thinking conventionally will get you killed.  You will be martyrs and not winners.

If you want to die for your country or die for your cause, you can do that by thinking conventionally. If you want to win, you need to think unconventionally. We have to embrace new paradigms. In the 21st century, you can choose where to locate your body, your friends and family. You can choose where to locate your mind. You can spend your time on Twitch or Netflix or YouTube or Reddit or reading whatever you like. There's infinite choices. You can be wherever you want to be with any group you want to be with in cyberspace in your head. You can also choose where to locate your business, your P & L. Where do you generate cash flow in order to pay your expenses? You want that to be a streaming YouTube channel? You want that to be a bakery on Venice Beach?  You choose, there are consequences.

And finally, you can choose where to place your wealth. That is, what will your bank be? How will you store your life savings? Every dime that you earn this year will be stored, where? You don't have to work where you live, and you don't have to think where you live, and you don't have to store where you live. If you live in Venezuela and you make money in bolivars, or if you live in Argentina and you're making pesos, you don't have to save your pesos in an Argentine bank. You could choose to place your wealth in a different location than your business interest, while your mind is in one place and your body is in another. The idea of crypto, the great achievement of Satoshi Nakamoto, is the concept of creating a truly decentralized network, giving it to billions of people, allowing people in a decentralized way, protect that network, support that network, serve that network, benefit from that network, transcending the constraints of a CEO, a corporation, a country, a city, a company. What if we could create something which is truly a utilitarian, egalitarian and economically and philosophically empowering computer network created on the strength of the power of cryptography.

And cryptography is a machine with a mechanical advantage instead of a Roman construction crane with a 180-to-one mechanical advantage that lets you move a one-ton block with your hands -- we're talking about cryptography where it becomes billions or trillions of times harder to break the code than it is to create the code. It's a trillion-to-one advantage. It's a quadrillion-to-one advantage. If you can create a mechanical advantage in cyberspace, then you can create something which is going to transcend beyond the reach of the collective. And you finally have a tool with which to fight back.

Bitcoin is a shining city in cyberspace, and you can go there once you understand it. Bitcoin and Objectivism, they have a common cause. Ayn Rand, in 1959, said: “I'm for the separation of state and economics, in the same way and for the same reasons as the separation of church and state.” Whereas, Hayek, in 1984, said: “I don't believe we shall ever have good money again before we take the thing out of the hands of the government. That is, we can't take it violently out of the hands of the government. All we can do is by some sly roundabout way, introduce something that they can't stop.”

Clearly, both movements are thinking about separating economics from the state and from the collective.

The difference is for thousands and thousands of years, the technology for doing that was imperfect. The technology of gold to separate the power from the state doesn't work when they just shoot you and take your gold. The technology of cows or tobacco or fiat currency or buildings, they don't work that well to separate economics from the state. So although this was an ideal and aspiration, we never had the technology to realize it.

January 3rd, 2009 is the singularity. That's the point at which Satoshi Nakamoto developed the technology to transfer value through space without a trusted third party. Now, people say that a lot. They say he solved the Byzantine Generals problem. But if you can transfer something of value through cyberspace without a trusted third party, that means you can manifest something of value in cyberspace without a trusted third party. That means you can create and store and transfer energy in the digital realm.  The creation of digital property, digital money, digital energy, and digital matter was therefore effected on January 3rd, 2009. Most people don't realize this, but Satoshi opened a portal from the physical realm into the digital realm. And energy began to flow into cyberspace, bringing life to a formerly dead realm, consisting only of shadows and ghosts.  Bringing conservation of energy and matter, objectivity, truth, time, and consequence into the digital realm, delivering property rights, freedom, and sovereignty that is separate from the physical and the political realm, to humanity.

Most of the world, myself included, ignored this chain reaction for the next decade. It happened, it flickered, it burned. We ignored it except for the OG Bitcoin Cipher punks. And they can tell you that everybody thought they were crazy. In March of 2020, the world came to a grinding halt. Suddenly billions of people woke up to the prospect of an economic collapse, losing faith in their institutions and their governments. On August 10th, MicroStrategy, struggling with this existential crisis, adopts the Bitcoin standard. At that point, I concluded, the road to serfdom is working exponentially harder for a currency growing exponentially weaker. And we saw an escape from economic slavery in the form of what we thought was digital gold. But as I've explained, it turned out to be much more than digital gold.

On September 18th, after fully adopting the Bitcoin standard, and after talking to some more Bitcoiners, I had this epiphany. I went to Twitter and I posted the following: Bitcoin is a swarm of cyber hornets serving the goddess of wisdom, feeding on the fire of truth, exponentially growing ever smarter, faster, and stronger behind a wall of encrypted energy. And I think Ayn Rand would understand what I was saying.

What it means is, for the first time in the human race, we have unleashed a freedom virus, a truth virus. We've unleashed a sovereignty virus, which is also a monetary virus. And as you know, and as Heinlein once said, the only way to fight a virus is with another virus. You can't take it on. You can't take it head on. Bitcoin is something special. Galt's Gulch is the Bitcoin network. Rather than removing your labor from a corrupt economy, you should remove your money from a corrupt economy. Bitcoin's a protocol to create free ideas, free economies, and free assets beyond the control of corrupt institutions. It's a fast, fair, and equitable method to settle the differences of 8 billion people. We say in the Bitcoin world: Fix the money, fix the world.

Success. We want to succeed. This is the end of my speech. We could talk about the struggle and the human misery, and we could talk about the reasons why, and what people think about it. But ultimately it doesn't really much matter. I don't want to be a martyr. I don't want us to die for our country. I want us to be the winners. Success requires courage, clarity, and commitment.

Look, there's 20,000 cryptos. There's one that’s 95% dominant, which is ethically sound, technically sound, economically sound. Bitcoin is Rearden Metal. It's the hardest substance in the universe. Most people don't know this. Most people are afraid of it. Never done that before. When we bought Bitcoin, we bought 250 million. No one, no public company had ever bought any.

People thought we were crazy. So then we bought another 175 million. People thought we were crazy. Then we bought 600 million more. People said: You can't stand on it, it'll destroy you. It's like standing on a bridge made of steel. And I concluded it's the perfect engineered material to solve our problem, but people are living in fear. And how are we going to get them to not be fearful? And I was reminded of Andrew Carnegie's example. It's like, build the bridge. Go stand out in the middle of the bridge. You build an airplane, fly the airplane, show people that it's not going break. That's what MicroStrategy did. We said, Well, if it's good for a hundred million, it's good for a billion. If it's good for a billion, we might as well go for 4 billion, right? And at some point people will realize that they have more to fear by not embracing this technology than by embracing it.

Right now it's a $400 billion asset. There are $400 trillion of other assets floating around in our current fiat system. They're leaking energy, they're corrupt, they're inefficient, they're controlled by the collective. Bitcoin is 0.1% of the human race's liquid energy, 99.9% of the world doesn't get it. They're not there. That 99.9% haven't moved to Galt’s Gulch. That means you're still early. So plug in yourself, your company, your organization, your agency, your product, your service, your family, or your ideology.

I said to you at the beginning of the talk, Bitcoin's a union. The union gets more powerful as more people join. And in the war for the future of money, it's going to be won with money. As the money moves into the network, the monetary union gets more powerful. Everybody that joins the network has that much more power. And your only hope against the oppressive force of the collective is to unionize your own activities and organize your activities with people of like ideology that believe as you believe.  More money, more people, more power.

So in closing, Bitcoin is an economic machine based on a truth machine poised to emerge as a freedom machine.  It's the best choice we have to save our civilization and realize the ideal world envisioned by Ayn Rand and the Objectivist movement. Join us. Thank you.
