She said the last thing — the one that ties everything together — is that the membership pays you back only if you use the whole thing.

"Here's how it all fits together. Understand that the membership is the product, so Costco wants you to feel it's worth renewing. Choose Gold Star or Executive based on your actual yearly spending — about $3,250 is the break-even. If you're Executive, use the early hours, the monthly delivery credit, and the services perks. Buy your gas at Costco and pay with a card that earns extra on gas. Use the app for entry, checkout, and food court. Check Costco Travel, the Auto Program, and Services before big purchases. Use the pharmacy, optical, hearing, and tire centers. Buy discounted gift cards. Know when to shop in the warehouse and when online is better. And follow the new membership rules so you don't get stopped at the door."

She said the biggest mistake is treating Costco like a regular grocery store.

"Most members only use the cheap prices on the shelf. That's great, but it's only one piece. The 2% reward, gas, travel, services, optical, tires, and gift cards are where the membership really pays off. A family that uses all of it can get many times their membership fee back every year."

She said do a quick Costco checkup once a year.

"Before your renewal date, look at your total spending for the year in the app or on your receipts. Decide whether Executive makes sense. Check your reward certificate. Think about upcoming big purchases — a car, a vacation, tires, glasses — and check Costco first. And remember Costco's membership satisfaction guarantee: if you're truly unhappy, Costco has long offered a membership fee refund. Check the current terms."

She told her cousin the same thing she told members for 12 years:

"Your membership card isn't a ticket to get in the door. It's a key to a whole set of savings. The members who get the most out of Costco aren't the ones who spend the most. They're the ones who use everything they're already paying for."

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla
 shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's 
lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was 
worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for 
his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about
 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that 
same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it 
"unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall 
and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the
 judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, 
unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for 
his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by 
about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for
 the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 
billion?

Peterson: “mr. chief justice, and may it please the court. aedpa's restrictions on second or successive habeas applications reflect the balance struck by congress between finality and error correction. rather than pursue error correction at all costs, congress chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability. this court decided atkins v. virginia and announced the rule that the constitution prohibits capital punishment of the intellectually disabled before respondent even committed his crimes. and respondent relied on atkins v. virginia in his initial federal habeas application. the rule of atkins is not a new rule of constitutional law that was previously unavailable to him under section 2244(b)(2)(a), and moore v. texas, which was a legal change following respondent's initial federal habeas application, has not been made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this court. nor can respondent pass through the gateway of section 2244(b)(2)(b) because the facts underlying his claim are unrelated to his guilt for the underlying offense. this court should defer to congress's policy choices, correct the fifth circuit's interpretation of section 2244(b)(2)(a), and reverse. i welcome the court's questions. well, mr. peterson, would you, um, spend a minute or two on the fifth circuit's reasoning on unavailability? your honor, as we read the fifth circuit's opinion, it focused on the availability of a claim, rather than on the availability of a rule. and the fifth circuit might well have been right about whether or not the claim was available. obviously, a claim has two pieces, a legal rule and- what should unavailability focus on? under the text of 2244(b)(2)(a), it is the rule that must be unavailable, not the claim. and what's the source of that rule? uh, well, we look both at the last antecedent modifier, that's the only reasonable modification. i believe respondent now agrees from his merits brief that previously unavailable modifies rule and not claim. and we see this as well in section 2255(h)(2), which uses the identical phrase, "new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this court that was previously unavailable without any mention of claim." so what role does the dsm play in that analysis? we think that any claim based on the dsm or based on a diagnosis under an updated dsm would be properly reviewed under 2244(b)(2)(b). these sorts of updates in scientific evidence, the nacdl amicus brief correctly explains in our view, can provide new factual predicates for claims. but the respondent here has disclaimed any reliance on 2244(b)(2)(b). and so we see 2244(b)(2)(a) and (b)(2)(b) as dividing a claim into two pieces. if you're trying to read... well, why is the, um, why is the dsm a fact? why isn't it part of the law? in other words, when atkins was announced, we made clear that there was, um, it was going to be based in large part on psychological criteria that were developed, uh, under the dsm. you know, it was clear that it was going to evolve. it was clear that, uh, states were going to have a fair bit of flexibility in deciding how to use the dsm with respect to the rule. so we almost said in atkins that the dsm was going to be, and, and other studies or, or, uh, evidence of a similar kind was going to form the legal standard of atkins. so why think of it as factual matter rather than the thing that provides in, at least in large part, the legal standard and was contemplated in just that way? respectfully, your honor, i think that became most clear following hall versus florida and moore versus texas. and keep in mind, hall recognizes that the legal determination of intellectual disability is distinct from a medical diagnosis. so it's important to keep in mind the distinction between the dsm-5 as a scientific standard and the incorporation of that dsm into law, which occurred here in texas following moore versus texas. now, my friend hasn't raised a claim under moore versus texas. i think if this court had made moore versus texas retroactive to cases on collateral review, that's the claim that he would be bringing and he would be making essentially the same argument, arguments acknowledging that this is a moore claim. but my friend says the rule he relies on as a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review is atkins itself. yeah. i guess what i'm suggesting is that, um, atkins, uh, is more, there's, there's more than one atkins rule. there was an, there, there, there are different atkins rules in different states because different states, uh, articulate the standards differently and there are different atkins rules over time. um, and with respect to big changes like the change that occurred in the dsm, you might say that there's a kind of atkins 1 and an atkins 2. so to sort of think of it as one atkins rule is to misunderstand the nature of atkins itself. well, your honor, i can certainly accept that framing because in order for that framing to prevail, atkins 2, which i think is probably post moore versus texas, would itself need to be a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this court. now... can i ask you about that because i guess i'm not quite sure, um, that that interpretation of the term of art, new rule of constitutional law made retroactive is what this statute is doing. um, you talked at the beginning about congress's intent and how they were setting it up and i suppose there is an interpretation that sees new rule of constitutional law made retroactive as a term of art that was established during the teague v. lane, um, set of cases to describe a type of claim or a type of rule and really isn't about the timing of the rule. so what i mean by that is when the supreme court announces a rule and determines that it is so significant and monumental and momentous that even prisoners who have closed cases should benefit from it. it's going to be retroactive, says the supreme court. we're talking about a certain kind of new rule that is distinguished from other rules where the supreme court doesn't decide that they should be retroactive. if we read the statute in that way, then why wouldn't atkins, meaning the determination that a person who is intellectually disabled cannot be executed. why doesn't it satisfy that and mr. johnson here can take advantage of it in the way that justice kagan suggests, um, because it evolves as we understood with new medical standards over time. well, two pieces to that, your honor. i would distinguish the new rule definition from the previously available question. which one are you relying on in this? i'm relying on both of them. i'm asking the court to resolve the circuit split over previously unavailable, but certainly we acknowledge that our argument is that atkins was not a new rule with respect to mr. johnson. with respect to mr. johnson, and i guess what i'm suggesting is that the statute isn't really talking about is a new rule, uh, new with respect to a particular petitioner. that that part of the statute is just talking about the nature of this rule and is not relative to any individual petitioner. that you get to the individual petitioner in the previously unavailable part of the statute. and i think what that would be doing is taking half of the teague definition. part of the teague definition is looking at the state of the law at the time the prisoner's conviction became final on direct appeal. and then, of course, the statute 2244(b)(2)(a) requires that the rule have been made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this court. that makes perfect sense if the rule is being applied retroactively. if it is a rule that was announced by this court after the prisoner's conviction became final on direct appeal and is then being applied on collateral review. but that's the problem, which is teague is, you, you have to have a timing rule for teague to avoid the very issue of retroactivity. under teague announces a rule of timing to ensure that there's sort of a deadline for that. um, what cases is it going to apply to today? but that's not the issue here. the issue here is the use of previously unavailable. um, you argue that a new rule announced before a person's first habeas position can never be a new rule. that was previously under, uh, unavailable, but let me give you a stark example of a situation. um, let's assume that we announce you can't execute someone before they're 70. before they're 70. thank you. i'm sorry. after they're 70. that that would violate the constitution. you would argue that a person who's 28 sentenced to death would have to bring his rule, but when he turns 70, he can't. your honor, i think that rule would go to the type of claim that would not be considered second or successful. why? because that wouldn't be ripe until the time of execution. so this is not ripe until the time of execution, and today you're saying even if he is mentally disabled under our, the definition of mental disability that atkins said under the dm-5, let's assume there's no dispute that he wins under dm-5. why isn't it a question of ripeness? because your honor, this isn't about his competence or eligibility to be executed. this is about his sentencing, the imposition of capital punishment. i don't see what the difference is. what we have said under atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill. we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the dm-5 makes it right. now, there's a timing issue that's separate that the court below may have dealt with right or wrong. i don't know, but put that aside. if that wasn't available during his first habeas petition because it wasn't ripe yet, why isn't it ripe now? so your honor, with respect to ripeness, this is, it's not a competency to be executed claim. it's about the moral blameworthiness of the defendant at the time of, excuse me, at the time of the crimes. that's why we're not looking at the, there's a distinct line of authority for ford and panetti claims relating to competence. that i understand, but we're not talking about panetti. we're talking about a different constitutional right not to be executed if you're mentally ill. well, but his argument is not that he has become intellectually disabled. no, he's saying i've been mentally disabled. that's in fact the entire atkins claim. and he now believes that he has a way to establish his intellectual disability. that goes to availability. we respectfully disagree, your honor. we see that perhaps going to the availability of the claim, but not to the availability of the rule of atkins, that the constitution prohibits the imposition of capital punishment on the intellectually disabled. justice kagan, let me return to your question. and i think the helpful way of thinking about this is what the court recognized in montgomery versus louisiana, that when the constitution prohibits a particular form of punishment for a class of persons, an affected prisoner receives a procedure through which he can show that he belongs to the protected class. so we have a substantive rule in atkins protecting a class of persons, the intellectually disabled. and then what we have is hall and moore perhaps modifying the procedures by which a person can prove that he would belong to the protected class. but under edwards versus vannoy, those procedures wouldn't be new rules of constitutional law applied retroactively. and this court certainly hasn't made them so. but why are you saying that it's a modification of the procedures? it is a substantive change in who belongs in the class. it's not about, you know, evidence, right? it's not a change in what mr. johnson can offer to show that he's intellectually disabled. it is a substantive change in the criteria of the people who constitute that class. so first, every circuit that has recognized moore as a new rule has treated moore as a new procedural rule that is not retroactive. why are you talking about moore? i'm talking about atkins, right? atkins says you can't execute the intellectually disabled. and in the context of that very case, we indicated that who qualifies as intellectually disabled is keyed to medical standards and that medical standards might vary throughout the country. it might evolve over time. i don't understand why that's characterized as a procedural determination. atkins did leave the definition of intellectual disability to the states. and then even in hall, where this court placed a greater emphasis legally on updated medical definitions, it's still reiterated that the legal determination of intellectual disability is distinct from a medical diagnosis. no, i understand. but it's, so let me ask you this. the problem, i think, with your interpretation is that, as you said, we're supposed to be giving effect to the congress's policy choices. and as i understood this set of provisions, congress's policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims. this is what the whole scheme is about. you can't bring a second or successive claim if you've had the opportunity before and you didn't do it. the way you're interpreting this, mr. johnson will never get that opportunity because the criteria that makes him eligible for claiming that he's intellectually disabled came after his original habeas petition. but you're saying that because it relates to the rule that we had laid out before, he's foreclosed. and that seems like a really incongruous consequence given congress's policy determination in this case. respectfully, your honor, i disagree with the premise of the question. i think what you articulated was essentially the common law abuse of the writ doctrine that preceded aedpa. and what we see in 2244(b)(2) is congress restricting the abuse of the writ, taking away opportunities. and the best way of looking at that is the limitation that we see in 2244(b)(2)(b), romanette 2. we know that congress didn't intend to allow prisoners to raise any previously unavailable claim because that limitation in romanette 2 means that if a prisoner uncovers a new factual predicate for a claim that is unrelated to whether they would have been found guilty of the underlying offense, they do not have an opportunity to bring that claim. so we don't look at this as congress attempting to provide a full opportunity. we look at this as congress placing strict limitations on second or successive applications and favoring finality.”

The Chief Justice: “thank you, counsel. justice thomas, any further? justice alito?”

Justice Alito: “when i'm thinking of availability, i'm thinking of how we define the term under the plra, because for me, these two were passed essentially at the same time. and so the meaning we've given available is exactly the same meaning the fifth circuit gave it. and it's the meaning that our precedents have given it in the plra. why isn't that the precedent that we should be following?”

Peterson: “your honor, when i look at the plra, booth v. turner recognizes that the meaning of a phrase involving available depends heavily on what must be available. in that case, the court had to determine what it meant for a remedy to be available. i'll note that booth rejects a futility exception under the plra. and ross v. blake, when it talks about what might make an administrative remedy unavailable under the plra, identifies procedural impediments to the filing of that sort of claim, the inability to take advantage of it by even asserting those sorts of arguments, not this fact that it would have been nonmeritorious.”

The Chief Justice: “justice kagan?”

Justice Kagan: “well, there, the impediments were procedural, but ross v. blake talks about you run into just a dead end. you run into a brick wall. and if something makes you run into a brick wall, you know, it's not available to you. so here, it wouldn't be procedures. it would just be this rule was of no use to me prior to the dsm-5. i was just -- i was going to lose any atkins claim i brought. so why isn't that -- it's not about procedures, but it has the same connotation of i couldn't do anything with this new rule before now. when we look at ross, that dead end phrase, i think the court explained it, involved officers unable or consistently unwilling to provide any relief to aggrieve inmates. i think that would be a circumstance where, for example, you might have a district clerk who would simply refuse to file a petition. well, that would be a closer analogy to the specific facts in ross. i agree with you there. but the idea, i think, is broader than that. and it reflects what available means, and it reflects even your own definitions of available, which is like i couldn't use it to achieve my purposes, whatever the "it" is. here it's the new rule. and if i couldn't use this rule to achieve any of my purposes, if i was going to be laughed out of court, then really the rule was unavailable to me. what we would say is it was capable of being used, simply not useful. that's the usage by this court in perry v. new hampshire, referring to constitutional safeguards available to defendants, including compulsory process. compulsory process remains a constitutional safeguard available to a defendant, even one who doesn't have any use for it. so in this case, we think of the two pieces of a claim. if the prisoner has the legal rule available to him that he can bring to court that would serve as a rule of decision, even if he doesn't have the factual predicate for that claim, that rule is available. and that's consistent with how we see the structure of 2244(b)(2). thank you.”

The Chief Justice: “justice gorsuch.”

Justice Gorsuch: “sure. just so i understand the exact rule that you're articulating on previously unavailable, what if the new rule is announced by this court during the pendency of the first federal habeas? i want to be precise about what you think happens then.”

Peterson: “your honor, we think that is a difficult question that is not presented on the facts of this case and that you don't need to address in order to resolve this case. i got that part. however, we agree with the eleventh circuit's interpretation in bowles. that's what we have consistently argued for. if a prisoner can say, even though this court announced the rule while i had an initial federal habeas petition or a federal habeas petition pending, i could not have actually brought that rule before the district court. i was not in a position to invoke that rule. i would not have been permitted to invoke it. because it was too late in that litigation? is that what you're suggesting? your honor, i think of an extreme hypothetical. if this court were to announce a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review the day that a district court enters final judgment or the day before a district court enters final judgment, the court could adopt a bright line rule based on banister and rivers, but we might acknowledge that under some circumstances such as those a prisoner would be able to say that rule was not available to me, even though theoretically if i had been able to amend my pending petition the day before final judgment, it would not have constituted a second or successive application. and second, we could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing previously unavailable, correct? yes, your honor, you could. now the state's asking you to resolve it based on previously unavailable in part because of the pending kathy case that we have. and kathy atkins was a new rule because it was announced after his conviction became final on direct appeal, and that would still leave the acknowledged split between at least the fifth and the eleventh circuits. thank you.”

The Chief Justice: “mr. spirit?”

Mr. Spirit: “picking up on justice kavanaugh's first question, would the state support a rule that said that whether the claim was available is measured from the time the habeas, the first habeas petition is filed? i suspect that would go a bit too far, your honor. we can, certainly we would say if it was announced before the filing of the initial federal habeas application, we do agree that it would have been available. i don't think we would say that every rule announced after the filing of the initial federal habeas petition would be unavailable. this court did in bannister and rivers recognize that filings before the entry of final judgment during a pending federal habeas application are not second or successive. we certainly think in the mine run of cases, a prisoner is going to be able to take advantage of a new rule announced while a pending, excuse me, while a federal habeas petition is pending. how would you propose, let's imagine, assume for the purposes of this question that we agree with your position, how would you recommend writing that so it fudges that issue? i think what you would write is to say the question presented in this case, and we tried to narrow it slightly in the merits brief, was to talk about this is a rule that had been announced before the filing of the petitioner's initial federal habeas application and made retroactive to cases on collateral review. we conclude. so just describing it with reference to the facts of this case. yes, your honor, you could do that, and that's going to solve, we think, 99 percent of the cases. certainly just adopting our understanding of previously unavailable is going to avoid the problems that might result with publication of, say, the dsm-6 when new prisoners would come forward saying, "i am now intellectually disabled," when i wasn't previously. so at one point in this litigation, the issue was cast as a matter of a judicially created futility exception. how, if at all, do you understand the current argument about previously unavailable to differ from the futility argument? we would characterize respondent's argument the same way. their theory is that a claim is, as i understand the argument, it is that a rule is unavailable when a claim is unavailable or a claim would lack merit and it would be futile to raise that claim. so i think they still are tying in the availability of a rule to the futility of asserting a claim under that rule. thank you.”

The Chief Justice: “justice jackson?”

Justice Jackson: “can i just get clarification on that? so they say the rule is unavailable if i could not take advantage of it, and your argument in response to that is what, it's still available if it just existed. the rule was available to be used for whatever purpose the prisoner could make use of it. so remember, as we define rule that is capable of being used, it is not necessarily useful to a particular prisoner. so the way of thinking of it here is there are two pieces of a claim. there is the legal predicate for the claim and the factual predicate. the prisoner may well have the legal rule available to him. he can always make any use of it that he wants to and indeed respond and use that rule in his initial federal habeas application. not the same way he is using it now, but he did rely on site atkins, urge a court to follow it and account for it in the arguments he was making. what he lacked at the time of that initial federal habeas application was the factual predicate. right. so what do you do with the fact that we have sort of rejected, i noted that your brief didn't cite panetti versus quarterman, but the same kind of analysis came up with respect to ford claims. this is kind of what justice sotomayor was exploring with you. a ford claim is one in which we have said that states are prohibited from executing people when they can't understand why they're being killed and that kind of factual circumstance arises later and the government in ford said, too bad, you needed to make the claim originally because it was available to you because ford existed and the fact that you didn't have that factual predicate, you know, sorry. and we said, no, that doesn't really make sense because it doesn't enable this defendant to ever make the claim. and here similarly, i think the same kind of thing is happening. and your honor, we see those as qualitatively different claims that panetti and ford are about the defendant's competence to be executed, which is focused on the defendant's status at the moment of execution, whereas an atkins claim concerns the defendant's status at the time of the crime and conviction, the onset of disability of the intellectual disability during the developmental period. but if the standards change as to whether or not at the time of the initial conviction he was intellectually disabled, you're saying that doesn't matter. he didn't have the factual predicate at the relevant time... 1/3

text:
Here is a selection of quotes or texts intended to help understand the Importance of Creativity category or phase. 

"Creativity is the key to success in the future, and primary education is where teachers can bring creativity in children at that level." - A.P.J. Abdul Kalam

"Imagination will often carry us to worlds that never were. But without it we go nowhere." - Carl Sagan

"We need to make the world safe for creativity and intuition, for it's creativity and intuition that will make the world safe for us." - Edgar Mitchell, Apollo Astronaut

"The future of humanity is going to bifurcate in two directions: Either it's going to become multiplanetary, or it's going to remain confined to one planet and eventually there's going to be an extinction event." - Elon Musk

"Happiness lies in the joy of achievement and the thrill of creative effort." - Franklin D. Roosevelt

"Ideas are the factors that lift civilization. They create revolutions. There is more dynamite in an idea than in many bombs." - John H. Vincent

"Creativity will always be the most powerful tool that we will ever use," - Sir John Hegarty

"Recent research shows that people who consistently engage in creative tasks tend to have brains that function several years younger than their chronological age. Creative engagement keeps your neural networks active, helping your brain become more adaptable and resilient." - Dr. Joseph Mercola

"Science consistently produces a new crop of miraculous truths and dazzling devices every year." - Kary Mullis

"Creativity is as important now in education as literacy and we should treat it with the same status." - Ken Robinson

"Nobody will stop you from creating. Do it tonight. So it tomorrow. That is the way to make your soul grow." - Kurt Vonnegut

"Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood. Now is the time to understand more, so that we may fear less." - Marie Curie

"You can't use up creativity. The more you use, the more you have." - Maya Angelou

"A moment's insight is sometimes worth a life's experience." - Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr.

"Fostering creativity in children is as important as any other part of the school curriculum because it feeds the soul. A daily dose of creativity helps children imagine a better world and then create it." - Renee Fleming

"What I can't create I don't understand" - Richard P. Feynman

"Everything around you that you call life was made up by people that were no smarter than you and you can change it, you can influence it, you can build your own things that other people can use." - Steve Jobs

"There is a grandeur in any act of creativity. There is mystery in the formation of a new idea. A new idea is one of the most precious things in the world. It comes along all too seldom. But when it does, revolutions are caused, industries are born, and in some cases, other industries die as a result of the same idea. It is a marvelous thing to know you have thought something no one else has ever thought, and done something no one else has ever done." - Thomas P. Carney, chemical engineer, former chairman of Notre Dame trustees

"Genius means little more than the faculty of perceiving in an unhabitual way." - William James

"Music is a means capable of expressing dark dramatism and pure rapture, suffering and ecstasy, fiery and cold fury, melancholy and wild merriment – and the subtlest nuances and interplay of these feelings which words are powerless to express and which are unattainable in painting and sculpture." - Dmitri Shostakovich

"There is no doubt that creativity is the most important human resource of all. Without creativity, there would be no progress, and we would be forever repeating the same patterns." - Edward de Bono

"The practical applications of new discoveries in science sometimes extend faster and further than the knowledge of the general principles on which they depend." - William Smith "Father of English Geology" And Author of the First Geologic map of Britain

"The greatest real thrill that life offers is to create, to construct, to develop something useful. Too often we fail to recognize and pay tribute to the creative spirit. It is that spirit that creates our jobs." - Alfred P. Sloan

"There are certain things that our age needs. It needs, above all, courageous hope and the impulse to creativeness." - Bertrand Russell

"People have told me, 'My dad passed on, but I have great memories of watching your shows with him.' It doesn't get any better than that." - Bob Newhart

"The life of a scientist is all about the creative process." - John C. Mather

"In my view, aiming at simplicity and lucidity is a moral duty of all intellectuals: lack of clarity is a sin, and pretentiousness is a crime. Creativity, in this sense, is about finding clear and simple solutions to complex problems." - Karl Popper

"I'm a musician. I play harmonica for relaxation. A good way to relax and entertain people. An excellent way to have fun." - Stan Musial "The Man"

"What is the use of living, if it be not to strive for noble causes and to make this muddled world a better place for those who will live in it after we are gone?" - Winston Churchill

"When learning is purposeful, creativity blossoms. When creativity blossoms, thinking emanates. When thinking emanates, knowledge is fully lit. When knowledge is lit, economy flourishes." - A.P.J. Abdul Kalam

"Still the question recurs "can we do better?" The dogmas of the quiet past, are inadequate to the stormy present. The occasion is piled high with difficulty, and we must rise with the occasion. As our case is new, so we must think anew, and act anew." - Abraham Lincoln (December 1, l862, Annual Message to Congress)

"The question is, who is interested in creativity? And my answer is that practically everybody is. This interest is no longer confined to psychologists and psychiatrists. Now it has become a question of national and international policy as well." - Abraham Maslow

"I like living. I have sometimes been wildly, despairingly, acutely miserable, racked with sorrow, but through it all I still know quite certainly that just to be alive is a grand thing." - Agatha Christie

"To create is to live twice." - Albert Camus

"Creating is the most intense excitement one can come to know." - Anni Albers

"Art makes life worth living, and in my opinion, it's what makes humans worth the fight. Like all of the things that we leave behind, all the creations, wouldn't it be so unfortunate if there's nobody on the other side to witness and observe them?" - Ayisha Siddiqa

"As we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours, and this we should do freely and generously." - Benjamin Franklin

"What we shall desire for individuals is now clear: strong creative impulses, overpowering and absorbing the instinct of possession; reverence for others; respect for the fundamental creative impulse in ourselves. A certain kind of self-respect or native pride is necessary to a good life; a man must not have a sense of utter inward defeat if he is to remain whole, but must feel the courage and the hope and the will to live by the best that is in him, whatever outward or inward obstacles it may encounter. So far as it lies in a man's own power, his life will realize its best possibilities if it has three things: creative rather than possessive impulses, reverence for others, and respect for the fundamental impulse in himself." - Bertrand Russell

"The best life is the one in which the creative impulses play the largest part and the possessive impulses the smallest." - Bertrand Russell

"Humor's a weapon if you want to make it one." - Bob Newhart

"Why should we all use our creative power....? Because there is nothing that makes people so generous, joyful, lively, bold and compassionate, so indifferent to fighting and the accumulation of objects and money." - Brenda Ueland

"Where there's music there can be no evil." - Miguel de Cervantes

"Music bypasses the brain and goes straight to the heart. I wish my life had more of it." - Dick Cavett

"I think it's tremendously important at this particular time to keep thinking about creativity in geology, because this is an era in which it is extremely easy to fall into the belief that advanced technology and hardware can do our thinking for us." - Dr. Stanley M. Totten

"What does music mean to you? What would you do without music?" - Duke Ellington

"Writers do not merely reflect and interpret life, they inform and shape life," - E. B. White

"A creative life is an amplified life. It's a bigger life, a happier life, an expanded life, and a hell of a lot more interesting life"" - Elizabeth Gilbert

"When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favor." - Elon Musk

"We are not making science for science. We are making science for the benefit of humanity." - Françoise Barré-Sinoussi

"The key role of entrepreneurs, like the most crucial role of scientists, is not to fill in the gaps in an existing market or theory, but to generate entirely new markets or theories. . .They stand before a canvas as empty as any painter's; a page as blank as any poet's." - George Gilder

"Since new developments are the products of a creative mind, we must therefore stimulate and encourage that type of mind in every way possible." - George Washington Carver

"What we were aiming at was getting people well, and the satisfaction of that is much greater than any prize you can get." - Gertrude Elion

"Today we are engaged in a contest for human freedom. During the last war we crushed one type of totalitarian tyranny in a military sense, but the ideological fight has not been won, for we cannot eliminate ideas by physical means and yet maintain freedom of thought . Only better and more inspiring ideas can be used to fight tyrannical ideas." - Harold Urey

"There is no greater joy than that of feeling oneself a creator. The triumph of life is expressed by creation." - Henri Bergson

"It  is art that makes life, makes interest, makes importance, and I know of no substitute for the force and beauty of it's process." - Henry James

"To live in the world of creation -to get into it and stay in it- to frequent it and haunt it... to think intently and fruitfully, to woo combinations and inspirations into being by a depth and continuity of attention and meditation -this is the only thing." - Henry James

"Imagination, as well as reason is necessary to perfection in the philosophical mind. A rapidity of combination, a power of perceiving analogies, and of comparing them by facts, in the creative source of discovery. Discrimination and delicacy of sensation, so important in physical research, are other words for taste; and the love of nature is the same passion, as the love of the magnificent, the sublime and the beautiful." - Sir Humphry Davy (1778-1829)

"History proves abundantly that pure science, undertaken without regard to applications to human needs, is usually ultimately of direct benefit to mankind." - Irving Langmuir

"You are today where your thoughts have brought you; you will be tomorrow where your thoughts take you." - James Allen

"I think music is an instrument. It can create the initial thought patterns that can change the thinking of people." - John Coltrane

"The art of drawing which is of more real importance to the human race than that of writing ...should be taught to every child just as writing is." - John Ruskin

"Progress toward a more abundant material life does not come like manna from heaven... The ultimate resource is people—especially skilled, spirited, and hopeful young people endowed with liberty—who will exert their wills and imaginations for their own benefit and inevitably benefit the rest of us as well." - Julian Simon

"The main fuel to speed the world's progress is our stock of knowledge, and the brake is our lack of imagination. The ultimate resource is people – skilled, spirited, hopeful people – who will exert their wills and imaginations for their own benefit as well as in a spirit of faith and social concern. Inevitably they will benefit not only themselves but the poor and the rest of us as well." - Julian L. Simon

"There is a general place in your brain, I think, reserved for melancholy of relationships past. It grows and prospers as life progresses, forcing you finally, against your better judgment, to listen to country music." - Kary Mullis

"We know that the way the way to improve the world is to work, is to create, is to build. And the problem with WOKE culture is that it has trained too many young minds like your to forget about that." - Konstantin Kisin

"No matter how corrupt, greedy, and heartless our government, our corporations, our media, and our religious & charitable institutions may become, the music will still be wonderful." - Kurt Vonnegut

"The key to the mystery of a great artist is that for reasons unknown, he will give away his energies and his life just to make sure that one note follows another... and leaves us with the feeling that something is right in the world." - Leonard Bernstein

"Science makes people reach selflessly for truth and objectivity; it teaches people to accept reality, with wonder and admiration, not to mention the deep awe and joy that the natural order of things brings to the true scientist." - Lise Meitner

"Science is a creative endeavor, and creativity thrives on diversity of thought and perspective." - Mae Jemison

"[Marc Andreessen says that America's strategic advantage lies not in mimicking China's centralized system but in doubling down on what we're good at:] "What if we become more like us? And what if we lean even harder into innovation, and even harder into creativity, and even harder into entrepreneurship? And isn't there so much more that we could do if we got to be more like us?"" - Marc Andreessen

"I shall devote only a few lines to the expression of my belief in the importance of science … it is by this daily striving after knowledge that man has raised himself to the unique position he occupies on earth, and that his power and well-being have continually increased." - Marie Curie

"It would be a sad day if human beings, adjusting to the Computer Revolution, become so intellectually lazy that they lost their power of creative thinking." - Martin Gardner

"As for the individual himself, failure to use such an abundant inherent treasure as creativity, whether it be because of unawareness that it exists, indifference, or deliberate stultification, is more than a waste, it is self-betrayal." - Masatoshi Yoshimura

"Innovation is the central issue in economic prosperity." - Michael Porter

"When this happens we will be practicing the art of finding oil and gas as true scientists -- as pure, thoroughly trained, well-rounded petroleum explorers --- not as unilateral specialists limited in scope, in knowledge and thinking power." - Michel T. Halbouty

"Creativity is a central source of meaning in our lives ...most of the things that are interesting, important, and human are the results of creativity ...when we are involved in it, we feel that we are living more fully than during the rest of life." - Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi

"Talent ... must be stimulated. The country will not manage without it." - Mikhail Gorbachev (1990)

"Human ingenuity has always been successful in overcoming crises that once seemed inevitable." - Nicholas Vardy

"Art washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life." - Pablo Picasso

"We usually find oil in new places with old ideas. Sometimes, also, we find oil in an old place with a new idea, but we seldom find much oil in a old place with an old idea. Several times in the past we have thought we were running out of oil whereas actually we were only running out of ideas." - Parke A. Dickey, Geologist

"I was born with music inside me. Music was one of my parts. Like my ribs, my kidneys, my liver, my heart. Like my blood. It was a force already within me when I arrived on the scene. It was a necessity for me - like food or water." - Ray Charles

"I call the age we are entering the creative age because the key factor propelling us forward is the rise of creativity as the primary mover of our economy." - Richard Florida

"We are at the very beginning of time for the human race. It is not unreasonable that we grapple with problems. But there are tens of thousands of years in the future. Our responsibility is to do what we can, learn what we can, improve the solutions, and pass them on." - Richard P. Feynman

"In the end, however, the most satisfying and powerful way to feel this connection is through creative activity. Engaged in the creative process we feel more alive than ever, because we are making something and not merely consuming, Masters of the small reality we create. In doing this work, we are in fact creating ourselves." - Robert Greene (Mastery)

"In my view, the composer, just as the poet, the sculptor or the painter, is in duty bound to serve Man, the people. He must beautify life and defend it. He must be a citizen first and foremost, so that his art might consciously extol human life and lead man to a radiant future." - Sergei Prokofiev

"To show your true ability is always, in a sense, to surpass the limits of your ability, to go a little beyond them: to dare, to seek, to invent; it is at such a moment that new talents are revealed, discovered, and realized" - Simone de Beauvoir

"There is a fountain of youth: it is your mind, your talents, the creativity you bring to your life and the lives of people you love. When you learn to tap this source, you will truly have defeated age." - Sophia Loren

"The most important thing that I learned in all of this is that we could build something ourselves that could change the world." - Steve Jobs

"Thanks to generations of curious, daring, intrepid explorers of the past, we may know enough, soon enough, to chart safe passage for ourselves far into the future." - Sylvia A. Earle

"Our duty, as men and women, is to proceed as if limits to our ability did not exist. We are collaborators in creation." - Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

"What we tried to do is to sing a song as simple as possible, get to the meaning of the song that you are doing, such as to the where the person is listening can enjoy, sing along with it or hum along, as long as you can get the people to do that, I think that is a wonderful thing." - Don Mills, The Mills Brothers

"Creativity is the cornerstone of differentiation in business." - Tom Kelley

"Odd how the creative power at once brings the whole universe to order"" - Virginia Woolf

"Where oil is first found, in the final analysis, is in the minds of men. The undiscovered oil field exists only as an idea in the mind of some oil-finder. When no man any longer believes more oil is left to be found, no more oil fields will be discovered, but so long as a single oil-finder remains with a mental vision of a new oil field to cherish, along with freedom and incentive to explore, just so long new oil fields may continue to be discovered." - Wallace E. Pratt, 1952, Petroleum Geologist

"We are the same. There is no difference anywhere in the world. People are people. They laugh, cry, feel, and love, and music seems to be the commons denomination that brings us all together. Music cuts through all boundaries and goes right to the soul." - Willie Nelson

text:
Janet Elaine Parks -

🇺🇸 LAST NIGHT WAS A WAKE-UP CALL FOR REPUBLICANS. HERE'S MY HONEST TAKE ON WHAT HAPPENED..

I'm not going to sugarcoat it.

Democrats won the House.
Democrats won the Senate.
And they did it in places nobody expected.. 

🔹 Texas elected a Democratic senator, James Talarico, and a Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, beating Greg Abbott.
🔹 Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932.
🔹 Ohio sent Sherrod Brown back to the Senate.
🔹 Maine voted out Susan Collins.
🔹 Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina flipped too.

Seven Republican Senate seats flipped to Democrats in one night.. 

And here in Florida, a state we were told was "safe red," the governor's race came down to a few tenths of a point for most of the night before Byron Donalds pulled ahead.. 

So what actually happened?

1️⃣ PRICES

About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a major factor in their vote.. 

Gas was over $4 a gallon on Election Day.

I've spent months explaining that a lot of this didn't start with Trump: the 20% price jump from 2021 to 2024, refinery problems around the world, Russia and Ukraine. 
I still believe that.. 

But voters don't vote on explanations. They vote on what they pay at the pump and the grocery store.. 
And right now, that hurts.

2️⃣ THE IRAN WAR

About 6 in 10 voters said attacking Iran was the wrong decision, according to exit polls.. 

I've defended the goal. 
Every president for decades promised Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and Trump is the first one who actually acted on it.. 

But promises made on a campaign stage feel different when the war goes on for months, Americans die, and gas prices climb.. 

Voters felt the cost before they saw the result.. 

3️⃣ TARIFFS

In Maine, 69% of voters said tariffs had hurt their local economy.. 

I believe tariffs are bringing factories back. 
But a factory that opens in 2030 doesn't help a family paying more today.

The benefits are slow. 
The costs are immediate. 
And midterms don't wait.

4️⃣ TRUMP HIMSELF

Trump's approval was 38% in the exit polls.. 

About one in five people who voted for him in 2024 now disapprove of how he's doing.. 

That's not just Democrats. 
That's our own voters sending a message.. 

5️⃣ THE NEW NEIGHBORS

This is my own opinion, but I think it's part of the story.. 

Over the last several years, millions of Americans have left states like California, New York and Illinois for places like Texas, Florida and the Carolinas. 
Many came for lower taxes, safer streets and more freedom.. let’s get keep that part factual.. red states were safer, bottom line. 

And yet I can't help but wonder how many of them are voting for the same policies they moved away from.. 

To be fair, there is research showing people who move to red states tend to be more conservative than the people they left behind. 
They're a mix, not a blue voting bloc. 
And Texas and Kansas didn't flip just because of newcomers. 
They flipped because longtime voters changed their minds.

But in places as close as Florida was last night, every new voter matters. 
If you moved here for what this state offers, I hope you'll think about what made it that way.. 

TO BE FAIR

Democrats ran on real concerns: health care, prices and a war many people didn't want. 
Their candidates connected with voters, and they deserve credit for that.. 

And Republicans can't blame the media, the weather or anyone else. 
Voters told us exactly what they care about.. even if I believe it was the wrong move, 

MY TAKE

I'm still conservative. 
That didn't change overnight.

But I've always said: principles over politicians. And a party that won't learn from a loss like this will keep losing.

Lower prices. 
End the war with a real win.. 

That's what we need to see over the next two years.. 

Congratulations to the winners, including those I didn't vote for. 
And congratulations to Governor-elect Byron Donalds, Florida's first Black governor, on a historic night here at home..

text:
Turbulent flow around a car body, simulated with a solver that also shows how design changes affect the result.

This video presents large-eddy simulations of the Ahmed body, a reference geometry in road-vehicle aerodynamics, at a Reynolds number of 768,000 and rear slant angles of 25° and 35°. It walks through the measured geometry and its representation in the solver, the 94-million-cell grid, and the governing equations and turbulence model. It then explores the transient vortex structures and wake, before comparing the results with laser-Doppler measurements.
What sets the framework apart is the combination of experimental validation, full differentiability and efficient GPU performance.

Reverse-mode differentiation runs through the entire solver, including the pressure projection and the immersed body. The resulting gradients agree with finite differences within the precision those checks can resolve. A single backward pass gives the sensitivity of drag to the slant angle.

The solver is built for GPUs and runs in double precision, from a single GPU to multi-node jobs on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper nodes of the Alps supercomputer @cscsch. On one GPU, it achieves around half the peak memory bandwidth. In scaling tests, a billion-cell grid advances by one time step in 78 milliseconds on 32 GPUs.

These capabilities matter because foundation and world models for physics are only as good as the data they learn from. They need reference simulations of known accuracy and, increasingly, gradients alongside snapshots to learn how a flow responds to changes in shape or operating conditions. A validated, differentiable solver that runs efficiently on modern GPUs can provide exactly this kind of training and test data.

The analysis also offers a sobering reminder of the challenge: small errors in this flow grow a millionfold within roughly twice the time it takes the flow to travel the length of the body. A learned model of this wake should therefore be judged by its statistics and its response to design changes, rather than by how closely it follows a single trajectory.

More is coming. Stay tuned.

text:
The country is sick, and both wings of the modern Republican Party are treating symptoms while ignoring the disease. MAGA populism and neo-conservative globalism have each claimed the conservative label while abandoning the principles that once defined it. One inflames grievance without restraint. The other expands government abroad while neglecting the foundations at home. Between them, the party has lost its way. It is not permanently dead, but it will remain hollow until it returns to ordered liberty, limited government, and moral accountability under God.

Populist energy is not the same as conservative principle. It can rally crowds and punish elites, yet it rarely produces lasting restraint on power. When every disagreement becomes betrayal and every institutional limit is treated as an obstacle, the result is not restoration. It is further erosion. Neo-conservatism and globalist foreign policy have done the same from the opposite direction. Decades of nation-building, open-ended commitments, and the assumption that 

America must manage the world’s problems have drained resources, stretched military capacity, and distracted from the collapse of fiscal discipline and cultural order inside our own borders. Neither approach prioritizes the hard work of governing a free people under the rule of law.

True conservatism begins with the recognition that government is limited by nature and by design. The Declaration of Independence grounds rights in the Creator, not in the state. The Constitution enumerates powers rather than granting a general license to solve every problem. 

Ordered liberty requires virtue among the people and restraint among those who hold office. When a nation abandons those foundations, debt, division, and moral confusion follow. Recent figures illustrate the point. Total public debt has reached approximately $40.5 trillion, after rising roughly $2.5 trillion in a single year and adding more than $2.5 trillion in fiscal 2026 alone. That is not abstract accounting. It is the predictable result of spending without limit while promising both domestic largesse and global engagement. Interest costs compound the problem and crowd out priorities that actually belong to the federal government.

Scripture offers the same diagnosis in clearer terms. “If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8, ESV). The principle scales. 

A people that cannot order its own house has no standing to lecture or manage others. Jesus distinguished the things that belong to Caesar from the things that belong to God (Matthew 22:21). He did not confuse the two, nor did He instruct 

His followers to seize Caesar’s sword in order to force the kingdom. The call is to faithful citizenship under legitimate authority while remaining loyal first to the Lord. National health begins with repentance, personal responsibility, and the recovery of institutions that restrain power rather than expand it.

The path forward is not a new slogan or a different strongman. It is a return to the foundations: constitutional limits, fiscal honesty, protection of life and property, and the moral order that makes free government possible. Focus on repairing this country before attempting to manage the world. Vote for candidates who demonstrate actual restraint, not merely rhetorical opposition to the other party. Demand that elected officials treat the national debt as the moral and practical failure it is, rather than a tool for short-term advantage. A nation that does not serve God will not long preserve the liberty He has given.

text:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) (PART D) 
Faith is the human side of the Divine activity carried on by the Holy Spirit. Faith is therefore implied in the Spirit's action and is the result of or response to it in its various forms. But faith is primarily and essentially faith in Jesus Christ. Hence, we find in Paul that Christ is represented as doing substantially everything that the Spirit does. Now we are not to see in this any conflicting conceptions as to Christ and the Spirit, but rather Paul's intense feeling of the unity of the work of Christ and the Spirit. The “law” of the Spirit's action is the revelation and glorification of Christ. In his Gospel, which came later, John, as we have seen, defined the Spirit's function in precisely these terms. Whether or not John was influenced by Paul in the matter we need not here consider.
(a) The Spirit and Jesus
We begin with a brief reference to the connection in Paul's thought between the Spirit and Jesus. The Holy Spirit is described as the Spirit of God's Son (Rom_8:14; Gal_4:6), as the Spirit of Christ (Rom_8:9). He who confesses Jesus does so by the Holy Spirit, and no one can say that Jesus is anathema in the Holy Spirit (1Co_12:3). Christ is called a life-giving Spirit (1Co_15:45); and in 2Co_3:17 the statement appears, “Now the Lord is the Spirit.” All of this shows how completely one Paul regarded the work of Christ and the Spirit, not because they were identical in the sense in which Beyschlag has contended, but because their task and aim being identical, there was no sense of discord in Paul's mind in explaining their activities in similar terms.
(b) In Bestowing Charismatic Gifts
The Spirit appears in Paul as in Acts imparting all kinds of charismatic gifts for the ends of the Messianic kingdom. He enumerates a long list of spiritual gifts which cannot receive separate treatment here, such as prophecy (1Th_5:19 f) ; tongues (1 Cor 12-14); wisdom (1Co_2:6); knowledge (1Co_12:8); power to work miracles (1Co_12:9 f); discerning of spirits (1Co_12:10); interpretation of tongues (1Co_12:10); faith (1Co_12:9); boldness in Christian testimony (2Co_3:17 f); χαρισματα, charismata generally (1Th_1:5; 1Th_4:8, etc.). See SPIRITUAL GIFTS. In addition to the above list, Paul especially emphasizes the Spirit's action in revealing to himself and to Christians the mind of God (1Co_2:10-12; Eph_3:5). He speaks in words taught by the Spirit (1Co_2:13). He preaches in demonstration of the Spirit and of power (1Co_2:4; 1Th_1:5).
In the above manifestations of the Spirit, as enumerated in Paul's writings, we have presented in very large measure what we have already seen in Acts, but with some additions. In 1 Cor 14 and elsewhere Paul gives a new view as to the charismatic gifts which was greatly needed in view of the tendency to extravagant and intemperate indulgence in emotional excitement, due to the mighty action of God's Spirit in the Corinthian church. He insists that all things be done unto edification, that spiritual growth is the true aim of all spiritual endowments. This may be regarded as the connecting link between the earlier and later New Testament teaching as to the Holy Spirit, between the charismatic and moral-religious significance of the Spirit. To the latter we now direct attention.
(c) In the Beginnings of the Christian Life
We note the Spirit in the beginnings of the Christian life. From beginning to end the Christian life is regarded by Paul as under the power of the Holy Spirit, in its inner moral and religious aspects as well as in its charismatic forms. It is a singular fact that Paul does not anywhere expressly declare that the Holy Spirit originates the Christian life. Gunkel is correct in this so far as specific and direct teaching is concerned. But Wood who asserts the contrary is also right, if regard is had to clear implications and legitimate inferences from Paul's statements (op. cit., 202). Rom_8:2 does not perhaps refer to the act of regeneration, and yet it is hard to conceive of the Christian life as thus constituted by the “law of the Spirit of life” apart from its origin through the Spirit. There are other passages which seem to imply very clearly, if they do not directly assert, that the Christian life is originated by the Holy Spirit (1Th_1:6; Rom_5:5; Rom_8:9; 1Co_2:4; 1Co_6:11; Tit_3:5).
The Holy Spirit in the beginnings of the Christian life itself is set forth in many forms of statement. They who have the Spirit belong to Christ (Rom_8:9). We received not the Spirit of bondage but of adoption, “whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom_8:15). “The Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are children of God” (Rom_8:16). The Spirit is received by the hearing of faith (Gal_3:2). See also Rom_5:5; Rom_8:2; 1Co_16:11; Gal_3:3, Gal_3:14; Eph_2:18. There are two or three expressions employed by Paul which express some particular aspect of the Spirit's work in believers. One of these is “first-fruits” (Rom_8:23, ἀπαρχή, aparchḗ), which means that the present possession of the Spirit by the believer is the guarantee of the full redemption which is to come, as the first-fruits were the guarantee of the full harvest. Another of these words is “earnest” (2Co_1:22; 2Co_5:5, ἀρραβών, arrabō̇n), which also means a pledge or guarantee. Paul also speaks of the “sealing” of the Christians with the Holy Spirit of promise, as in Eph_1:13 (ἐσφραγίσθητε, esphragı́sthēte, “ye were sealed”). This refers to the seal by which a king stamped his mark of authorization or ownership upon a document.
(d) In the Religious and Moral Life
Paul gives a great variety of expressions indicating the presence and activity of the Holy Spirit in the religious and moral life of the Christian. In fact at every point that life is under the guidance and sustaining energy of the Spirit. If we live after the flesh, we die; if after the Spirit, we live (Rom_8:6). The Spirit helps the Christian to pray (Rom_8:26 f). The kingdom of God is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom_14:17). Christians are to abound in hope through the Holy Spirit (Rom_15:13). “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, self-control” (Gal_5:22). Christians are warned to grieve not the Holy Spirit (Eph_4:30), and are urged to take the sword of the Spirit (Eph_6:17). The flesh is contrasted with the Spirit at a number of points in Paul's writings (e.g. Rom_8:5 f; Gal_5:17). The Spirit in these passages probably means either the Spirit of God or man's spirit as under the influence of the Spirit of God. Flesh is a difficult word to define, as it seems to be used in several somewhat different senses. When the flesh is represented as lusting against the Spirit, however, it seems equivalent to the “carnal mind,” i.e. the mind of the sinful natural man as distinct from the mind of the spiritual man. This carnal or fleshly mind is thus described because the flesh is thought of as the sphere in which the sinful impulses in large part, though not altogether (Gal_5:19), take their rise.
Paul contrasts the Spirit with the letter (2Co_3:6) and puts strong emphasis on the Spirit as the source of Christian liberty. As Gunkel points out, spirit and freedom with Paul are correlatives, like spirit and life. Freedom must needs come of the Spirit's presence because He is superior to all other authorities and powers (
Die Wirkungen des heiligen Geistes, etc., 95). See also an excellent passage on the freedom of the Christian from statutory religious requirements in DCG, article “Holy Spirit” by Dr. James Denney, I, 739.
(e) In the Church
Toward the end of his ministry and in his later group of epistles, Paul devoted much thought to the subject of the church, and one of his favorite figures was of the church as the body of Christ. The Holy Spirit is represented as animating this body, as communicating to it life, and directing all its affairs. As in the case of the individual believer, so also in the body of believers the Spirit is the sovereign energy which rules completely. By one Spirit all are baptized into one body and made to drink of one Spirit (1Co_12:13). All the gifts of the church, charismatic and otherwise, are from the Spirit (1Co_12:4, 1Co_12:8-11). All spiritual gifts in the church are for edification (1Co_14:12). Prayer is to be in the Spirit (1Co_14:15). The church is to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph_4:3). Love (Col_1:8); fellowship (Php_2:1); worship (Php_3:3) are in the Spirit. The church is the habitation of the Spirit (Eph_2:22). The church is an epistle of Christ written by the Spirit (2Co_3:3). Thus the whole life of the church falls under the operation of the Holy Spirit.
(f) In the Resurrection of Believers
The Spirit also carries on His work in believers in raising the body from the dead. In Rom_8:11 Paul asserts that the present indwelling in believers of the Spirit that raised up Jesus from the dead is the guarantee of the quickening of their mortal bodies by the power of the same Spirit. See also 1Co_15:44 f; Gal_5:5.
We have thus exhibited Paul's teachings as to the Holy Spirit in some detail in order to make clear their scope and comprehensiveness. And we have not exhausted the material supplied by his writings. It will be observed that Paul nowhere elaborates a doctrine of the Spirit, as he does in a number of instances his doctrine of the person of Christ. The references to the Spirit are in connection with other subjects usually. This, however, only serves to indicate how very fundamental the work of the Spirit was in Paul's assumptions as to the Christian life. The Spirit is the Christian life, just as Christ is that life.
The personality of the Spirit appears in Paul as in John. The benediction in 2Co_13:14 distinguishes clearly Father, Son and Spirit (compare also Eph_4:4). In many connections the Spirit is distinguished from the Son and Father, and the work of the Spirit is set forth in personal terms. It is true, references are often made to the Holy Spirit by Paul as if the Spirit were an impersonal influence, or at least without clearly personal attributes. This distinguishes his usage as to the Spirit from that as to Christ and God, who are always personal. It is a natural explanation of this fact if we hold that in the case of the impersonal references we have a survival of the current Old Testament conception of the Spirit, while in those which are personal we have the developed conception as found in both Paul and John. Personal attributes are ascribed to the Spirit in so many instances, it would seem unwarranted in us to make the earlier and lower conception determinative of the later and higher.
In Paul's writings we have the crowning factor in the Biblical doctrine of the Holy Spirit. He gathers up most of the preceding elements, and adds to them his own distinctive teaching or emphasis. Some of the earlier Old Testament elements are lacking, but all those which came earlier in the New Testament are found in Paul. The three points which Paul especially brought into full expression were first, the law of edification in the use of spiritual gifts, second, the Holy Spirit in the moral life of the believer, and third, the Holy Spirit in the church. Thus Paul enables us to make an important distinction as to the work of the Spirit in founding the kingdom of God, namely, the distinction between means and ends. Charismatic gifts of the Spirit were, after all, means to ethical ends. God's kingdom is moral in its purpose, “righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” Christianity is, according to Paul, inherently and essentially supernatural. But its permanent and abiding significance is to be found, not in extraordinary phenomena in the form of “mighty works,” “wonders,” “tongues” and other miracles in the ordinary sense, but in the creation of a new moral order in time and eternity. The supernatural is to become normal and “natural” in human history, therefore, in the building up of this ethical kingdom on the basis of a redemption that is in and through Jesus Christ, and wrought out in all its details by the power of the Holy Spirit.
(5) The Holy Spirit in Other New Testament Writings
There is little to add to the New Testament teaching as to the Holy Spirit. Paul and John practically cover all the aspects of His work which are presented. There are a few passages, however, we may note in concluding Our general survey. In He the Holy Spirit is referred to a number of times as inspiring the Old Testament Scriptures (Heb_3:7; Heb_9:8; Heb_10:15). We have already referred to the remarkable statement in Heb_9:14 to the effect that the blood of Christ was offered through the eternal Spirit. In Heb_10:29 doing “despite unto the Spirit of grace” seems to be closely akin to the sin against the Holy Spirit in the Gospels. In Heb_4:12 there is a very remarkable description of the “word of God” in personal terms, as having all the energy and activity of an actual personal presence of the Spirit, and recalls Paul's language in Eph_6:17. In 1 Pet we need only refer to Eph_1:11 in which Peter declares that the “Spirit of Christ” was in the Old Testament prophets, pointing forward to the sufferings and glories of Christ.
Literature

🚩 My Election Day poll-watching observations at Vizcaya Village Garage in Miami on November 3, 2026, serving precincts 562, 582, 634, 651 and 657:

❌Within minutes of my arrival, a man identifying himself as Andres Blanco, also known as Andy White, approached and questioned the outgoing poll watcher and me without displaying credentials. He claimed to be an attorney, a non-U.S. citizen, and working for President Trump. He said he did this every day to help Republicans. He did NOT attempt to vote and should probably be investigated. 

❌ I asked the clerk to file an incident report about that encounter. She later said she had not filed one.

❌ The clerk said she did not know what I meant by “pollbook” or “check-in numbers.” No final sitewide check-in total was provided. She said, “Everything would be posted on the door outside.”

❌ The clerk reported ZERO provisional ballots all day. I observed people turned away over registration issues, including someone who was not offered a provisional ballot.

❌ About 1/3 of voters arrived at the wrong precinct because they did not realize the early voting location was not their Election-Day polling place. They were directed elsewhere, including City Hall, Simpson Park, First Presbyterian Church, and other Precincts within minutes of the polls closing. I highly doubt many of them made it on time. 

❌ People identifying themselves as first-time voters received applause and cheers. Some were subsequently turned away because they were not registered.

❌ Voters signed electronic check-in devices with their fingers, as no stylus was provided. I could not determine how signatures were being validated or even close to being correct. I could not even get my own signature to resemble my ID. 

❌ A voter reported harassment by people representing candidates outside. No incident-report reference was provided to me, as the Clerk stated she did not file a report. 

 ❌ A voter needed a replacement ballot. I also observed the clerk tear a surrendered mail-in ballot and provide another ballot. The clerk said surrendered ballots were retained “as evidence.” I requested clarification of the accounting and cancellation records.

❌ Public Count versus Protected Count explanations remained unclear. The recorded changes showed Protected Counts increasing by twice the Public Count changes. The final combined Public Count was 443.

❌ Opening Public Counts were zero according to the clerk, but she did not show me the opening or zero tapes when requested. Opening Protected Counts were not verified.

❌ The technician, Mike, rolled a machine outside for approximately 5 minutes, saying he could not get it to connect to the internet. I do not believe the connection ever succeeded.

❌ The clerk called Mike away while he was explaining the machines and issues to me, preventing that conversation from continuing.

❌ I observed the clerk consulting an instruction book. She said she had not received training on any pollbooks and did not know my reference.

❌ Polls were announced closed at approximately 7 p.m. all while X reported Florida polls closing at 8pm. People arriving afterward were denied entry because they had not been in line by closing. The last voter left around 7:20 p.m.

❌ The clerk and technician appeared concerned that I wanted to stay to observe closing procedures. While they allowed me to stay in, I remained inside until after 8 p.m., when the machines left the building; then I moved outside at the clerk’s direction.

❌ The blue boxes below the machines could easily have ballots inserted prior to any clerk tabbing the boxes. I did not see any ballot insertions, but I did not accompany the machine that was rolled outside. The clerks add the plastic tabs onto the machines. 

❌ I was not allowed to review the receipt tapes inside, nor was I permitted to witness the Clerk and the technician sign a form. At first, two tapes were posted on the door, then removed and replaced with multiple tapes.

❌ Darkness, rain, flashing lights, and security alarms made it difficult to document and read the posted tapes.

❌ Spotty internet prevented me from accessing the reporting form or filing a report on my phone during my shift.

I prepared a full report, submitted it, and am requesting readable tapes, check-in totals, ballot-accounting records, equipment logs, and incident reports. These observations warrant documented answers; they do not, by themselves, establish improper tabulation.

Dear @GOP @RNC @JoeGruters @kc4gop @JDVance @alinagarcia  - 
While Republicans may have won Florida this time, I have filed a report with the Election Integrity Team regarding my observations. Please reach out if. you need me to testify to anything. These issues are serious technological matters, and I was named Cox Communications' First Female Tech Exec, so I understand technology.
