text:
Trump's defeat has changed the price of loyalty inside the Republican Party. That matters more for Ukraine than any election-night speech. A president can keep his office after a midterm rout. He has a harder time keeping every senator, donor and committee chair obedient when association with him starts costing them their own careers.

The counts

• Democrats hold 54 Senate seats and are competing for two more in Alaska and Mississippi.

Republicans have won zero toss-up states before the vote. Alaska remains their possible pickup among those contests.

• South Carolina, generally treated as safe Republican territory, went Democratic. Florida came close to flipping. In Mississippi, the Democrat leads by roughly 50 votes as counting continues.

• In the House, Democrats have 228 seats to Republicans' 139, with 68 districts still being counted. The Democratic projection is 255–260 seats.

• Republicans have also lost five governorships: Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada.

Those numbers describe a party losing well beyond the districts where it expected a fight. The Iran war, tariffs, Trump's handling of the Kremlin and his own unpopularity have become liabilities for candidates who had to put their names on the ballot. Republicans can argue over which issue did the most damage. They cannot look at South Carolina, Texas and Ohio and pretend their problem was a handful of weak campaigns.

The 2028 calculation

Trump will still control the White House. His influence over Republicans depends on their belief that following him helps them win. After this result, every Republican planning a 2028 campaign has to consider two more years of the same presidency. Every member of Congress has staff, donors and local interests tied to keeping an office. Self-preservation can produce dissent faster than a sudden outbreak of principle.

Expect Trump to blame candidates, advisers and party officials. That is his usual way of protecting the brand; this time it risks making the internal fight worse. People he blames will have their own accounts of why they lost, and some will have votes in Congress. Before asking them to carry his defeat, a president needs their cooperation and should think carefully.

Texas makes this especially painful. Republicans lost both the Senate race and the governorship there. Business donors who once expected a friendly state administration now have practical matters to settle with Democrats in power. They will still have their politics. They will also need decisions made, relationships maintained and access that a feud with the new administration will not provide. That shift reaches beyond one election cycle: a major Republican funding base has to adjust to a changed state government while the national party argues over Trump.

The Kremlin channel

For Ukraine, the immediate opening lies in the growing political cost of the White House's Kremlin contacts. Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff, Lynch and others around Trump could previously count on a Republican Congress showing little appetite to examine those relationships. A Democratic majority in both chambers changes the incentives. Committees can hold hearings, request records and ask who authorized conversations, what was offered and whether sanctions or Ukraine's security were treated as bargaining material.

Witkoff deserves particular attention while Republicans are absorbing the scale of the defeat. He has been central to the administration's dealings with Moscow. If members of Trump's own party want distance from that record, congressional committees should move before his team has time to settle on a new account of its actions. Call him to testify. Seek the documents. Put the relevant officials' decisions on the record. Ukraine has an interest in making clear to its American partners which contacts and proposals require scrutiny, while Congress does the investigating under its own authority.

This pressure works even without a dramatic revelation. Officials and intermediaries behave differently when they know that messages, meetings and proposed deals may be examined in public. The people whispering to Trump about business with the Kremlin have reason to speak more carefully when the next conversation could become a question at a hearing. This practical constraint limits a dangerous channel of influence.

Vance is watching the same party arithmetic. Before the election, he had begun moving toward a more balanced posture associated with Marco Rubio, even referring to Putin as a “little dictator.” His change in tone coincided with Peter Thiel, his principal patron, publicly criticizing Trump's performance. Nobody should confuse a phrase with a policy reversal. It does show that ambitious Republicans are testing how much distance they may need from an electoral liability.

Congressional influence

The new Congress takes office on January 3. Until then, Trump retains room to act under the current balance of power. After that, Democrats will control the budget process in both chambers and can force negotiations over spending. Before the vote, Trump called himself “Mr. Veto.” Following the result, he began talking about making deals. The change in language reflects a change in influence.

Getting the limit right matters. A veto override requires two-thirds support in both chambers: 67 votes in a full Senate and 290 in a full House. Even 56 Democratic senators and a House caucus of 255–260 would need substantial Republican support to clear those thresholds. This rout makes defections more plausible while leaving Democrats short of a veto-proof majority. Their nearer-term power comes from controlling what Congress funds, what it investigates and which compromises the White House needs to keep government working.

That creates an opening on sanctions. Congress can press to reverse sanctions relief granted under Trump and pursue new measures against Moscow. Republicans trying to separate themselves from his Kremlin policy may have an incentive to join them. The relevant legislation will still need votes, and executive implementation will still matter. But the White House must now expect that proposals to ease pressure on Russia will face scrutiny and that some Republicans will not defend them.

Ukraine assistance belongs in those negotiations too. Democrats can seek a new package through the budget process and try to build bipartisan support around it. After nearly two years of Trump cutting back support, even a limited package represents a consequential shift. What matters for Ukraine is the content: appropriated money, usable authorities and a route from congressional approval to deliveries. A headline number that the administration can slow-roll through implementation will do less good than a smaller package that actually moves.

The Senate's control of appointments adds another lever. Democrats can scrutinize and reject new nominees, particularly for the Pentagon, and push the White House toward candidates capable of working with Congress and allies. Current officials such as Pete Hegseth, Kash Patel or Robert F. remain in place. Kennedy Jr. Hearings and oversight can examine their conduct; confirmation votes apply to future appointments. The distinction matters because Ukraine needs a functioning Pentagon to turn any renewed assistance into contracts, transfers and coordination with partners. A congressional vote alone does not put air-defense missiles where they are needed.

Iran remains part of this picture. The war has contributed to Trump's domestic political damage, while its effect on oil prices matters to the pressure Western governments can sustain on Russia. A new Congress may create space to challenge the administration's choices and demand a different approach. Nobody should promise that an election result will settle the conflict or bring oil prices down. The useful change: the White House will have less freedom to treat its Iran policy as immune from political consequences.

Ukraine should use this opening with discipline. Build relationships in both parties, make the case for specific aid and sanctions provisions, and press for serious oversight of the Kremlin-facing figures around Trump. The Republican Party has been given a blunt warning by its own voters. Whether its members act on that warning will determine how much of this electoral defeat becomes actual policy.

Trump has lost votes. From January, Congress can start testing where he has lost obedience.

text:
The most common way a sound arbitration agreement fails isn't its own text. It's another document signed the same day.

In Cluck v. GEO Secure Services (2026), the employee signed an arbitration agreement and a confidentiality agreement during onboarding. Read together, he had to arbitrate the claims he was most likely to bring, while the employer could litigate its likely confidentiality, competition, and nonsolicitation claims in a Florida court. That lack of mutuality supported a finding of substantive unconscionability.

The court also found procedural unconscionability in the opt-out process. A new hire had to obtain an employee number, prepare a separate written statement, and send it to the legal department within 30 days.

That followed the California Supreme Court's decision in Fuentes v. Empire Nissan (2026): small, difficult-to-read print bears on procedural unconscionability, and a high degree of procedural unconscionability requires correspondingly less substantive unfairness.

What to check:

→ Every carve-out, in every document. Confidentiality, non-solicitation, and invention-assignment agreements, offer letters, and handbooks. If any of them sends the employer's claims to court, fix the inconsistency.

→ Mutuality. Claims the employer is likely to bring should be arbitrated on the same terms as claims the employee is likely to bring.

→ Forum. An out-of-state forum for the employer's claims against a California employee is a red flag on its own (see Labor Code § 925).

→ Presentation. Legible font, a standalone document, and an opt-out process a new hire can actually use.

Bottom line: read the onboarding packet the way a court will, all at once.

All five ways California employers lose arbitration, and what to review before January 1, 2027: https://t.co/8lMP0Mb6Ri

text:
The Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod is rolling out a new website.

And, well, I have some thoughts.

The new site at lcms[.]org actually invites visitors to offer feedback. "Pardon our dust," it says. "We're still building our new site. Let us know what you think."

Well, you asked.

As an LCMS pastor who also happens to run a church digital marketing business, I figured I'd take a look. I recorded a video offering a little micro-roast of the new homepage.

And then I decided to go a step further.

I spent about thirty minutes putting together my own proposed homepage for the fictional "Lutheran Church Mystery Synod." Any resemblance to an actual confessional Lutheran church body is, of course, entirely incidental.

But here's the thing. My biggest objection to the new LCMS website isn't the mobile formatting problems, the overlapping navigation elements, or even the rather confusing assortment of buttons and news stories.

My biggest objection is that I can't figure out what the website is actually trying to get people to do.

And I think that's a pretty fundamental problem.

I'm increasingly convinced that websites ought to be understood as *decision media*. They're not primarily places to dump everything your organization produces. We have YouTube for videos, Spotify for podcasts, and all sorts of other platforms for distributing content.

A website is where you have the greatest control over guiding visitors toward a particular decision.

So what's the decision we want somebody visiting the LCMS website to make?

Donate money? Read about our institutional activities? Download resources? Learn about the March for Life?

Those are all fine things. Good, right, and salutary, even.

But they're not the main thing.

I want people visiting our churches.

I want them crossing the thresholds of LCMS congregations, hearing the Gospel of Jesus Christ, receiving the forgiveness of sins, and encountering God's grace and mercy in Word and Sacrament.

And I think our synodical website ought to be designed around that objective.

In fact, I'd love to see Synod establish a little operation where a sweet-tea-drinking Lutheran lady from the Deep South personally follows up with people who express interest in our churches, while some rather less saccharine fellow from the Rust Belt makes sure the local congregations actually contact them.

I'm only half joking.

But in the meantime, we have a perfectly good church locator. Why not put it front and center?

So that's what I did in my proposed redesign.

One clear objective. One primary call to action. Everything else organized around helping people take that next step.

And no, I'm not claiming that thirty minutes of tinkering produces a finished replacement for a major institutional website. But I do think it demonstrates how a different set of priorities could produce a very different homepage.

I've put together a new article featuring both videos: my critique of the existing LCMS website and a walkthrough of my proposed redesign.

I love our Synod. I want it to succeed. And I think we can do better here.

Take a look, and tell me what you think.

What should the primary purpose of the LCMS website be?

The risk of a widening uranium supply deficit has several drivers:

▪️ LIFE EXTENSIONS
Keeping reactors operating for 60–80 years preserves decades of fuel demand that would otherwise disappear with retirement.

▪️ NEW NUCLEAR
Around 80 reactors are under construction worldwide. The World Nuclear Association’s reference scenario projects annual uranium requirements rising from roughly 69,000 tonnes in 2025 to more than 150,000 tonnes by 2040.

▪️ YEARS OF UNDERINVESTMENT
Weak uranium prices discouraged exploration and mine development for years. Spending is recovering, but rebuilding the project pipeline takes time.

▪️ TOO FEW NEW MINES ADVANCING FAST ENOUGH
Recent production growth has relied heavily on restarts and expansions. Uranium mine development typically takes 15–20 years.

▪️ EXISTING MINES DEPLETING
Future projects must replace declining production as well as supply additional reactors. Inventories and other secondary supplies have helped to help bridge the gap, but not for much longer.

Now add Kazakhstan’s latest move.
On November 3, Kazatomprom’s CEO briefed President Tokayev on work to establish a national strategic uranium reserve.

The broader proposal envisages reserving at least 150,000 tonnes of uranium by 2050 through a combination of deposits kept underground, physical uranium stocks and finished nuclear fuel. Implementation details remain under development.

text:
Fei Tong Fan Xiang (Beyond the Ordinary)
November 4, 2026
Speaker: Tong Wen-hsun (童文薰)

https://t.co/3DKuHel7JY

Chapter 1: Opening — Thank Goodness for Trump!
Hello, everyone! Welcome to Fei Tong Fan Xiang. Let's discuss the important issues of our time.
Today is November 4, 2026, Taipei time. By now, we should have a fairly clear picture of the final results of the U.S. elections. Although a few states are still counting votes, President Trump appears to have lost both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Some people will be happy today, while others will be disappointed. Those who are happy can open a bottle of champagne. As for those who are disappointed, I encourage you to stay and listen carefully to my analysis.
First, I must say that I want to begin today's program with just one statement:
Thank goodness for Trump! Thank goodness the world has Donald Trump!
As a fellow human being, I have come to admire him even more.
I have always maintained that I am not a devoted Trump supporter. I simply evaluate him based on the facts. Yet, after seeing today's election results, on the very day the Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, why would I make such a statement?
Because I believe I understand very clearly why Trump is taking action against Iran and why he is using tariffs to put pressure on the Chinese Communist Party.
Nuclear weapons are not merely an American concern. They are a concern for all humanity.
When a regime constantly threatens to destroy others, who can sleep peacefully knowing that regime possesses nuclear weapons?
The same principle applies to tariffs. They are not merely about how much money Americans have in their pockets. They are about restructuring a global supply chain that has been taken over and hollowed out by China.
These policies have far-reaching implications for the common interests of humanity. At the same time, they can address America's underlying crises.
But what are many voters looking at?
They are looking at this month's bills and the price of groceries at the supermarket.
I understand that. When people feel their lives are becoming more difficult, they have a vote and can use it to express their dissatisfaction and punish politicians.
But here is my question: If life has become difficult, why blame Trump, the person who is trying to solve the problems?
Who created the problems of inflation, border security, and national debt in the first place?
You blame the person trying to solve the problems while letting those who created them escape responsibility. Worse still, you return political power to the very people who caused those problems.
I simply cannot understand that logic.
So today, I want to begin with a particular quotation.

Chapter 2: Speaker Mike Johnson — Our Duty Is Ours; the Results Belong to God
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted a photograph on X.
It showed the U.S. Capitol at night, accompanied by a single quotation attributed to America's sixth president, John Quincy Adams:
“Duty is ours, results are God's.”
In other words, our responsibility is to do our duty; the outcome belongs to God.
In response, I posted a verse from the Book of Proverbs. We will return to that verse at the end of today's program.
But first, I want to emphasize that this statement is the key to understanding this entire episode.
Trump and his team have done everything they could.
How much effort did they put in? We will examine the numbers shortly.
As for the outcome, it rests in God's hands.
This election is not the final judgment.
And I want to tell you something else: The election results will have almost no effect on the major objectives Trump is pursuing.
Almost none at all.
You may find that surprising.
So let us first examine the election results.

Chapter 3: Election Results and Trump's Response
As of approximately 10:50 p.m. Eastern Time on November 3, according to the Associated Press, the Democratic Party had secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Trump had also given a telephone interview to The New York Times, in which he indicated that he accepted the election results.
Some details remain unresolved because several states have not completed their vote counts.
Alaska, for example, does not close its polls until the early hours of the morning, and its ranked-choice voting system means the final results could take several weeks.
However, Trump presumably already had access to internal polling and information reflecting voters' actual preferences.
That may explain why, on November 2, Eastern Time, he had already begun preparing the public for a possible defeat during an appearance in front of the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial.
He said that regardless of who occupies the White House—whether Republican or Democrat, whether a good president, a great president, or a poor president—incumbent presidents somehow tend to lose midterm elections.
Nevertheless, he said, his team had given the campaign everything they had.
What he said was true.
As we discussed previously, throughout American history, only three presidents have managed to win midterm elections under exceptional circumstances.
At other times, presidents have generally suffered electoral losses.
There is, therefore, an established tendency in how voters behave during midterm elections.
This time, Trump did not produce another Trump miracle.
But from a constitutional perspective, does he understand that the results of a midterm election do not substantially diminish the powers of the presidency?
Of course he does.
That is why, during a telephone interview with CBS on election night, he told everyone to remember one thing.
We will return to this point at the end of the program.
He said that he possessed an ultimate power.
That power is the veto.
“I have veto power.”
Before going to bed, he posted an image of a cap featuring that very message: “I have veto.”
Yet, in his telephone interview with The New York Times, he also said that he accepted the election results and that his administration might reach certain agreements with the Democrats.
“We'll work it out.”
This is characteristic of Trump's larger-than-life, godfather-like personality.
If he can negotiate with the Chinese Communist Party, Russia, and North Korea, he can certainly negotiate with the Democrats.
But if the midterm election results have so little impact on his presidential authority, why did he campaign so vigorously?
If he lost enough congressional support for his opponents to command two-thirds majorities in both chambers, that would certainly matter.
But the results are nowhere near that threshold. The likelihood of such an outcome is extremely low.
Nevertheless, Trump worked tirelessly, holding 30 campaign rallies.
Why would he push himself so hard?
Because he has a personality that refuses to accept defeat.
History tells him he is likely to lose, but he insists on holding those 30 rallies anyway.
If he manages to produce another Trump miracle, it would indeed be a miracle.
If he fails, he will still have fulfilled his responsibility.
The outcome remains in God's hands.
In fact, Trump believes that he should have won.
He has four major reasons for believing so.

Chapter 4: Trump's Four Reasons for Believing He Should Have Won
First, he prevented Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
That represents an enormous contribution to both the United States and the world.
But the question is whether American voters recognize that achievement.
After all, the people casting ballots are American citizens, not citizens of the world.
Second, Trump believes that oil prices are not an especially serious problem.
He predicts that after the election, oil prices will fall like a rock.
The problem, however, is that American voters are deeply concerned about fuel prices.
Many middle-class and lower-middle-class families have little or no savings. Their immediate financial concerns leave them little room to think about broader regional risks.
They are also accustomed to attributing their frustrations directly to politics.
Consequently, this has become a recurring pattern in American midterm elections: People identify someone to blame for their personal difficulties.
Third, Trump has implemented tax cuts and accomplished many other things.
But restoring American strength requires time.
We are now in America's golden age, according to Trump.
Investment is flowing into the country. Employment has been preserved. Inflation has not become excessively severe. Economic growth has reached new highs, while unemployment has fallen to record lows.
Yet, despite all these achievements, he still lost the midterm elections.
Fourth, Trump believes he should have won because the Democratic candidates were too extreme.
Some were Muslims whose political positions, he argues, went beyond socialism. Yet candidates like these were elected to Congress.
All four reasons are plainly visible.
Nevertheless, voters still chose the Democrats.
So I want to ask a question:
Is it justice for America to defeat a Trump administration that has worked so tirelessly?
When life becomes difficult because of inflation, rising prices, and border problems, who left these problems behind?
Why blame the people working to solve them rather than those who created them?
Everyone has done their duty. The outcome must now be entrusted to God.
But the voters themselves are not God.
So here is my question to you:
If you are an American citizen and life has become difficult, whom do you blame?
The people currently governing, or the Democrats who left behind this mess?
Now, let us examine ten things that will not change after the election.

Chapter 5: Ten Things That Will Not Change After the Election
There are ten things that absolutely will not change as a result of the election, and everyone should understand them.
First, whether the United States takes military action against Iran is up to Trump. When such action might occur is also up to Trump.
During a telephone interview on November 2, Trump said that regardless of the election outcome—“either way”—his administration would take action.
So what has changed?
Nothing.
Second, has the red line concerning Iran's nuclear weapons program shifted?
No, it has not.
Since that red line remains unchanged, should Iran be opening champagne?
Not necessarily. In fact, Iran might face even more severe military action.
Third, there are the U.S.–China port fees.
The suspension of these fees runs through November 9.
That is why the Chinese Communist Party has remained relatively quiet. It would be wise for Beijing not to comment too extensively on the American midterm elections.
But China's rare-earth export restrictions have been an issue since last year. A full year has passed since the Busan meeting, and the relevant arrangement expires on November 10.
Will China continue imposing export restrictions?
My assessment is that Beijing will not dare to do so.
Why?
Because who controls tariffs?
Not Congress, but Trump.
Fourth, there is the APEC meeting in Shenzhen.
Many people have been awaiting the midterm election results, wondering whether they will affect the Shenzhen APEC meeting.
Will they?
No.
Look at the red cap Trump posted, bearing the word “veto.”
He has placed his bargaining chip directly on the table.
What can the Democrats do about it?
Nothing.
It is rather like the Chinese Communist Party playing games with rare-earth minerals.
Trump has described China's rare-earth tactics as a minor nuisance, like playing in the mud.
The Democrats are doing something similar.
They can continue their political mud fights and even keep the federal government shut down.
But those activities do not prevent Trump from carrying out his major objectives.
What is affected?
The legislative process.
Trump has many legislative proposals he wants to advance, and those efforts will certainly face substantial interference.
As a result, his opportunities to reshape domestic policy have become more limited.
But Trump possesses seemingly inexhaustible energy.
Where will he direct it?
Naturally, toward foreign affairs.
Therefore, whether in diplomacy, military affairs, tariffs, or domestic executive administration, he will intensify his efforts.
During the next two years, he will do everything he can to accomplish his objectives.
The election results also reveal that many people are afraid of Trump.
They hoped the Republicans would lose so that Congress could be used to restrain him.
But the American constitutional system was not designed in the way they imagine.
Let us finish examining these ten points before turning to the constitutional framework.
Sixth, arms sales to Taiwan remain on Trump's desk.
Regarding this issue, we have two episodes in our Event Files playlist.
In one episode, our AI news presenter, Kevin, provides a comprehensive analysis of a New York Times article concerning arms sales to Taiwan.
Kevin offers no personal commentary, but I have provided my own assessment in a separate episode.
Both episodes are available in the Event Files playlist.
I do not consider this issue particularly significant.
Nevertheless, the decision still rests with Trump, not Congress.
Seventh, there is the issue involving Jensen Huang and advanced semiconductor chips.
Trump has said that advanced chips must be examined very carefully.
Neither Democrats nor Republicans will permit advanced chips to flow into China.
Therefore, as far as Jensen Huang and the challenges confronting his business are concerned, nothing fundamental has changed.
Eighth, there is Taiwan itself.
Some people in Taiwan really do hope that Trump will lose, or that they can simply wait until he leaves office.
Well, they will have a long wait!
Trump's position regarding Taiwan having taken away America's semiconductor business has not changed at all.
This issue has even produced an amusing incident.
Later, in Tong Tong Tells Jokes, I will share it with you.
When Trump spoke about semiconductors, he also remarked that America had previously had terrible presidents. Otherwise, he suggested, the Taiwan Strait crisis would never have occurred.
A reporter then raised this statement during a press conference with China's Taiwan Affairs Office.
The response reminded me of a joke Ronald Reagan once told.
You can watch that episode in our Tong Tong Tells Jokes playlist.
Ninth, there are the proposed trilateral negotiations among Russia, Ukraine, and the United States.
Much depends on Russia's attitude.
What has the Kremlin said?
It has said that regardless of the midterm election results, Trump will continue pursuing his foreign policy.
Of course, some people in Moscow believe that after Trump's electoral setback, Russia may have a better opportunity to recover its frozen assets.
But they should not open their champagne too quickly.
Tenth, there is Canada.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that, if necessary, Canada can wait until Trump leaves office before proceeding.
If he wants to wait, he can wait another two years!
As we have discussed before, Congress controls appropriations and can conduct hearings.
But decisions concerning tariffs, the timing of arms sales, and whether to use military force fall within presidential authority, as the speaker presents it.
This brings us to another question:
Who are the ten major forces obstructing Trump?

Chapter 6: Ten Forces Holding Trump Back — Who Is Celebrating?
If the confrontation with Iran had ended on February 18, and Iran had admitted defeat rather than prolonging the conflict, would Trump really have lost the midterm elections?
If voters are so concerned about oil prices, then Iran is obviously the first party obstructing Trump.
Iran has been trying to prolong the situation until after the midterm elections.
We will see whether that strategy actually produces a better outcome for Iran.
Next comes Canada's Mark Carney.
He says he would rather wait for the next American administration.
But can he himself remain in office long enough to see that next administration?
We will have to wait and see.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also said that his province is in no hurry to conclude a trade agreement with the United States.
Then go ahead and wait!
The Chinese Communist Party, comparatively speaking, has been more restrained.
Its state-run media rushed to report the election results, but the Chinese government itself has avoided saying very much officially.
This has been the pattern for quite some time.
Even when Beijing openly criticizes the United States, it often avoids criticizing Trump by name.
Next is the European Union.
The EU is now trying to buy time.
European leaders say they want to wait and see, hoping that Trump will become weaker.
Many within European countries are betting that Trump will become a lame-duck president.
But in reality, they are waiting for an outcome that will never occur.
What about Russia?
As we have already discussed, Russia is also obstructing Trump, particularly through the war in Ukraine.
Next comes Mexico.
Mexico's attitude amounts to openly applauding and supporting the Democrats.
Just wait and see whether Trump retaliates after the election.
Of course, Trump's greatest domestic opponent is the Democratic Party.
The Democrats hope to use the election results to restrain Trump, as Nancy Pelosi has suggested.
But how exactly will they restrain him?
I have only two questions:
What are these people expecting, and what will they ultimately achieve?
Looking at the entire list, we are primarily dealing with diplomacy, tariffs, and military affairs.
These are fundamentally matters of presidential authority within the American constitutional system.
All the buttons remain in Trump's hands.
Yet when we examine this whole group, we see that those entertaining mistaken expectations include Tehran, Beijing, Moscow, and Canada.
They believe Trump's midterm election defeat means they can finally breathe a sigh of relief.
So here is my question:
Whose interests are American voters actually serving through the results of this election?
This is the second question I want to ask our audience.
Who do you think is happiest about Trump's defeat in the midterm elections?
Let us consider four possibilities: Iran, China, the European Union, and Canada.
Which one do you think it is?
Now, let us examine Trump's upcoming trip to Asia.

Chapter 10: Is the Voice of the People the Voice of God?
Vox populi, vox Dei.
This is a Latin expression meaning:
“The voice of the people is the voice of God.”
But is there something wrong with this statement?
In fact, one of the earliest recorded historical references to this expression, specifically a rejection of it, dates to A.D. 798.
At that time, a scholar named Alcuin wrote a letter to Charlemagne.
The substance of his warning was this:
Do not listen to those who claim that the voice of the people is the voice of God.
The clamor of the crowd often comes dangerously close to madness.
I intend to devote another episode specifically to this subject.
This reminds me of the founding of the United States.
Do you imagine that everyone in America supported the American Revolution?
Of course not.
Strictly speaking, there were no Americans in the modern national sense at that time. They were residents of Britain's colonies.
Perhaps one-third supported independence.
Some strongly opposed it.
And what about many of the others?
They remained indifferent, watching events unfold without becoming involved.
Among those who opposed independence were people who wanted to remain under the British Crown.
These were the people who would become associated with what is now Canada.

Chapter 11: Exodus and the Gospel of Luke
We have covered a great deal of information today.
But I want to conclude the main discussion with words from the Bible.
Why use Scripture to conclude our discussion?
Because when America was founded, its Declaration of Independence and the principles underlying its establishment were deeply connected with religious faith.
Without faith, I believe, America would not have become the nation it is today.
Therefore, to understand this country, you must interpret it through the Bible.
This is also what I discuss in my book under the concept of GI—God Intelligence.
Artificial intelligence can help you interpret many things. It can gather information and analyze it for you.
But without GI, you will never truly understand what Trump is doing.
The Book of Exodus contains this instruction:
“You shall not follow a multitude to do evil; nor shall you testify in a dispute so as to turn aside after a multitude to pervert justice.”
Then there is the Gospel of Luke:
“But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.”
The voice of the crowd can prevail.
But winning does not necessarily mean being right.
So what kind of constitutional safeguards did America's founders, who established this nation with their faith in God, leave behind?

Chapter 12: Why Does the U.S. Constitution Give the President Veto Power?
Why does the U.S. Constitution give the president the power to veto legislation?
If the will of the people were truly the voice of God, and public opinion were the ultimate authority, then the president would simply have to follow the will of the majority.
But that is not how the American constitutional system works.
At the time of the nation's founding, the founders understood that perhaps more than 70 percent of the population had not actually rolled up their sleeves and participated in building the new nation.
It was a minority who established the country.
Therefore, the founders clearly understood that the voice of the people was not necessarily the voice of God.
To put it more precisely, the text of the U.S. Constitution does not mention God.
Nevertheless, those who framed the Constitution possessed a remarkably clear understanding of human nature.
James Madison wrote in The Federalist Papers, No. 51:
“If men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
Human beings are not angels.
Nor do people suddenly become angels simply because they belong to a majority.
Having large numbers on your side does not make you morally infallible.
This reflects the same principle expressed in Scripture:
“You shall not follow a multitude to do evil.”
That is why Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution provides that the president may veto legislation passed by Congress.
If Congress wishes to override that veto, both the House of Representatives and the Senate must approve the measure by a two-thirds majority.
That is how a properly functioning constitutional system should operate.
It stands in sharp contrast, in my view, to the ugly political maneuvering we are witnessing in Taiwan today.
So let us consider the current American midterm elections.
Even though control of both the House and the Senate has shifted, do the Democrats possess two-thirds majorities in both chambers?
No.
That is why Trump could declare on election night that he still possessed an ultimate power.
He still has the authority to veto legislation.
Only when you understand this can you properly assess the significance of the midterm election results.
And what is that significance?
In many respects, very little has changed.
Of course, there will be consequences for domestic policy and legislation.
There is also another concern.
We had better hope that nothing happens to any of the Supreme Court justices during this period, because confirming a replacement could become very difficult.
If vacancies occur in the federal judiciary, Trump may find it impossible to appoint conservative judges without negotiating with the Democrats.
So let us return to where we began.

Chapter 13: Returning to Proverbs 21:31
Speaker Mike Johnson posted this quotation:
“Duty is ours, results are God's.”
What was my response?
I replied with a verse from the Book of Proverbs:
“The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory belongs to Yahweh.”
Victory belongs to Yahweh!
Therefore, our responsibility is to do our duty.
Trump, like a horse prepared for battle, spent 32 days campaigning and participated in 30 rallies.
He fulfilled his responsibility.
But the final judgment rests with God.
And thank goodness for Trump!
America truly has produced a president willing to shoulder responsibilities that concern all humanity.
Look around the world.
Which other national leader is capable of carrying the burdens Trump is carrying today?
That is Trump's courage.

Chapter 14: The New Book — Weapons Denuclearization
We need to understand Trump correctly.
And we need to understand just how important weapons denuclearization is for Taiwan.
The English-language e-book is now available for preorder.

Dr. Kathy Hull is a Bay Area clinical psychologist and the pioneering founder of George Mark Children’s House (GMCH), the first freestanding, independent pediatric palliative care facility in the United States. While working with pediatric oncology patients and families at Children’s Hospital Oakland, now UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, Kathy saw the unmet need for exceptional medical care provided in a nurturing, home-like setting, with support for the entire family. Kathy founded and opened GMCH in San Leandro in 2004. The house is named after her brothers, George and Mark, whose deaths at young ages shaped her commitment to pursuing a career that offers comfort and honors relationships. Kathy remains deeply involved as GMCH’s staff psychologist and is a current member of its Board of Directors, helping the organization expand its services to a continuum that includes respite, transitional, end-of-life care, and bereavement support. She also advances pediatric palliative care through clinical education, mentoring, and public speaking. Her 2016 TedWomen talk has received more than one million views. Her honors include being the recipient of the Minerva Award from the State of California, being named a Purpose Prize Fellow, the Junior League of the East Bay Sustainer of the year, a California Senate Local Hero, and, most recently, receiving an Honorary Doctorate from Santa Clara University. text:
Yvonne De Carlo, born Margaret Yvonne Middleton in Vancouver in 1922, rose from modest beginnings to become a familiar face in Hollywood films of the 1940s and 1950s. 

Her father departed early in her childhood, leaving her mother to raise her and nurture her interest in performance. 

As a teenager she headed for California, working as a nightclub dancer while pursuing film roles, and gradually established herself as a leading actress.

By the mid-1950s her screen credits included a prominent part as Sephora in the epic The Ten Commandments (1956), opposite Charlton Heston. 

That same year she married stuntman Bob Morgan; the couple later had two sons. Their life changed abruptly in 1962 when Morgan was severely injured during a train sequence on the production of How the West Was Won. 

He lost a leg and suffered lasting damage to one eye. The resulting medical costs placed heavy financial pressure on the family, prompting De Carlo to seek reliable work after stepping back from her career to care for him.

An unexpected opportunity arrived in the form of a television role: Lily Munster, the elegant yet undead matriarch of a comic horror household. 

For an actress associated with dramatic features, the part was an unusual departure, yet it offered steady employment at a critical moment. 

When The Munsters premiered in 1964, De Carlo shared the screen with Fred Gwynne as Herman and Al Lewis as Grandpa. 

The series quickly became a popular favorite and introduced her to a new generation of viewers, effectively revitalizing her career during a difficult personal period.
Her marriage to Morgan later ended in divorce. 

She continued to appear in films, television, and stage productions for years afterward. De Carlo died in 2007 at the age of 84. 

While audiences most readily recall her as Lily Munster, the role that secured that lasting recognition was taken, in part, to help stabilize her family’s finances after her husband’s accident.🌹

Charging Perks offers a $50 enrollment credit and $150 annually for letting Xcel help manage charging around grid demand. You can override the schedule when needed.

WeaveGrid handles the smart charging integration. Eligible Tesla owners can connect their vehicles directly, while compatible ChargePoint, Emporia and Wallbox chargers are also supported.

There's a catch. The $500 installation rebate is tied to a different charging program, so don't assume all these incentives can be combined.

text:
FINGLAS M50/N2 HOMELESS ENCAMPMENT
 
A man beaten with planks and metal bars. Nine people still without homes. Four years of engagement. How much longer must people wait?

Streetlink Homeless Support is raising the alarm following a serious incident of violence at the homeless encampment near the M50/N2 interchange in Finglas, Dublin, where one of our clients was brutally assaulted last night.

When our team arrived at the camp this morning, we found the man suffering significant injuries. According to the information available to us, he had been attacked by several individuals and beaten with wooden planks and metal bars. He had sustained injuries to his head, chest and legs and was experiencing difficulty breathing, with suspected broken ribs affecting his chest and back.

Dublin City Fire and Ambulance attended the scene, provided emergency first aid and transported him to Connolly Hospital in Blanchardstown for medical treatment.

Dr Richard Healy, Chairperson of Streetlink Homeless Support, said:

“After four years of engagement, nine people remain living in appalling conditions beneath a motorway, and now one of our clients has been seriously assaulted. Dublin spends hundreds of millions of euro on homelessness services, yet we must ask what that expenditure is actually delivering for people on the ground. Engagement without housing is not a solution, and public money must deliver real outcomes. These people deserve safety, healthcare and a place to call home, not another year of waiting.”

This is a deeply disturbing incident. But it must not be treated as an isolated emergency, disconnected from the conditions in which people are being forced to live.

This is not simply a story about one man being assaulted. It is a damning reminder of what happens when people are left to survive in unsafe conditions, without the security of a home and without adequate access to essential supports.

Four years of engagement. Nine people still without homes.

Streetlink Homeless Support has been engaging with people living at this encampment for more than four years. Throughout that period, the location and the circumstances of those living there have been brought to the attention of the Dublin Region Homeless Executive (DRHE) and homelessness services.
Yet, as of this morning, nine individuals remain unhoused at the site, according to Streetlink's current information.

They are living in conditions that can only be described as an environmental and public health hazard, a makeshift encampment surrounded by accumulated rubbish, vermin and unsanitary conditions, exposed to the elements and lacking the basic security and facilities that most people take for granted.

This is not a newly discovered problem. The encampment beneath the M50/N2 interchange has already been documented in national media. In June 2025, The Irish Times reported on residents living amid rats, rubbish, needles and human excrement, with some having remained there for years. The report also documented the involvement of outreach services and the DRHE's awareness of the location.

Public awareness is not the issue. Awareness among the relevant services is not the issue.

The question is why, after years of engagement, people are still living in these conditions.

How many assessments, referrals, outreach visits and meetings does it take before meaningful action is taken?

Engagement cannot become a substitute for progress. Recording that people are sleeping rough is not the same as securing them a home. Offering contact with a service is not the same as ensuring access to healthcare, appropriate accommodation and sustained support.

If nine people remain trapped in these circumstances after years of engagement, the authorities must explain what has been done, what barriers remain and what concrete action will now be taken.

Public expenditure demands public accountability
Ireland spends hundreds of millions of euro every year responding to homelessness in Dublin. Official figures supplied to the Dáil show that Exchequer funding for Dublin's homeless accommodation and related services reached approximately €318.9 million in 2025, compared with €217.5 million in 2020.

Focus Ireland's analysis of 2024 expenditure further found that 88.4% of Dublin's Section 10 homelessness service spending went towards emergency accommodation.

These figures raise serious questions about the balance between managing homelessness and ending it.

Streetlink recognises that homelessness services operate under significant pressure and that frontline outreach workers are not responsible for every failure within the housing system. Many workers and volunteers make extraordinary efforts to support people in difficult circumstances.

However, public funding must be judged not only by the amount allocated or spent, but also by the outcomes it achieves for the people it is intended to serve.

When nine people remain unhoused at a known encampment, when the location has been the subject of years of engagement, and when a resident is now being taken to hospital following a serious assault, the public is entitled to demand answers.

Where has the intervention failed?

What accommodation options have been offered to these nine individuals? What barriers have prevented them from accessing appropriate housing? What health and social supports have been made available? What measurable outcomes have the responsible agencies achieved at this location?

We are not alleging that funding has been misappropriated. We are demanding transparency about what public expenditure is delivering and why people remain exposed to such dangerous living conditions despite the resources committed to homelessness services.

Homelessness is not a safe alternative to housing
No individual should have to live beneath a motorway interchange, surrounded by vermin and waste, with no secure front door to close against violence and no safe place to recover when injured.

People experiencing homelessness are entitled to dignity, safety and access to healthcare. They should not have to wait for a serious assault, a medical emergency or a preventable death before their circumstances receive the urgency they deserve.

The incident at Finglas must prompt more than another round of expressions of concern. It must trigger a coordinated and immediate response from the DRHE, the relevant local authorities, health services and the organisations responsible for supporting those living at the site.

Streetlink is calling for:

An immediate review of the nine residents' circumstances, including individual assessments of their accommodation, health and support needs.

A clear accommodation plan with deadlines, setting out how the responsible authorities intend to move each person out of unsafe living conditions and into suitable, secure accommodation.

Urgent access to healthcare and ongoing support, including appropriate assessment of physical injuries, mental-health needs and any other medical or social-care requirements identified by the individuals themselves.

A formal review of four years of engagement at the site, identifying the interventions undertaken, the outcomes achieved, the obstacles encountered and the reasons nine people remain unhoused.

Transparency regarding public expenditure and service delivery, including the resources allocated to outreach, accommodation and support, and the measurable outcomes achieved for people sleeping rough in this area.
 
A coordinated safety and environmental response, addressing the accumulation of rubbish, vermin and other hazards without simply displacing residents to another unsafe location.

We cannot continue to accept this as normal
Streetlink Homeless Support will continue to work with people experiencing homelessness, providing practical assistance, advocacy and support wherever possible. We will continue to raise concerns when people are left in conditions that threaten their health, dignity and safety.

But voluntary outreach cannot replace a functioning housing and healthcare response. Charities cannot independently resolve a crisis that requires sustained action from statutory agencies, adequate housing provision and accountable public expenditure.

The man taken to hospital this morning is a person, not a statistic. The other eight individuals living alongside him are not statistics either. They are people whose circumstances demand a meaningful response, not another year of waiting.

The Finglas encampment has been visible, documented and known to services for years. Yet people remain exposed to conditions that no one should be expected to endure.

Four years of engagement must lead to more than four years of survival. Public money must deliver more than reports, referrals and repeated promises. And people experiencing homelessness must not be left waiting for a crisis to prove that their lives matter.

Streetlink Homeless Support is calling on the DRHE and the relevant authorities to act now, account for the lack of progress and provide a clear, time-bound plan to ensure that the people living at this encampment can access safe accommodation and the support they need.

A tent beneath a motorway is not a home. Survival is not a housing policy. And leaving people in danger is not an acceptable outcome.

text:
POST OFFICE SCANDAL WITHIN A SCANDAL

She remortgaged her house to repay money she never took. @PostOffice still refuses to call her conviction unsafe, which is a bold review for a service that ended in a remortgage.

Her name is Teju Adedayo. In 1999 she moved to Gillingham in Kent with her then husband and 3 young children to run the Rainham Road branch. Horizon, the Post Office computer system, arrived in 2000 and the problems started straight away. What a thoughtful welcome gift.

She says she asked for help and was told to roll the losses over into the next week. Cutting edge customer support, and I would recommend it to nobody.

By 2005 the gap sat around £50K. Investigators questioned her in the flat above her own shop with no lawyer present. 

She says they threatened her with prison, so she made up a confession on the spot. Nothing says fair process like a story invented under threat.

Then she remortgaged the house to pay back money she never took. She was convicted of false accounting in 2006. 

Vandals spray painted thief across her shop door, customers stayed away and the business failed within about a year. Work was out of reach with a conviction, and she hid behind pillars outside the probation office so nobody would see her. 

A court quashed the conviction on 14 May 2021, 15 years later. Natasha Bernard, the Post Office investigator who questioned her, told the Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry @PostOffInquiry in 2023 that she did not believe the confession was reliable, according to reports. It was reliable enough to prosecute a mother, apparently.

Teju says that confession kept her out of the compensation others received. In January 2024 the UK Government said she could claim in full or take a £600K offer. 

Soon after, Post Office told the Inquiry hers was the one case where it still did not accept the conviction was unsafe. Her barrister Edward Henry KC told the Inquiry about it. Consistency is clearly a company value.

A court cleared her name in 2021. Post Office is still reading the paperwork.

Sources: @JEPnews, @ccrcupdate, @exeterebjl @nickwallis @guardian, others

text:
@Lj_era8 is gonna be a @MiamiDolphins IN 2027! 

Lamar Jackson holds all the leverage. He has a no-trade clause, a no-tag clause, and an $84M cap hit. Because of that, Baltimore is facing three choices: trade him to a team of his choice on terms favorable to the acquiring team, cut him and get nothing, or keep him on the roster with an $84M cap hit.

If Lamar wanted Miami, the Dolphins could potentially offer Malik Willis plus a conditional 2028 2nd-round pick that could become a 2029 1st-round pick. From Baltimore's perspective, that's a better return than letting Lamar play out the final year of his contract and potentially ending up with only a 2029 compensatory 3rd-round pick.

Miami is projected to have around $100M in cap space, and trading for a top-5 QB may be a better use of those resources than overspending in free agency, especially when the front office has traditionally preferred to draft and develop talent.

Including Willis would help offset some of the cap concerns, and Lamar's roughly $52M cap hit in 2026 could be lowered through an extension. I could also see Miami using a front-loaded structure, taking advantage of its cap space in 2026 while maintaining flexibility down the road.

The biggest benefit for Miami is that it accelerates the retool. Instead of spending years hoping to find and develop a franchise QB, Miami would already have one in place while still being able to draft and develop a young quarterback such as LaNorris Sellers behind him. That potentially shortens the timeline back to contention while giving the Dolphins both a proven veteran and a long-term plan at the position.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/hJJxr2DmcE | Author: @TasmanianTgrUSA NAS3™ .50 BMG Ammunition Clears Belt-Fed Test 
Final major validation complete as SST moves its .50 BMG NAS3 case toward sample-lot production.

Eubank, Ky. (November 2026) – Shell Shock Technologies, LLC (SST), a leading innovator in the ammunition industry, today announced that its .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) NAS3 ammunition has successfully completed live-fire testing in a belt-fed machine gun. The cases and ammunition fed, fired, extracted, and cycled as designed, marking the final major validation SST sought before moving the .50 BMG NAS3 case into production. Following minor tooling refinements, the company expects to begin producing its first sample lots in November 2026.

The test was conducted by Detroit Ammo on Oct. 1, 2026, using an M2Hb belted machine gun, with 10 consecutive rounds fired. Belt-fed operation places different demands on a cartridge case than a test barrel or bolt-action rifle. In automatic fire, the case must withstand high-speed feeding from a linked belt, chambering, firing, and rapid extraction, cycle after cycle. The NAS3 case met each of those demands.

The belt-fed results build on SST’s earlier test-barrel and bolt-action evaluations, including independent live-fire testing conducted by Vairog US, LLC and announced in July 2026. That testing recorded zero primer or case failures across nine charge weights. The SST .50 BMG NAS3 case offers approximately 13.5 percent greater internal capacity than standard brass, enabling a higher powder charge for improved velocity and downrange energy. In testing at standard SAAMI pressures, the NAS3 case produced approximately 280 feet per second more velocity than comparable brass at approximately 54,000 PSI.

At approximately 33.7 grams, the .50 BMG NAS3 case is roughly 40 percent lighter than a comparable brass case, saving approximately 46 pounds per 1,000 rounds. For crew-served, belt-fed weapons, where crews carry, stage, and feed ammunition in volume, that reduction delivers direct logistics and mobility value. The case’s nickel-stainless steel alloy construction also supports clean extraction, faster heat dissipation than brass, and corrosion resistance under sustained fire and adverse conditions.

“This was the test I was waiting for. We had already seen very strong results through test barrels and bolt-action rifles, but numbers from a test barrel only tell part of the story. The real question was simple: How does it run in a belt-fed machine gun? Now we know. It fed, fired, extracted, and cycled exactly the way we wanted it to. After all the engineering, tooling, and testing that went into reaching this point, watching that belt run was a significant milestone for our entire team,” said Peter Foss, Managing Partner and CEO of Shell Shock Technologies.

With belt-fed validation complete, SST is finalizing tooling adjustments ahead of its first sample lots and will continue gathering performance data as it moves into production. The .50 BMG NAS3 case is engineered for professional end-users who require every performance advantage the platform can deliver, and for precision shooters pushing the limits of extreme long-range capability.

text:
Let me tell you about the most expensive house I ever bought.

It was 2003, and I was newly married. I was earning about $20,000 a year working in the nonprofit world and my wife was still a student. We found a for sale by owner house that was listed for $105,000 (I live in Oklahoma). We went to an open house and loved it.

The big problem was credit. Specifically that I had none. Banks were not exactly lining up to loan me money with my paltry income. Only one bank would offer me a loan, but it came with a hard-core condition. I had to put up 50% of the house’s value as a down payment in order to get financing for the other half.

I didn’t have any other options, and the only thing of value I had was shares in a small company that made money sending people things in the mail on a subscription plan. I sold all $50,000 worth to make the down payment and buy the house.

What was the stock that I sold in 2003?
Netflix.

I sold something like $20 million in today’s value for $50,000 to make a down payment. For that reason, my very first house will always be the most expensive house I’ll ever buy. It was a very rude introduction to the idea of opportunity cost.

This is where I initially bought NFLX.
It’s been a 600x return since then.

text:
@kenblackwell posted this on FB:

🇺🇸 LAST NIGHT, REPUBLICANS SAW WHAT HAPPENS WHEN WE DRIFT FROM OUR PRINCIPLES. HERE'S MY TAKE.

There's no way to soften what happened. Dems won the House & Senate.  They flipped 7 R Senate seats in one night, in TX, KS, OH, ME, IA, NC and SC.

KS elected its first Dem senator since 1932.

TX elected a Dem senator and governor.

OH voters sent Sherrod Brown back to the Senate. Amy Acton won the governor's race by 7 points in a state President Trump carried by 11 points two years ago.

When I read the exit polls, I see a party that drifted from the principles that built it. Voters noticed, and they let us know.

Here's where we went wrong.

1. SPENDING
Just under 8 in 10 voters told exit pollsters that inflation is causing hardship for their families. Gas prices are up 34% from a year ago.

Conservatives have always known that Washington's spending habit shows up in the price of everything families buy.

The national debt passed $40 trillion in August. 

Washington ran a $2T deficit this year.

We now pay more in interest on that debt than we spend on our entire military.

Republicans ran the House, the Senate and the White House while that happened. Voters held us responsible, and they had every right to.

2. TARIFFS
For decades, other countries took advantage of American workers. China dumped cheap steel on our market, stole American technology and kept our products out of its own. Too many presidents looked the other way.

President Trump was right to push back. Tariffs gave him leverage at the bargaining table, and he used it.

A tariff is a tool for getting a better deal. When it stays in place too long, American families and businesses end up paying for it.

In ME, most voters told exit pollsters that tariffs had hurt their local economy. Susan Collins lost her seat after five terms.

The lasting answer to unfair trade is the one conservatives have always offered: lower taxes, fewer regulations and American energy that make this the best country in the world to build things.

3. THE WAR IN IRAN
Iran must never get a nuclear weapon. I stand by that goal.

However, a majority of voters objected to the war anyway, according to the NBC News exit poll. Many of them felt it first at the gas pump.

Peace through strength has always meant a clear mission, the support of the American people and a plan to bring our troops home. Washington owes voters all three.

4. CHARACTER
In Texas, James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1988. Ken Paxton faced a string of scandals that turned off independents and even some Republicans.

Conservatives have said for decades that character counts. We have to mean it when we choose our own candidates, too.

5. PRINCIPLES OVER PERSONALITY
President Trump's approval among voters was lower than any sitting president's on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the NBC News exit poll.

The Goldwater-Reagan conservative movement was built on ideas. Limited government, free markets, strong families and a strong national defense were here before any one candidate, and they will outlast every one of them.

TO BE FAIR
Dems ran on real worries about prices, health care and a war many Americans didn't want. Their candidates connected with voters, and they earned their wins.

Reps can't blame the media or the map. Voters told us exactly what they care about.

MY TAKE
I'm as conservative this morning as I was yesterday. A loss like this reminds us what happens when we stop living up to what we say we believe.

The next two years are our chance to earn back trust. That means cutting spending, using tariffs to win fair deals without leaving families to foot the bill, finishing the job in Iran with a clear plan, and nominating candidates of character.

Congrats to the winners, including those I didn't vote for.

Now comes the hard part, holding everyone accountable, on both sides.

And remember, no matter what, God is in control. 🙏🏾

Short version: it stopped being about AI. It's about the electric bill.

Home electricity prices are up 10%+ since 2024 (EIA). On the PJM grid, Ohio and Maryland bills picked up about $16 to $18 a month in capacity charges, and more than 60% of that increase traces to expected data center demand.

Now look at the deal a town gets offered. A big data center runs on roughly 157 permanent jobs. States handed out about $6B in sales tax breaks to them over five years. So voters see a higher bill, a handful of jobs and a tax break for Big Tech.

That's why it's not left vs right. Gallup: 70% oppose a data center near their home. Only 53% oppose a nuclear plant. There are 570+ local bans or moratoriums across 46 states, and candidates in both parties ran on pausing them.

Texas is the extreme case. Data centers and other big users have asked to plug 400+ GW into the Texas grid, about 5x its all-time peak. Even Abbott backed an audit of new data centers before the vote. Hinojosa, who won last night, wants a moratorium until the legislature writes protections.

The market got it in one morning: Microsoft +6.8%, Amazon +6.7%, Vistra -13.4%, NRG -13.6%. Nobody is killing AI. The fight is over who pays for the power.

Where it lands: Pennsylvania's "build, bring or buy" rule. Data centers bring their own power or pay for it. The bill moves from your house to theirs.

text:
A rude stranger in a parking lot can still be souring your dinner three hours later.

Why does that happen, biologically? The popular answer is "stress hormones linger". The real answer is more interesting, and more hopeful: most of what lingers is something we can actually change.

🧠 Emotion vs mood: weather vs climate

An emotion is a weather event. A trigger, a fast response, seconds to minutes. Someone cuts you off, and there's a flash of anger.

A mood is the climate. A background state that lasts hours or days, often without one clear cause.

Psychologist James Russell calls the core of it "core affect": how pleasant or unpleasant you feel, and how calm or activated.

Lisa Feldman Barrett's influential theory goes a step further. The brain is constantly managing the body's "budget", predicting its needs for energy, sleep and repair, and mood partly reflects how that budget is going. It's why sleep debt, hunger or a looming cold can colour everything.

So mood isn't just "serotonin levels". It emerges from brain and body working together.

🚗 Why one bad moment lingers

1️⃣ The stress chemistry
Adrenaline clears in minutes. Cortisol, the main stress hormone, rises more slowly and has a half-life of roughly an hour.

A 2004 meta-analysis of 208 studies found cortisol typically peaks 20 to 40 minutes after a stressor starts. The biggest, slowest-to-recover responses came from situations that were both uncontrollable and involved being judged by others.
A rude stranger checks both boxes.

2️⃣ The replay
But three hours later, the stranger is long gone. What usually keeps it going is the replay.

Researchers call this perseverative cognition. Replaying a stressful event, or rehearsing what you should have said, re-triggers the stress response: higher heart rate, blood pressure and cortisol, as if it were happening again.

3️⃣ Leftover arousal transfers
Psychologist Dolf Zillmann described "excitation transfer": leftover arousal from one situation amplifies your reaction to the next. A minor irritation at home lands harder because your body is still revved from earlier.

4️⃣ Rudeness changes what we see
In studies by Trevor Foulk and colleagues, people exposed to rudeness were quicker to spot rude words, more likely to read an ambiguous message as hostile, and more likely to act spitefully towards the next person.
Rudeness spreads a bit like a cold.

Paul Ekman describes a related "refractory period" after strong emotion, when we struggle to take in information that contradicts what we're feeling.

📉 Is a bad mood just stress?

Not exactly. Some bad moods are high-energy, like anger and anxiety, and look a lot like the stress response. Others are low-energy, like sadness or flatness.

But when stress becomes chronic, it shows up in the body. In a classic 1991 study, 394 volunteers were deliberately exposed to cold viruses. The more psychological stress people reported, the more likely they were to catch a cold.

Stress also hampers the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain behind flexible thinking. It's harder to be creative, patient or articulate when your stress system is running hot.

Why good moods matter: Barbara Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory proposes that positive emotions widen attention and thinking, helping us build skills and relationships over time.

One important nuance: the goal isn't permanent happiness. Research on "emodiversity" found that experiencing a wide range of emotions, including negative ones, was linked to better mental health. Bad moods carry information.

🛠️ What the evidence supports for resetting

🏷️ Name it, precisely
In a 2007 UCLA brain-imaging study, simply labelling the emotion in a face ("angry", "afraid") reduced amygdala activity and increased activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex.
Naming it as "frustrated and embarrassed" works better than just "upset". Precision seems to help.

🌬️ Breathe out longer than you breathe in
In a 2023 Stanford randomised trial, five minutes a day of "cyclic sighing" for a month (two inhales through the nose, then a long, slow exhale) improved mood more than the same time spent on mindfulness meditation, and lowered breathing rate.
Heart rate naturally slows on the exhale, which is part of why long exhales calm.

🚶 Move, ideally outdoors
In a 2015 Stanford study published in PNAS, a 90-minute walk in nature reduced rumination and activity in a brain region linked to it, the subgenual prefrontal cortex. An urban walk did neither.

🔄 Reappraise rather than bottle it up
In James Gross's classic 1998 experiment, 120 students watched a disturbing film. Those told to view it in a detached, reframed way felt less disgust. Those told to simply hide their feelings felt just as disgusted, and showed higher sympathetic nervous system activation.
Hiding a feeling isn't the same as resolving it.

💧 Cool water on the face
Cool water on the face triggers the dive reflex, which slows the heart rate. It's used as a calming skill in dialectical behaviour therapy. The evidence is stronger for the physiology than for mood itself, and anyone with a heart condition should check with a doctor first.

🛡️ Dealing with people who repeatedly sour your mood

The "grey rock" method, becoming as dull and unreactive as possible, is popular online. But no published research has tested whether it works. And with an abusive person, it can backfire and escalate things. In those situations, safety and support come first.

There's also a twist from the Gross study: a flat face over a boiling inside costs the body. Calm on the outside works better when it's backed by a genuine reframe on the inside, such as recognising that the other person's behaviour isn't really about you.

Feel for, not with. Research by Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki found that training people in empathy, sharing others' distress, increased negative feelings. Training in compassion, caring without absorbing the distress, increased positive feelings and engaged different brain networks linked to reward and connection.

And where you can, limit exposure. Given how rudeness spreads, distance is a legitimate strategy, not a weakness.

⚠️ When it's more than a bad day

If low mood or loss of interest lasts most days for two weeks or more, or starts affecting work, sleep or relationships, it's worth talking to a doctor or mental-health professional.
In India, Tele-MANAS offers free mental-health support around the clock on 14416.

🎓 The takeaway

The stress-hormone surge from a rude stranger peaks within about 20 to 40 minutes and then starts to fade. Much of what comes after is our own replay of the scene.

That's the bad news and the good news at once. The part that lingers is mostly the part we can do something about: naming it, breathing it down, walking it off and reframing it.

Educational only, not medical advice.

text:
@Lj_era8will be a @MiamiDolphins in 2027!  

Lamar Jackson holds all the leverage. He has a no-trade clause, a no-tag clause, and an $84M cap hit. Because of that, Baltimore is facing three choices: trade him to a team of his choice on terms favorable to the acquiring team, cut him and get nothing, or keep him on the roster with an $84M cap hit.  

If Lamar wants Miami, the Dolphins could potentially offer Malik Willis plus a conditional 2028 2nd-round pick that could become a 2029 1st-round pick. From Baltimore's perspective, that's a better return than letting Lamar play out the final year of his contract and potentially ending up with only a 2029 compensatory 3rd-round pick.  

Miami is projected to have around $100M in cap space, and trading for a top-5 QB may be a better use of those resources than overspending in free agency, especially when the front office has traditionally preferred to draft and develop talent.  Including Willis would help offset some of the cap concerns, and Lamar's roughly $52M cap hit in 2026 could be lowered through an extension. I could also see Miami using a front-loaded structure, taking advantage of its cap space in 2026 while maintaining flexibility down the road.  

The biggest benefit for Miami is that it accelerates the retool. Instead of spending years hoping to find and develop a franchise QB, Miami would already have one in place while still being able to draft and develop a young quarterback such as LaNorris Sellers behind him. That potentially shortens the timeline back to contention while giving the Dolphins both a proven veteran and a long-term plan at the position.  

This would still allow the Dolphins to draft a top 5 talent in 2027 

 #PhinsUp

Wednesday Futures: The Rest Of The Week
November 4, 2026

Commodity and financial markets enter the first Wednesday session of November navigating a broad fundamental pullback across major boards as performance tracks since Monday’s open. 

In agricultural markets, heavy seasonal harvest pressure continues to dominate price discovery across the central Corn Belt, keeping December corn near $4.47 per bushel while December Chicago wheat pulls back to $6.06 1/4 per bushel. 

Outside the ag pits, energy futures are undergoing a sharp mid week correction; December WTI Crude Oil has pulled back further from its October highs, slipping to $88.34 per barrel as traders digest temporary easing in maritime transport friction alongside macroeconomic demand checks. 

In livestock, the post-report rally has met resistance ahead of late week cash trade; December live cattle are easing toward $217.625 per cwt, while November feeder cattle slide to $331.675 per cwt as feedlots weigh lower feed costs against lighter packer kill schedules.

This Morning

GrainsThis morning, row crops are under harvest-related pressure as Midwestern combines complete final field passes. December corn (/ZCZ26) is trading near $4.47 per bushel, pressed by heavy seasonal cash marketings despite the official crop insurance harvest price metrics.

December Silver (/SILZ26) holds near $52.30 per ounce.

Wednesday Corn & Ethanol Report
Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026

The grain and energy complexes are navigating a mix of macro energy adjustments and accelerating harvest activity this morning as nationwide corn combining reaches 74% completion. 

Energy markets have moderated off recent peaks, with West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil trading at $88.34 per barrel following a period of profit taking. Despite lower crude benchmarks, interior grain fundamentals remain firmly supported by a massive surge in weekly EIA fuel ethanol production which jumped to 1.143 million barrels per day and a record daily sale of 1.73 million metric tons of U.S. corn to Mexico. CBOT December corn futures are holding firm near $4.47 0/4.

Top News Story: Record 16 Billion Bushel Harvest Forecast Weighs on Corn Board

The agricultural trade continues to digest the USDA's expanded supply baseline, which projects national corn production at a massive 16.03 billion bushels on an 181.2 bushel per acre national yield. While the record crop estimates sent December futures down from early autumn highs, steady interior processor grinding demand and a massive daily export sale of 1.73 million metric tons to Mexico are establishing an active commercial floor as combining reaches 74% complete.

Futures & Market News

CBOT corn futures are trading flat to slightly firmer near midday, supported by a surge in weekly ethanol refinery output and strong export sales that offset pressure from $88.34 WTI crude oil.

December 2026 (Z): $4.47 0/4  holding nearby support as active harvest pressure absorbs

March 2027 (H): $4.60 2/4  maintaining a modest carry structure

May 2027 (K): $4.68 4/4

Key Driver: Clear weather across the Midwest allowed harvest combines to reach 74% completion nationwide. While weekly export inspection totals (885,000 MT) showed mixed trends, a massive single day sale to Mexico and weekly ethanol output surging to 1.143 million bpd continue to defend interior processing bids.

Commitments of Traders: Funds & Open Interest Deflates

Managed money accounts maintain a balanced to light net long stance, leaning on strong ethanol processing margins and major export bookings to absorb seasonal harvest hedge pressure.

Net Position: Non commercial funds hold a stable net long posture, supported by biofuel complex strength (1.143 million bpd ethanol) and solid commercial demand.

Short Covering Surge: Speculative short exposure remains contained, with trading activity dominated by commercial elevator hedging against physical receipts.

Market Impact: Board liquidity remains solid. Processor bid structures remain protective as refiners work to secure spot bushels against robust biofuel demand.

USDA Crop Progress: Development Phase
Monday afternoon’s USDA Crop Progress report showed harvest operations making rapid progress over the past week, moving toward the home stretch nationwide.

National Progress: Domestic corn harvest advanced 14 percentage points on the week to 74% complete nationwide. Fieldwork trails the five year average of 77% by 3 points, but dry weather has allowed combines to recover significant ground.

Crop Condition: Tennessee became the first monitored state to officially finish harvesting, while fieldwork across the central I States and Western Corn Belt accelerates rapidly under open skies.
