text:
$MSFT Microsoft possesses multiple, deep competitive moats. Even as market trends shift, the company’s performance remains remarkably resilient.

First, its "AI + Azure" combination is exceptionally strong. Microsoft has forged a deep partnership with OpenAI, and Azure has become the cloud platform of choice for enterprises deploying AI workloads. Companies are not merely testing AI on Azure; they are building their entire production systems—leveraging Azure, Foundry, and Copilot—on the platform. This generates consistent, recurring revenue rather than relying on one-off transactions.

Second, its enterprise ecosystem is unrivaled. With tools like Microsoft 365, Teams, SharePoint, LinkedIn, and Dynamics, Microsoft is embedded in virtually every large enterprise. Copilot integrates seamlessly across this entire suite, making upselling effortless. Microsoft doesn’t need to scramble for new customers; it can simply offer additional AI capabilities to its massive existing user base—a significant advantage that most other AI vendors cannot match.

Third, its balance sheet is rock-solid. Backed by robust cash flow and sustained profitability, Microsoft can easily invest billions of dollars into GPUs and data center infrastructure. While many smaller AI startups are burning through cash, Microsoft has the capital to continuously scale its AI foundation. Furthermore, the company regularly pays dividends and repurchases shares, cementing its status as a stable, high-quality tech stock—even during periods of market volatility.

Fourth, its revenue streams are well-diversified. Whether through Windows OEM, the Xbox gaming business, search advertising, or enterprise cloud services, Microsoft is not dependent on any single product. If growth slows in one segment, other areas can step in to fill the gap.

text:
Someone offers to get your business on Wikipedia for a fee. Here's what that fee can't buy.

• Approval. Volunteer editors review drafts, and no outside service can guarantee they'll accept one or keep it up.
• Control. Once a page exists, other editors can revise it, add sourced information, or propose deleting it. Being the subject doesn't let you remove accurate details you'd rather not see.
• A guaranteed ranking boost. Wikipedia generally applies nofollow to external links. The link can send readers your way, but don't pay for a page expecting it to lift your rankings.

Wikipedia doesn't charge anything to publish. A writer can charge for research and drafting, so treat the offer as paid work with an uncertain outcome.

Before you agree, ask:

• Will you assess my existing coverage before charging for a full draft?
• Where will you disclose that you're being paid? Wikipedia requires paid contributors to disclose their employer, client, and relevant affiliations.
• Who's writing it? English Wikipedia's guidelines prohibit using AI writing tools to generate or rewrite article content, with narrow exceptions.
• Does the agreement separate your fee from any promise of publication?

If they claim they can approve the page themselves or protect it from edits, treat that as a red flag. No writer can sell you those rights.

Bitcoin solved a fundamental problem: transferring value between strangers without depending on a bank, company or central administrator. Its strength comes from a network of independent participants verifying transactions under shared rules.

But Bitcoin was designed to prioritise security, not to run every kind of application. It cannot natively handle complex checkout systems, subscriptions, conditional payments or marketplaces.

This creates an interesting challenge. Can digital commerce benefit from Bitcoin's security without forcing Bitcoin itself to become something it was never designed to be?

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗚𝗢𝗔𝗧 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗔𝗖𝗛

GOAT Network is building infrastructure that brings programmable execution into the Bitcoin ecosystem.

Its architecture combines Ethereum-compatible execution through a zkEVM with Ziren, its in-house zero-knowledge proving system.

The important detail is verification. GOAT's design attaches zero-knowledge proofs to transaction batches, allowing their correctness to be checked mathematically without repeating all the computation.

It also uses decentralised sequencers rather than relying on a single company to operate the entire transaction pipeline.

𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗕𝗜𝗧𝗩𝗠𝟯 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗦

The bridge is one of the most important parts of this architecture.

GOAT's BitVM3 design aims to let Bitcoin verify withdrawals and allow anyone to challenge invalid claims. Its proposed withdrawal process includes a challenge period of at least one week before finalisation.

This distinction between a rollup and a sidechain matters. A system that asks users to trust its own operators offers different security guarantees from one designed to make settlement disputes answerable to Bitcoin.

BitVM3 remains under development. Its design and security assumptions must continue to face independent scrutiny before its intended guarantees can be treated as established in production.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗡𝗚𝗘: 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗖𝗘

AI agents are moving beyond answering questions. They are increasingly expected to search for services, make decisions and complete transactions.

But autonomous software needs more than intelligence. It needs a payment method and an identity that other participants can verify.

GOAT's ecosystem addresses these requirements through three important components:

• AgentKit gives developers tools to build and connect agents.

• x402 enables payment directly within internet requests, allowing an agent to receive a price, pay in stablecoins and access a service.

• ERC-8004 provides portable onchain identity and reputation, helping agents establish a verifiable record.

These components address a practical gap between software that can recommend a purchase and software that can actually complete one.

𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗧𝗢 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗟 𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗦

GOAT Flow brings this idea closer to businesses through a checkout system designed for both people and AI agents. Customers can pay by card or crypto, while agents can make stablecoin payments.

The October 2026 agreement with Square Tech in South Korea is another development worth watching. The proposed programme explores stablecoin payments for foreign tourists at participating Korean merchants, with verifiable agent identities, spending limits and transaction records.

This is a more concrete use case than simply discussing AI and blockchain as separate trends.

𝗠𝗬 𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘

Bitcoin provides the settlement foundation. GOAT adds programmable execution and verification. AgentKit, x402 and ERC-8004 explore how autonomous software can participate in an economy where payments and identity matter.

text:
This got me thinking, and I couldn't get it out of my head. Here's what I came up with.

How HL3 could switch Half-Life back from cosmic horror to epic sci-fi, close the G-Man mystery, tie in Portal, and end the Combine for good.

THE PREMISE
The Shu'ulathoi (Advisors) are the Combine's brains, and its slaves themselves. Some still have their own minds and want out. They built the G-Man as an untraceable proxy: they are his "e-e-employers". His "restrictions" are operational security: he can only nudge, never confront, or the rebels quickly get exposed and killed by the Combine loyalist core. The Combine knows he's a threat (hence the HL:A vault) but not where he came from or what he is.

This is the moment where the genre changes. The Combine isn't unbeatable by nature. Its nature is explained, so it becomes beatable in principle. It was unbeatable in practice, because it's coordinated by a hive mind at an inhuman level. But the coordinators are slaves themselves, and want out. 

Combine borrows medical language and treats individuals of the species it co-opted and enslaved as cells of an interdimensional body - expendable, interchangeable, infinitely obedient. To stop it we don't need to destroy every single cell, we just need the brain stem to defect.

THE SPINE: "Unforeseen Consequences"
The Combine and Advisors run on prediction, and humans are the one thing the hive mind can't model. Humanity wasn't chosen for its strength, but for unpredictability. Gordon is the unforeseen consequence. 

It also explains G-Man's habits: rebel tech and direct intervention leave a psionic trace and risk exposure; a free human choice doesn't. So he must "hire", "employ" and "offer a choice". The bureaucrat act is agency laundering, protecting his employers.

HL2 E3: BOREALIS
  - Starts from the HL:A epilogue. Eli alive, Alyx taken. Saving Eli broke G-Man's own rules, and the Combine heard it.
  - Eli's "destroy the Borealis" explained: it can open a door into G-Man's Space Between. Now it's the only way to reach Alyx, so Eli makes a U-turn.
  - Aboard: Cave Johnson tapes talk about "the consultant", a man in a blue suit who handed Aperture the portal maths. Black Mesa had the same consultant, the Aperture vs Black Mesa rivalry was engineered.
  - The Borealis is the one thing the G-Man didn't give them or predict, so it works outside his control.
  - Gordon and Eli use the Borealis to crash into the Space Between and upset G-Man's plans.
  - Finale: every HL ends with the protagonist frozen while G-Man talks. This time, you walk. Into his realm of frozen moments, to Alyx in stasis. You can't fight him, but the Borealis sits in his space like a lighthouse the Combine can see. This is leverage we use to negotiate with G-Man, not just obey him.

Alyx freed, G-Man contract renegotiated, his parting words: "My employers are closer to your enemies than you might imagine."

HALF-LIFE 3
1. The Second Voice: an Advisor makes contact and doesn't attack. The Vorts confirm a dissenting voice in the Vortessence. The painful reveal: killing the Nihilanth was the plan. It was the barrier keeping the Combine away, and G-Man had Gordon remove it to put Earth in the Combine's path. Humanity was used, knows it, and fights anyway, on its own terms.
2. Enrichment: raid Aperture's buried facility for industrial portal tech. GLaDOS dormant, Chell asleep in her vault (Portal 2 canon intact). Gordon gets a portal gun. Then off-world to the Overworld.
3. Unforeseen Consequences: the rebels can cut the Combine's psionic lattice only while it's fixated on a threat it can't predict - humanity. With Aperture's tech and rebels' help - Freeman can portal directly into the Combine Brain Core, bypassing the infinite layers of protection built in the normal space-time. Final boss is the loyalist Advisor core, powerful, but killable like the Nihilanth. 
HL1 killed the Vortigaunts' enslaver. 
HL3 kills everyone's.

Once the Brain Core is gone - the Combine isn't blown up, it dissolves. Conscripted species stop obeying, striders stand still, gunships land and start munching antlions, transhuman soldiers drop guns and take off their masks. The threat really was that strong. It was strong because it was held together by an unyielding interdimensional will. 
With the will gone - the empire falls apart.

EPILOGUE
Gordon and Alyx alive on a quiet Earth. G-Man straightens his tie: "My employers have no further need of my services. And it seems, Dr. Freeman, neither... do you." He walks off, and the screen doesn't cut to black. You keep control, nobody's employee.

text:
The decision to buy Twitter for $44 billion began, by Elon Musk's own account, as something between a joke and an impulse. It ended as the most expensive content moderation decision in history and the only business move that people close to him have described as the one time the pattern broke.

The timeline: in early 2022, Elon began buying Twitter shares quietly. By April, he owned 9.2 percent. Twitter offered him a board seat. He accepted. Then he rejected it. Then on April 14, he made an unsolicited offer to buy the entire company for $54.20 per share ($44 billion total). The price, like the $420 Tesla tweet before it, contained a marijuana reference. The man was bidding $44 billion on a company and embedding a weed joke in the offer price.

The market assumed it was a negotiating tactic. It was not. Twitter's board adopted a poison pill defense. Elon secured financing from banks. The offer became legally binding. And then the regret reportedly began.

Over the following months, Elon attempted to withdraw from the deal citing concerns about the number of bot accounts on the platform. Twitter sued him to enforce the agreement. The lawsuit was headed to trial in Delaware Chancery Court. The legal consensus was that Elon would lose. The contract was binding. He was going to own Twitter whether he wanted to or not.

On October 27, 2022, he closed the deal. He walked into Twitter headquarters carrying a kitchen sink (a visual pun: "let that sink in"). He fired 80 percent of the staff. He changed the name to X. He became the world's most controversial CEO overnight, adding the most divisive company in tech to a portfolio that already included the most complicated car company and the most ambitious rocket company on earth.

The vulnerability is this: every other major Elon decision (SpaceX, Tesla, Neuralink, Boring Company) was made from first principles analysis. The Twitter acquisition was made from something else. Frustration with censorship. Personal grievance with the platform. The impulse of a man who could afford anything choosing the most chaotic possible thing to purchase. The pattern of calculated risk that defined his career was interrupted by a $44 billion emotional purchase.

People close to him have said it is the only decision they have seen him make that they believe he would undo if he could. The man who has never regretted starting SpaceX on a 10 percent probability, never regretted splitting his last $20 million between two dying companies, and never regretted sleeping on a factory floor for months reportedly has one regret. And it is the one decision that started with a joke and ended with $44 billion leaving his bank account.

The richest man alive made the most expensive impulse purchase in business history. The purchase contained a weed joke. The consequences are still unfolding. And the man who calculates everything got caught by the one moment where the calculation was replaced by something he couldn't spreadsheet.

The study’s focus on limited training data is particularly relevant to healthcare, where access to large, representative datasets can be challenging. While further validation with independent clinical datasets is needed, this research demonstrates how quantum computing is being explored for applications in data-constrained environments with meaningful real-world implications.

text:
Hollywood socialite Zsa Zsa Gabor married 9 times, including the founder of the Hilton hotel empire. One of those marriages lasted a single day, and her last husband was a "prince" who had paid a real princess to adopt him.

She was born in Budapest in 1917. At 19 she was crowned Miss Hungary, then disqualified for lying about her age.

In America she met Conrad Hilton, the man building the Hilton hotels. She says that on the first night he offered her $20,000 to fly to Florida with him. In 1942 they married. She was 25.

When they divorced five years later, she got $35,000 and $2,500 a month until she married again. They had one daughter, Francesca.

Then the list just kept growing. An Oscar-winning actor. An oil heir. The designer behind the Barbie doll. Then her own divorce lawyer, the one who had handled her previous split.

In 1983 she married husband number eight, a Mexican actor. The next day the marriage was annulled, because her divorce from the lawyer was not final yet.

Husband number nine was Frederic Prinz von Anhalt, around 26 years younger than her. He was born the son of a German police officer. In 1980 he reportedly paid an elderly, broke German princess to adopt him as an adult, and that is how he got the "Prince" in his name.

That marriage lasted 30 years, until her death in 2016 at 99. Along the way the couple reportedly charged other men up to $2 million each to be adopted into the "royal" family.

Her most famous line was that she was a marvelous housekeeper, because every time she left a man, she kept his house.

In the video below, six months after her ninth wedding, David Letterman goes through her husbands one by one on live TV, and she corrects him on what they actually did.

9 weddings and a bought crown. Was she marrying for love or for the house?

text:
TV legend Larry King married 8 times, to 7 different women. When he died, his wife of 22 years found out he had secretly written a new will by hand that left her nothing.

He married for the first time at 19. Their parents had the marriage annulled a year later. Then the list just kept growing.

One of his wives was a Playboy Bunny named Alene Akins. He married her in 1961, divorced her in 1963, married someone else, and then married Alene again in 1968. They split for good three years later.

In 1997 he married wife number seven, singer and actress Shawn Southwick. It became the longest marriage of his life. They had two sons, and for a while it looked like this one would last.

In 2010 they both filed for divorce, then changed their minds. In August 2019, at 85, Larry filed again.

Two months later he took out a pen. On October 17, 2019 he wrote a new will by hand, saying 100% of his money should be split equally between his five children. Shawn's name was not in it. It also replaced his 2015 will, the one that had named her as executor.

Then the family started falling apart. In 2020 two of the five children named in that will died, weeks apart. In January 2021 Larry died at 87, still legally married to Shawn.

Shawn went to court. She said the handwritten will was not valid, that his eldest son had pressured him, and that Larry had a secret account he used to send gifts without her knowledge, including more than $266,000 to that same son.

The will covered about $2 million. Reports had put his total fortune much higher, with most of it believed to be in trusts. In the end the two sides settled in private, and nobody said who got what.

In the video below, Larry explains his obsession with marriage on the radio, and why he kept walking down the aisle instead of just dating.

8 weddings, and the last word was a note in his own handwriting. Would you call that love or a habit?

text:
Nick Cannon, host of The Masked Singer and Mariah Carey's ex-husband, has 12 children with 6 different women. Five of them were born in a single year, and he says he does not pay child support to any of their mothers.

It started with Mariah. They married in 2008 and had twins in 2011. The marriage fell apart, and by 2016 they were officially divorced.

What came next is hard to believe. Between 2017 and 2022 he had ten more children with five more women: three with model Brittany Bell, three with DJ Abby De La Rosa, two with model Alyssa Scott, one with Selling Sunset star Bre Tiesi, and one with LaNisha Cole, a model from The Price Is Right.

Five of those babies arrived in 2022 alone, from five different mothers.

The press quickly ran the numbers. One estimate said his child support would cost about $3 million a year. Nick said that was wrong in the other direction: he spends a lot more than that, and he never plans to deal with the government child support system at all.

His rule is simple. The mothers get no fixed monthly amount. Whatever the kids need, they get. He has also said he makes around $100 million a year, so $3 million is "not a lot of money."

In 2024 he took it one step further and insured his testicles for $10 million. Later he joked that his only regret was not making it $12 million, one for each kid.

The critics call him a deadbeat dad. He says Bob Marley and Muhammad Ali had big families too.

In the video below, Nick admits on The Breakfast Club that it all started from pain after his divorce from Mariah, that he never did the work on himself, and that one day he just looked up and had 12 kids.

Is this a father providing for his family, or a man who just keeps paying for his mistakes?

text:
What African Leaders Should Learn from America’s Midterm Reckoning

The 2026 United States midterm elections delivered a clear verdict. @TheDemocrats captured control of both the House and the Senate, flipping seats and governorships in places that had long been written off as permanently Republican. #Kansas elected a Democratic senator for the first time in 94 years. Texas produced both a Democratic senator and governor. South Carolina, Iowa, Ohio, and other traditional strongholds moved. The results were driven less by any sudden Democratic brilliance than by widespread frustration over the cost of living, energy prices linked to the Iran conflict, and a sense that the governing side had lost touch with daily realities.

For #African countries, these outcomes contain practical lessons that go beyond slogans about democracy. Many of the continent’s political systems feature dominant parties, personalized leadership, carefully managed electoral rules, and constituencies that rarely change hands. The American results show what happens when material conditions deteriorate and voters are given a credible chance to register dissatisfaction. They also show the limits of several common tactics used to protect incumbents.

The most immediate lesson is that sustained economic pain overrides personality, historical loyalty, and safe geography. American voters ranked the cost of living as their top concern. Large majorities blamed the administration’s policies for higher prices. Tariffs and the energy disruptions caused by the Iran war, particularly restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz, turned abstract decisions into higher fuel and household costs. Even districts that had supported the president by double digits two years earlier swung or became competitive.

African governing parties that treat inflation, currency weakness, fuel shortages, or unemployment as secondary to ethnic arithmetic, regional bargains, or the leader’s personal brand face the same risk wherever elections remain competitive enough for voters to punish failure. Promises of future growth or appeals to loyalty do not neutralize rising prices at the market or the pump. Parties that deliver measurable improvements in living standards retain more room to manoeuvre; those that do not discover that “safe” rural or peripheral areas can move when the pain is prolonged and visible.

A related point is that foreign policy and security choices carry domestic electoral costs. The Iran conflict became a major liability precisely because it raised energy prices and diverted resources at a moment of existing affordability strain. Polling showed majority opposition to the use of force and widespread belief that the war lacked a clear endgame. African governments that become involved in prolonged regional interventions, expensive security commitments, or alliances that raise import costs or divert budgets from domestic needs can face comparable judgment. Voters notice when fuel, food, or transport become more expensive because of decisions made elsewhere. Leaders who calculate that external adventures will be accepted as long as the political machine holds at home underestimate how quickly household economics can reorder priorities.

The midterms also demonstrated that safe seats and permanent majorities are rarer than parties assume. Historic flips occurred not only in swing states but in places that had not elected the opposing party to statewide office in decades. This is relevant in African systems where ruling parties often dominate large rural areas through patronage, limited competition, or the absence of strong local alternatives. Those advantages erode when material conditions worsen, and opposition candidates present credible local faces focused on prices, jobs, and services. Parties that treat certain regions as automatic remain vulnerable to sudden shifts once voters conclude that continuity has failed them.

Candidate selection proved equally consequential. The president intervened in Republican primaries to favour personal loyalists and ideological allies over more established or electable alternatives. In Texas, he backed Ken Paxton over a long-serving senator; Paxton then lost. In South Carolina, he pressed a political novice, the sister of a late senator, into a race in a state he had carried by nearly 18 points; she lost. Similar patterns appeared in other races. High success rates in primaries did not translate into general-election strength once the national environment turned.

African parties that centralize nomination around a leader’s personal preferences, rewarding loyalty, family ties, or factional deals while sidelining candidates with broader local appeal or fewer liabilities, absorb both the leader’s unpopularity and the nominee’s weaknesses. More open internal processes, whether competitive primaries, greater weight for local branches, or explicit tests of electability, produce stronger general-election candidates. They also reduce the chance that one person’s choices become the party’s ceiling.

Finally, efforts to manipulate the electoral map and process delivered limited protection. Republicans pursued mid-decade redistricting in several states, including Texas, Florida, and North Carolina, to create additional House seats and blunt expected losses. Many of the targeted districts still went to Democrats or remained competitive. California’s counter-redistricting offset gains elsewhere. Maps drawn on the assumption that the previous election’s coalition would hold proved fragile when that coalition frayed.

Structural advantages in constituency boundaries, voter registration rules, or administrative procedures can create temporary edges, but they are vulnerable to large shifts in public mood. When turnout rises and grievances are widely shared, engineered maps do not reliably deliver the expected results. Over-reliance on such tactics can also reduce a party’s incentive to address underlying voter concerns and can damage legitimacy when outcomes diverge sharply from the intended design.

These patterns do not require the full institutional density of the United States. They mainly require that elections remain competitive enough for material failure to be punished and that parties cannot fully insulate themselves from the consequences of high living costs or expensive external commitments. Practical steps follow. Governing parties should treat measurable improvements in prices, fuel availability, and employment as first-order political priorities, not secondary ones. Candidate selection should weigh local popularity and electability more than loyalty tests.

Electoral commissions and courts that maintain independence on boundary delimitation and process integrity make map manipulation less attractive and less effective. Civil society and media that focus public attention on household economics, rather than solely on elite personalities, raise the cost of ignoring living standards. Opposition parties that organize around concrete economic delivery rather than abstract critiques stand a better chance of converting dissatisfaction into seats.

The American midterms do not offer a template to copy. They do illustrate that voters respond to the gap between promises and daily experience, that loyalty and geography are not permanent shields, and that attempts to engineer outcomes through candidate imposition or map drawing have clear limits when conditions deteriorate. African parties and leaders who internalise those constraints early, by delivering on costs of living, opening nomination processes, and accepting competitive rules, reduce the chance of sudden, large-scale reversals. Those who treat the same constraints as optional discover, as American Republicans did, that the bill arrives at the ballot box.

text:
What if the Midterms didn’t go your way?

I have an Op-Ed under review for publication, but until then I wanted to share this abridged version for time's sake. I hope these quick points encourage fellow Christians. 

Some Christians reviewed the midterm results the morning after and probably began mourning. I know many are disappointed with the results. I am disappointed, but certainly not surprised. Dear Christians, if your candidates and ballot measures failed, let me offer a few reminders. 

(1) God is still the sovereign Lord and judge of all the earth. 

Politicians come and go, governments come and go, even nations have risen and fallen, but our God stays the same yesterday, today, and tomorrow. God is working all things out according to the counsel of His will.

(2) Christ is still the King of Kings and Lord of Lords

Nothing that happened in the midterms changes the fact that Christ has been given the name above all names and that one day every knee will bow and tongue confess that Jesus the Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10-11).

(3) The Great Commission is still our mission

Nothing in the midterm results changes the mission for the Christian. Jesus gave us our marching orders in Matthew 28:18-20. This charge from Christ is still active no matter the outcome of American elections. Our mission is to take the truth, love, and grace of Jesus to everyone. The church’s mission is not politics; it’s evangelism and discipleship. 

(4) Don’t let politics replace your heart for lost people

Related to point three, we need to be careful not to let our politics replace our love for lost people. Our mission involves taking the gospel of Jesus to people who need to hear about Him. If we are not careful, we can let politics replace people. We can become so political that we forget the unsaved people who voted opposite us are not our foes; they are our mission field. 

(5) Don't become politically apathetic

Even though politics is not the mechanism for fulfilling the Great Commission, Christians must not become politically apathetic. Politics does matter. Ballot measures impact moral issues, and politicians are people with a moral vision. If you are disappointed with the midterm results, do not let that make you politically apathetic. The temptation is to think your vote does not matter, so why bother. If more of us think like this, it only makes it easier for our country to become morally worse off. 

Here is a case study tying my points together. As a Missouri resident, I am particularly disappointed that Amendment 3 did not pass. But that does not mean I will stop advocating for the biblical moral principle that all life, even the preborn, is made in God’s image and must be protected. Amendment 3 did not pass, but my trust in God is not shaken. Amendment 3 did not pass, but that does not stop me from taking part in evangelism, missions, and discipleship. More of my Missouri neighbors obviously voted the opposite of me concerning Amendment 3. However, this does not change my desire to see my lost neighbors come to faith in Christ and be saved. 

Dear Christians, if the midterms did not go your way, take heart because our God reigns, Christ is Lord, and our unsaved neighbors still need Jesus.

text:
A CITY LOST IN THE DESERT FOR 600 YEARS… AND THE MYSTERIES IT LEFT BEHIND

Deep in the vast Gobi Desert of northwestern China stands one of the most haunting ancient ruins in the world: Khara-Khoto, also known as the Black City. Built around the 11th century, this once-thriving settlement was an important military and trading center of the Western Xia Dynasty. Its strong defensive walls, busy streets, Buddhist temples, and remarkable architecture once made it a significant city in this remote desert region.

But its story took a dramatic turn in 1372, when Ming Dynasty forces besieged the city. According to historical accounts and local legends, the attackers cut off its water supply by diverting the nearby river. Without water in the middle of the desert, survival became almost impossible. The city eventually fell, and its people disappeared from history, leaving behind a settlement that would slowly become buried beneath the desert sands.

Today, its massive mud-brick walls still rise above the golden dunes. Ancient towers, ruined buildings, and the remains of religious structures offer a glimpse into a civilization that once flourished here. For centuries, the city remained largely forgotten until Russian explorer Pyotr Kozlov reached the ruins in 1908. His expedition uncovered thousands of ancient manuscripts, Buddhist paintings, books, and other remarkable artifacts, revealing valuable details about the forgotten Tangut civilization.

What makes Khara-Khoto especially fascinating is how much of its history survived beneath the sand. A city that once supported thousands of people, welcomed travelers, and played an important role in regional trade was eventually reduced to silent ruins.

Today, the desert surrounds its ancient walls as if trying to hide them once again. Yet every surviving structure tells a story of human ambition, faith, war, and the passage of time.

How many other lost cities are still waiting to be discovered beneath the world’s deserts?

Sources: International Dunhuang Programme (British Library) – Revisiting Kharakhoto; National Institute of Informatics, Japan – Silk Road in Rare Books.

text:
In the first days of November 1846, snow trapped the Donner Party in the Sierra Nevada, a few miles short of getting over the mountains into California. What happened that winter became one of the most horrifying stories of the American West.

They left Springfield, Illinois, in April 1846: the families of brothers George and Jacob Donner, and the family of a prosperous businessman named James Reed. Reed's family traveled in a huge custom wagon with two levels and a built-in stove. His children later called it the Pioneer Palace Car.

From Independence, Missouri, they followed the Oregon Trail across Kansas. Reed's mother-in-law, Sarah Keyes, was 70 and very sick. She died near the Big Blue River, at a place called Alcove Spring, and was buried there. Her name and Reed's are still carved into the rocks nearby.

Along the way they read a guidebook by a promoter named Lansford Hastings. He wrote about a new shortcut south of the Great Salt Lake that would save hundreds of miles. What the book didn't say was that Hastings had never taken a wagon over it. In late July, the Donners, the Reeds, and several other families split off from the main trail to try it. They elected George Donner as their captain.

The shortcut was a disaster. In the Wasatch Mountains of Utah, there was no road, so the men had to chop one through thick brush and trees, sometimes making only a mile or two a day. It took weeks. Then came the Great Salt Lake Desert. Hastings said it was 40 miles across. It was closer to 80. Oxen died of thirst or wandered off in the night. Reed had to abandon his big wagon.

By the time they rejoined the main California Trail in Nevada, they were weeks behind schedule, short on food, and turning on each other. In October, two wagons got tangled on a steep hill and a fight broke out. A teamster named John Snyder hit Reed with a whip. Reed pulled a knife and killed him. The group banished Reed, and he rode ahead alone to California, leaving his family behind.

At the end of October they reached the foot of the Sierra Nevada. The snow came early that year, and hard. They tried to force their way up to the pass, now called Donner Pass, and couldn't get through. Most of the group fell back to a lake, now Donner Lake, and built rough cabins. The Donner families were stuck about six miles back at Alder Creek, living in tents and brush shelters.

Then it kept snowing. That winter the snow got deeper than 20 feet.

They slaughtered their oxen. Then they ate their dogs. Then they boiled ox hides into a gluey paste, and ate bones, bark, and twigs. People started dying of starvation in December. An Irish immigrant named Patrick Breen kept a diary in one of the cabins, writing down each day's weather, the deaths, and his prayers.

On Dec 16, 15 of the strongest left on snowshoes made from oxbows and rawhide to try to reach help. They had about six days of food. They got lost in the mountains, and a storm caught them at Christmas. Several died. The survivors, starving, ate the bodies of the dead. Two Native American men who had been sent from Sutter's Fort with supplies were with them. One of the survivors shot and killed them.

After about a month, a man named William Eddy staggered into a ranch in the Sacramento Valley. Only seven of the 15 had survived: two men and all five women.

Rescue parties started heading into the mountains. The first one reached the lake in February 1847 and found people starving in cabins buried under snow. Those still alive had been forced to eat the dead too.

James Reed, who had been banished, came back leading a second rescue party. On the way in he ran into his wife and two of his children being brought out. His two youngest had been too weak to make the trip, so he kept going up to the lake and found them alive. His 8-year-old daughter Patty had carried a tiny wooden doll hidden in her dress through the entire ordeal. It's in a museum in California today.

At Alder Creek, Tamsen Donner refused to leave her dying husband George, even when rescuers offered to take her out. She stayed, and she died. When the last rescue party reached the lake in April, they found one survivor left, a German immigrant named Lewis Keseberg, alone in a cabin with what was left of the dead. Rumors spread that he had murdered people for food, but nothing was ever proven.

Of about 87 people who started, only around half lived. Most of the men in their prime died. More of the women and children survived.

That spring, 13-year-old Virginia Reed wrote a long letter to her cousin back in Illinois describing what they'd been through. At the end she gave advice for anyone else coming west: never take no cutoffs, and hurry along as fast as you can.

Today there's a monument at Donner Lake. Its pedestal is 22 feet tall, the depth of the snow that winter.

text:
🇺🇸 A prisoner was being beaten to death.

Another American stepped forward and offered to take the rest of his punishment.

In April 1942, Lieutenant Richard Antrim was a prisoner of the Japanese at Makassar, on the island of Celebes (today’s Sulawesi, Indonesia).

The US Navy officer had survived the sinking of the destroyer USS Pope. Now he was living behind barbed wire.

One day, a Japanese guard began brutally punishing a fellow American officer. Antrim intervened, trying to persuade the guard to stop. But the beating continued. The prisoner lost consciousness after fifteen blows. The guard then began kicking him.

Around 2,700 Allied prisoners watched. Antrim stepped forward again. He offered to take the rest of the punishment himself.

He had no weapon, no authority over the guards, and no guarantee that his intervention would save either man.

But the beating stopped.

According to Antrim’s Medal of Honor citation, his action saved his fellow prisoner’s life and prompted a cheer from the assembled prisoners. It also changed his standing in the camp. The citation records that his captors developed a new respect for him, helping improve conditions for the other prisoners.

Antrim survived captivity and returned home after the war. On January 30, 1947, President Harry Truman presented him with the Medal of Honor.

His was an extraordinary act of courage performed as a prisoner, with no means of defending himself.

Rear Admiral Antrim died in Mountain Home, Arkansas on March 7, 1969. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia

text:
President Donald Trump never hesitates to tell us what he thinks of a person.

Saul Alinsky famously said "Use ridicule."

"Ridicule is man's most potent weapon. There is no defense. It is almost impossible to counterattack ridicule. Also it infuriates the opposition, who then react to your advantage."

I've found that to be exactly what it says, the most infuriating political tactic, which is exactly the reaction Alinsky and Leftist activists want. What ought to be a source of shame for them is simply something they have grown proud of doing. It's certainly worked. For as long as I can remember, the Left has called Republicans racist bigots, greedy, you name it. It's a reflex form of abuse and has been since I was a child.

Reagan fought back. You can look up his campaigns and speeches. He called the Soviet Union "the evil Empire" which outraged Democrats. He used the term "liberal" constantly as a pejorative. He told endless jokes about Democrat behavior, socialist views of the world, and made it clear that his views on the economy were bound up within a philosophy that viewed the battle as one of good versus evil. This absolutely outraged the Left, apparently because they believed they had a monopoly on "using ridicule." But Reagan also, if you look at the old speeches, rarely if ever directly called someone a fool. Perhaps one can fight back, yet still somehow turn the other cheek?

---

Since I formed this account in 2009, I've deleted my history a few times. It wasn't that I changed my views, but it was the way I expressed them that made me want to make a fresh start. A rant can be amusing, but it can also slip into a kind of ridicule that's shameful, at least in my hands I've discovered that too many times. However, each time I wiped my public posting, I found I regretted the decision, because it can be worthwhile to go back more than ten years to find where one has been consistent, and not.

The point being, I've been of two minds about the value of speaking one's mind bluntly, to the point of attacking one's opponent, not just their ideas, by essentially calling them fools. Or, as we've seen over the past few years, "retards."

The Left's faux gasping, and its hall monitor policing of language has nothing whatsoever to do with this. Southpark does a better job of explaining the difference between humor and real ridicule. This isn't about verbotten words.

It may simply be a matter of style and "type" of personality. Trump has always been who he is. If you were against him, no kind of ridicule seemed off limits.

Close observers might say that Trump actually is much more careful than he comes across. What appears to be careless, snap judgments and breathtaking insults are arguably what gamblers might call "table image." He picks and chooses his spots, but good businessmen and excellent poker players know that to make sure the others at the table really, truly believe the image you're projecting, you must back it up with stacks of chips, and keep doing it over time, to the point that when it really counts, they simply cannot discern the difference. That is how tournaments are won, deals done, and peace made, at times. It can be done at a clumsy, amateur level, or it can be a lifelong work. Donald Trump in his entire, very public life, has never once stopped fighting, throwing gut punches, and responding on his feet, on the fly, rapidly. Is that table image, just who he is, or both? It has served him well, and anyone who doesn't see the benefit of having a President who is that sharp, and willing to speak without a teleprompter to anyone on the planet, including journalists, has their own issues to deal with.

So, if Alinsky, and his acolytes like Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, and so many others under the Leftist activist religion can "use ridicule", so can Donald Trump and Republicans. They call you greedy racists constantly and get offended when you elect someone who fights fire with fire. The comedy is there and it's okay to enjoy it.

But don't forget, that is their method. They are manipulating you, and pretending to be offended, because as Saul Alinsky taught (rule 11):

"If you push a negative hard and deep enough it will break through into its counterside; this is based on the principle that every positive has its negative."

If this has its moments of comedy, that will inevitably be the highest source of it. Rule 11: "Hold a bazooka to your own face."
...

Except the one thing that has been making me more uncomfortable with my own side than the past is religion.

I have always wanted to flee the room when it sounds like an evangelist is speaking. The same religion that gives me the New Testament, which I have been re-reading lately, also produces the con artists of mega churches that I grew up flipping by on television on Sunday mornings in Dallas between ball games. This was at a time when you would go to the store and if it was a Sunday, some aisles would have blue tape across them, meaning you could not shop there, because on Sundays in parts of the South, including Texas, certain purchases might violate Christian doctrine. You might be able to buy a hammer, but not the nails to go with it, because you weren't supposed to work on a Sunday. In other nations and places in the West, shops were simply closed, by law, so let's not rip on the South. 

But my own discomfort with the particularly cloying evangelism of con artist preachers has made me always hesitate to talk about the Bible, my own Christianity, the requirements of my religion to view the resurrection of Christ as a fact truer and more important than any other, including any law of physics. That is the Nicene Creed, and it is spoken in Catholic and Protestant Churches every Sunday. And for people who believe in science and reason, there is real fear of hypocrisy in reciting the creed while wondering how much we really believe it. Of course, the Church addresses it, and has, in many ways, through time, but it comes down to your own conscience, too, and your relationship with God, and the words which are there whether a Church run by flawed humans is or not.

One can have doubts. One can have interpretations. But the words of Jesus Christ are not secret. And in this past month or so, reading Matthew slowly, because this time around, I've been looking at several translations at once as I go, there really is little room for a wide range of interpretation:

Matthew 5:22 (KJV, NASB, ESV, NIV)

KJV

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

NASB

But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be answerable to the court; and whoever says to his brother, ‘You good-for-nothing,’ shall be answerable to the supreme court; and whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be guilty enough to go into the fiery hell.

ESV

But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the hell of fire.

NIV

But I tell you that anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will be subject to judgment. Again, anyone who says to a brother or sister, ‘Raca,’ is answerable to the court. And anyone who says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of hell.

---

President Trump has had a few words on the topic himself:

“I mean, you know, I’m being a little cute. I don’t think there’s anything going to get me in heaven. Okay. I really don’t. I think I think I’m not maybe heaven bound. I may be in heaven right now as we fly on Air Force One. I’m not sure I’m going to be able to make heaven, but I’ve made life a lot better for a lot of people.”

“I want to try and get to heaven, if possible. I’m hearing I’m not doing well. I am really at the bottom of the totem pole. But if I can get to heaven, this will be one of the reasons.”

However, tongue in cheek at times he may be, I find these statements fascinating, and appropriate in ways and on levels many don't give the man credit for. I think he will go down as a great President. He may have helped turn the tide that is so strong against this nation he'll be up there with Washington himself, surpassing even Reagan, who I grew up admiring and who is one of the reasons I have always been a Republican and have never voted for a Democrat in my entire life.

But for my part, I'm tired of trying to adopt the style of the Alinsky acolytes. I'm tired of instantly thinking of half the population as idiots and fools, which is something I have often done, and no doubt still will. It's odd, extremely odd to me that I can have read the words I quoted above several times in my life, and yet go through long spans of time ignoring them, only to come back once again and read them like a punch in the gut. I don't think I'm high on the totem pole myself.

And I speak only for myself, but I do think that whenever in polemics the proverbial pendulum swings, we see a release of bottled-up frustrations. Republicans and right wingers having been accused of racism and bigotry for so long they spent generations tamping down natural, logical, fair objections to liberal policy, as it grew insane before our eyes, wake up one post-election morning and think victory has happened, and is complete, and out comes the flood. I don't believe half the people even believe what they're saying, and I am certain that many who utter phrases that confirm the Left's worst accusations were baited into it for so long, it's pure Oedipus. The Left can say, "See we were right!" in a prophecy they feared so much they manifested it.

The crash of the Lear Jet a few days ago is just one of so many examples. Even if we completely throw out the thousands of bots and jokers trying to get a rise out of anyone with comments about the fear in the co-pilot's voice—and so many who instantly assumed she was the pilot—the fact that even reasonably well-respected voices on the Right could not wait a single day to offer their invaluable opinion of the fear and death of this woman and the people on the plane, is just sad.

We are not the activist mentality. We've had to adapt to it. We will continue to have to adapt to it, and to gather together as collective people, no matter how individualistic we are, and no matter how much we believe in individual freedom, but we are not the people who believe activism-as-way-of-life is the highest purpose.

We believe we cannot serve two masters. Politics is politics. We are up against what we believe to be evil in this world: a philosophy of politics based purely in envy, and a theory of organization that leads to only one thing, a slave state. But God is God. We have the instruction manual. Right?

I can't speak for you. I'm truly asking, is that not correct?

Matthew 13:35

"I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world."

If one side in this conflict is using a set of rules that are fundamentally a despicable way of manipulating the minds and hearts of the masses, no matter how effective they seem to be in the short term, and even over decades of our lives, and the other side has a rule book that is The Rule Book ... why start, or at least continue to dabble with the other's way of doing things?

text:
Regardless of politics, I have been in full Christmas mode since November 1st. Let me introduce you to the Krampus!

USA residents are deeply acquainted with the generous magic of Santa Claus, but just across the Atlantic, the Alpine traditions of Austria weave a much darker, wilder narrative into the Advent season. If you misbehave in central Europe, you aren't met with a harmless lump of coal—you might just find yourself face-to-face with the Krampus!

Let's dive into the fascinating, ancient history of this fearsome holiday creature, exploring how an old pagan spirit became the ultimate symbol of Christmas discipline.

The Ancient Origins of the Christmas Demon

The roots of Krampus trace back long before the first Christmas tree was ever decorated. Believed to originate from pre-Christian Alpine pagan traditions, this horned, half-goat, half-demon figure was likely tied to winter solstice rituals aimed at warding off evil spirits and surviving the longest, darkest nights of the year. In fact, some folklorists believe Krampus is the son of Hel, the Norse goddess of the underworld, with his name likely deriving from the Old High German word krampf, meaning "claw".

As Christianity swept through Europe, church officials repeatedly attempted to ban these primal, terrifying traditions. But the Alpine people refused to let their protective winter spirits die. The ultimate compromise? A brilliant cultural merger. Krampus was paired with Saint Nicholas, creating a powerful moral dualism.

The Yin-Yang of Alpine Christmas

This brings us to Krampusnacht (Krampus Night), celebrated every year on the evening of December 5th. While Saint Nicholas arrives as the benevolent bringer of gifts, praising the virtuous, Krampus serves as his dark enforcer.

The mythology is brutally effective. Towering and covered in fur, Krampus clatters through the streets wielding heavy chains (a symbol of the Christian concept of "binding the devil") and large cowbells. For the truly naughty, Krampus carries a bundle of birch branches to swat them, and in the darkest versions of the legend, a basket on his back to drag the worst offenders straight to the underworld. When children wake up on December 6th—Saint Nicholas Day—they either find sweet rewards or nurse the sting of the birch.

The Thrill of the Krampuslauf (Krampus Run)

Today, the tradition is kept intensely alive through the Krampuslauf, or Krampus Run. Men in Alpine towns don elaborate, hand-carved wooden masks and heavy fur suits to transform into the demonic entity. These processions are not quaint parades; they are sensory spectacles of fire, smoke, and primal noise.

Spectators deliberately crowd the streets, with many actively seeking the thrill of being chased or lightly whipped by a Krampus. These costumes are considered highly valuable pieces of folk art, with masks passed down through generations and ancient wooden faces proudly displayed in local museums.

Krampus’s unsettling presence permeates Austrian culture in ways that extend far beyond a single winter night. Visually, he is meant to leave a lingering sense of unease, traditionally depicted in vintage greeting cards and folklore artwork with an eerie, asymmetrical stride of one human foot and one cloven hoof. To keep that disciplinary magic alive throughout the year, some families would even spray paint a bundle of his infamous birch twigs gold, hanging them on the wall as a constant, glittering reminder for children to behave. Yet, this deeply rooted cultural icon hasn't always been welcomed by those in power; the chaotic nature of the folklore was viewed as such a threat in the 1930s that the tradition was actually banned by the Dollfuss fascist regime, who absurdly pledged to arrest the creature on sight.

Encountering a demon on a cold winter night requires fortitude. It is a long-standing tradition to offer a roaming Krampus a shot of strong fruit schnapps to appease him during his run.

So, the next time you find yourself longing for the holiday spirit, remember that in the snow-capped peaks of Austria, the magic of the season isn't just about joy and generosity—it is also about honoring the shadows, respecting the dark, and maintaining absolute discipline.

Have you been good this year? Because Krampus is watching.
